question: What does the juxtaposition of where white families lived across different decades convey?
answer: It shows that suburbs gradually became white-only neighborhoods.
distractor1: White families increasingly preferred the suburbs.
distractor3: Central cities became less and less popular.

question:
1
00:00:17,730 --> 00:00:21,989
This was Levittown, Pennsylvania, shortly
after World War II.

2
00:00:21,989 --> 00:00:27,000
In a suburb that explicitly promised a
white-only neighborhood.

3
00:00:27,000 --> 00:00:29,380
And it wasn't some outlier.

4
00:00:29,380 --> 00:00:31,250
It was the prototypical suburb,

5
00:00:31,250 --> 00:00:36,730
built by the father of suburbia — Bill
Levitt — who created several suburbs around

6
00:00:36,730 --> 00:00:39,280
the US, all named Levittown.

7
00:00:42,670 --> 00:00:46,280
But one reason Levitt wanted a white-only
community was because the US government was

8
00:00:46,280 --> 00:00:48,900
subsidizing it — and that's what they wanted.

9
00:00:48,900 --> 00:00:53,770
They said they didn't want "racially inharmonious
groups" lowering property values.

10
00:00:53,770 --> 00:00:56,700
That's why Levitt didn't just sell cookie-cutter
houses.

11
00:00:59,600 --> 00:01:04,080
He sold a meticulously crafted, affordable,
utopian lifestyle.

12
00:01:06,600 --> 00:01:11,240
So as the courts integrated public spaces,
like schools, more and more white people fled

13
00:01:11,240 --> 00:01:12,240
to these suburbs.

14
00:01:12,240 --> 00:01:17,520
And these patterns are still the defining
characteristic of America's racial geography.

15
00:01:19,640 --> 00:01:22,800
But we now spend most of our time at work.

16
00:01:22,800 --> 00:01:25,920
It gets a lot more complicated.

17
00:01:31,060 --> 00:01:36,860
"More than a million persons each year have
pulled up stakes in the city and turned commuter…"

18
00:01:37,760 --> 00:01:44,000
Shortly after the first Levittown broke ground
in 1947 in Long Island, New York, about 80 percent

19
00:01:44,009 --> 00:01:47,549
of men still commuted the hour to
Manhattan.

20
00:01:47,549 --> 00:01:52,469
And while neighborhoods were getting deeply
segregated, these workplaces were getting

21
00:01:52,469 --> 00:01:53,260
more diverse.

22
00:01:54,900 --> 00:01:59,229
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned employment
discrimination.

23
00:01:59,229 --> 00:02:04,020
More companies explicitly said they were "equal
opportunity employers."

24
00:02:04,020 --> 00:02:06,960
And segregation within our workplaces declined.

25
00:02:07,980 --> 00:02:12,940
This meant the workplace was a crucial environment
for us to interact with people of other races.

26
00:02:16,080 --> 00:02:18,580
Except that's not exactly how it turned out.

27
00:02:19,360 --> 00:02:24,200
A few months ago, researchers at Cornell and
Penn State shared a dataset with me — and

28
00:02:24,200 --> 00:02:26,680
when I mapped it, it kind of blew my mind.

29
00:02:28,720 --> 00:02:31,520
This is a map of where people work in modern-day
Chicago.

30
00:02:33,080 --> 00:02:37,120
The taller an area,
the more people there are.

31
00:02:37,130 --> 00:02:40,920
But now, let's color in each neighborhood
by the percentage of white people.

32
00:02:40,920 --> 00:02:43,550
You can see the city centers are pretty diverse.

33
00:02:44,880 --> 00:02:47,680
But, now, here's what happens when they go
home.

34
00:02:51,940 --> 00:02:55,620
What's even more astounding is what happens
when we map people of color.

35
00:02:55,630 --> 00:02:58,090
Here's where black people work in Chicago.

36
00:02:58,090 --> 00:03:01,040
Again, they're concentrated in diverse city
centers.

37
00:03:02,280 --> 00:03:06,840
[Insert subtitle here]

38
00:03:06,840 --> 00:03:08,200
[Insert subtitle here]

39
00:03:09,820 --> 00:03:12,240
And we can see the same patterns in DC.

40
00:03:14,800 --> 00:03:15,900
Detroit.

41
00:03:20,100 --> 00:03:21,560
Philadelphia.

42
00:03:24,460 --> 00:03:26,220
Pretty much everywhere in the US.

43
00:03:27,820 --> 00:03:32,440
These maps shows just how stubborn residential
segregation is.

44
00:03:32,440 --> 00:03:36,220
But they also show what looks like a glimmer of
hope for integration:

45
00:03:36,220 --> 00:03:37,510
cities are remarkably

46
00:03:37,510 --> 00:03:40,150
diverse during the work day.

47
00:03:40,150 --> 00:03:44,180
This got researchers interested in looking
closer at what's at work.

48
00:03:47,720 --> 00:03:50,380
Let's look at how segregation has changed
in recent year.

49
00:03:50,380 --> 00:03:57,660
From 2000 to 2010, residential segregation
between black and white people got slightly better.

50
00:03:58,320 --> 00:04:03,070
For the most part, segregation just mostly plateaued for all racial groups.

51
00:04:03,070 --> 00:04:07,370
But when researchers looked at how segregation
changed during the day, when we're at work,

52
00:04:07,370 --> 00:04:11,470
they found that segregation increased slightly
across all racial groups.

53
00:04:11,470 --> 00:04:13,440
When we zoom in some more to the company level,

54
00:04:13,440 --> 00:04:15,980
we can see a bit more of what's actually happening.

55
00:04:15,980 --> 00:04:20,740
Researchers at Stanford and Harvard found,
within a company, segregation levels have

56
00:04:20,750 --> 00:04:22,820
gone down very little.

57
00:04:22,820 --> 00:04:27,760
In other words, we're exposed to about as
much diversity now... as we were a generation ago.

58
00:04:28,220 --> 00:04:32,220
But there are a lot more people of color now
than there were in 1980.

59
00:04:33,020 --> 00:04:35,280
So what's going on?

60
00:04:37,720 --> 00:04:42,220
Well, they aren't being more represented at
these white-majority companies, which would

61
00:04:42,220 --> 00:04:43,340
look like this.

62
00:04:45,000 --> 00:04:47,840
Rather, they are getting
opportunities at companies that are mostly

63
00:04:47,840 --> 00:04:49,660
non-white, over here.

64
00:04:51,129 --> 00:04:55,719
So this means that, when we look at this from
a company level, segregation has actually

65
00:04:55,720 --> 00:04:58,460
gotten worse than a generation ago.

66
00:05:00,840 --> 00:05:03,660
Of course, some places are pretty diverse.

67
00:05:03,669 --> 00:05:08,090
So researchers looked at what kinds of places
actually have less segregation during the day.

68
00:05:09,630 --> 00:05:13,590
But they found that, if a place is diverse
during the daytime, it's likely not because

69
00:05:13,590 --> 00:05:16,400
people of all races are working alongside
each other.

70
00:05:16,400 --> 00:05:21,739
Rather, it's likely because most of the higher
status workers, like managers, are white.

71
00:05:21,740 --> 00:05:25,920
and the lower-status workers, like janitors,
are people of color.

72
00:05:32,560 --> 00:05:36,240
American policies engineered our segregated
homes.

73
00:05:36,240 --> 00:05:38,800
But work — where we spend most of our time?

74
00:05:38,800 --> 00:05:42,060
Many thought that could be a space where we
form meaningful relationships with people

75
00:05:42,060 --> 00:05:43,660
of other racial backgrounds.

76
00:05:46,340 --> 00:05:48,080
That hasn't quite happened.

77
00:05:48,080 --> 00:05:51,220
And we can see it in the most personal parts
of our lives.

78
00:05:52,680 --> 00:05:57,779
In 2014, the Public Religion Research Institute
asked Americans to list the people with whom

79
00:05:57,779 --> 00:06:01,800
they "discussed important matters" in
the past six months.

80
00:06:01,800 --> 00:06:03,500
In other words, our friends.

81
00:06:05,500 --> 00:06:08,479
Most Hispanic people had friends of other
races.

82
00:06:08,480 --> 00:06:10,760
About one in three black people did, too.

83
00:06:12,030 --> 00:06:17,720
But 75 percent of white people only had
white friends.

84
00:06:19,260 --> 00:06:23,660
In short, we may be exposed to diverse spaces,

85
00:06:24,620 --> 00:06:27,940
but we still live very segregated lives.

86
00:06:28,220 --> 00:06:35,720
"The whole trouble with this integration business is that in the end it probably will end up with mixing, socially."
answer: But when black workers go home, they go to very segregated neighborhoods, clustered in the poorer areas.

question:
1
00:00:01,199 --> 00:00:06,606
In September 2021, the CDC
recommended Covid-19 booster shots,

2
00:00:06,606 --> 00:00:09,750
an additional vaccine dose,
for the elderly

3
00:00:09,750 --> 00:00:12,897
and those at high risk in the US.

4
00:00:12,897 --> 00:00:18,221
That echoed the booster shot rollout 
in places like the UK and Singapore.

5
00:00:18,221 --> 00:00:22,161
But in November, the CDC announced 
a new recommendation:

6
00:00:22,161 --> 00:00:24,512
all adults could get a booster shot.

7
00:00:24,512 --> 00:00:29,000
And that idea had been a contentious
question among scientists.

8
00:00:29,000 --> 00:00:32,787
"I do believe that all of us are going 
to need another shot at some point."

9
00:00:32,787 --> 00:00:36,760
"It's much more of a gray area for 
younger people, particularly under 50s."

10
00:00:36,760 --> 00:00:39,457
"I don't think we should get hung up 
on should, may...

11
00:00:39,457 --> 00:00:41,060
just go out and get boosted."

12
00:00:41,060 --> 00:00:43,550
"FDA's Dr. Marion Gruber and Dr. Phil Krause

13
00:00:43,550 --> 00:00:47,927
say there's currently no need for boosters
for the general population."

14
00:00:47,927 --> 00:00:51,320
Dr. Celine Gounder was one of those scientists.

15
00:00:51,320 --> 00:00:55,220
She wasn’t convinced that we all 
needed more shots.

16
00:00:55,220 --> 00:00:57,103
Up until recently.

17
00:00:57,103 --> 00:01:00,215
So, to help me figure out what’s going on
with boosters,

18
00:01:00,215 --> 00:01:01,503
I called her up.

19
00:01:01,503 --> 00:01:07,790
GOUNDER: I had not planned to get boosted,
and yesterday scheduled a third dose.

20
00:01:07,790 --> 00:01:11,469
And that's really a decision that was made
based on the emergence of omicron.

21
00:01:14,181 --> 00:01:17,041
To start us off, can you sort of just 
walk us through

22
00:01:17,041 --> 00:01:20,083
what the science of needing boosters is?

23
00:01:20,083 --> 00:01:21,830
GOUNDER: When you get vaccinated

24
00:01:21,830 --> 00:01:24,859
you're stimulating different branches
of your immune system.

25
00:01:24,859 --> 00:01:30,086
You're stimulating B cells, 
T cells, antibody levels.

26
00:01:30,086 --> 00:01:36,149
Those antibody levels are what protect
you robustly against infection,

27
00:01:36,149 --> 00:01:40,000
particularly soon after vaccination.

28
00:01:40,000 --> 00:01:42,889
But those antibody levels wane.

29
00:01:42,889 --> 00:01:47,815
[Insert subtitle here]

30
00:01:47,815 --> 00:01:53,120
[Insert subtitle here]

31
00:01:53,120 --> 00:01:58,443
But Dr. Gounder emphasized that 
charts like this shouldn’t alarm us.

32
00:01:58,443 --> 00:02:02,612
GOUNDER: Once those antibodies fade
away, the B cells are still there.

33
00:02:02,612 --> 00:02:06,471
B cells are these little factories
to make antibodies.

34
00:02:06,471 --> 00:02:09,340
So when you get re-exposed 
to the virus,

35
00:02:09,340 --> 00:02:13,340
the B cells recognize the virus
and kick back into gear

36
00:02:13,340 --> 00:02:15,668
and produce antibodies all over again.

37
00:02:15,668 --> 00:02:18,840
You're not fully protected 
against all infection,

38
00:02:18,840 --> 00:02:24,209
but you still have very strong, very
long-lived memory B cell responses

39
00:02:24,209 --> 00:02:29,310
that are still there to protect you from
severe disease, hospitalization, and death.

40
00:02:29,888 --> 00:02:34,769
So if we still have that protection 
from severe cases,

41
00:02:34,769 --> 00:02:37,396
why do we need more
antibodies from a booster?

42
00:02:37,396 --> 00:02:42,000
GOUNDER: There are certain groups in
which we do see a reduction in protection

43
00:02:42,000 --> 00:02:44,879
against even some of those
more severe outcomes.

44
00:02:44,879 --> 00:02:47,042
And those are specifically older people.

45
00:02:47,042 --> 00:02:49,840
In addition, people who are highly
immunocompromised

46
00:02:49,840 --> 00:02:53,477
also do benefit from getting
additional doses of vaccine.

47
00:02:53,477 --> 00:02:57,600
That was the reasoning behind initially 
limiting boosters to the vulnerable:

48
00:02:57,600 --> 00:03:02,064
that while boosters for all adults in general
could help replenish antibodies

49
00:03:02,064 --> 00:03:04,397
to prevent any infections,

50
00:03:04,397 --> 00:03:07,851
they weren't necessary for 
preventing severe cases,

51
00:03:07,851 --> 00:03:11,400
which vaccines continue to do
effectively for most people.

52
00:03:11,906 --> 00:03:16,140
But many scientists like Dr. Gounder 
have changed their mind on that stance

53
00:03:16,140 --> 00:03:20,849
based on the information available about the
omicron variant at the time of this video.

54
00:03:20,849 --> 00:03:24,530
GOUNDER: Now that you've had the rise of 
the omicron variant,

55
00:03:24,530 --> 00:03:27,189
it's a different conversation
about boosters.

56
00:03:27,189 --> 00:03:30,219
The concern about 
the Omicron variant is that

57
00:03:30,219 --> 00:03:34,249
our vaccines may not fully protect 
against this variant,

58
00:03:34,249 --> 00:03:37,921
which has more than 30 mutations 
in the spike protein.

59
00:03:37,921 --> 00:03:41,540
B cells that would have recognized
earlier strains of the virus

60
00:03:41,540 --> 00:03:43,680
may not recognize omicron.

61
00:03:43,680 --> 00:03:46,030
It has changed so much

62
00:03:46,030 --> 00:03:49,768
that your memory immune responses 
don't recognize it.

63
00:03:49,768 --> 00:03:53,195
But that's a prediction based on
looking at the genetic sequence.

64
00:03:53,195 --> 00:03:55,995
By giving additional doses 
of vaccine,

65
00:03:55,995 --> 00:04:01,471
you can override that
relative immune evasion.

66
00:04:05,000 --> 00:04:09,014
It’s not clear yet whether or not we’ll
need a new vaccine for the new variant.

67
00:04:09,014 --> 00:04:13,469
That was actually a question companies like
Pfizer had with the other variants, too.

68
00:04:22,833 --> 00:04:26,402
So even though there are still 
a lot of unknowns about omicron,

69
00:04:26,402 --> 00:04:30,220
experts like Dr. Gounder say boosters 
may be a good tool against it,

70
00:04:30,220 --> 00:04:33,380
especially if it turns out to be as bad 
as some fear.

71
00:04:34,030 --> 00:04:37,833
So at what point after our first round 
of vaccinations

72
00:04:37,833 --> 00:04:39,658
should we get boosted?

73
00:04:39,658 --> 00:04:44,030
GOUNDER: So you should wait six months 
after your second dose of COVID vaccine,

74
00:04:44,030 --> 00:04:48,040
if you got the Pfizer or Moderna vaccine, 
before getting a boost,

75
00:04:48,040 --> 00:04:52,144
and you should wait two months after getting
the Johnson & Johnson vaccine

76
00:04:52,144 --> 00:04:54,283
before getting a boost.

77
00:04:54,283 --> 00:04:59,483
To really get to peak antibody levels,
you really want to wait about two weeks.

78
00:04:59,483 --> 00:05:03,688
So if you're, say, planning to go
visit family over the holidays,

79
00:05:03,688 --> 00:05:06,490
I would recommend getting that 
additional dose of vaccine,

80
00:05:06,490 --> 00:05:10,240
that booster dose, about two weeks 
prior to travel.

81
00:05:10,240 --> 00:05:13,433
And that booster doesn’t have to be the
same one you originally got.

82
00:05:13,433 --> 00:05:16,280
GOUNDER: The NIH conducted a study 
looking at,

83
00:05:16,280 --> 00:05:19,700
do you start with Johnson & Johnson, 
Pfizer, or Moderna,

84
00:05:19,700 --> 00:05:23,940
and then do you boost with Johnson & Johnson,
Pfizer, or Moderna?

85
00:05:23,940 --> 00:05:27,103
The study found that 
not only is mixing vaccines safe:

86
00:05:27,103 --> 00:05:29,010
all combinations work.

87
00:05:29,010 --> 00:05:33,320
In the US, if you got initial doses of 
an mRNA vaccine,

88
00:05:33,320 --> 00:05:36,043
you can get either one as a third shot.

89
00:05:36,043 --> 00:05:39,153
But it’s recommended that if you got 
Johnson & Johnson first,

90
00:05:39,153 --> 00:05:43,058
it’s most effective to get boosted with
an mRNA vaccine.

91
00:05:43,058 --> 00:05:46,330
Similarly, in countries like Germany and Korea,

92
00:05:46,330 --> 00:05:50,307
most people who got AstraZeneca 
will be offered an mRNA vaccine.

93
00:05:50,307 --> 00:05:54,780
GOUNDER: There is some thought
that the different vaccine technologies

94
00:05:54,780 --> 00:06:00,171
teach the immune system to recognize
the spike protein in slightly different ways,

95
00:06:00,171 --> 00:06:04,798
and that as a result, the immune system,
you could say, remembers better.

96
00:06:04,798 --> 00:06:09,220
Considering that the vaccines have been so
unequally distributed around the world,

97
00:06:09,220 --> 00:06:12,960
should we be concerned about 
the ethics of getting a third shot

98
00:06:12,960 --> 00:06:15,706
when so many people haven’t
even had their first?

99
00:06:15,706 --> 00:06:21,799
GOUNDER: I think we should be worried about
that at a policy level, at a macro level,

100
00:06:21,799 --> 00:06:26,627
but whether you yourself as the individual
choose to get a booster dose or not

101
00:06:26,627 --> 00:06:29,877
is really not going to have an impact 
on global vaccine supply,

102
00:06:29,877 --> 00:06:34,431
because those decisions
are being made far upstream

103
00:06:34,431 --> 00:06:38,689
from you going into your local drugstore 
and getting a vaccination.

104
00:06:38,689 --> 00:06:41,637
As for whether we’ll all 
need boosters for years:

105
00:06:41,637 --> 00:06:43,160
it’s really too soon to tell.

106
00:06:43,160 --> 00:06:45,880
It depends on how much Covid is spreading.

107
00:06:45,880 --> 00:06:48,113
GOUNDER: Look, boosters are not going to 
end the pandemic.

108
00:06:48,113 --> 00:06:51,257
What is going to end the pandemic 
is vaccinating people

109
00:06:51,257 --> 00:06:52,739
who are not vaccinated.

110
00:06:52,739 --> 00:06:59,829
Your risk of infection is proportional to
how much virus is circulating in the community.

111
00:06:59,829 --> 00:07:01,810
Even if you've been boosted.

112
00:07:01,810 --> 00:07:06,403
We still have a long way to go 
to vaccinate the unvaccinated.

113
00:07:06,403 --> 00:07:11,730
But Dr. Gounder also emphasized 
that we can do two things at once:

114
00:07:11,730 --> 00:07:14,790
we can continue to vaccinate the unvaccinated

115
00:07:14,790 --> 00:07:19,311
while also strengthening the defenses 
of the vaccinated.

116
00:07:19,311 --> 00:07:22,070
GOUNDER: Boosters do provide another 
layer of protection,

117
00:07:22,070 --> 00:07:25,000
especially with the rise of the omicron variant.

118
00:07:25,000 --> 00:07:29,270
I think there is broader consensus
now among doctors and scientists that

119
00:07:29,270 --> 00:07:33,697
everyone 18 and up in the United States who
can get a booster should get a booster.

120
00:07:33,697 --> 00:07:36,090
That boost won't last forever,

121
00:07:36,090 --> 00:07:37,413
but it does buy you time.

If the internet is any gauge, the world LOVES

Sadly, there are sixty million feral cats
living on the streets in the USA today.

10
00:00:43,670 --> 00:00:49,730
55% of all household cats in the US are overweight,

And cats have powerful night vision, allowing

20

question:
1
00:00:00,207 --> 00:00:03,050
- Can we still trust polls?

2
00:00:03,050 --> 00:00:05,570
After the 2016 U.S. presidential election,

3
00:00:05,570 --> 00:00:08,168
a common reaction from
across the political spectrum

4
00:00:08,168 --> 00:00:11,200
was that polling must be broken.

5
00:00:11,200 --> 00:00:13,215
Now that researchers
have had time to dig into

6
00:00:13,215 --> 00:00:17,100
what happened in 2016 and
in polling more generally,

7
00:00:17,100 --> 00:00:19,370
we can bring a lot
of data to bear on this.

8
00:00:19,370 --> 00:00:20,950
Here are the basics,

9
00:00:20,950 --> 00:00:22,210
Some people who were surprised

10
00:00:22,210 --> 00:00:24,020
by the outcome of the 2016 election

11
00:00:24,020 --> 00:00:26,000
still can't get past the feeling

12
00:00:26,000 --> 00:00:27,700
that they were led astray by the polls.

13
00:00:27,700 --> 00:00:29,053
But the fact of the matter is

14
00:00:29,053 --> 00:00:32,372
that [Insert subtitle here]

15
00:00:32,372 --> 00:00:35,870
[Insert subtitle here]

16
00:00:35,870 --> 00:00:37,370
[Insert subtitle here]

17
00:00:37,370 --> 00:00:38,810
[Insert subtitle here]

18
00:00:38,810 --> 00:00:40,420
[Insert subtitle here]

19
00:00:40,420 --> 00:00:42,200
- When a commission got down to the data and

20
00:00:42,200 --> 00:00:44,710
looked at what happened in the 2016 election,

21
00:00:44,710 --> 00:00:46,000
they found that most of the problems

22
00:00:46,000 --> 00:00:48,645
were in the state-level,
where there are folks who are

23
00:00:48,645 --> 00:00:50,459
trying to do this kind of polling with

24
00:00:50,459 --> 00:00:53,950
not the resources you might
have at the national level.

25
00:00:53,950 --> 00:00:55,560
What happened with some
of those polls was that

26
00:00:55,560 --> 00:00:57,850
they were out of the field
and missed a late swing

27
00:00:57,850 --> 00:01:00,610
among those undecided
voters toward Donald Trump.

28
00:01:00,610 --> 00:01:03,352
Another issue they
had was under-representing

29
00:01:03,352 --> 00:01:06,740
people who didn't have college educations.

30
00:01:06,740 --> 00:01:08,710
And all those let to big surprises

31
00:01:08,710 --> 00:01:10,480
in the Midwest on election night.

32
00:01:10,480 --> 00:01:12,696
- Another common criticism
is that pollsters favor

33
00:01:12,696 --> 00:01:14,513
a particular political party.

34
00:01:14,513 --> 00:01:18,000
But a look at the direction
of polling misses in the U.S.

35
00:01:18,000 --> 00:01:20,340
over time shows that whether
the polls tend to miss

36
00:01:20,340 --> 00:01:22,881
in the Republican direction
or the Democratic direction

37
00:01:22,881 --> 00:01:25,415
is pretty much just a coin flip.

38
00:01:25,415 --> 00:01:27,891
Some of the best evidence
about the performance

39
00:01:27,891 --> 00:01:30,427
of election polling comes
from rigorous analyses

40
00:01:30,427 --> 00:01:34,210
of the accuracy of polls over time.

41
00:01:34,210 --> 00:01:37,480
If anything, national polling
in presidential elections

42
00:01:37,480 --> 00:01:40,910
is more accurate now than
it was a few decades ago.

43
00:01:40,910 --> 00:01:43,560
Since 2000 the average absolute error

44
00:01:43,560 --> 00:01:45,112
in national presidential polls

45
00:01:45,112 --> 00:01:48,340
has been around two or
three percentage points,

46
00:01:48,340 --> 00:01:51,330
which historically-speaking,
is really quite good.

47
00:01:51,330 --> 00:01:54,130
- And an even broader look
at polling in 45 countries

48
00:01:54,130 --> 00:01:56,450
around the world over the past 75 years,

49
00:01:56,450 --> 00:01:59,040
done by Will Jennings
and Christopher Wlezien,

50
00:01:59,040 --> 00:02:00,360
found a similar result.

51
00:02:00,360 --> 00:02:03,750
Election polls worldwide have
a good record of accuracy,

52
00:02:03,750 --> 00:02:07,200
and despite some forecasting
misses of the past few years,

53
00:02:07,200 --> 00:02:10,900
the average level of
accuracy has not declined.

54
00:02:10,900 --> 00:02:12,716
- While those overall
trends are reassuring,

55
00:02:12,716 --> 00:02:15,330
unexpected election outcomes still rattled

56
00:02:15,330 --> 00:02:17,260
the public's confidence in polls.

57
00:02:17,260 --> 00:02:19,170
A good example of this is Brexit.

58
00:02:19,170 --> 00:02:22,140
Believe it or not, Brexit was
not a massive polling failure.

59
00:02:22,140 --> 00:02:25,179
While betting markets in
Britain did strongly suggest

60
00:02:25,179 --> 00:02:28,640
that Britons would vote to
remain in the European Union,

61
00:02:28,640 --> 00:02:30,580
the polls were actually
showing a close race,

62
00:02:30,580 --> 00:02:32,180
and for most of the final month,

63
00:02:32,180 --> 00:02:34,940
the polling showed "leave" ahead.

64
00:02:34,950 --> 00:02:36,660
So while Brexit was certainly not

65
00:02:36,670 --> 00:02:38,627
a shining moment in
the history of polling,

66
00:02:38,627 --> 00:02:42,847
it also wasn't an instance
where the polls were wildly off.

67
00:02:42,847 --> 00:02:47,660
- The fixation on election
polls is totally understandable

68
00:02:47,660 --> 00:02:49,660
and probably unavoidable,

69
00:02:49,660 --> 00:02:51,670
but they're just not the best barometer

70
00:02:51,670 --> 00:02:53,550
for how good a job polling is doing.

71
00:02:53,550 --> 00:02:56,020
And that's because election
polls have to do something

72
00:02:56,020 --> 00:02:57,690
that other polls measuring policies

73
00:02:57,690 --> 00:02:59,196
or attitudes don't have to do.

74
00:02:59,196 --> 00:03:02,060
They have to figure out, of the people they're talking to on the phone,

75
00:03:02,060 --> 00:03:04,021
who is actually going to go out and vote

76
00:03:04,021 --> 00:03:08,150
in some day in the future and
then how are they going to vote?

77
00:03:08,150 --> 00:03:10,773
For those of you who have
studied human behavior,

78
00:03:10,773 --> 00:03:13,130
even if it's just in
your friends and family,

79
00:03:13,130 --> 00:03:15,940
You know that those kind of
predictions are really hard.

80
00:03:15,940 --> 00:03:18,680
- While polls may not always
be able to call the winner

81
00:03:18,680 --> 00:03:21,500
in very close elections, they
remain very well equipped

82
00:03:21,500 --> 00:03:25,840
for reliably tracking the
contours of social attitudes,

83
00:03:25,840 --> 00:03:28,190
measuring peoples values,
their preferences,

84
00:03:28,190 --> 00:03:30,950
priorities and concerns.

85
00:03:30,950 --> 00:03:32,930
Take the trend over time in attitudes

86
00:03:32,930 --> 00:03:34,842
toward same-sex marriage.

87
00:03:34,842 --> 00:03:37,960
This is an example of
polling, not from an election,

88
00:03:37,960 --> 00:03:40,287
where real world events arguably validated

89
00:03:40,287 --> 00:03:42,580
the ability of polls to track

90
00:03:42,580 --> 00:03:44,450
real movement in public opinion.

91
00:03:44,450 --> 00:03:46,050
- You had different polling organizations

92
00:03:46,050 --> 00:03:48,410
using different questions
to measure support

93
00:03:48,410 --> 00:03:50,810
for a legal right for gays
and lesbians to marry,

94
00:03:50,810 --> 00:03:53,350
but all of them told the
same story over time:

95
00:03:53,350 --> 00:03:56,050
majority opposition in
the 1990s and early 2000s,

96
00:03:56,050 --> 00:03:58,090
followed by gradual gains in support

97
00:03:58,090 --> 00:04:00,900
through the last decade and
the emergence of majority

98
00:04:00,900 --> 00:04:02,740
support in recent years.

99
00:04:02,740 --> 00:04:04,627
And these trends were
corroborated to some extent

100
00:04:04,627 --> 00:04:07,566
by the fact that supporters
of same-sex marriage

101
00:04:07,566 --> 00:04:11,220
began winning statewide
referenda on the issue

102
00:04:11,220 --> 00:04:14,670
about the time majority
support emerged in the polling.

103
00:04:14,670 --> 00:04:17,310
- Another way to evaluate
the performance of polls

104
00:04:17,310 --> 00:04:18,710
is called benchmarking.

105
00:04:18,710 --> 00:04:21,400
We take some questions asked
in large federally-funded

106
00:04:21,400 --> 00:04:23,180
studies with high response rates

107
00:04:23,180 --> 00:04:26,420
and ask those same questions
in our regular polls.

108
00:04:26,420 --> 00:04:29,280
The difference between our
poll numbers and the numbers

109
00:04:29,280 --> 00:04:30,970
from the benchmark surveys,

110
00:04:30,970 --> 00:04:34,150
gives us some sense as to our accuracy.

111
00:04:34,150 --> 00:04:36,660
We recently benchmarked
our telephone surveys

112
00:04:36,660 --> 00:04:39,080
against some high profile federal surveys

113
00:04:39,080 --> 00:04:41,750
and found our polls get very
similar numbers on issues

114
00:04:41,750 --> 00:04:43,320
like "What share of Americans

115
00:04:43,320 --> 00:04:45,934
identify as Republicans versus Democrats?"

116
00:04:45,934 --> 00:04:48,307
- And the same goes for "What
share of Americans identify as

117
00:04:48,307 --> 00:04:51,720
Protestant, Catholic, another religion,

118
00:04:51,720 --> 00:04:53,600
or no religious affiliation?"

119
00:04:53,600 --> 00:04:56,260
In these analyses, the fact
that the trends from the polls

120
00:04:56,260 --> 00:04:59,200
line up very closely with the trends
from the benchmark surveys

121
00:04:59,200 --> 00:05:02,480
is evidence that the polls
remain quite accurate.

122
00:05:02,480 --> 00:05:05,610
During the timeline shown, the
response rate was declining,

123
00:05:05,610 --> 00:05:07,405
but despite what some people claim,

124
00:05:07,405 --> 00:05:10,680
the accuracy of these polls
has basically held steady.

125
00:05:10,680 --> 00:05:13,070
- Pew Research Center takes
the accuracy of polling

126
00:05:13,070 --> 00:05:15,340
very seriously because we that believe polls

127
00:05:15,340 --> 00:05:18,217
have a very important role
to play in a democracy.

128
00:05:18,217 --> 00:05:20,360
They're designed to give every citizen,

129
00:05:20,360 --> 00:05:22,420
whether rich or poor, well-educated

130
00:05:22,420 --> 00:05:25,658
or less educated, an equal voice.

131
00:05:25,658 --> 00:05:28,470
They also serve as a check on politicians

132
00:05:28,470 --> 00:05:30,977
on both sides of the aisle
who could otherwise just claim

133
00:05:30,977 --> 00:05:33,090
to know what the public thinks

134
00:05:33,090 --> 00:05:34,990
or why they voted the way they did.

135
00:05:34,990 --> 00:05:37,301
- Now, that doesn't mean
that people in government

136
00:05:37,301 --> 00:05:39,610
should be slaves to poll numbers

137
00:05:39,610 --> 00:05:41,330
or that all polls are trustworthy.

138
00:05:41,330 --> 00:05:44,920
But polls do perform a valuable
function as a reality check

139
00:05:44,920 --> 00:05:47,250
on how the public is
thinking about major issues

140
00:05:47,250 --> 00:05:50,440
and what's going well or going
poorly in people's lives.

141
00:05:50,440 --> 00:05:52,660
- And even though some recent
elections have put a spotlight

142
00:05:52,661 --> 00:05:55,451
on the limits to just how
accurate polls can be,

143
00:05:55,451 --> 00:05:58,340
there is a lot of research
showing that well-designed polls

144
00:05:58,340 --> 00:06:00,978
still work and still
produce useful information.

145
00:06:00,978 --> 00:06:03,367
So, bottom line, can polls be trusted?

146
00:06:03,367 --> 00:06:06,220
As long as we're realistic
about the precision

147
00:06:06,220 --> 00:06:08,919
that polls can actually provide, yes.

148
00:06:08,919 --> 00:06:11,919
(light soft sounds)

question:
1
00:00:00,640 --> 00:00:04,660
China and Japan are two countries that have
been culturally intertwined from as early

2
00:00:04,660 --> 00:00:06,580
as 400 AD.

3
00:00:06,580 --> 00:00:10,750
This relationship led to Japan adopting the
Chinese writing system, the religion of Buddhism,

4
00:00:10,750 --> 00:00:15,960
similar political systems, as well as developing
in matters of food, fashion, law, and more,

5
00:00:15,960 --> 00:00:17,609
under the influence of China.

6
00:00:17,609 --> 00:00:20,789
Although the countries are currently at peace,
relations have remained somewhat tense over

7
00:00:20,789 --> 00:00:21,800
the last century.

8
00:00:21,800 --> 00:00:25,570
Today, we’ll compare the two nations in
a hypothetical military match-up, in this

9
00:00:25,570 --> 00:00:28,560
episode of The Infographics Show, China vs.
Japan.

10
00:00:28,560 --> 00:00:31,460
Don’t forget to subscribe and click the
bell button so that you can be part of our

11
00:00:31,460 --> 00:00:32,800
Notification Squad.

12
00:00:32,800 --> 00:00:37,690
[Insert subtitle here]

13
00:00:37,690 --> 00:00:42,930
It’s followed by China with a nominal GDP
of 11.8 trillion dollars, and then Japan with

14
00:00:42,930 --> 00:00:45,850
a GDP of around 4.8 trillion dollars.

15
00:00:45,850 --> 00:00:50,489
The European Union would take second place,
but the EU is a combination of 28 states.

16
00:00:50,489 --> 00:00:55,359
While China has experienced economic prosperity
in recent years, it’s per capita GDP ranks

17
00:00:55,359 --> 00:01:01,820
low, globally in 70th place, at around 8,000
dollars, with Japan’s per capita GDP much

18
00:01:01,820 --> 00:01:04,390
higher at around 39,000 dollars.

19
00:01:04,390 --> 00:01:08,490
There is certainly less money to go around
in China as it has the world’s largest population

20
00:01:08,490 --> 00:01:15,060
of 1.38 billion people, compared to Japan’s
126-plus million population.

21
00:01:15,060 --> 00:01:19,560
In terms of military spending, China ranks
third behind Russia and the military-minded

22
00:01:19,560 --> 00:01:26,180
USA, with a defense budget of around $147
billion, which is 2.1% of its GDP.

23
00:01:26,180 --> 00:01:31,520
Japan sits in 7th place on this list, with
a $43 billion defense budget, which is 0.9%

24
00:01:31,520 --> 00:01:32,740
of its GDP.

25
00:01:32,740 --> 00:01:37,360
It’s also worth mentioning here that military
pundits often state China spends much more

26
00:01:37,360 --> 00:01:41,619
on its military than the number that is reported,
although China’s finance minister denied

27
00:01:41,619 --> 00:01:47,070
this secrecy in 2017, saying, “Let me be
very clear, there is no such thing as opacity

28
00:01:47,070 --> 00:01:48,979
in China’s military spending.”

29
00:01:48,979 --> 00:01:52,759
While Japan is regarded as being a military
powerhouse, it’s number of military personnel

30
00:01:52,759 --> 00:01:57,810
is actually quite small, and very much inferior
to the number of personnel the Chinese employ.

31
00:01:57,810 --> 00:02:04,470
Japan has around 250,000 active military personnel,
with another 57,900 people acting as reserve

32
00:02:04,470 --> 00:02:05,490
personnel.

33
00:02:05,490 --> 00:02:12,640
China on the other hand has a massive 2,335,000
active frontline personnel and 2,300,000 active

34
00:02:12,640 --> 00:02:15,480
reserve personnel and paramilitary forces.

35
00:02:15,480 --> 00:02:19,150
Japan’s personnel numbers may be small,
but it's protected with some of the world’s

36
00:02:19,150 --> 00:02:20,650
best military equipment.

37
00:02:20,650 --> 00:02:28,439
This includes 678 Tanks, 2,850 armored fighting
vehicles, 202 self-propelled guns, 500 Towed-Artillery,

38
00:02:28,439 --> 00:02:30,569
and 99 multiple launch rocket systems.

39
00:02:30,569 --> 00:02:35,150
It’s large fleet of land artillery includes
two machines often on the list of the world’s

40
00:02:35,150 --> 00:02:40,511
most advanced tanks, those being the Japanese-made
Type 10 Main Battle Tank and Type 90 Main

41
00:02:40,511 --> 00:02:41,511
Battle Tank.

42
00:02:41,511 --> 00:02:51,140
China, however, outguns Japan considerably
with a total of 9,150 tanks, 4,788 AFVs, 1,710

43
00:02:51,140 --> 00:02:55,930
SPGs, 6,246 Towed-Artillery, and 177 MLRSs.

44
00:02:55,930 --> 00:03:00,950
China’s Type 99 main battle tank is also
highly rated, while the country also claims

45
00:03:00,950 --> 00:03:04,780
to have developed the most advanced tank in
the world in its VT-4.

46
00:03:04,780 --> 00:03:09,170
China is not alone in making such boastful
claims, with the USA and Russia also stating

47
00:03:09,170 --> 00:03:14,629
they have the best tanks in the M1A2 Abrams
and the T-14 Armata, respectively.

48
00:03:14,629 --> 00:03:19,080
The VT-4 is as much a Chinese war machine
as it is a profitable export, with Thailand

49
00:03:19,080 --> 00:03:23,530
placing a big order of the tanks, and other
countries showing interest in buying.

50
00:03:23,530 --> 00:03:28,380
Both countries have strong air forces, with
China owning around 2,900-plus aircraft and

51
00:03:28,380 --> 00:03:30,440
206 attack helicopters.

52
00:03:30,440 --> 00:03:35,599
Japan has around 1,590 aircraft and 119 attack
helicopters.

53
00:03:35,599 --> 00:03:41,239
In terms of strength, China’s aerial piece
de resistance is its new Chengdu J-20 stealth

54
00:03:41,239 --> 00:03:46,110
fighter, which the air force, and some aviation
experts, have stated can match America’s

55
00:03:46,110 --> 00:03:50,450
highly advanced Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor
and F-35.

56
00:03:50,450 --> 00:03:54,650
China is also the only country to have bought
the Russian beasts of the skies, the Sukhoi

57
00:03:54,650 --> 00:03:56,709
Su-35 multipurpose fighter.

58
00:03:56,709 --> 00:04:01,200
If you’ve seen our shows on these aircraft,
you’ll know the Su-35 alone is an impeccable

59
00:04:01,200 --> 00:04:02,819
piece of engineering.

60
00:04:02,819 --> 00:04:07,200
Japan would be hard pushed to equal such aerial
military might, but the country is no slouch

61
00:04:07,200 --> 00:04:08,590
when it comes to aircraft.

62
00:04:08,590 --> 00:04:12,860
Japan is said to have created a veritable
equal to China’s J-20, having joined the

63
00:04:12,860 --> 00:04:15,610
stealth leagues with its own Mitsubishi X-2.

64
00:04:15,610 --> 00:04:20,640
Japan has some formidable combat aircraft
in its homemade Mitsubishi F-2, as well as

65
00:04:20,640 --> 00:04:24,560
American made F-4 Phantom IIs and F-15 Eagles.

66
00:04:24,560 --> 00:04:29,140
The country is also the proud owner of the
USA’s highly touted F-35 Lightning II.

67
00:04:29,140 --> 00:04:33,310
Japan currently has one of these aircraft,
but another 42 have been ordered.

68
00:04:33,310 --> 00:04:36,800
With this in mind, the two countries seem
to be fairly evenly matched in terms of air

69
00:04:36,800 --> 00:04:40,110
force equipment, with Japanese imports being
a major factor.

70
00:04:40,110 --> 00:04:44,540
As far as naval power is concerned, a matter
of significance given the history of naval

71
00:04:44,540 --> 00:04:48,110
invasions, and the fact that the countries
are separated by a stretch of water.

72
00:04:48,110 --> 00:04:52,080
Both countries are credited with having very
strong navies, although most analysts rank

73
00:04:52,080 --> 00:04:53,760
China above Japan.

74
00:04:53,760 --> 00:04:58,540
The People’s Liberation Army Navy is said
to have grown from a fairly weak outfit consisting

75
00:04:58,540 --> 00:05:03,800
of old ships to a formidable foe due to massive
injections of money since China’s economic

76
00:05:03,800 --> 00:05:04,800
boom.

77
00:05:04,800 --> 00:05:09,250
The navy not only has well over 100,000 personnel,
but has a large fleet of ships.

78
00:05:09,250 --> 00:05:15,620
This includes one aircraft carrier, 35 destroyers,
51 frigates, 35 corvettes, 31 mine warfare,

79
00:05:15,620 --> 00:05:21,410
3 amphibious transports, 8 nuclear attack
submarines, and around 50 conventional attack

80
00:05:21,410 --> 00:05:22,410
submarines.

81
00:05:22,410 --> 00:05:28,370
By comparison, the Japanese navy consists
of around 114 ships and 45,800 personnel,

82
00:05:28,370 --> 00:05:33,470
and according to nationalinterest.org, its
fleet of 17 submarines is as good as any submarine

83
00:05:33,470 --> 00:05:34,470
fleet in the world.

84
00:05:34,470 --> 00:05:40,350
In total, Japan has 3 Aircraft Carriers, 43
Destroyers, 6 Coastal Defense Craft, 0 Frigates,

85
00:05:40,350 --> 00:05:43,000
0 Corvettes, and 25 mine warfare.

86
00:05:43,000 --> 00:05:45,830
A matter of importance is each country’s
nuclear capabilities.

87
00:05:45,830 --> 00:05:49,750
Japan doesn’t have any nuclear weapons,
although it is protected by the United States

88
00:05:49,750 --> 00:05:51,140
under the nuclear umbrella.

89
00:05:51,140 --> 00:05:54,880
The country is well known for its highly advanced
industries and technology, and there is no

90
00:05:54,880 --> 00:05:59,320
doubt that it could develop its own nuclear
weapons given its nuclear energy infrastructure.

91
00:05:59,320 --> 00:06:03,750
This has so far not happened due to a non-nuclear
weapons policy, although being positioned

92
00:06:03,750 --> 00:06:08,460
so close to North Korea, many Japanese politicians
and military officials have called for a change

93
00:06:08,460 --> 00:06:09,990
in nuclear weapons policy.

94
00:06:09,990 --> 00:06:14,220
China, on the other hand, is one of 9 nations
with nuclear weapons, with a considerable

95
00:06:14,220 --> 00:06:16,330
arsenal of around 260 warheads.

96
00:06:16,330 --> 00:06:19,310
It’s first nuclear test was in 1964.

97
00:06:19,310 --> 00:06:23,000
The number of weapons, however, and China’s
development of nuclear weapons, has been a

98
00:06:23,000 --> 00:06:24,820
matter of wide speculation.

99
00:06:24,820 --> 00:06:28,600
For instance, a Georgetown University study
claimed that China’s nuclear weapons arsenal

100
00:06:28,600 --> 00:06:31,630
is not in the hundreds, but possibly 3,000.

101
00:06:31,630 --> 00:06:34,760
The study claimed the weapons were hidden
in secret underground tunnels.

102
00:06:34,760 --> 00:06:38,460
The prospect of any kind of conflict involving
these weapons of mass destruction, however,

103
00:06:38,460 --> 00:06:40,180
is highly unlikely.

104
00:06:40,180 --> 00:06:44,640
We cannot forget that almost every single
tank, aircraft, or naval unit needs fuel to

105
00:06:44,640 --> 00:06:45,640
operate.

106
00:06:45,640 --> 00:06:48,770
China currently consumes approximately 12
million (11,968,000) barrels of oil a day,

107
00:06:48,770 --> 00:06:51,820
but it only produces about 4 million (3,980,000)
barrels daily.

108
00:06:51,820 --> 00:06:55,210
That said, it does have 25 billion barrels
in reserves.

109
00:06:55,210 --> 00:07:00,980
Japan, on the other hand, consumes 4.15 million
barrels of oil a day, but it only produces

110
00:07:00,980 --> 00:07:03,890
a meager 3,900 barrels daily.

111
00:07:03,890 --> 00:07:07,870
Worse yet, it only has 44 million barrels
of oil in reserves.

112
00:07:07,870 --> 00:07:10,330
So, who do you think has a stronger military?

113
00:07:10,330 --> 00:07:11,330
China or Japan?

114
00:07:11,330 --> 00:07:12,730
Let us know why in the comments!

115
00:07:12,730 --> 00:07:15,360
And be sure sure to check out our military
comparisons playlist.

116
00:07:15,360 --> 00:07:18,160
Thanks for watching, and, as always, don’t
forget to like, share, and subscribe.

117
00:07:18,160 --> 00:07:18,820
See you next time!

question: What is the temperature difference between the lower bound of the outer core and the average temperature of the Mesosphere?
What is the thickness of the core layer in kilometers?
What percentage of Earth's surface is water?

1
00:00:00,520 --> 00:00:02,520
Planet Earth is the home of every lifeform,

2
00:00:02,520 --> 00:00:04,520
known to us, in the universe.

3
00:00:05,120 --> 00:00:07,820
Its age is about 1/3 of the age of the universe

4
00:00:07,820 --> 00:00:09,580
and, admitted,

5
00:00:09,580 --> 00:00:11,080
It is a thing of beauty.

6
00:00:11,800 --> 00:00:14,120
a slightly squashed fair with a heavy metal core,

7
00:00:14,120 --> 00:00:15,800
and a lighter surface crust,

8
00:00:15,800 --> 00:00:18,120
wrapped in a thin sliver of sweet air to breathe,

9
00:00:18,640 --> 00:00:20,140
with vast oceans,

10
00:00:20,140 --> 00:00:21,200
fertile plains,

11
00:00:21,200 --> 00:00:22,700
magnificent mountains,

12
00:00:23,040 --> 00:00:25,840
fresh water rivers, streams, lakes and aquifers,

13
00:00:26,120 --> 00:00:28,120
orbiting a star which warms us,

14
00:00:28,120 --> 00:00:29,780
and gives us energy.

15
00:00:30,400 --> 00:00:32,480
But how did our home come in to existence,

16
00:00:32,480 --> 00:00:34,480
and what's it made of?

17
00:00:41,980 --> 00:00:43,780
4.6 billion years ago,

18
00:00:43,780 --> 00:00:46,120
Earth was created from the remnants of dead stars,

19
00:00:46,120 --> 00:00:48,720
that collected in a giant, dirty gas cloud.

20
00:00:49,360 --> 00:00:51,440
The gas cloud became denser in its center,

21
00:00:51,440 --> 00:00:53,440
and formed an accretion disk.

22
00:00:53,880 --> 00:00:56,260
small particles started clumping together,

23
00:00:56,260 --> 00:00:58,340
and building larger and larger objects,

24
00:00:58,340 --> 00:01:01,140
until they form the objects we call "Planets" today.

25
00:01:01,960 --> 00:01:04,360
This process took 10 to 20 million years,

26
00:01:04,360 --> 00:01:06,360
and is still not very well understood.

27
00:01:07,160 --> 00:01:10,220
At about this time, when the solar system was young and chaotic,

28
00:01:10,220 --> 00:01:12,560
a giant object, about as big as Mars,

29
00:01:12,560 --> 00:01:14,560
collided with our home.

30
00:01:14,560 --> 00:01:16,280
The impact was violent,

31
00:01:16,280 --> 00:01:18,280
and if the object had been more massive,

32
00:01:18,280 --> 00:01:20,220
it might have destroyed Earth.

33
00:01:20,660 --> 00:01:22,660
Materials from Earth were smashed out into orbit,

34
00:01:22,660 --> 00:01:24,180
and formed the Moon,

35
00:01:24,180 --> 00:01:27,500
which is the biggest satellite in relation to its planet in the solar system.

36
00:01:28,440 --> 00:01:30,760
At this time, Earth was a hot hell,

37
00:01:30,760 --> 00:01:33,100
constantly being hit by asteroids,

38
00:01:33,100 --> 00:01:34,260
with seas of lava,

39
00:01:34,260 --> 00:01:35,400
and a toxic atmosphere.

40
00:01:36,080 --> 00:01:38,720
But something was about to change drastically.

41
00:01:38,720 --> 00:01:40,240
Earth cooled down.

42
00:01:40,700 --> 00:01:42,700
Water from the inside of the Earth

43
00:01:42,700 --> 00:01:45,500
wandered to the surface and rained down on Earth,

44
00:01:45,500 --> 00:01:47,840
only to vaporize again and become clouds.

45
00:01:48,560 --> 00:01:51,660
Millions of asteroids brought more and more water to our planet.

46
00:01:52,680 --> 00:01:56,780
All the water on Earth has about this volume compared to Earth.

47
00:01:57,480 --> 00:01:58,180
Today,

48
00:01:58,180 --> 00:02:00,480
the surface of Earth is 71% water,

49
00:02:00,480 --> 00:02:01,960
and 29% land.

50
00:02:02,580 --> 00:02:05,240
97.5% is saline water,

51
00:02:05,240 --> 00:02:07,740
while only 2.5% is fresh water.

52
00:02:08,480 --> 00:02:11,540
The Fresh water is 69% ice and snow,

53
00:02:11,540 --> 00:02:13,460
30% are ground waters,

54
00:02:13,460 --> 00:02:17,160
and only about 1% make up the remaining ground waters.

55
00:02:17,680 --> 00:02:19,980
But even this small part is mostly frozen.

56
00:02:20,620 --> 00:02:23,840
Only a tiny part of our water is actually lakes and rivers.

57
00:02:23,840 --> 00:02:27,100
and an even tinier part is bound in living things.

58
00:02:27,880 --> 00:02:30,240
So, gradually the Earth cooled down,

59
00:02:30,240 --> 00:02:32,240
and the surface formed a thin crust.

60
00:02:32,240 --> 00:02:35,720
But inside the earth, hot rock continue to swirl about,

61
00:02:35,720 --> 00:02:38,680
moving the crust from below and breaking it apart.

62
00:02:39,320 --> 00:02:41,840
This process is called "Plate Tectonics",

63
00:02:41,840 --> 00:02:43,800
and is happening right now.

64
00:02:43,800 --> 00:02:45,980
We'll make a whole video about it in the future.

65
00:02:46,480 --> 00:02:47,020
For now,

66
00:02:47,020 --> 00:02:49,200
let's just say that the crust of Earth consisted of

67
00:02:49,200 --> 00:02:51,380
separate giant plates that move around.

68
00:02:51,580 --> 00:02:54,500
As they meet, they crumble, and create mighty mountains.

69
00:02:55,000 --> 00:02:55,500
OR:

70
00:02:55,500 --> 00:02:57,940
violently plunge back down, deeper into Earth,

71
00:02:57,940 --> 00:02:59,660
creating deep trenches.

72
00:03:00,160 --> 00:03:03,080
That's the way the highest place on Earth was formed: Mt.Everest,

73
00:03:03,080 --> 00:03:05,160
and the deepest: the Mariana Trench.

74
00:03:05,820 --> 00:03:07,200
From our perspective,

75
00:03:07,200 --> 00:03:10,140
Earth's mountains and trenches are mighty indeed,

76
00:03:10,140 --> 00:03:12,340
but when you look at the Earth in cross-section,

77
00:03:12,340 --> 00:03:14,440
you can see how tiny they actually are.

78
00:03:15,080 --> 00:03:17,080
The part we stand on is the crust,

79
00:03:17,080 --> 00:03:18,760
which is about 50 kilometers thick,

80
00:03:18,760 --> 00:03:21,500
though it can vary between 5 and 70 kilometers

81
00:03:22,000 --> 00:03:22,500
By the way,

82
00:03:22,500 --> 00:03:24,320
[Insert subtitle here]

83
00:03:24,320 --> 00:03:26,520
[Insert subtitle here]

84
00:03:27,060 --> 00:03:29,060
After the crust, comes the mantle.

85
00:03:29,060 --> 00:03:30,520
It's a silicate rocky shell,

86
00:03:30,520 --> 00:03:33,260
and about 2,900 kilometers thick.

87
00:03:33,620 --> 00:03:36,660
The mantle consists of the upper mantle, and the lower mantle.

88
00:03:37,320 --> 00:03:39,680
The upper mantle has different regions, too.

89
00:03:39,680 --> 00:03:42,500
It's upper part, which is viscous and carries the crust,

90
00:03:42,500 --> 00:03:43,820
is called the "Lithosphere."

91
00:03:44,200 --> 00:03:46,440
After that, there comes the "Asthenosphere,"

92
00:03:46,440 --> 00:03:49,640
which consists of less mobile, mostly solid material.

93
00:03:50,420 --> 00:03:53,540
The lower mantle reaches deep down to the outer core of Earth.

94
00:03:54,180 --> 00:03:57,000
Earth's outer core is a liquid layer of iron and nickel,

95
00:03:57,000 --> 00:04:00,180
about 2,266 kilometers thick.

96
00:04:00,580 --> 00:04:03,260
Temperatures vary from 4,000℃(7,232℉)

97
00:04:03,260 --> 00:04:05,720
to 5,700℃(10,292℉).

98
00:04:06,260 --> 00:04:08,600
And in the center, is the inner core.

99
00:04:09,260 --> 00:04:10,560
It's mostly solid,

100
00:04:10,560 --> 00:04:12,800
a ball made of an iron-nickel alloy.

101
00:04:12,800 --> 00:04:15,420
with a radius of about 1,200 kilometers.

102
00:04:15,660 --> 00:04:17,500
70% of the size of the moon,

103
00:04:17,500 --> 00:04:20,100
and about the temperature of the surface of the Sun.

104
00:04:20,540 --> 00:04:21,940
It is slowly growing

105
00:04:21,940 --> 00:04:24,900
at an estimated rate of about 1mm/year.

106
00:04:25,620 --> 00:04:27,060
Now, for some respective,

107
00:04:27,440 --> 00:04:31,740
this small layer of crystallized melt products of former molten mantle,

108
00:04:31,740 --> 00:04:33,240
is where we live.

109
00:04:33,600 --> 00:04:36,020
Then, there's Earth's magnetic field.

110
00:04:36,420 --> 00:04:38,040
It's an invisible phenomenon

111
00:04:38,040 --> 00:04:41,620
that diverts high energy particles coming from the Sun and other sources,

112
00:04:41,620 --> 00:04:43,420
allowing for a stable environment

113
00:04:43,420 --> 00:04:46,240
with comparatively little radiation impact on Earth.

114
00:04:46,920 --> 00:04:48,040
But why is it there?

115
00:04:48,580 --> 00:04:51,500
Actually, we don't really know a terrible lot about that.

116
00:04:51,960 --> 00:04:54,340
We know, it has something to do with the core of Earth.

117
00:04:54,340 --> 00:04:56,060
Inside this metal sphere,

118
00:04:56,060 --> 00:04:59,040
large electrical currents flow in complicated patterns.

119
00:04:59,620 --> 00:05:01,320
They cause a magnetic field,

120
00:05:01,320 --> 00:05:05,160
that sort of stabilizes itself according to the laws of electrodynamics.

121
00:05:05,540 --> 00:05:08,060
This entire system is called the "Dynamo."

122
00:05:08,460 --> 00:05:11,340
But, don't let us fool you into thinking we have it all figured out.

123
00:05:12,360 --> 00:05:14,600
Speaking of breathtaking information,

124
00:05:14,980 --> 00:05:17,480
what about the airy stuff that surrounds us?

125
00:05:17,894 --> 00:05:18,994
By volume,

126
00:05:19,000 --> 00:05:21,500
dry air consists mostly of Nitrogen,

127
00:05:21,500 --> 00:05:22,440
Oxygen,

128
00:05:22,440 --> 00:05:23,180
Argon,

129
00:05:23,180 --> 00:05:24,080
Carbon,

130
00:05:24,080 --> 00:05:25,840
a variable mount of water vapor,

131
00:05:25,840 --> 00:05:27,620
and small amounts of other gases.

132
00:05:28,360 --> 00:05:31,740
Humans are very dependent on the lowest layer of the atmosphere:

133
00:05:31,740 --> 00:05:34,140
the Troposphere - Where the weather is.

134
00:05:34,154 --> 00:05:36,154
It's 12 kilometers thick on average.

135
00:05:36,600 --> 00:05:38,180
Above that is the Stratosphere,

136
00:05:38,180 --> 00:05:40,180
which is where the ozone layer protects us

137
00:05:40,180 --> 00:05:42,180
from the sun's most aggressive type of light.

138
00:05:42,920 --> 00:05:46,100
Above that is the Mesosphere - the coolest place on Earth,

139
00:05:46,100 --> 00:05:49,600
with an average temperature around -85℃(-121℉).

140
00:05:50,580 --> 00:05:53,800
At about 80 kilometers up, the Thermosphere starts.

141
00:05:54,000 --> 00:05:57,360
The transition to space is a fluent one, without clear borders.

142
00:05:57,360 --> 00:06:00,040
but humans decided that space starts here.

143
00:06:00,520 --> 00:06:03,740
At about 100 kilometers, Earth stops, and space begins,

144
00:06:03,740 --> 00:06:06,040
though the atmosphere extends a bit further.

145
00:06:06,660 --> 00:06:08,660
In this region, we find the Ionosphere,

146
00:06:09,040 --> 00:06:10,260
the aurora borealis,

147
00:06:10,920 --> 00:06:11,900
and the ISS,

148
00:06:12,720 --> 00:06:15,240
and the outermost layer is the Exosphere,

149
00:06:15,240 --> 00:06:17,700
stretching up to 10,000 kilometers.

150
00:06:18,080 --> 00:06:20,220
It merges fluently with outer space,

151
00:06:20,220 --> 00:06:21,960
where there's no atmosphere at all.

152
00:06:22,420 --> 00:06:25,460
The atoms and molecules in this area are so far apart,

153
00:06:25,460 --> 00:06:27,620
that they can travel hundreds of kilometers

154
00:06:27,620 --> 00:06:29,320
without colliding with each other.

155
00:06:29,880 --> 00:06:30,380
OK.

156
00:06:30,800 --> 00:06:32,380
Humans, in their present form,

157
00:06:32,380 --> 00:06:35,060
have only been around for 200,000 years.

158
00:06:35,060 --> 00:06:38,700
- that's 0.004% of Earth's history.

159
00:06:39,040 --> 00:06:40,020
Not long, really.

160
00:06:40,540 --> 00:06:41,980
And, here we are now,

161
00:06:41,980 --> 00:06:45,380
living in a thin, moist layer on a small, wet rock.

162
00:06:45,380 --> 00:06:47,380
We call this rock: Earth.

163
00:06:48,040 --> 00:06:50,920
It is the product of the universe's deepest workings,

164
00:06:50,920 --> 00:06:54,980
the result of a constant process of creation and destruction,

165
00:06:54,980 --> 00:06:57,920
happening all of the universe, all the time,

166
00:06:57,920 --> 00:06:59,280
helped by chance,

167
00:06:59,280 --> 00:07:02,240
the laws of the universe and random events,

168
00:07:02,880 --> 00:07:04,200
we are really lucky.

question:
1
00:00:00,658 --> 00:00:04,800
What is hydraulic fracturing – or fracking ?

2
00:00:04,800 --> 00:00:09,800
Since the industrial revolution our energy consumption has risen unceasingly.

3
00:00:09,800 --> 00:00:17,383
The majority of this energy consumption is supplied by fossil fuels like coal or natural gas.

4
00:00:17,383 --> 00:00:21,800
Recently there has been a lot of talk about a controversial method of extracting natural gas:

5
00:00:21,800 --> 00:00:25,800
Hydraulic fracturing or fracking.

6
00:00:25,800 --> 00:00:30,577
Put simply, fracking describes the recovery of natural gas from deep layers inside the earth.

7
00:00:30,577 --> 00:00:34,632
In this method, porous rock is fractured by the use of water, sand and chemicals

8
00:00:34,632 --> 00:00:39,497
in order to release the enclosed natural gas.

9
00:00:39,497 --> 00:00:42,777
The technique of fracking has been known since the 1940s.

10
00:00:42,777 --> 00:00:48,856
Nonetheless, only in the last ten years has there been quite a “fracking boom”,

11
00:00:48,856 --> 00:00:51,134
especially in the USA.

12
00:00:51,134 --> 00:00:57,633
This is because most conventional natural gas sources in America and on the European continent have been exhausted.

13
00:00:57,633 --> 00:01:03,299
Thus prices for natural gas and other fuels are rising steadily.

14
00:01:03,299 --> 00:01:10,658
Significantly more complicated and expensive methods, like fracking, have now become attractive and profitable.

15
00:01:10,658 --> 00:01:17,098
In the meantime, fracking has already been used more than a million times in the USA alone.

16
00:01:17,098 --> 00:01:22,498
[Insert subtitle here]

17
00:01:22,498 --> 00:01:26,800
Now let’s take a look at how fracking actually works:

18
00:01:26,800 --> 00:01:31,800
First, a shaft is drilled several hundred meters into the earth.

19
00:01:31,800 --> 00:01:37,097
From there, a horizontal hole is drilled into the gas-bearing layer of rock.

20
00:01:37,097 --> 00:01:42,098
Next, the fracking fluid is pumped into the ground using high-performance pumps.

21
00:01:42,098 --> 00:01:46,049
On average, the fluid consists of 8 million liters of water

22
00:01:46,049 --> 00:01:50,133
which amounts to about the daily consumption of 65,000 people.

23
00:01:50,133 --> 00:01:55,656
plus several thousand tons of sand and about 200,000 liters of chemicals.

24
00:01:55,656 --> 00:02:01,048
The mixture penetrates into the rock layer and produces innumerable tiny cracks.

25
00:02:01,048 --> 00:02:05,264
The sand prevents the cracks from closing again.

26
00:02:05,264 --> 00:02:07,965
The chemicals perform various tasks

27
00:02:07,965 --> 00:02:10,465
among other things, they condense the water,

28
00:02:10,465 --> 00:02:11,965
kill off bacteria

29
00:02:11,965 --> 00:02:14,884
or dissolve minerals.

30
00:02:14,884 --> 00:02:18,216
Next, the majority of the fracking fluid is pumped out again.

31
00:02:18,216 --> 00:02:22,050
And now the natural gas can be recovered.

32
00:02:22,050 --> 00:02:26,337
As soon as the gas source is exhausted, the drill hole is sealed.

33
00:02:26,337 --> 00:02:32,578
As a rule, the fracking fluid is pumped back into deep underground layers and sealed in there.

34
00:02:32,578 --> 00:02:37,216
However, fracking is also associated with several considerable risks.

35
00:02:37,216 --> 00:02:41,099
The primary risk consists in the contamination of drinking water sources.

36
00:02:41,099 --> 00:02:44,097
Fracking not only consumes large quantities of fresh water,

37
00:02:44,097 --> 00:02:49,216
but in addition the water is subsequently contaminated and is highly toxic.

38
00:02:49,216 --> 00:02:56,216
The contamination is so severe that the water cannot even be cleaned in a treatment plant.

39
00:02:56,216 --> 00:02:59,965
Even though the danger is known and theoretically could be managed,

40
00:02:59,965 --> 00:03:06,337
in the USA already sources have been contaminated due to negligence.

41
00:03:06,337 --> 00:03:09,616
No one yet knows how the enclosed water will behave in the future,

42
00:03:09,616 --> 00:03:14,298
since there have not yet been any long-term studies on the subject.

43
00:03:14,298 --> 00:03:17,576
The chemicals used in fracking vary from the hazardous to the

44
00:03:17,576 --> 00:03:24,738
extremely toxic and carcinogenic, such as benzol or formic acid.

45
00:03:24,738 --> 00:03:32,577
The companies using fracking say nothing about the precise composition of the chemical mixture.

46
00:03:32,577 --> 00:03:39,178
But it is known that there are about 700 different chemical agents which can be used in the process.

47
00:03:39,178 --> 00:03:43,537
Another risk is the release of greenhouse gases.

48
00:03:43,537 --> 00:03:47,418
The natural gas recovered by fracking consists largely of methane,

49
00:03:47,418 --> 00:03:53,465
a greenhouse gas which is 25 times
more potent than carbon dioxide.

50
00:03:53,465 --> 00:03:57,457
Natural gas is less harmful than coal when burned.

51
00:03:57,457 --> 00:03:59,383
But nonetheless, the negative effects of fracking

52
00:03:59,383 --> 00:04:02,134
on the climate balance are overall greater.

53
00:04:02,134 --> 00:04:07,496
Firstly, the fracking process requires
a very large consumption of energy.

54
00:04:07,496 --> 00:04:11,738
Secondly, the drill holes are quickly exhausted and it is necessary to drill

55
00:04:11,738 --> 00:04:16,633
fracking holes much more frequently than for classical natural gas wells.

56
00:04:16,633 --> 00:04:24,496
In addition, about 3% of the recovered gas is lost in the extraction and escapes into the atmosphere.

57
00:04:24,496 --> 00:04:27,258
So how is fracking and its expected benefits to be assessed

58
00:04:27,258 --> 00:04:31,497
when the advantages are balanced against the disadvantages?

59
00:04:31,497 --> 00:04:34,258
When properly employed, this technique offers one way

60
00:04:34,258 --> 00:04:41,050
in the short to medium term for meeting our demand for lower-cost energy.

61
00:04:41,050 --> 00:04:44,633
But the long-term consequences of fracking are unforeseeable

62
00:04:44,633 --> 00:04:49,258
and the risk to our drinking water thus should not be underestimated.

63
00:05:01,000 --> 00:05:04,000
Subtitles by the Amara.org community
answer: Over 60% of all new oil and gas wells are drilled by using fracking.

question:
1
00:00:00,210 --> 00:00:03,164
American moms are starting a new trend.

2
00:00:03,164 --> 00:00:06,150
Thirties are now the new 20s.

3
00:00:06,150 --> 00:00:08,980
In 2016, for the first time ever,

4
00:00:08,980 --> 00:00:10,670
more American women had babies

5
00:00:10,670 --> 00:00:13,650
in their early 30s than in their 20s.

6
00:00:13,650 --> 00:00:16,430
And women are now 25% older when they

7
00:00:16,430 --> 00:00:19,250
give birth compared to 50 years ago.

8
00:00:19,250 --> 00:00:23,420
But isn't having kids at an
older age harder on your body?

9
00:00:23,420 --> 00:00:26,140
And couldn't that mean
more risk to the baby?

10
00:00:26,140 --> 00:00:29,380
Come to think of it,
what is the difference

11
00:00:29,380 --> 00:00:33,463
between giving birth in
your 20s versus your 30s?

12
00:00:34,330 --> 00:00:37,670
Giving birth at any age is a big change.

13
00:00:37,670 --> 00:00:40,690
For one, you'll have a child to support.

14
00:00:40,690 --> 00:00:45,690
They cost the average household
around $230,000 to raise,

15
00:00:46,150 --> 00:00:48,460
but there are some major differences

16
00:00:48,460 --> 00:00:50,850
based on when you give birth.

17
00:00:50,850 --> 00:00:55,127
Take fertility: Between
the ages of 20 and 24,

18
00:00:55,127 --> 00:00:57,440
women have an 86% chance

19
00:00:57,440 --> 00:00:59,950
of conceiving after trying for a year.

20
00:00:59,950 --> 00:01:04,580
But that chance falls to
around 50% in your late 30s.

21
00:01:04,580 --> 00:01:06,510
And then there's your health.

22
00:01:06,510 --> 00:01:09,740
20-somethings have a lower
chance of miscarrying

23
00:01:09,740 --> 00:01:12,450
and of conditions like
gestational diabetes,

24
00:01:12,450 --> 00:01:15,210
preeclampsia, and high blood pressure.

25
00:01:15,210 --> 00:01:17,510
But when it comes to your
health later in life,

26
00:01:17,510 --> 00:01:20,950
waiting until your 30s
to give birth is better.

27
00:01:20,950 --> 00:01:23,340
Research shows that moms
who first gave birth

28
00:01:23,340 --> 00:01:25,960
in their early 30s report higher energy,

29
00:01:25,960 --> 00:01:28,420
better fitness, and fewer aches and pains

30
00:01:28,420 --> 00:01:32,110
compared to moms who first
gave birth in their early 20s.

31
00:01:32,110 --> 00:01:36,090
And that might help explain
another scientific finding.

32
00:01:36,090 --> 00:01:40,110
Women who have kids in their
30s might also live longer.

33
00:01:40,110 --> 00:01:43,340
According to a paper published in 2015,

34
00:01:43,340 --> 00:01:46,630
women who had their
last child after age 33

35
00:01:46,630 --> 00:01:49,560
were twice as likely to live past 95

36
00:01:49,560 --> 00:01:50,810
compared to women who had their

37
00:01:50,810 --> 00:01:53,930
last child before their 30th birthday.

38
00:01:53,930 --> 00:01:56,410
And perhaps they'll also have more

39
00:01:56,410 --> 00:01:59,530
money to spend in those extra years.

40
00:01:59,530 --> 00:02:02,140
A Danish study found that
college-educated mothers

41
00:02:02,140 --> 00:02:05,220
who were 31 to 34 when they gave birth

42
00:02:05,220 --> 00:02:08,980
earned around $5,000 more
income over their lifetime

43
00:02:08,980 --> 00:02:11,720
compared to the average
woman with a college degree,

44
00:02:11,720 --> 00:02:14,560
whereas [Insert subtitle here]

45
00:02:14,560 --> 00:02:19,560
[Insert subtitle here]

46
00:02:19,800 --> 00:02:24,800
Of course, that's just
moms. What about the kids?

47
00:02:25,080 --> 00:02:27,000
If their moms gave birth in their 30s

48
00:02:27,000 --> 00:02:29,300
instead of their 20s, those kids

49
00:02:29,300 --> 00:02:32,820
might be safer, smarter, or even taller.

50
00:02:32,820 --> 00:02:36,220
On top of that, there
might be more of them.

51
00:02:36,220 --> 00:02:39,450
That's right, because if
you wait until your 30s,

52
00:02:39,450 --> 00:02:42,150
you're more likely to have twins.

53
00:02:42,150 --> 00:02:44,470
Older women have higher
levels of a hormone

54
00:02:44,470 --> 00:02:48,270
called FSH, which stimulates the ovaries.

55
00:02:48,270 --> 00:02:51,500
Normally, women release just enough FSH

56
00:02:51,500 --> 00:02:54,320
to ovulate or release one egg,

57
00:02:54,320 --> 00:02:57,930
but near menopause, they
produce a ton of it,

58
00:02:57,930 --> 00:03:00,300
which can cause two eggs to ovulate

59
00:03:00,300 --> 00:03:03,150
and ultimately result in twins.

60
00:03:03,150 --> 00:03:07,520
Now, whether having twins is
a benefit, that's up to you.

61
00:03:07,520 --> 00:03:12,150
But one thing's for sure,
whether you have kids at 21

62
00:03:12,150 --> 00:03:15,685
or 35, you will never be the same again.
answer: College-educated women who had their first kid before 25 earned around $80,000 less.

People are talking a lot about

Shocking, right? 80% percent of the world's

the richest 2%, they have more wealth than

Now let's show how the world's total

is distributed. The vast majority have practically nothing

Nothing with which to educate their

they've accumulated 43% of our world's

26

8 out of every 10 people - have just 6% between

But even this

doesn't show how extreme things have

wealth than the populations of India, China,

We can also see this inequality geographically,

36

For most of history, things were much more equal. 200 years ago, rich countries were only

37
00:02:12,080 --> 00:02:17,530
3 times richer than poor countries. By the
end of colonialism in the 1960s, they were

00:02:17,530 --> 00:02:23,370
35 times richer. Today, they're about 80 times richer.

39
00:02:23,370 --> 00:02:27,300
Rich countries try to compensate for this
by giving aid to poor countries - about

40
00:02:27,300 --> 00:02:31,500
130 billion dollars each year. That's a
lot of money.

41
00:02:31,500 --> 00:02:34,050
So then why does the wealth gap keep getting
bigger?

42
00:02:34,050 --> 00:02:39,160
One reason I found is that large corporations
are taking more than 900 billion dollars

43
00:02:39,160 --> 00:02:41,970
out of poor countries each year through a

44
00:02:41,970 --> 00:02:45,620
form of tax avoidance called trade mispricing.

45
00:02:45,620 --> 00:02:50,690
On top of this, each year poor countries are
paying about 600 billion dollars in debt service

46
00:02:50,690 --> 00:02:55,350
to rich countries, on loans that have already
been paid off many times over.

47
00:02:55,350 --> 00:02:59,800
And then there's the money that poor countries
lose from trade rules imposed by rich countries

48
00:02:59,800 --> 00:03:05,000
to get access to more resources and cheaper
labor. Economists from the University of Massachusetts

49
00:03:05,000 --> 00:03:10,130
calculate that this costs poor countries about
500 billion dollars a year.

50
00:03:10,130 --> 00:03:14,500
All together, that's more than 2 trillion
dollars that flows from some of the poorest

51
00:03:14,500 --> 00:03:20,200
parts of the world to the richest, every year.
Rich governments like to say they're helping

52
00:03:20,200 --> 00:03:24,540
poor countries develop, but who's developing
who here?

53
00:03:24,540 --> 00:03:28,099
This makes me think that there's something
wrong with the basic rules of the global economy.

54
00:03:28,099 --> 00:03:32,520
It can't be right that the wealth of our
planet is becoming so concentrated in the

55
00:03:32,520 --> 00:03:37,650
hands of such a tiny number of people.
The only reasonable response, it seems to me,

56
00:03:37,650 --> 00:03:40,840
and our only hope, is to change the rules.
answer: The richest 1% have so much more than everybody else.
