00:00:01,230 --> 00:00:04,130
The modern United States is the most powerful country in human history.

2
00:00:04,130 --> 00:00:10,320
With over 800 military bases and 37% of global military spending, the United States

3
00:00:10,320 --> 00:00:14,101
has become the leader of a vast interconnected global system that has helped usher in an

4
00:00:14,101 --> 00:00:18,180
era of unprecedented prosperity and low levels
of conflict.

5
00:00:18,180 --> 00:00:22,589
To understand America’s position in the
world, and why it’s so pivotal for world

6
00:00:22,589 --> 00:00:25,820
politics as we know it, you have to go back
to the country’s founding — back to when

7
00:00:25,820 --> 00:00:29,360
America wasn’t a global power in any sense
of the word.

8
00:00:29,360 --> 00:00:33,140
During the first 70 years of its existence,
the United States expanded in both territory

9
00:00:33,140 --> 00:00:37,750
and influence in North America eventually
reaching the Pacific Ocean in a wave of expansionism

10
00:00:37,750 --> 00:00:41,550
that resulted in the wholesale slaughter of
the indigenous people who populated the continent.

11
00:00:41,550 --> 00:00:46,340
But early Americans were deeply divided as
to whether the country should expand beyond

12
00:00:46,340 --> 00:00:48,250
the Pacific and Atlantic oceans.

13
00:00:48,250 --> 00:00:52,420
This became a major debate after the civil
war, when some leaders, like post-war

14
00:00:52,420 --> 00:00:57,030
Secretary of State Seward, argued that America
should push to become a global power.

15
00:00:57,030 --> 00:01:00,960
Seward succeeded in pushing a plan to purchase
Alaska from Russia, but his attempts to buy

16
00:01:00,960 --> 00:01:06,160
Greenland and Iceland, as well as annex territory
in the Caribbean, were all blocked by Congress.

17
00:01:06,160 --> 00:01:11,770
That’s because some Americans, including
many on Capitol Hill, had a strong anti-imperialist bent.

18
00:01:12,770 --> 00:01:16,080
These people worried about America getting
more involved in global politics, as well

19
00:01:16,080 --> 00:01:20,170
as having to integrate populations from “inferior”
races.

20
00:01:20,170 --> 00:01:24,040
And this opposition applied major checks on
the imperialist urge to expand.

21
00:01:24,040 --> 00:01:28,880
But something was happening in the late 1800s
that would change the debate about American expansionism.

22
00:01:28,880 --> 00:01:32,740
[Insert subtitle here], and the bigger US economy

23
00:01:32,740 --> 00:01:37,150
required a more centralized state and bureaucracy
to manage the growing economy.

24
00:01:37,150 --> 00:01:41,290
Power became concentrated in the federal government,
making it easier for expansionist presidents,

25
00:01:41,290 --> 00:01:45,180
like William Mckinley, to unilaterally push
United States influence abroad.

26
00:01:45,180 --> 00:01:49,470
The key turning point came in 1898, when President
McKinley dragged the country into war with

27
00:01:49,470 --> 00:01:53,610
Spain over the island of Cuba despite intense
opposition.

28
00:01:53,610 --> 00:01:58,480
The rising US easily defeated the moribund
Spanish empire, acquiring Puerto Rico, Guam,

29
00:01:58,480 --> 00:02:01,080
and the Philippines in the process (1898).

30
00:02:01,080 --> 00:02:04,410
Over the next two years, the US would annex
the Kingdom of Hawaii (1898), Wake Island

31
00:02:04,410 --> 00:02:05,670
(1899), and American Samoa (1900).

32
00:02:05,670 --> 00:02:09,560
A few years later the US took control of the
Panama Canal Zone (1903) and sent troops to

33
00:02:09,560 --> 00:02:13,920
occupy the Dominican Republic (1916), it also
purchased the American Virgin Islands (1917).

34
00:02:13,920 --> 00:02:18,069
This period of rapid acquisition of far flung
territories put the US on the map as a truly

35
00:02:18,069 --> 00:02:19,959
global power.

36
00:02:19,959 --> 00:02:23,819
During this time, America also began using
its influence to protect its growing commercial

37
00:02:23,819 --> 00:02:28,299
and military interests abroad, installing
pro-American regimes in places like Nicaragua

38
00:02:28,299 --> 00:02:34,189
and playing a major role in international
diplomacy regarding the Western presence in China.

39
00:02:34,189 --> 00:02:36,929
World War I showed how just how much America’s
influence had grown.

40
00:02:36,929 --> 00:02:41,009
Not only was American intervention a decisive factor in the war's end

41
00:02:41,680 --> 00:02:44,959
But President Wilson attended the Paris Peace
Conference which ended the war and attempted

42
00:02:44,959 --> 00:02:46,980
to set the terms of the peace.

43
00:02:46,980 --> 00:02:51,340
He spearheaded America’s most ambitious
foreign policy initiative yet, an international

44
00:02:51,340 --> 00:02:57,560
organization, called the League of Nations,
designed to promote peace and cooperation globally.

45
00:02:57,560 --> 00:03:02,200
The League, a wholesale effort to remake global
politics, showed just how ambitious American

46
00:03:02,200 --> 00:03:04,940
foreign policy had become.

47
00:03:04,940 --> 00:03:07,489
Yet isolationism was still a major force in
the United States.

48
00:03:07,489 --> 00:03:08,489
Yet isolationism was still a major force in
the United States.

49
00:03:09,580 --> 00:03:13,580
Congress blocked the United States from joining
the League of Nations, dooming Wilson’s

50
00:03:13,580 --> 00:03:14,260
project.

51
00:03:15,280 --> 00:03:18,549
During the Great Depression and the rise of
Hitler, the US was was much more focused on

52
00:03:18,549 --> 00:03:23,099
its own region than on European affairs
Ultimately, though, America’s ever-growing

53
00:03:23,099 --> 00:03:27,519
entanglements abroad made it impossible for
it to stay out of global affairs entirely.

54
00:03:27,519 --> 00:03:32,019
In East Asia, the growing Japanese empire
posed a the direct threat to American possessions

55
00:03:32,019 --> 00:03:36,599
and troops bringing the United States and Japan into conflict.

56
00:03:36,599 --> 00:03:40,060
This culminated in the Pearl Harbor attack bringing the United States into World War II.

57
00:03:40,060 --> 00:03:43,170
World War Two would transform America’s
global presence forever.

58
00:03:43,170 --> 00:03:48,629
The United States was the only major power
to avoid economic ruin during the war, and

59
00:03:48,629 --> 00:03:51,120
it was the sole country equipped with atomic
weapons.

60
00:03:51,120 --> 00:03:55,659
As such, it was in unique position to set
the terms of the peace — and, with the aim

61
00:03:55,659 --> 00:03:58,329
of preventing another war in mind, it took
advantage.

62
00:03:58,329 --> 00:04:01,670
The most famous example of this is the creation
of the United Nations.

63
00:04:01,670 --> 00:04:06,349
The UN charter set up a system of international
law prohibiting wars of conquest, like the

64
00:04:06,349 --> 00:04:08,879
ones waged by the Nazis and the Japanese.

65
00:04:08,879 --> 00:04:13,169
It also served as a forum in which the international
community could weigh in on disputes, and

66
00:04:13,169 --> 00:04:14,430
help resolve them.

67
00:04:14,430 --> 00:04:18,510
This way, the Americans hoped, great powers
could resolve their differences through compromise

68
00:04:18,510 --> 00:04:20,810
and law rather than war.

69
00:04:20,810 --> 00:04:25,700
But while the UN is the most famous of the
post-war institutions, it isn’t the only one.

70
00:04:26,700 --> 00:04:32,260
730 delegates from all 44 Allied nations
came together in a small vacation haven in

71
00:04:32,260 --> 00:04:37,340
New Hampshire. Their goal? To establish a global financial system that would prevent another Great Depression

72
00:04:37,340 --> 00:04:38,380
and World War.

73
00:04:40,060 --> 00:04:44,280
The resulting agreement, called the Bretton Woods Agreement  ultimately became backbone of the

74
00:04:44,280 --> 00:04:46,280
global financial system.

75
00:04:46,280 --> 00:04:48,280
Resulting in the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.

76
00:04:52,820 --> 00:04:56,190
By creating these institutions the United
States committed itself to being deeply

77
00:04:56,190 --> 00:04:58,800
involved in the world’s problems.

78
00:04:58,800 --> 00:05:02,650
The issue, though, is that the world’s second-largest
power — The Soviet Union — saw things

79
00:05:02,650 --> 00:05:03,970
differently.

80
00:05:03,970 --> 00:05:07,920
World War II had made allies out of the democratic
West and communist East in the fight against

81
00:05:07,920 --> 00:05:10,160
Hitler, but that couldn’t last.

82
00:05:10,160 --> 00:05:14,000
The United States saw Soviet expansion in
Eastern Europe and elsewhere as a direct threat

83
00:05:14,000 --> 00:05:17,680
to its vision of a free-trading world.

84
00:05:17,680 --> 00:05:20,540
"To a substantial degree, in one form or another"

85
00:05:21,740 --> 00:05:23,740
Socialism has spread the shadow of human regimentation

86
00:05:24,740 --> 00:05:26,740
Over most of the nations of the earth

87
00:05:27,380 --> 00:05:30,980
And... the shadow is encroaching on our own liberty.

88
00:05:31,710 --> 00:05:35,940
Fearful of Soviet intentions towards Western
Europe, the US and other European nations

89
00:05:35,940 --> 00:05:40,610
created the North Atlantic Treaty Organization,
a military alliance meant to stop Russia from

90
00:05:40,610 --> 00:05:44,610
invading other countries in Europe.

91
00:05:44,610 --> 00:05:49,721
Globally, the US committed to a strategy called
“containment” — so called because it

92
00:05:49,721 --> 00:05:54,050
was aimed at containing the spread of Communism
everywhere on the globe.

93
00:05:54,050 --> 00:05:57,590
This new global struggle meant that the US
had to exert influence everywhere, all the

94
00:05:57,590 --> 00:05:58,660
time.

95
00:05:58,660 --> 00:06:02,220
Instead of disbanding the massive military
machine created for World War II, its wheels

96
00:06:02,220 --> 00:06:04,920
mostly kept turning.

97
00:06:06,720 --> 00:06:12,050
This had two main results: first, the US was
pulled into unlikely alliances with countries

98
00:06:12,050 --> 00:06:17,370
like Saudi Arabia, Israel, and South Korea,
seeing each of them as bulwarks against communist

99
00:06:17,370 --> 00:06:18,740
influence in their region.

100
00:06:18,740 --> 00:06:24,490
Secondly, the US began intervening, often
secretly, in dozens of countries to contain

101
00:06:24,490 --> 00:06:25,970
Soviet influence.

102
00:06:25,970 --> 00:06:30,820
Sometimes this meant propping up sympathetic
dictators like in Iran, other times

103
00:06:30,820 --> 00:06:37,810
supplying rebels with arms and money like
in Afghanistan in 1979 and Nicaragua in 1985.

104
00:06:37,810 --> 00:06:42,360
Over the course of the Cold War, the US intervened
in hundreds of disputes around the globe,

105
00:06:42,360 --> 00:06:46,970
ending up with a complicated set of alliances, tensions, and relationships in basically every corner

106
00:06:46,970 --> 00:06:48,490
of the earth.

107
00:06:51,490 --> 00:06:54,930
After the Berlin wall fell, the US could have
withdrawn from this system, severing ties

108
00:06:54,930 --> 00:06:57,980
with its allies and drawing down the size
of its military.

109
00:06:57,980 --> 00:07:01,560
And while the US did military
spending, much of the military

110
00:07:01,560 --> 00:07:05,130
infrastructure and alliances from the Cold War war remained.

111
00:07:05,130 --> 00:07:09,380
Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton
decided that it was in both America and the

112
00:07:09,380 --> 00:07:13,290
world’s interests for the United States,
now the sole superpower on earth, to continue

113
00:07:13,290 --> 00:07:15,070
actively managing global affairs.

114
00:07:16,300 --> 00:07:18,300
" We should be and we must be Peacemakers"

115
00:07:18,310 --> 00:07:25,210
NATO, created solely as a tool for countering
the Soviets, stayed together and even expanded,

116
00:07:25,210 --> 00:07:30,020
a way of keeping European nations united in
the absence of the Soviet threat.

117
00:07:30,020 --> 00:07:35,200
Washington’s support for countries like
Israel and Japan stayed intact, ostensibly

118
00:07:35,200 --> 00:07:38,080
as a means of preventing war in those regions.

119
00:07:38,080 --> 00:07:41,620
The global system of alliances and institutions
created to keep the peace during the Cold

120
00:07:41,620 --> 00:07:45,870
War became permanent — as did the American
military and political commitments needed to

121
00:07:45,870 --> 00:07:46,870
keep them running .

122
00:07:46,870 --> 00:07:51,501
This system remains in operation today, and no leading
American politician since the Cold War has

123
00:07:51,501 --> 00:07:56,720
seriously called for dismantling them — except, perhaps for Donald Trump.

124
00:07:56,720 --> 00:07:58,520
Trump has said contradictory things about
these commitments.

125
00:07:59,520 --> 00:08:03,380
But he’s consistently argued that American
allies are not paying America enough for its

126
00:08:03,380 --> 00:08:06,680
protection, and questioned the value of free trade.

127
00:08:06,680 --> 00:08:08,680
That calls NATO and even the World Trade Organization into question.

128
00:08:09,940 --> 00:08:13,500
At some point, we have to say, you know what, we're better off if Japan

129
00:08:13,500 --> 00:08:17,140
protects itself against this maniac in North Korea.

130
00:08:17,140 --> 00:08:21,260
We're better off if South Korea is going to start to protect itself

131
00:08:21,260 --> 00:08:22,160
-- and Saudi Arabia?--

132
00:08:22,160 --> 00:08:23,700
Saudi Arabia? Absolutely.

133
00:08:23,700 --> 00:08:27,560
This is a sharp divergence from the consensus
that has dominated US foreign policy since

134
00:08:27,560 --> 00:08:32,190
1945, and something closer to the isolationism
that came before it.

135
00:08:32,190 --> 00:08:36,870
So will President Trump act on some of candidate Trump's ideas, and reverse decades

136
00:08:36,870 --> 00:08:39,669
worth of institution building and alliances?

137
00:08:39,669 --> 00:08:41,029
We'll find out, soon enough.

4
00:00:10,700 --> 00:00:15,480
Fortunes disappeared overnight, and the value

5
00:00:15,480 --> 00:00:20,320
But the people in charge of those companies
had an idea.

6
00:00:20,320 --> 00:00:25,920
They started buying shares of their own company's stock from investors.

7
00:00:25,920 --> 00:00:30,130
Which meant there were fewer stocks out there
for other people to buy.

8
00:00:30,130 --> 00:00:34,140
And when there’s less of something, the
price goes up.

9
00:00:34,140 --> 00:00:37,960
Normally, to raise their stock prices, these companies would have had

11
00:00:38,460 --> 00:00:40,690

12
00:00:40,690 --> 00:00:46,040
invent a new product, or a different way of doing things.

13
00:00:46,040 --> 00:00:48,489
But with this, corporations had discovered a kind of magic trick.

14
00:00:48,489 --> 00:00:53,820
They could jack up their stock price without
really doing anything.

15
00:00:53,820 --> 00:00:55,440
This is a stock buyback.

16
00:00:55,440 --> 00:01:01,079
An attempt by the owners of America’s biggest
corporations to hang on to their wealth

17
00:01:01,079 --> 00:01:06,420
while the rest of the country suffered the
worst Depression ever.

18
00:01:06,420 --> 00:01:11,380
This practice helped fundamentally reshape the American economy,

19
00:01:11,400 --> 00:01:13,960
and it set the stage for a century long fight

20
00:01:13,960 --> 00:01:15,251
we’re still having.

21
00:01:15,251 --> 00:01:16,251
It was a choice.

22
00:01:16,251 --> 00:01:17,450
And it was about greed.

23
00:01:17,450 --> 00:01:20,040
Someone has forgotten about the human element.

24
00:01:20,040 --> 00:01:22,869
A fight about where American wealth comes from,

25
00:01:22,869 --> 00:01:26,220
and who should keep it.

26
00:01:26,220 --> 00:01:31,000
You could have saved these jobs, but you chose
not to.

27
00:01:35,960 --> 00:01:42,710
In 1932, the New York Times reported on the
“many abuses alleged” among companies

28
00:01:42,710 --> 00:01:45,560

29
00:01:45,560 --> 00:01:50,810
Abuses like “using the corporations’ funds

30
00:01:50,810 --> 00:01:56,500

The President signed a new law to make them

And they pretty much stopped doing them.

35
00:02:11,999 --> 00:02:18,189
And without buybacks for an option, corporations
basically had three choices for what to do

36
00:02:18,189 --> 00:02:19,939
with their profits.

37
00:02:19,939 --> 00:02:23,209
Option one: reinvest back in the company.

38
00:02:23,209 --> 00:02:24,349
Build new factories.

39
00:02:24,349 --> 00:02:25,870
Create new products.

40
00:02:25,870 --> 00:02:27,980
Option two: raise wages for employees

41
00:02:27,980 --> 00:02:34,840
Option three: issue a dividend and hand profits
over to investors

42
00:02:34,840 --> 00:02:39,799
Most American companies did a mix of all three,
with the bulk of profits going towards reinvestment

43
00:02:39,799 --> 00:02:40,909
and wages.

44
00:02:40,909 --> 00:02:44,459
Over time, technology improved.

45
00:02:44,459 --> 00:02:46,069
Workers made more stuff.

46
00:02:46,069 --> 00:02:51,650
The productivity of American workers nearly doubled in
the thirty years after World War II.

47
00:02:51,650 --> 00:02:53,689
And so did hourly wages.

48
00:02:53,689 --> 00:02:56,010
This helped build the American middle class.

49
00:02:56,010 --> 00:02:59,079
But things didn’t stay that way.

50
00:02:59,079 --> 00:03:02,559
Productivity kept rising, but wages flat lined.

51
00:03:02,559 --> 00:03:08,180
A new political and economic philosophy had
taken hold.

52
00:03:08,180 --> 00:03:11,599
Government is not the solution to our problems.

53
00:03:11,599 --> 00:03:13,090
Government is the problem.

54
00:03:13,090 --> 00:03:16,140
When Ronald Reagan was elected, the Securities and Exchange Act

55
00:03:16,160 --> 00:03:18,260
had successfully been scaring companies away

56
00:03:18,269 --> 00:03:20,599
from doing stock buybacks for fifty years.

57
00:03:20,599 --> 00:03:25,790
But that changed after Reagan appointed
a former investment banker named John Shad

58
00:03:25,790 --> 00:03:27,699
to the top enforcement job.

59
00:03:27,699 --> 00:03:32,150
Shad wanted companies to put less of their
profits into reinvestment and wages.

60
00:03:32,150 --> 00:03:34,140
He thought more should go to investors.

61
00:03:34,140 --> 00:03:37,010
So in 1982, he changed the rules.

62
00:03:37,010 --> 00:03:42,589
For the first time since the 1930s, companies
could buy back shares of their own stock from

63
00:03:42,589 --> 00:03:43,589
investors.

64
00:03:43,589 --> 00:03:47,019
They didn’t have to worry about the government
coming after them.

65
00:03:47,019 --> 00:03:50,049
Buybacks were back.

66
00:03:50,049 --> 00:03:53,579
It was a really good time to be an investor.

67
00:03:53,579 --> 00:03:56,329
Investors wanted to keep that money flowing.

68
00:03:56,329 --> 00:03:59,499
So they changed the way CEOs got paid.

69
00:03:59,499 --> 00:04:05,469
Instead of just earning a salary, CEOs could get a bonus if the company’s stock price went up.

70
00:04:05,469 --> 00:04:11,090
The quickest way to raise the stock price
was to do a buyback, so CEOs started doing

71
00:04:11,090 --> 00:04:13,469
them all the time.

72
00:04:13,469 --> 00:04:19,479
[Insert subtitle here]

73
00:04:19,479 --> 00:04:20,479
[Insert subtitle here]

74
00:04:20,479 --> 00:04:26,129
By 2008, just before the recession, that share
had jumped to 77 percent.

75
00:04:26,129 --> 00:04:31,689
Fast forward to today, and companies are spending
65% of their profits buying back shares of

76
00:04:31,689 --> 00:04:33,370
their own stock.

77
00:04:33,370 --> 00:04:42,520
The pay gap between American CEOs and workers
has grown from 15:1 to 220:1 in less than

78
00:04:42,520 --> 00:04:44,830
a single lifetime.

79
00:04:44,830 --> 00:04:50,050
You can what a uniquely American phenomenon this is when you compare the compensation

80
00:04:50,050 --> 00:04:56,960
for General Motors' CEO with her counterparts
at Volkswagen in Germany and Toyota in Japan.

81
00:04:56,960 --> 00:05:03,110
And you can see part of the reason for this
gap when you look at how much of their profits

82
00:05:03,110 --> 00:05:06,139
three companies spend on buybacks.

83
00:05:06,139 --> 00:05:12,530
Volkswagen hasn’t done any since 2012, and
Toyota’s biggest buyback years are roughly

84
00:05:12,530 --> 00:05:15,360
the size of GM’s smallest.

85
00:05:15,360 --> 00:05:21,000
The more of their profits GM gave to executives
and shareholders, the less was left over for

86
00:05:21,000 --> 00:05:23,150
reinvestment, and for workers.

87
00:05:25,100 --> 00:05:29,819
In 2000, GM had the largest market share of
any automaker in the world.

88
00:05:29,819 --> 00:05:33,819
By 2017, it had fallen to number 4.

89
00:05:33,819 --> 00:05:38,360
And as their market share shrank, GM shuttered
plants across the US,

90
00:05:38,360 --> 00:05:42,250
and tens of thousands of workers lost their
jobs.

91
00:05:42,250 --> 00:05:48,600
For decades, this General Motors plant in Lordstown, Ohio was the biggest employer in the county.

92
00:05:48,600 --> 00:05:53,600
It opened in the 1960s, and started
out making big sedans and muscle cars.

93
00:05:53,600 --> 00:05:59,229
When people's preferences changed or one model
was discontinued, GM would re-tool the plant

94
00:05:59,229 --> 00:06:01,210
to make a different kind of car.

95
00:06:01,210 --> 00:06:06,840
But in 2015, GM promised investors another
massive stock buyback.

96
00:06:06,840 --> 00:06:11,819
To cut costs,  they started eliminating shifts at the Lordstown plant.

97
00:06:11,819 --> 00:06:14,999
Another cutback— the second shift will be
dropped in two months

98
00:06:14,999 --> 00:06:15,999
Where am I going to go?

99
00:06:15,999 --> 00:06:18,199
Everybody's got to find a place now.

100
00:06:18,199 --> 00:06:22,939
It is the end of the line for the General
Motors plant in Lordstown, Ohio

101
00:06:22,939 --> 00:06:30,219
The cuts come as the automaker is reporting
a near-record $12-billion profit last year.

102
00:06:30,219 --> 00:06:35,120
A few months after the GM plant closed down,
the local supplier that built the rear suspensions

103
00:06:35,120 --> 00:06:36,719
went out of business.

104
00:06:36,719 --> 00:06:40,039
Same with the local factory that built the
seats.

105
00:06:40,039 --> 00:06:43,159
Plans for a new hospital building in town
were put on hold.

106
00:06:43,159 --> 00:06:47,349
As paychecks dried up, a local restaurant
closed its doors.

107
00:06:47,349 --> 00:06:49,999
Economists call it the “multiplier effect.”

108
00:06:49,999 --> 00:06:55,120
One study predicted that every four jobs lost
at GM’s Lordstown plant would trigger three

109
00:06:55,120 --> 00:06:58,960
more job losses among suppliers and other
local businesses.

110
00:06:58,960 --> 00:07:05,650
That’s why laid off auto workers aren't the only ones in Lordstown who understand the effects of GM’s choices.

111
00:07:05,650 --> 00:07:07,520
So do teachers.

112
00:07:07,520 --> 00:07:09,729
There were some students who just changed
tremendously.

113
00:07:09,729 --> 00:07:13,669
This is all tremendous upheaval for them

114
00:07:13,669 --> 00:07:17,490
When you look around, you drive around our town, there's a lot of farming,

115
00:07:17,490 --> 00:07:19,710
but General Motors is pretty much the town.

116
00:07:19,710 --> 00:07:23,300
There was a time where the budget was made up mostly of General Motors.

117
00:07:23,300 --> 00:07:27,509
If we lose that revenue from General Motors, that’s going to be really tough for us.

118
00:07:27,509 --> 00:07:30,910
I hesitate to use the word traumatic but it
is.

119
00:07:30,910 --> 00:07:35,669
Because when something this sudden happens, it rocks
your world.

120
00:07:35,669 --> 00:07:40,860
A year before GM shut down the Lordstown plant,
President Trump and Republicans in Congress

121
00:07:40,860 --> 00:07:46,159
lowered the corporate tax rate from 37 percent
to 21 percent.

122
00:07:46,159 --> 00:07:51,509
Those who supported the cuts predicted that corporations would reinvest those tax savings, and that

123
00:07:51,509 --> 00:07:53,669
workers would benefit the most.

124
00:07:53,669 --> 00:07:57,970
The vast majority of businesses are going
to do just what we say— reinvest in their

125
00:07:57,970 --> 00:08:00,389
workers, reinvest in their factories.

126
00:08:00,389 --> 00:08:01,569
Pay people more money.

127
00:08:01,569 --> 00:08:07,240
When our businesses pay less in taxes, they
reinvest that money into their companies.

128
00:08:07,240 --> 00:08:12,949
But according to the non-partisan Congressional
Research Service, that's not what happened.

129
00:08:12,949 --> 00:08:17,470
The CRS studied the effects of the new tax law
a year and a half after it passed.

130
00:08:17,470 --> 00:08:22,900
And they found “very little growth in wage rates”
among ordinary workers

131
00:08:22,900 --> 00:08:29,030
What they did find was evidence for “a record
breaking amount of stock buybacks, with $1

132
00:08:29,030 --> 00:08:33,560
trillion announced by the end of 2018”

133
00:08:33,560 --> 00:08:37,900
For decades, stock buybacks have been secretly
re-shaping the American economy.

134
00:08:37,900 --> 00:08:42,219
And now, politicians are taking notice.

135
00:08:42,219 --> 00:08:46,810
Republican Senator Marco Rubio has suggested
giving extra tax breaks to companies when

136
00:08:46,810 --> 00:08:50,480
they reinvest their profits instead of doing
buybacks.

137
00:08:50,480 --> 00:08:54,980
Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie
Sanders have called for getting rid of the

138
00:08:54,980 --> 00:08:58,750
Reagan-era rule that protects companies when
they do buybacks.

139
00:08:58,750 --> 00:09:02,230
They want to make it easier for the SEC to
investigate these companies, in the hopes

140
00:09:02,230 --> 00:09:09,230
that they’ll be too scared to do buybacks,
just like they were in the 1930s.

141
00:09:09,230 --> 00:09:13,959
Warren is also calling for a new rule that
would give workers mandatory seats on corporate

142
00:09:13,959 --> 00:09:14,959
boards.

143
00:09:14,959 --> 00:09:19,880
That way, they’d have a chance to vote on
those big bonuses that CEOs get when a company’s

144
00:09:19,880 --> 00:09:20,940
stock price goes up.

145
00:09:20,940 --> 00:09:26,080
That’s how German companies have done things
for decades, and buybacks there are way less common.

146
00:09:26,640 --> 00:09:29,540
But in America, they have a long history.

147
00:09:29,540 --> 00:09:36,190
Buybacks began in an era when less than 1 percent
of America’s population held nearly a quarter

148
00:09:36,190 --> 00:09:38,300
of its wealth.

149
00:09:38,300 --> 00:09:40,860
Today, buybacks are back.

150
00:09:40,860 --> 00:09:45,860
And the American economy looks a lot like
it did in the 1920s.

151
00:09:45,860 --> 00:09:50,120
The question now is whether we want it to
stay that way.

The surface area of the moon is huge.

To give you some perspective, it's as big as the whole European
continent, China, the USA, Brazil, and South Africa together.

6
00:00:21,353 --> 00:00:25,534

7
00:00:25,534 --> 00:00:28,061

8
00:00:28,358 --> 00:00:33,528

the solar system in relation to its planet,

[Insert subtitle here]

00:00:39,884 --> 00:00:46,589

how far away is it from us to seem this small in the night sky?

00:00:47,169 --> 00:00:55,900

The IKEA brand is as iconic and loved as Disney,

Although, despite its colors, names, and advertised

00:01:49,659 --> 00:01:50,939

00:01:50,939 --> 00:01:54,509

27
00:01:54,509 --> 00:01:58,580
What are the secrets behind IKEA’s enormous

28
00:02:01,280 --> 00:02:07,710
Although not nearly the same company it is
today, Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA in 1943

29
00:02:07,710 --> 00:02:12,760
as a traveling salesman, selling staples like
matches, pencils, and watches.

30
00:02:12,760 --> 00:02:15,800
Seven years later, he began selling furniture.

31
00:02:15,800 --> 00:02:21,090
Seeing the logistical difficulty of shipping
large items far away, Ingvar decided to flat-pack

32
00:02:21,090 --> 00:02:25,620
the furniture, which also reduced the chance
of damage during transport.

33
00:02:25,620 --> 00:02:31,120
The company created a catalog that customers
could browse through and order with from afar.

34
00:02:31,120 --> 00:02:36,720
The first showroom was built in 1953 in the
same small town, followed by the first of

35
00:02:36,720 --> 00:02:41,290
the company’s iconic giant warehouses in
1965.

36
00:02:41,290 --> 00:02:45,430
The business model has more or less remained
consistent ever since.

37
00:02:45,430 --> 00:02:50,459
Rather than try to compete with department
stores in city centers, IKEA has always preferred

38
00:02:50,459 --> 00:02:55,560
large multi-story buildings away from the
bustle, with only a few exceptions like in

39
00:02:55,560 --> 00:02:57,360
cramped Hong Kong.

40
00:02:57,360 --> 00:03:02,940
With this far cheaper real estate, the company
can build equally giant attached parking lots.

41
00:03:02,940 --> 00:03:09,800
The average size of a store is around 35,000
square meters or 370,000 square feet, with

42
00:03:09,800 --> 00:03:12,290
over 8,000 unique items.

43
00:03:12,290 --> 00:03:16,480
Inside, the experience is unlike any other.

44
00:03:16,480 --> 00:03:21,340
Customers are guided through the store by
a one-way path, which begins in the showroom,

45
00:03:21,340 --> 00:03:25,959
flows into the “Market Hall” where small
items can be picked up instantly, and ends

46
00:03:25,959 --> 00:03:30,400
in the warehouse, where previously selected
items can be picked off the shelves and then

47
00:03:30,400 --> 00:03:32,989
paid for at the register.

48
00:03:32,989 --> 00:03:38,209
Most retailers design their stores to maximize
the time you spend inside, spreading out staples

49
00:03:38,209 --> 00:03:40,570
like bread, milk, and bananas.

50
00:03:40,570 --> 00:03:43,900
IKEA takes this approach to the extreme.

51
00:03:43,900 --> 00:03:48,430
By arranging its stores like a transit line,
the company has total control over the shopping

52
00:03:48,430 --> 00:03:52,700
experience and forces you to look through
all its departments.

53
00:03:52,700 --> 00:03:57,030
Placed toward the beginning of the journey
are usually its largest drivers of profit:

54
00:03:57,030 --> 00:03:58,810
bedroom and kitchen.

55
00:03:58,810 --> 00:04:04,299
The restaurant and kids’ play area not only
keep customers inside longer but also communicate

56
00:04:04,299 --> 00:04:09,220
low prices and value, which spill over onto
the brand, as a whole.

57
00:04:09,220 --> 00:04:14,630
The average visit lasts a whole hour and a
half at many of its stores, and, by one estimate,

58
00:04:14,630 --> 00:04:18,209
60% of items purchased at IKEA are unplanned.

59
00:04:18,209 --> 00:04:21,750
Nudged towards, in other words, by the store
psychology.

60
00:04:21,750 --> 00:04:27,030
Research also suggests we attach more value
to things we help make ourselves - turning

61
00:04:27,030 --> 00:04:30,530
IKEA’s self-assembly from a flaw to a feature.

62
00:04:30,530 --> 00:04:37,040
It also helps reduce manufacturing and shipping
costs - another ingredient in the IKEA formula.

63
00:04:37,040 --> 00:04:42,620
Low prices are its self-proclaimed mission
- to, quote, “Democratize furniture”.

64
00:04:42,620 --> 00:04:48,070
Whatever its true motivation, IKEA has remained
inexpensive despite its ubiquity.

65
00:04:48,070 --> 00:04:53,479
The price of its most popular chair, for example,
has gone down dramatically over time, adjusted

66
00:04:53,479 --> 00:04:54,970
for inflation.

67

The company reportedly sets a target price
for a product before sending it off to its

68
00:04:59,270 --> 00:05:03,670
small team of around 20 designers, who work
within those constraints.

69
00:05:03,670 --> 00:05:08,830
Finally, the warehouse design eliminates the
need for a large staff, which greatly reduces

70
00:05:08,830 --> 00:05:10,850
operating expenses.

71
00:05:10,850 --> 00:05:16,539
This low-cost image is so important that,
before he died in 2018, the founder and CEO

72
00:05:16,539 --> 00:05:22,039
claimed only to fly economy, never stay in

73
00:05:22,039 --> 00:05:24,250
true to the company’s values.

only 50, and 17 countries or territories have

00:06:31,330 --> 00:06:36,610

00:06:36,610 --> 00:06:42,330

Its bright blue and yellow stores announce

But since colors can't be patented,

19

nothing stops other with the same idea.

20

A number of countries
that aspire to join the EU

21
00:01:09,250 --> 00:01:11,510
have changed their
passports to burgundy too.

22
00:01:13,670 --> 00:01:17,880
Meanwhile, Britain has
decided to leave the club.

23
00:01:17,880 --> 00:01:21,080
Its government has announced
that the UK passports

24
00:01:21,080 --> 00:01:24,000
will revert back to
navy blue after Brexit.

25

If you have a passport from

you're in position of

Having to get a visa is a hassle.

But there are unexpected upsides

47

Middle-ranking Namibia is one

49
00:02:51,640 --> 00:02:54,440

50
00:02:55,750 --> 00:02:58,490
India is one of only three countries

51
00:02:58,490 --> 00:03:01,160
whose citizens have
visa-free access into Bhutan.

52
00:03:03,068 --> 00:03:06,240
A low-ranking passport
limits your choices,

53
00:03:06,240 --> 00:03:08,430
but not your sense of adventure.

00:00:37,230 --> 00:00:43,170

bit more and yet make a lot more money.

11
00:00:43,170 --> 00:00:48,420

00:00:48,420 --> 00:00:56,629

00:01:21,990 --> 00:01:22,990
Every part of an attack is a fascinating lesson

00:01:22,990 --> 00:01:30,360
And with profit margins of over 30%, even

21
00:01:30,360 --> 00:01:35,740

22
00:01:35,740 --> 00:01:41,420

only led to drought and famine, but also left

23
00:01:41,420 --> 00:01:44,659
the country without a unified, central government.

24
00:01:44,659 --> 00:01:50,310
To the north are the independent but unrecognized
states of Somaliland and Puntland.

25
00:01:50,310 --> 00:01:55,720
In the south, control is split between the
federal government based in the capital, Mogadishu,

26
00:01:55,720 --> 00:01:58,149
and large, terrorist factions.

27
00:01:58,149 --> 00:02:03,200
This makes building infrastructure like schools
and hospitals extremely difficult.

28
00:02:03,200 --> 00:02:08,300
Which, in turn, makes building a formal economy,

29

[Insert subtitle here]

00:02:25,830 --> 00:02:33,040

00:02:33,040 --> 00:02:36,170

00:02:59,810 --> 00:03:05,720
Those that survived are now caught illegally

42
00:03:05,720 --> 00:03:10,640

have nearly zero healthcare, and a per capita

$104, or twenty-eight cents, per person, per

00:03:28,120 --> 00:03:35,440
The average ransom, on the other hand, is

It all begins by identifying a target.

49
00:03:39,340 --> 00:03:44,390
The ideal victim comes from a rich country,
is traveling slowly, and near the coast.

50
00:03:44,390 --> 00:03:51,560
Or, in the case of luxury cruise ship Star

51
00:03:51,560 --> 00:03:53,620
The next step is financing.

52
00:03:53,620 --> 00:04:00,840
A single attack may cost $30,000 up-front,
which is already a lot, but especially in

53
00:04:00,840 --> 00:04:01,840

54
00:04:01,840 --> 00:04:07,291
So the risk is usually spread between 3-5

00:04:07,291 --> 00:04:08,400

56
00:04:08,400 --> 00:04:10,330
Now comes the attack.

57
00:04:10,330 --> 00:04:16,359
With one, large mother ship, anywhere between

00:04:16,359 --> 00:04:18,680

59
00:04:18,680 --> 00:04:23,680
Once they get close, they switch to one or
two small chaser boats, and use rope and ladders

60
00:04:23,680 --> 00:04:24,680

61
00:04:24,680 --> 00:04:30,030
Of course, the crew is trying to speed up,
or change directions, and fight back, but

62
00:04:30,030 --> 00:04:35,800

00:04:46,099 --> 00:04:51,860
In areas like South East Asia, the goal is
often stealing oil, selling it to anyone smart

67
00:04:51,860 --> 00:04:54,770
enough not to ask why it’s so cheap.

68
00:04:54,770 --> 00:04:58,789
But here, in Somalia, pirates rarely touch
the cargo.

69
00:04:58,789 --> 00:05:03,009
The crew is, by far, the most valuable thing
on board.

70
00:05:03,009 --> 00:05:08,830
They steer the ship to a nearby port, where
the most tense part of the operation begins.

71
00:05:08,830 --> 00:05:14,080
With only one buyer and one seller, almost
none of the rules of a normal negotiation

72
00:05:14,080 --> 00:05:15,229
apply.

73
00:05:15,229 --> 00:05:20,530
Neither party has all the information and
both have great incentive to lie.

74
00:05:20,530 --> 00:05:24,780
The owner of the ship wants to appear poor,
driving down the ransom.

75
00:05:24,780 --> 00:05:29,340
The pirates, meanwhile, need to seem rash
enough to deliver on their threats and yet

76
00:05:29,340 --> 00:05:31,879
patient enough to wait for a deal.

77
00:05:31,879 --> 00:05:33,939
Because, the clock is ticking.

78
00:05:33,939 --> 00:05:39,659
As time goes on, the value of the ship and
its cargo goes down, and the average ransom

79
00:05:39,659 --> 00:05:41,220
generally goes up.

80
00:05:41,220 --> 00:05:47,999
Talks, therefore, can last three, four, five
hundred days, all spoken through a translator,

81
00:05:47,999 --> 00:05:50,669
often with several different negotiators.

82
00:05:50,669 --> 00:05:55,860
If the owner has Kidnapping & Ransom Insurance,
negotiations are made by a professional, who

83
00:05:55,860 --> 00:06:00,000
reduces the chance of death from 9% to just
two.

84
00:06:00,000 --> 00:06:03,009
But companies aren’t allowed to say they
have insurance.

85
00:06:03,009 --> 00:06:07,819
In fact, many corporate travelers don’t
know they have K&R insurance.

86
00:06:07,819 --> 00:06:10,370
If they did, it would be invalidated.

87
00:06:10,370 --> 00:06:14,779
Because of the incentives, an agreement is
almost always reached.

88
00:06:14,779 --> 00:06:18,529
Pirates bring the crew up to the top deck,
confirming their safety.

89
00:06:18,529 --> 00:06:24,599
And then, a helicopter flies overhead and
drops a waterproof container full of cash.

90
00:06:24,599 --> 00:06:27,810
Finally, comes a pirate’s favorite job:
accounting.

91
00:06:27,810 --> 00:06:32,520
First, investors get their guaranteed cut
of at least 30%,

92
00:06:32,520 --> 00:06:36,930
The port, who looked the other way while they
parked the ship, gets 5-10%.

93
00:06:36,930 --> 00:06:43,080
And the rest is split between the attackers,
with a bonus of around $10,000 for being first

94
00:06:43,080 --> 00:06:44,279
to board the ship.

95
00:06:44,279 --> 00:06:49,340
This scenario plays out hundreds of times
a year, and costs shipping companies a total

96
00:06:49,340 --> 00:06:56,039
of 4.9 to $8.3 billion a year - including
security and insurance.

97
00:06:56,039 --> 00:07:03,289
Even just speeding up from 13 to 18 knots
costs an extra $88,000 in fuel, per ship,

98
00:07:03,289 --> 00:07:04,410
per day.

99
00:07:04,410 --> 00:07:07,249
And those costs are passed on to you and me.

100
00:07:07,249 --> 00:07:09,889
We all pay a hidden “piracy tax”.

101
00:07:09,889 --> 00:07:11,849
So, what can be done?

102
00:07:11,849 --> 00:07:14,710
The obvious answer is fighting back.

103
00:07:14,710 --> 00:07:21,759
NATO’s Operation Ocean Shield greatly reduced
attacks from 2009 to 16 by patrolling dangerous

104
00:07:21,759 --> 00:07:22,759
waters.

105
00:07:22,759 --> 00:07:27,290
And any shippers now hire private security
companies to fill that role.

106
00:07:27,290 --> 00:07:32,340
But this creates a free rider problem, other
companies and countries benefit from that

107
00:07:32,340 --> 00:07:35,389
security without paying for it themselves.

108
00:07:35,389 --> 00:07:40,909
Likewise, everyone would be better off if
no one paid ransoms, but it’s always in

109
00:07:40,909 --> 00:07:43,639
each company’s best interest to pay them.

110
00:07:43,639 --> 00:07:48,099
All of these solutions reduce piracy, but
none of them solve it.

111
00:07:48,099 --> 00:07:55,449
For 30 - $75,000 per attack, there will always
be someone willing to take that risk, no matter

112
00:07:55,449 --> 00:07:57,550
how high it becomes.

113
00:07:57,550 --> 00:08:03,319
The only real solution is economic, giving
pirates alternative ways to make money.

114
00:08:03,319 --> 00:08:09,259
Rebuilding a country like Somalia is a major
undertaking, but giving locals new skills

115
00:08:09,259 --> 00:08:13,900

solution.

big shifts that's happened in the economy

that is lead in part to a decline in union membership.

7
00:00:32,880 --> 00:00:38,160
But one if the biggest drivers of inequality is hiding here, in these 2,000 pages.

8
00:00:38,160 --> 00:00:39,900
It's the US tax code.

9
00:00:39,900 --> 00:00:44,160
President Trump and Republicans in Congress have a plan to alter that code.

10
00:00:44,160 --> 00:00:48,780
and if they get their way it'll get even better for the richest Americans.

11
00:00:51,700 --> 00:00:54,360
First let's look at a few things that Trump and the Republicans

12
00:00:54,360 --> 00:00:56,780
don't want to change about the tax code.

13
00:00:56,780 --> 00:01:00,080
the charitable deduction and 
the mortgage interest deduction.

14
00:01:00,080 --> 00:01:02,160
Here's how they favor the rich:

15
00:01:02,160 --> 00:01:07,680
Let's say Dan makes $100 donation to his church. 
He makes about $30,000 a year.

16
00:01:07,680 --> 00:01:10,840
Roughly, the median income for individuals in the US.

17
00:01:10,840 --> 00:01:13,780
[Insert subtitle here]

18
00:01:13,780 --> 00:01:17,940
[Insert subtitle here]

19
00:01:17,940 --> 00:01:23,100
But let's say Dan's boss Steve makes the same donation to his church.

20
00:01:23,100 --> 00:01:27,960
Steve makes $500,000 a year which puts him in the top tax bracket.

21
00:01:27,960 --> 00:01:34,140
And the same $100 donation could save Steve $39.60 on his taxes.

22
00:01:34,140 --> 00:01:37,040
Dan and Steve give the same amount to their church

23
00:01:37,040 --> 00:01:39,620
but Steve saves more than twice as much.

24
00:01:43,500 --> 00:01:45,500
Small examples like this add up.

25
00:01:45,500 --> 00:01:52,040
People making $100,000 or more account for about 57% of all the charitable contributions in the US

26
00:01:52,040 --> 00:01:55,480
but they get 76% of the tax benefits.

27
00:01:55,480 --> 00:01:57,820
This deduction is also really expensive.

28
00:01:57,820 --> 00:02:01,180
The US spends $70,000,000,000 a year on it.

29
00:02:01,180 --> 00:02:05,580
More than eight times what it spends on Head Start the federally funded preschool program

30
00:02:05,580 --> 00:02:09,920
and more than twice what it spends on Pell grants for low-income students to go to college.

31
00:02:09,920 --> 00:02:12,380
Plus there's all kinds of ways to bend the rules.

32
00:02:12,380 --> 00:02:16,460
Billionaire Mitchell Rales gets tax break for donating his collection of modern art

33
00:02:16,460 --> 00:02:20,400
to a museum that he built right next door to his house.

34
00:02:20,400 --> 00:02:22,940
A museum that's only open for private tours.

35
00:02:22,960 --> 00:02:24,900
But the worst thing about about the charitable deduction?

36
00:02:24,900 --> 00:02:27,820
There's not great evidence that it works.

37
00:02:27,820 --> 00:02:32,520
Turns out you don't need a tax break to
encourage people to be generous to others.

38
00:02:32,520 --> 00:02:38,070
In the 1980's the top tax rate
for the richest people was 70%

39
00:02:38,070 --> 00:02:40,520
and through a series of reforms it dropped to 28%

40
00:02:40,520 --> 00:02:44,780
and the Council on Foundations, it's kind of a trade group for charities,

41
00:02:44,780 --> 00:02:48,660
said, 'Oh my God, you do that we're going to lose all our contributions.'

42
00:02:48,660 --> 00:02:54,800
Guess what? No difference. People gave just as much with a much lower tax rate.

43
00:02:54,860 --> 00:02:59,020
Austria, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland, and New Zealand

44
00:02:59,020 --> 00:03:01,920
have all gotten rid of their deductions for charitable contributions

45
00:03:01,920 --> 00:03:04,760
and that hasn't had an impact on
donation rates.

46
00:03:04,760 --> 00:03:06,980
One easy way to make things more fair?

47
00:03:06,980 --> 00:03:09,640
Replace the tax deduction with a tax credit.

48
00:03:09,640 --> 00:03:12,580
If Dan and Steve both give $100 to their church,

49
00:03:12,580 --> 00:03:15,400
give them each a $15 tax credit.

50
00:03:15,400 --> 00:03:17,160
That's how they do it in Canada.

51
00:03:17,160 --> 00:03:22,240
A tax credit reduces the amount you owe, so the same donation gets the same benefit

52
00:03:22,240 --> 00:03:23,920
no matter how rich you are.

53
00:03:24,460 --> 00:03:27,720
There's another tax deduction that's a boon for the wealthy.

54
00:03:27,720 --> 00:03:33,020
The mortgage interest deduction costs about $100,000,000,000 a year to the Treasury.

55
00:03:33,020 --> 00:03:37,880
We could use that money to treat wounded veterans, to build hospitals, to build highways

56
00:03:37,880 --> 00:03:40,520
but instead we give it to rich homeowners.

57
00:03:40,520 --> 00:03:41,780
Here's how it works:

58
00:03:41,780 --> 00:03:46,440
Let's say Dan buys a house for $100,000.
He doesn't pay for that all at once.

59
00:03:46,440 --> 00:03:49,520
Each month he writes a check to the bank for $1,000.

60
00:03:49,520 --> 00:03:52,000
Let's say $800 goes to paying for the house,

61
00:03:52,000 --> 00:03:54,540
and the bank keeps $200. That's interest!

62
00:03:54,560 --> 00:03:59,632
Dan writes twelve of these checks a year, so he pays $2,400 a year in interest.

63
00:03:59,640 --> 00:04:04,780
The mortgage interest deduction let's Dan subtract that interest from his taxable income

64
00:04:04,780 --> 00:04:08,520
which could save him as much as $362.

65
00:04:08,520 --> 00:04:12,820
"Nice," thinks Dan, that is until he hears about Steve.

66
00:04:12,820 --> 00:04:15,820
Steve also buys a house for $100,000.

67
00:04:15,820 --> 00:04:20,100
He also writes a $1,000 check each month paying $200 in interest.

68
00:04:20,100 --> 00:04:25,680
So after a year, Steve can also deduct the $2,400 from his taxable income.

69
00:04:25,680 --> 00:04:30,340
But that same deduction can save Steve more than $960.

70
00:04:30,340 --> 00:04:35,220
Nearly three times as much as Dan for the exact same mortgage payments.

71
00:04:35,220 --> 00:04:40,300
It doesn't stop there. Steve can buy a second home, deduct the interest, and save even more.

72
00:04:40,300 --> 00:04:45,840
Or he can get a mortgage for his yacht, count it as a second home, and deduct the interest.

73
00:04:45,840 --> 00:04:48,720
Sorry Dan, your fishing boat doesn't count.

74
00:04:48,720 --> 00:04:50,740
There are deductions everywhere.

75
00:04:50,740 --> 00:04:53,480
The money you lose from gambling? Deduct it.

76
00:04:53,480 --> 00:04:55,340
Fancy business dinners? Yep.

77
00:04:55,340 --> 00:04:58,340
Money you put in a retirement account? That too.

78
00:04:58,340 --> 00:05:03,660
You can even deduct the fees you pay an accountant to help you find more deductions.

79
00:05:03,660 --> 00:05:07,780
And while theoretically Dan could take advantage of these same deductions

80
00:05:07,780 --> 00:05:11,300
the fact is, people like Steve benefit a whole lot more.

81
00:05:11,300 --> 00:05:16,700
People who make about $400,000 a year or more make up about 5% of taxpayers

82
00:05:16,700 --> 00:05:20,600
but they get more than half the benefits from these tax deductions.

83
00:05:20,600 --> 00:05:25,140
Now there's a third part of the tax code that Trump and the Republicans want to keep

84
00:05:25,140 --> 00:05:29,720
and it's even better for the richest Americans than all of these deductions

85
00:05:29,720 --> 00:05:33,640
The preferred rate for capital gains. Here's how it works:

86
00:05:33,640 --> 00:05:37,080
According to the US tax code, there are two different kinds of income.

87
00:05:37,080 --> 00:05:41,900
Earned income is when you go to work and somebody pays you a salary or wage a paycheck.

88
00:05:41,900 --> 00:05:49,020
That's earned income and we have a whole set of income tax rates for that income that go up to 39.6%.

89
00:05:49,020 --> 00:05:51,720
This is where Dan and Steve's tax rates come from.

90
00:05:51,720 --> 00:05:54,560
Unearned income means guys who trade paper.

91
00:05:54,560 --> 00:05:58,800
Guys who sell stock or buy commodities and then sell it.

92
00:05:58,800 --> 00:06:01,620
Invest in real estate properties and then sell them.

93
00:06:01,620 --> 00:06:05,420
That's capital income and we tax that at a lower rate.

94
00:06:05,420 --> 00:06:09,020
Let's say Steve earns $500,000 a year as a surgeon

95
00:06:09,020 --> 00:06:12,440
and Laurie earns the same amount as a hedge fund manager.

96
00:06:12,440 --> 00:06:17,100
Even though their income is the same, Steve's tax rate is 39.6%

97
00:06:17,100 --> 00:06:21,380
but Laurie's tax rate is nearly half that, 23.8%.

98
00:06:21,380 --> 00:06:24,880
So Steve ends up with a much higher tax bill.

99
00:06:24,880 --> 00:06:29,500
This is why billionaire investor Warren Buffet pays a lower tax rate than his secretary.

100
00:06:29,500 --> 00:06:33,160
His money comes from capital gains while hers comes from a salary.

101
00:06:33,160 --> 00:06:38,100
Debbie works just as hard as I do and she pays at twice the rate I pay.

102
00:06:38,100 --> 00:06:40,400
Ronald Reagan thought the same thing.

103
00:06:40,400 --> 00:06:44,200
Reagan had been a very high, high bracket taxpayer.

104

In fact, he paid at the 90% rate in the 1950s. He was a movie star.

105
00:06:48,280 --> 00:06:52,920
His accountant kept telling him well sign these documents and that'll shift your income

106
00:06:52,920 --> 00:06:56,940
from labor to capital income and Reagan saw that that was hokey.

107
00:06:56,940 --> 00:06:59,030
Why should that be?

108
00:06:59,030 --> 00:07:06,040
Reagan's landmark 1986 tax bill tax capital income and labor income at the same rate.

109
00:07:17,480 --> 00:07:21,960
People said, "Oh my God, you can't do that. Then nobody will invest. Investments will plummet."

110

This chart shows the value of the S&P 500, a stock market metric that measures

111

how well big businesses are doing.

112
00:07:29,760 --> 00:07:35,060
After Reagan raised the capital gains rate in 1986, businesses continued to prosper.

113
00:07:35,060 --> 00:07:41,180
Reagan's successors, George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton also raise taxes and the on the wealthiest Americans.

114
00:07:41,180 --> 00:07:46,620
And the 1990s saw America's longest period of consecutive economic growth ever.

115
00:07:46,620 --> 00:07:49,360
But the changes that Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress

116
00:07:49,360 --> 00:07:52,260
want to make to the tax code look very different.

117
00:07:52,280 --> 00:07:55,820
While the Trump and GOP plans get rid of some deductions

118
00:07:55,820 --> 00:08:00,120
neither gets rid of the charitable
contribution or mortgage interest deductions

119
00:08:00,120 --> 00:08:05,280
Both plans would lower taxes on capital income for people like Laurie the hedge fund manager.

120
00:08:05,280 --> 00:08:09,200
And both plans would reduce the number of tax brackets from seven to three.

121
00:08:09,200 --> 00:08:13,760
and cut the top tax rate. Which would mean big tax savings for someone like Steve

122
00:08:13,760 --> 00:08:17,440
and minimal savings for working and middle-class people like Dan.

123
00:08:17,440 --> 00:08:22,080
Rather than working to reduce the growing gap between the richest Americans and everyone else

124
00:08:22,080 --> 00:08:26,120
these new tax plans would make that gap even wider.

Or ask friends about it.

8
00:00:18,380 --> 00:00:21,580
But all of these seem so imprecise.

9
00:00:21,580 --> 00:00:24,820
Plus, it's kind of weird to
visit dozens of playgrounds.

10
00:00:25,240 --> 00:00:28,720
So, these days, you would probably Google the school.

11
00:00:28,720 --> 00:00:31,620
And you'll almost certainly end up on this website:

12
00:00:31,620 --> 00:00:37,080
GreatSchools.org.
GreatSchools is a nonprofit school ratings website.

13
00:00:37,080 --> 00:00:40,600
They provide a number rating for almost every public school in America.

14
00:00:40,600 --> 00:00:44,480
The worst schools are a 1, and
the best schools are a 10.

15
00:00:44,480 --> 00:00:49,800
There are other websites and organizations that rate schools, but GreatSchools is the big one.

16
00:00:55,760 --> 00:00:58,420
Well, we dug into the data to find out.

17
00:00:58,420 --> 00:01:06,440
And what we found, is that this score often ends up showing something other than how good a school is.

18
00:01:09,240 --> 00:01:11,500
GreatSchools started in the late 1990s.

19
00:01:11,500 --> 00:01:16,220
They visited schools around the San Francisco Bay Area, and talked to each school's principal.

20
00:01:16,220 --> 00:01:19,560
But that method of profiling schools wasn't exactly scalable.

21
00:01:19,560 --> 00:01:21,780
They couldn't go visit every single school in the country.

22
00:01:21,780 --> 00:01:24,740
That would be prohibitively expensive; it was hard enough as it was.

23
00:01:24,740 --> 00:01:28,440
Matt Barnum is a reporter at Chalkbeat, a site that covers education.

24
00:01:28,440 --> 00:01:29,720
He helped us report
this story.

25
00:01:29,720 --> 00:01:32,800
Going to every single school was just not a sustainable model.

26
00:01:32,800 --> 00:01:37,060
Then, in 2001, something huge happened for GreatSchools.

27
00:01:37,060 --> 00:01:40,660
Congress passed a national
education law called "No Child Left Behind."

28
00:01:40,660 --> 00:01:44,500
No Child Left Behind required
schools to give state standardized tests,

29
00:01:44,500 --> 00:01:47,280
each year, in grades three through eight, to figure out how many of them

30
00:01:47,280 --> 00:01:50,420
met a standard called "proficiency."

31
00:01:50,420 --> 00:01:54,920
"Proficiency" is basically each US state's standard for what kids should know at a certain grade level.

32
00:01:55,000 --> 00:01:59,600
So that gave them a lot of data to rate schools all across the country.

33
00:01:59,600 --> 00:02:04,000
After No Child Left Behind, GreatSchools had the numbers they could base their scores on.

34
00:02:04,000 --> 00:02:07,660
Today, they say this proficiency score is the biggest factor

35
00:02:07,660 --> 00:02:12,840
in the ratings it gives each elementary and middle school; accounting for about half the score.

36
00:02:12,840 --> 00:02:17,840
But when we start looking at GreatSchools' data, we notice something.

37
00:02:17,840 --> 00:02:22,500
Here are basically all the public elementary and middle schools in Denver and a few of its suburbs.

38
00:02:22,500 --> 00:02:25,660
With the help of journalists at Chalkbeat, we sorted them by the percentage of

39
00:02:25,660 --> 00:02:28,000
low-income students in each school.

40
00:02:28,000 --> 00:02:29,620
These schools have more low-income students,

41
00:02:29,620 --> 00:02:31,600
and these schools have fewer.

42
00:02:31,600 --> 00:02:38,080
Now, let's highlight the schools that got a GreatSchools rating of at least a 7, which is what they consider above average.

43
00:02:38,080 --> 00:02:41,820
You can see that almost all of these better-rated schools are more affluent.

44
00:02:41,820 --> 00:02:48,980
And this is true in basically every city from San Francisco to Detroit.

45
00:02:48,980 --> 00:02:53,640
And this correlation also appears when
we sort these schools by racial demographics.

[Insert subtitle here]

of 7 or above?

49
00:03:02,880 --> 00:03:07,820
It's schools with more white and Asian kids, who tend to come from more affluent neighborhoods.

50
00:03:07,820 --> 00:03:12,200
GreatSchools' ratings seem to confirm
something that many people already assume:

51
00:03:16,920 --> 00:03:20,560
Here's the problem: That's not necessarily true.

52
00:03:20,560 --> 00:03:24,920
And to understand why, we need to look at one of the big issues with measuring proficiency.

53
00:03:24,920 --> 00:03:27,320
America's neighborhoods are highly unequal.

54
00:03:27,320 --> 00:03:29,660
And when children show up
to school in affluent neighborhoods,

55
00:03:29,660 --> 00:03:32,990
that are mostly white and Asian, they're
better-prepared for school

56
00:03:32,990 --> 00:03:36,040
than children in poor, mostly black and Hispanic areas.

57
00:03:36,220 --> 00:03:41,740
So when we look at proficiency, we're actually often measuring how prepared these kids were coming in.

58
00:03:41,740 --> 00:03:45,000
Not what happens inside the school.

59
00:03:45,000 --> 00:03:48,180
So, if proficiency is more about measuring the student than the school,

60
00:03:48,180 --> 00:03:51,160
how could we
actually measure the school's performance?

61
00:03:51,160 --> 00:03:56,700
Well, another common way of measuring schools is to see how much a school helps a student improve.

62
00:03:56,700 --> 00:03:58,600
This is called a "growth score."

63
00:03:58,600 --> 00:04:02,880
Now, Growth is still just based on test scores, which not everyone is a fan of.

64
00:04:02,880 --> 00:04:06,160
But it's how many schools
prefer we measure them.

65
00:04:06,160 --> 00:04:09,640
The principals I talked to felt that it was more fair to judge them on growth.

66
00:04:09,640 --> 00:04:13,760
If you're a school that is serving a lot of students who
are coming in at a low level, you could

67
00:04:13,760 --> 00:04:18,260
be doing a great job with those students,
but it might not be showing up in proficiency.

68
00:04:18,280 --> 00:04:23,400
Not all states report growth scores, which is a problem in itself. But most do.

69
00:04:23,400 --> 00:04:27,540
And growth scores show that there are many low-income schools that are pretty good.

70
00:04:27,540 --> 00:04:29,260
Here's every Denver school again.

71
00:04:29,260 --> 00:04:32,400
And again, sorted by the percentage of low-income students.

72
00:04:32,400 --> 00:04:36,100
And now, if we highlight the schools that have an above-average growth score,

73
00:04:36,100 --> 00:04:38,858
which is data we got from GreatSchools' own website,

74
00:04:38,860 --> 00:04:43,700
we can see that there are lots of schools in poor neighborhoods that are very good at educating their students.

75
00:04:43,700 --> 00:04:48,640
And this is true in other cities, too: Like
Indianapolis...

76
00:04:48,640 --> 00:04:50,320
and Detroit.

77
00:04:50,320 --> 00:04:55,520
But in the GreatSchools rating system, growth only matters about half as much as proficiency does.

78
00:04:55,520 --> 00:04:59,060
Which is why these schools are rarely rated highly,

79
00:04:59,060 --> 00:05:02,900
even if they do a great job teaching students.

80
00:05:02,900 --> 00:05:05,220
We talked to GreatSchools. They said the important thing

81
00:05:05,220 --> 00:05:08,340
is that they give parents a "broader picture of school quality,"

82
00:05:08,340 --> 00:05:12,100
and that their site
helps "underserved families" make good choices.

83
00:05:12,100 --> 00:05:14,380
They also stressed that they've
actually changed the rating system to

84
00:05:14,400 --> 00:05:17,505
start considering growth, alongside
proficiency.

85
00:05:17,505 --> 00:05:19,640
And the data reflects this. But:

86
00:05:19,640 --> 00:05:22,500
There's still this really stark
correlation with race and class of

87
00:05:22,500 --> 00:05:25,640
students, but it is lower than what it
was before.

88
00:05:25,640 --> 00:05:29,820
That's not entirely their fault. Not every state reports growth scores.

89
00:05:29,820 --> 00:05:35,140
But even where growth scores are available, GreatSchools still weights proficiency a lot more.

90
00:05:35,140 --> 00:05:39,720
And that muddles the difference between two definitions of "good" schools:

91
00:05:39,720 --> 00:05:42,680
The ones that do the best job teaching students,

92
00:05:42,680 --> 00:05:45,520
and the ones that get kids who are already high-achieving,

93
00:05:45,520 --> 00:05:48,020
who tend to be from white and
affluent families.

94
00:05:48,020 --> 00:05:50,660
So maybe, the real question is:

95
00:05:50,660 --> 00:05:55,880
Which one do parents actually want?

1

- How polarizing is Donald Trump?

Richard Nixon may come to mind,

4

or maybe George W. Bush or Barack Obama.

5

But no president in
the modern polling era,

6
00:00:14,040 --> 00:00:16,070
dating back to the 1950s,

7
00:00:16,070 --> 00:00:18,910
has had a larger partisan gap
in his job approval ratings

8
00:00:18,910 --> 00:00:20,010
than Donald Trump.

9
00:00:20,010 --> 00:00:21,370
The approval gap is one measure

10
00:00:21,370 --> 00:00:23,700
how politically divided Americans are,

11
00:00:23,700 --> 00:00:25,400
but it's not the only one.

12
00:00:25,400 --> 00:00:28,140
And the public's growing
partisan polarization

13
00:00:28,140 --> 00:00:31,420
was evident long before Trump took office.

14
00:00:31,420 --> 00:00:35,040
Flashback to the mid-1990s when
Bill Clinton was president.

15
00:00:35,040 --> 00:00:37,830
Republicans and Democrats
disagreed over many things,

16
00:00:37,830 --> 00:00:40,510
including healthcare and foreign policy,

17
00:00:40,510 --> 00:00:42,420
but on average, opinion differences

18
00:00:42,420 --> 00:00:44,200
between Republicans and Democrats

19
00:00:44,200 --> 00:00:47,470
were no larger than differences
between men and women,

20
00:00:47,470 --> 00:00:50,410
blacks and whites, or
those of other groups.

21
00:00:50,410 --> 00:00:53,810
Today, the partisan gap dwarfs
any of these other measures,

22
00:00:53,810 --> 00:00:56,093
and it's more than doubled since 1994.

23
00:00:57,630 --> 00:00:59,060
Look at the trajectory of attitudes

24
00:00:59,060 --> 00:01:01,790
on just a single issue: immigration.

25
00:01:01,790 --> 00:01:04,120
[Insert subtitle here]

26
00:01:04,120 --> 00:01:06,080
[Insert subtitle here]

27
00:01:06,080 --> 00:01:08,020
The dominant view in both parties was that

28
00:01:08,020 --> 00:01:11,233
immigrants did more to burden
than strengthen the country.

29
00:01:12,080 --> 00:01:14,810
But today, partisans are far apart.

30
00:01:14,810 --> 00:01:16,330
The vast majority of Democrats

31
00:01:16,330 --> 00:01:19,140
say immigrants do more to
strengthen the country,

32
00:01:19,140 --> 00:01:22,080
while Republicans remain
skeptical about the contributions

33
00:01:22,080 --> 00:01:23,553
immigrants make to the U.S.

34
00:01:24,549 --> 00:01:26,710
Partisan polarization encompasses

35
00:01:26,710 --> 00:01:28,160
more than just disagreements

36
00:01:28,160 --> 00:01:30,501
over policies and political values.

37
00:01:30,501 --> 00:01:33,160
Think for a minute: what type of community

38
00:01:33,160 --> 00:01:35,120
would you prefer to live in?

39
00:01:35,120 --> 00:01:37,140
Republicans express a strong preference

40
00:01:37,140 --> 00:01:41,210
for big houses and widely
spaced, drivable communities.

41
00:01:41,210 --> 00:01:43,940
Democrats for the most part
say they want a smaller house

42
00:01:43,940 --> 00:01:45,830
closer to amenities such as schools,

43
00:01:45,830 --> 00:01:47,363
stores and restaurants.

44
00:01:48,850 --> 00:01:50,900
Differences between
Republicans and Democrats

45
00:01:50,900 --> 00:01:53,700
now extend to issues
which you may not expect

46
00:01:53,700 --> 00:01:55,320
to be all that partisan,

47
00:01:55,320 --> 00:01:57,840
like views of the national economy.

48
00:01:57,840 --> 00:02:00,240
Throughout the 1990s there
wasn't much difference

49
00:02:00,240 --> 00:02:03,750
in how Republicans and Democrats
rated economic conditions,

50
00:02:03,750 --> 00:02:07,050
but since the early 2000s
- and especially today -

51
00:02:07,050 --> 00:02:09,313
the economy is viewed
through a partisan lens.

52
00:02:10,500 --> 00:02:11,990
We should keep this history in mind

53
00:02:11,990 --> 00:02:13,880
when thinking about Trump's presidency

54
00:02:13,880 --> 00:02:15,570
since we've been polarized for a while.

55
00:02:15,570 --> 00:02:18,940
But Trump may have distilled
our differences even further.

56
00:02:18,940 --> 00:02:20,120
While debates over issues

57
00:02:20,120 --> 00:02:22,458
from taxes to immigration continue,

58
00:02:22,458 --> 00:02:24,780
one of the most powerful expressions

59
00:02:24,780 --> 00:02:27,500
of the nation's deep
political divisions today

60
00:02:27,500 --> 00:02:30,343
is the public's opinion
of one man - Donald Trump.

Nothing is more frustrating than a paywall

cough

Long ago, deepwater navigation freed merchants

00:01:09,670 --> 00:01:15,500
buy, Now, they had access to the world’s

00:01:19,230 --> 00:01:25,130

22

23
00:01:26,659 --> 00:01:32,270
But when there are no barriers to entry, supply

24

25
00:01:33,729 --> 00:01:35,340

26
00:01:35,340 --> 00:01:38,810
Nobody wants to pay for music or news or apps,

27
00:01:38,810 --> 00:01:43,140
And yet musicians, and writers, and developers
need to get paid.

28
00:01:43,140 --> 00:01:48,120
The question is how, preferably in a way that
doesn’t suck.

29
00:01:48,120 --> 00:01:52,990
Spotify, Netflix, the New York Times, and

30
00:01:52,990 --> 00:01:54,020

31
00:01:54,020 --> 00:01:55,720
Some of which are thriving.

32
00:01:55,720 --> 00:01:59,060
Others, you might be surprised to learn, are
failing.

33
00:01:59,060 --> 00:02:05,100
So, what works?
and, maybe more importantly, what doesn’t?

34
00:02:05,100 --> 00:02:08,239
The iTunes music store opened in 2003.

35
00:02:08,239 --> 00:02:10,390
The App Store, in 2008.

36
00:02:10,390 --> 00:02:13,629
In other words, the music industry has a head
start.

37
00:02:13,629 --> 00:02:19,290
This graph of music revenue over time, adjusted
for inflation, tells the story pretty well.

38
00:02:19,290 --> 00:02:23,640
Earnings peaked in 1999, and they’ve been

39
00:02:23,640 --> 00:02:25,500
Like, really, really down.

40
00:02:25,500 --> 00:02:29,639
Now, I’d argue this period was somewhat
artificially high,

41
00:02:29,639 --> 00:02:34,810
If we zoom out a little, it looks more like
an anomaly, a ten-year spike in the long history

42
00:02:34,810 --> 00:02:36,659
of recorded music.

43
00:02:36,659 --> 00:02:39,389
People spent so much, because, they had to.

44
00:02:39,389 --> 00:02:44,879
Their choices were: buy music a whole album
at a time, or don’t listen at all.

45
00:02:44,879 --> 00:02:47,180
But then, the numbers just start falling.

46
00:02:47,180 --> 00:02:54,920
[Insert subtitle here]

47
00:02:54,920 --> 00:02:58,629
[Insert subtitle here] You can see this time is different.

48
00:02:58,629 --> 00:03:00,159
Nothing replaces the CD.

49
00:03:00,159 --> 00:03:01,549
At least, not immediately.

50
00:03:01,549 --> 00:03:04,349
You’d think people just stopped listening.

51
00:03:04,349 --> 00:03:07,290
Busy wondering why the world didn’t end
or something.

52
00:03:07,290 --> 00:03:12,170
But really, of course, they just stopped paying,
in favor of sites like Napster.

53
00:03:12,170 --> 00:03:15,639
iTunes tried to fight piracy by breaking up
the album.

54
00:03:15,639 --> 00:03:21,409
But nothing really changed until a Swedish
programmer, no, the other one realized something:

55
00:03:21,409 --> 00:03:24,559
“The problem with the music industry is
piracy…

56
00:03:24,559 --> 00:03:26,409
But you can’t beat technology.

57
00:03:26,409 --> 00:03:28,439
Technology always wins.

58
00:03:28,439 --> 00:03:31,689
But what if you can make a better product
than piracy?…

59
00:03:31,689 --> 00:03:36,120
It took a few minutes to download a song,
it was kind of cumbersome, you had to worry

60
00:03:36,120 --> 00:03:37,169
about viruses.

61
00:03:37,169 --> 00:03:39,870
It’s not like people want to be pirates.

62
00:03:39,870 --> 00:03:41,829
They just want a great experience.”

63
00:03:41,829 --> 00:03:44,219
And that’s how Spotify was born.

64
00:03:44,219 --> 00:03:50,669
The lesson is: Companies can fight change,
lobby for new laws, burden everyone with annoying

65
00:03:50,669 --> 00:03:56,959
restrictions, even more annoying ads, and
sue 12-year old girls for sharing songs.

66
00:03:56,959 --> 00:04:00,249
Or, they can adapt, see it as an opportunity.

67
00:04:00,249 --> 00:04:02,069
Because most of us are lazy.

68
00:04:02,069 --> 00:04:07,269
If we can pay a little more for a lot more
convenience, we usually will.

69
00:04:07,269 --> 00:04:09,290
That’s why streaming wins.

70
00:04:09,290 --> 00:04:15,620
Today, people listen to more music than ever
before - an average of 32 hours a week.

71
00:04:15,620 --> 00:04:16,739
That’s a lot.

72
00:04:16,739 --> 00:04:21,430
And revenue is actually growing, for the first
time since the 90’s.

73
00:04:21,430 --> 00:04:24,560
Now, Netflix seems to be in the same position,

74
00:04:24,560 --> 00:04:28,349
Both are $10, all-you-can-eat streaming subscriptions.

75
00:04:28,349 --> 00:04:34,020
An answer to piracy and, in this case, Blockbuster
making a killing on late fees.

76
00:04:34,020 --> 00:04:40,080
Before Netflix, the idea of letting users
watch any movie, from any device, at any time

77
00:04:40,080 --> 00:04:43,780
was… ridiculous, What if people share their
password?

78
00:04:43,780 --> 00:04:46,710
Netflix was like: Ah, good point, we should
make that easier.

79
00:04:46,710 --> 00:04:51,560
They don’t just accept it, they embrace
it, letting you make separate profiles on

80
00:04:51,560 --> 00:04:52,800
the same account.

81
00:04:52,800 --> 00:04:57,400
But then you look at money, and suddenly the
two companies couldn’t be more different.

82
00:04:57,400 --> 00:05:03,000
One has been profitable for 15 years, making
half a billion dollars last year alone.

83
00:05:03,000 --> 00:05:09,380
The other, reported almost the same number
a year earlier, except its number was… negative.

84
00:05:09,380 --> 00:05:10,389
Why is that?

85
00:05:10,389 --> 00:05:12,259
In a word: scalability.

86
00:05:12,259 --> 00:05:17,750
Spotify only takes a small cut of your $10
a month, the rest is distributed among the

87
00:05:17,750 --> 00:05:19,520
songs you listened to.

88
00:05:19,520 --> 00:05:24,710
In other words, no matter how many people
sign up, the economics never improve.

89
00:05:24,710 --> 00:05:26,590
More users, more costs.

90
00:05:26,590 --> 00:05:31,580
Netflix, on the other hand, licenses shows
for a set period of time.

91
00:05:31,580 --> 00:05:37,860
7 or 10.99 a month isn’t a lot of money,
but after they’ve paid for content, every

92
00:05:37,860 --> 00:05:40,629
additional user is pure profit.

93
00:05:40,629 --> 00:05:42,750
More users, more money.

94
00:05:42,750 --> 00:05:45,780
So why doesn’t Spotify just raise prices?

95
00:05:45,780 --> 00:05:47,670
Well, competition.

96
00:05:47,670 --> 00:05:52,330
Every company and their mother sells a music
service - just pick your favorite color.

97
00:05:52,330 --> 00:05:59,539
There’s also plenty of video sites, Netflix,
Prime, Hulu, Showtime, HBO, soon even more.

98
00:05:59,539 --> 00:06:04,220
The difference is, customers can and do pay
for several at a time.

99
00:06:04,220 --> 00:06:05,689
Music is winner-take-all.

100
00:06:05,689 --> 00:06:09,629
We expect every song to be available on every
service.

101
00:06:09,629 --> 00:06:10,960
They just... aren’t unique.

102
00:06:10,960 --> 00:06:16,729
They also can’t really take a bigger cut,
Because artists barely survive as it is.

103
00:06:16,729 --> 00:06:21,219
When Taylor Swift complains about money, you
can only imagine what it’s like for the

104
00:06:21,219 --> 00:06:22,660
average musician.

105
00:06:22,660 --> 00:06:27,509
For many, streaming is really just an ad for
their concerts, where they make almost all

106
00:06:27,509 --> 00:06:28,509
their money.

107
00:06:28,509 --> 00:06:34,099
The problem is musicians share their revenue
with producers, writers, and record labels,

108
00:06:34,099 --> 00:06:38,910
Just three of which: Sony, Universal, and
Warner, control most of the industry.

109
00:06:38,910 --> 00:06:44,170
Spotify, for example, pays between six and
eight-tenths of a penny per stream.

110
00:06:44,170 --> 00:06:49,330
But after everyone takes their cut, artists
are left with just over an estimated 1 tenth

111
00:06:49,330 --> 00:06:50,330
of a penny.

112
00:06:50,330 --> 00:06:55,740
So, here’s my prediction: Sites like Netflix
will focus almost entirely on exclusives - the

113
00:06:55,740 --> 00:06:59,659
Stranger Things and the West Worlds that make
their service unique.

114
00:06:59,659 --> 00:07:02,689
There won’t just be one winner, but several.

115
00:07:02,689 --> 00:07:05,550
For music, the future may not be so bright.

116
00:07:05,550 --> 00:07:10,030
Unless something drastic changes, like cutting
out the labels, services will land in one

117
00:07:10,030 --> 00:07:11,530
of two categories,

118
00:07:11,530 --> 00:07:17,050
those owned by a bigger company, like Apple
or Google, who use them as a loss-leader.

119
00:07:17,050 --> 00:07:20,729
Not to make profit directly, but to sell more
phones.

120
00:07:20,729 --> 00:07:24,710
And, everyone else, left with no way to make
money.

121
00:07:24,710 --> 00:07:26,639
This is already starting to happen.

122
00:07:26,639 --> 00:07:29,129
It’s just not obvious unless you’re looking.

123
00:07:29,129 --> 00:07:34,889
A MoviePass user can feel the business model
fail underneath them, Unlimited movies turns

124
00:07:34,889 --> 00:07:41,800
into most movies, turns into some movies turns
into only black comedy westerns starring Adam

125
00:07:41,800 --> 00:07:48,349
Sandler, only between the hours of 4 and 5
am... in select Wyoming theaters.

126
00:07:48,349 --> 00:07:52,259
But a Spotify user can just keep happily listening
away.

127
00:07:52,259 --> 00:07:53,259
For now.

128
00:07:53,259 --> 00:07:57,970
Every song ever written for less than the
price of a single album works only because

129
00:07:57,970 --> 00:07:59,550
investors pay for it.

130
00:07:59,550 --> 00:08:01,509
But that won’t last forever.

131
00:08:01,509 --> 00:08:07,189
The industry may look healthy in aggregate,
but it’s mostly the top 1% inflating the

132
00:08:07,189 --> 00:08:08,189
average.

133
00:08:08,189 --> 00:08:12,600
It’s not that I don’t think developers,
or musicians, or journalists will survive,

134
00:08:12,600 --> 00:08:15,479
I worry which ones survive.

135
00:08:15,479 --> 00:08:20,060
There are three kinds of companies, those
that make money honestly, those that make

136
00:08:20,060 --> 00:08:23,360
money dishonestly, and those that… don’t.

137
00:08:23,360 --> 00:08:29,330
When nobody pays for music or software, independent
musicians and developers lose, But there are

138
00:08:29,330 --> 00:08:33,150

good ones.

139
00:08:33,150 --> 00:08:36,630
Journalism won’t die, but the good kind

140
00:08:36,630 --> 00:08:39,450
Some would say, largely has.

141
00:08:39,450 --> 00:08:43,970
If you think there’s a problem with freemium
apps and in-app purchases today, just wait

142
00:08:43,970 --> 00:08:46,710

143

The good news is that these industries have
