question:
1
00:00:07,808 --> 00:00:10,839
A toothpaste brand claims
their product will destroy more plaque

2
00:00:10,839 --> 00:00:12,910
than any product ever made.

3
00:00:12,910 --> 00:00:16,411
A politician tells you their plan
will create the most jobs.

4
00:00:16,411 --> 00:00:18,951
We're so used to hearing these
kinds of exaggerations

5
00:00:18,951 --> 00:00:20,850
in advertising and politics

6
00:00:20,850 --> 00:00:23,131
that we might not even bat an eye.

7
00:00:23,131 --> 00:00:26,111
But what about when the claim
is accompanied by a graph?

8
00:00:26,111 --> 00:00:28,471
Afterall, a graph isn't an opinion.

9
00:00:28,471 --> 00:00:32,611
It represents cold, hard numbers,
and who can argue with those?

10
00:00:32,611 --> 00:00:36,403
Yet, as it turns out, there are plenty
of ways graphs can mislead

11
00:00:36,403 --> 00:00:38,192
and outright manipulate.

12
00:00:38,192 --> 00:00:40,745
Here are some things to look out for.

13
00:00:40,745 --> 00:00:45,760
In this 1992 ad, Chevy claimed to make
the most reliable trucks in America

14
00:00:45,760 --> 00:00:47,510
using this graph.

15
00:00:47,510 --> 00:00:51,963
Not only does it show that 98% of all
Chevy trucks sold in the last ten years

16
00:00:51,963 --> 00:00:53,592
are still on the road,

17
00:00:53,592 --> 00:00:57,338
but it looks like they're twice
as dependable as Toyota trucks.

18
00:00:57,338 --> 00:01:00,634
That is, until you take a closer look
at the numbers on the left

19
00:01:00,634 --> 00:01:05,472
and see that the figure for Toyota
is about 96.5%.

20
00:01:05,472 --> 00:01:09,313
The scale only goes between 95 and 100%.

21
00:01:09,313 --> 00:01:12,963
[Insert subtitle here]

22
00:01:12,963 --> 00:01:16,243
This is one of the most common
ways graphs misrepresent data,

23
00:01:16,243 --> 00:01:18,333
by distorting the scale.

24
00:01:18,333 --> 00:01:20,804
Zooming in on a small portion
of the y-axis

25
00:01:20,804 --> 00:01:25,703
exaggerates a barely detectable difference
between the things being compared.

26
00:01:25,703 --> 00:01:27,974
And it's especially misleading 
with bar graphs

27
00:01:27,974 --> 00:01:31,023
since we assume the difference
in the size of the bars

28
00:01:31,023 --> 00:01:33,233
is proportional to the values.

29
00:01:33,233 --> 00:01:36,125
But the scale can also be distorted
along the x-axis,

30
00:01:36,125 --> 00:01:40,414
usually in line graphs
showing something changing over time.

31
00:01:40,414 --> 00:01:44,747
This chart showing the rise
in American unemployment from 2008 to 2010

32
00:01:44,747 --> 00:01:47,996
manipulates the x-axis in two ways.

33
00:01:47,996 --> 00:01:50,395
First of all, the scale is inconsistent,

34
00:01:50,395 --> 00:01:53,416
compressing the 15-month span
after March 2009

35
00:01:53,416 --> 00:01:56,755
to look shorter than 
the preceding six months.

36
00:01:56,755 --> 00:02:00,106
Using more consistent data points
gives a different picture

37
00:02:00,106 --> 00:02:03,705
with job losses tapering off
by the end of 2009.

38
00:02:03,705 --> 00:02:06,675
And if you wonder why
they were increasing in the first place,

39
00:02:06,675 --> 00:02:10,615
the timeline starts immediately after
the U.S.'s biggest financial collapse

40
00:02:10,615 --> 00:02:12,626
since the Great Depression.

41
00:02:12,626 --> 00:02:15,219
These techniques are known as
cherry picking.

42
00:02:15,219 --> 00:02:18,869
A time range can be carefully chosen
to exclude the impact of a major event

43
00:02:18,869 --> 00:02:20,648
right outside it.

44
00:02:20,648 --> 00:02:24,762
And picking specific data points
can hide important changes in between.

45
00:02:24,762 --> 00:02:27,356
Even when there's nothing wrong
with the graph itself,

46
00:02:27,356 --> 00:02:30,937
leaving out relevant data can give
a misleading impression.

47
00:02:30,937 --> 00:02:33,997
This chart of how many people watch
the Super Bowl each year

48
00:02:33,997 --> 00:02:37,626
makes it look like the event's
popularity is exploding.

49
00:02:37,626 --> 00:02:40,198
But it's not accounting 
for population growth.

50
00:02:40,198 --> 00:02:41,967
The ratings have actually held steady

51
00:02:41,967 --> 00:02:45,109
because while the number 
of football fans has increased,

52
00:02:45,109 --> 00:02:47,959
their share of overall viewership has not.

53
00:02:47,959 --> 00:02:49,888
Finally, a graph can't tell you much

54
00:02:49,888 --> 00:02:53,318
if you don't know the full significance 
of what's being presented.

55
00:02:53,318 --> 00:02:56,457
Both of the following graphs
use the same ocean temperature data

56
00:02:56,457 --> 00:02:59,719
from the National Centers 
for Environmental Information.

57
00:02:59,719 --> 00:03:02,490
So why do they seem to give
opposite impressions?

58
00:03:02,490 --> 00:03:05,279
The first graph plots the average
annual ocean temperature

59
00:03:05,279 --> 00:03:07,987
from 1880 to 2016,

60
00:03:07,987 --> 00:03:10,149
making the change look insignificant.

61
00:03:10,149 --> 00:03:12,878
But in fact, a rise of even
half a degree Celsius

62
00:03:12,878 --> 00:03:15,799
can cause massive ecological disruption.

63
00:03:15,799 --> 00:03:17,219
This is why the second graph,

64
00:03:17,219 --> 00:03:19,858
which show the average temperature
variation each year,

65
00:03:19,858 --> 00:03:22,390
is far more significant.

66
00:03:22,390 --> 00:03:27,379
When they're used well, graphs can
help us intuitively grasp complex data.

67
00:03:27,379 --> 00:03:31,180
But as visual software has enabled
more usage of graphs throughout all media,

68
00:03:31,180 --> 00:03:35,900
it's also made them easier to use
in a careless or dishonest way.

69
00:03:35,900 --> 00:03:39,560
So the next time you see a graph,
don't be swayed by the lines and curves.

70
00:03:39,560 --> 00:03:40,882
Look at the labels,

71
00:03:40,882 --> 00:03:42,130
the numbers,

72
00:03:42,130 --> 00:03:43,048
the scale,

73
00:03:43,048 --> 00:03:44,360
and the context,

74
00:03:44,360 --> 00:03:46,780
and ask what story the picture
is trying to tell.

00:00:01,430 --> 00:00:05,510
We hold these truths to be self-evident: that
all men and women are created equal.

2
00:00:05,510 --> 00:00:08,230
[laughter] Just kidding, sorry, no.

3
00:00:08,230 --> 00:00:13,040
We're not all equal. Inequality,
in fact, gets a ton of attention these days.

4
00:00:13,050 --> 00:00:18,380
President Obama called it, quote, the defining
challenge of our time. But usually when people

5
00:00:18,380 --> 00:00:22,760
are talking about inequality, they're talking
about income inequality. And income inequality

6
00:00:22,760 --> 00:00:28,640
is at its highest level since the Great Depression.
Before taxes, the top 1% take home about 22.5%

7
00:00:28,640 --> 00:00:33,050
of the national income. Really think about
that for a second. For every dollar paid in

8
00:00:33,050 --> 00:00:37,540
income in the U.S., almost a quarter of it
goes to the top 1 percent -- a quarter!

9
00:00:37,540 --> 00:00:42,860
But income inequality is actually less dangerous
than its cousin, wealth inequality. The top

10
00:00:42,860 --> 00:00:47,980
1% hold close to 40% of the national wealth.
So for every dollar in American assets -- that's

11
00:00:47,980 --> 00:00:52,840
homes, stocks, savings, all of that -- 40
cents of it belongs to the top 1%. The top

12
00:00:52,840 --> 00:00:59,120
1% holds more wealth in America than the bottom
90% of the country, combined. And a lot of

13
00:00:59,120 --> 00:01:02,500
that money gets passed on to their children
or their children's children. Take the heirs

14
00:01:02,500 --> 00:01:07,080
of Sam Walden, founder of Walmart. None of
them founded Walmart. None of them were created

15
00:01:07,080 --> 00:01:12,240
equal either. The six of them have more than
$140 billion in wealth. That makes those six

16
00:01:12,240 --> 00:01:17,380
people wealthier than the bottom 40 percent
of Americans, combined. Now, there's an upside

17
00:01:17,380 --> 00:01:22,770
to income inequality. That income is a reward
for people who start businesses and do great

18
00:01:22,770 --> 00:01:26,080
things. You can like income inequality or
you can hate it but usually it is money they

19
00:01:26,080 --> 00:01:30,220
earned in this lifetime, usually through talent
or risk or hard work, with a little bit of

20
00:01:30,220 --> 00:01:33,900
luck. But wealth inequality isn't like that.
That money is often a reward for people who

21
00:01:33,900 --> 00:01:37,729
were just born into the right family. And
it's money that keeps growing. That's a big

22
00:01:37,729 --> 00:01:42,990
point economist Thomas Piketty makes in his
new book, Capital. [Insert subtitle here]

23
00:01:42,990 --> 00:01:48,290
[Insert subtitle here] So people who have

24
00:01:48,290 --> 00:01:51,579
a lot of wealth, they tend to get wealthier
and wealthier and wealthier unless something

25
00:01:51,579 --> 00:01:57,579
like a war or a tax intervenes. One way to
get wealthier, by the way, is politics. A

26
00:01:57,579 --> 00:02:01,100
lot of money can buy you a lot of political
speech, particularly now that the Supreme

27
00:02:01,100 --> 00:02:05,119
Court is systematically dismantling the limits
on buying political speech. This is the doom

28
00:02:05,119 --> 00:02:09,310
loop of oligarchy: wealth buys power, power
buys more wealth, more wealth means more power,

29
00:02:09,310 --> 00:02:13,230
more power means more wealth, and on and on
and on we go until a very small fraction of

30
00:02:13,230 --> 00:02:17,770
the population has a whole lot of power and
a whole lot of money.

31
00:02:17,770 --> 00:02:20,830
So no, all men and women aren't born equal.

32
00:02:20,830 --> 00:02:23,390
Some are born really, really
wealthy.

So as a result of that, what we're seeing

00:01:11,410 --> 00:01:13,160

00:01:13,160 --> 00:01:15,470

32
00:01:15,470 --> 00:01:17,690

00:01:17,690 --> 00:01:20,640

00:01:20,640 --> 00:01:21,860

We're seeing that public

00:01:39,620 --> 00:01:41,300

00:01:41,300 --> 00:01:43,860

00:02:04,660 --> 00:02:06,830
Trust in the research

00:02:06,830 --> 00:02:07,800
a sense that you believe

00:02:07,800 --> 00:02:09,610
that the vaccines are safe and effective

00:02:09,610 --> 00:02:12,460

00:02:12,460 --> 00:02:14,890
and there even dynamics around

00:02:14,890 --> 00:02:16,590
or experiences with other vaccines,

00:02:16,590 --> 00:02:17,917

00:02:17,917 --> 00:02:19,320
If you typically get a flu shot,

00:02:19,320 --> 00:02:22,070

00:02:22,070 --> 00:02:24,617

4
00:00:06,991 --> 00:00:08,071
What happened?

5
00:00:08,841 --> 00:00:12,545
In 2003, the US invaded Iraq because of
its alleged connections to terrorism

6
00:00:12,545 --> 00:00:14,068
and weapons of mass destruction.

7
00:00:14,278 --> 00:00:17,366
At the time, Saddam Hussein, a brutal
dictator, ruled the country.

8
00:00:17,576 --> 00:00:19,274
He was part of the Sunni minority

9
00:00:19,274 --> 00:00:21,179
and suppressed the Shia majority.

10
00:00:21,709 --> 00:00:23,331
Iraq was conquered fairly quickly,

11
00:00:23,331 --> 00:00:25,336
but the US had no plan for the country.

12
00:00:25,936 --> 00:00:29,355
The until-then suppressed Shia majority
took over

13
00:00:29,355 --> 00:00:31,140
and began oppressing the Sunnis,

14
00:00:31,140 --> 00:00:34,783
because suppressing other faiths has
proven to be such a good idea.

15
00:00:35,313 --> 00:00:38,046
Unsurprisingly, a Sunni rebel
uprising began

16
00:00:38,046 --> 00:00:40,910
and terrorist groups, like al-Qaeda,
trickled into Iraq

17
00:00:40,910 --> 00:00:43,839
and local forces, often former Sunni
military, began

18
00:00:43,839 --> 00:00:46,774
fighting the US troops and the newly
formed Iraqi state,

19
00:00:46,774 --> 00:00:49,304
peaking in a bloody civil war in 2006.

20
00:00:49,964 --> 00:00:53,319
Since then, people in Iraq have basically
been segregated by religion.

21
00:00:53,999 --> 00:00:58,030
So, in a tragic irony of history, the US
invasion led to the formation of

22
00:00:58,030 --> 00:01:01,292
the very terrorists the US wanted to
eliminate in the first place,

23
00:01:01,292 --> 00:01:04,670
because Iraq was now the perfect training
ground for terrorism.

24
00:01:05,580 --> 00:01:08,826
To understand this complicated conflict
better, we need to understand

25
00:01:08,826 --> 00:01:12,025
the relationship between the two main
branches of the Muslim faith:

26
00:01:12,025 --> 00:01:13,823
Shia and Sunni Islam.

27
00:01:14,273 --> 00:01:18,583
[Insert subtitle here]

28
00:01:19,033 --> 00:01:22,357
And the hard-liners on both sides don’t
like each other very much.

29
00:01:23,197 --> 00:01:26,873
Saudi Arabia and Iran are the two most
powerful players in the game of faiths.

30
00:01:27,553 --> 00:01:31,466
They both have no separation of state and
religion, domestic problems, and

31
00:01:31,466 --> 00:01:32,602
a lot of oil money.

32
00:01:32,952 --> 00:01:36,100
And they support groups that fight the
other religious orientation.

33
00:01:37,160 --> 00:01:40,317
And one of those terror organizations
supported by Saudi Arabia

34
00:01:40,317 --> 00:01:43,935
was the Islamic State in Iraq,
or ISI for short.

35
00:01:44,545 --> 00:01:46,374
In 2010, the Arab Spring happened

36
00:01:46,374 --> 00:01:48,779
and changed the whole situation
in the Middle East.

37
00:01:49,009 --> 00:01:52,702
In Syria, dictator Bashar al-Assad didn’t
think much of resigning

38
00:01:52,702 --> 00:01:55,494
and started a gruesome civil war
against his own people.

39
00:01:55,754 --> 00:01:58,996
The longer the war went on, the more
foreign groups joined the fight,

40
00:01:58,996 --> 00:02:00,677
most of them for religious reasons,

41
00:02:00,677 --> 00:02:03,539
and with the goal of building an
Islamic state in the region.

42
00:02:03,849 --> 00:02:06,669
And one of them was the infamous ISI,
which now became

43
00:02:06,669 --> 00:02:09,752
the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria,
or ISIS.

44
00:02:10,692 --> 00:02:13,006
They had fought in Iraq for years, and had

45
00:02:13,006 --> 00:02:16,030
thousands of well-trained and
fanatic soldiers.

46
00:02:16,520 --> 00:02:19,038
They already quasi-controlled parts of
northern Iraq

47
00:02:19,038 --> 00:02:22,098
and were very determined to build
their religious state.

48
00:02:22,458 --> 00:02:25,678
And they changed the game in Syria like
no-one expected.

49
00:02:26,078 --> 00:02:29,602
ISIS was so unbelievably violent and
radical that soon it was

50
00:02:29,602 --> 00:02:32,933
a war with almost every other faction of
the Syrian rebel armies.

51
00:02:32,933 --> 00:02:35,975
They attacked and killed member of other
Muslim terrorist groups.

52
00:02:35,975 --> 00:02:38,940
In the territories they controlled, they
built an Islamic state

53
00:02:38,940 --> 00:02:43,358
with rules so strict that even the
hard-liners of al-Qaeda and Saudi Arabia

54
00:02:43,358 --> 00:02:45,613
were shocked and withdrew their support.

55
00:02:46,123 --> 00:02:50,041
ISIS has been accused of responsibility
for multiple massacres against civilians,

56
00:02:50,041 --> 00:02:53,721
countless suicide bombings, the
hostage-taking of women and children,

57
00:02:53,721 --> 00:02:56,351
the execution of their prisoners, and
beheadings.

58
00:02:56,481 --> 00:03:00,209
All kinds of medieval hororrs we would
rather not have to illustrate.

59
00:03:00,429 --> 00:03:03,867
And this lovely gathering of human beings
recently decided it was time to

60
00:03:03,867 --> 00:03:05,383
take more territory in Iraq.

61
00:03:06,043 --> 00:03:09,463
Since the US left Iraq, the Shia prime
minister, Nouri al-Maliki,

62
00:03:09,463 --> 00:03:13,111
has monopolized power and discriminated
against Sunnis wherever possible.

63
00:03:13,731 --> 00:03:17,642
The government of Iraq is widely regarded
as being corrupt, incapable,

64
00:03:17,642 --> 00:03:20,466
and it’s cetainly hated by a large part
of its citizens.

65
00:03:21,006 --> 00:03:23,823
The Iraqi army, consisting of about
300,000 soldiers,

66
00:03:23,823 --> 00:03:27,115
was created using 25 billion US dollars in
tax money,

67
00:03:27,115 --> 00:03:29,198
but it’s not loyal to its government and

68
00:03:29,198 --> 00:03:32,968
has been withdrawing or completely
disbanding, giving up city after city.

69
00:03:33,508 --> 00:03:36,683
Because ISIS has announced that everyone
who opposes them will be killed,

70
00:03:36,683 --> 00:03:38,881
they have proven they mean business.

71
00:03:40,571 --> 00:03:43,442
By June 2014, they’d conquered a big
chunk of Iraq,

72
00:03:43,442 --> 00:03:46,384
including Mosul, Iraq’s second-largest
city.

73
00:03:47,084 --> 00:03:49,329
They’d stolen hundreds of millions from
captured banks,

74
00:03:49,329 --> 00:03:51,854
making them the richest terror
organization on Earth.

75
00:03:52,234 --> 00:03:54,440
And they are constantly working on
establishing

76
00:03:54,440 --> 00:03:56,148
a super-medieval religious state.

77
00:03:56,938 --> 00:04:00,485
Iran and the US are even considering
working together to fight them.

78
00:04:00,865 --> 00:04:02,839
That’s how gruesome the situation is.

79
00:04:03,339 --> 00:04:06,820
Events in Iraq show again that exploiting
the people you’ve defeated in a war,

80
00:04:06,820 --> 00:04:10,030
denying them power, a living, and a stake
in the rebuilding of the country

81
00:04:10,030 --> 00:04:13,198
is just sowing the seeds of the next bout
of violence.

82
00:04:13,978 --> 00:04:16,310
Somehow, we have to break this circle.

83

question: What percentage do the richest 20% own of the country's wealth in reality?

1
00:00:00,880 --> 00:00:05,440
In a poll of a thousand people, we asked

2

in an ideal world, if you were to share

3
00:00:05,440 --> 00:00:10,000
out the wealth of the country, what

4
00:00:07,279 --> 00:00:11,920
would you think is fair or equal? And

5
00:00:10,000 --> 00:00:14,000
it's kind of what you'd expect. The

6
00:00:11,920 --> 00:00:16,160
richest 20% would have a little bit

7
00:00:14,000 --> 00:00:18,320
more. [Insert subtitle here]

8
00:00:16,160 --> 00:00:21,279
[Insert subtitle here]

9
00:00:18,320 --> 00:00:23,359
[Insert subtitle here] And then we asked, how do you

10
00:00:21,279 --> 00:00:26,080
think the wealth of the country is

11
00:00:23,359 --> 00:00:28,320
actually shared? And unsurprisingly,

12
00:00:26,080 --> 00:00:30,640
yes. You thought it was unequal. You

13
00:00:28,320 --> 00:00:33,040
thought the wealthiest 20% would have

14
00:00:30,640 --> 00:00:36,640
almost 60% of the country's wealth and

15
00:00:33,040 --> 00:00:39,200
the poorest 20% will they just have 11%.

16
00:00:36,640 --> 00:00:42,800
So that's how unfair you think Ireland

17
00:00:39,200 --> 00:00:44,719
is. But do you want to see the reality?

18
00:00:42,800 --> 00:00:47,280
You believe the wealth gap in Ireland is

19
00:00:44,719 --> 00:00:49,520
bad, but it's worse than you think. So

20
00:00:47,280 --> 00:00:53,039
again, this is what we would like it to

21

22
00:00:53,039 --> 00:01:00,960
And this is the reality of wealth in

23
00:00:56,079 --> 00:01:03,680
Ireland. The richest 20% own 73% of the

24
00:01:00,960 --> 00:01:06,080
country's wealth. And the poorest 20%,

25
00:01:03,680 --> 00:01:10,080
they don't own the 11% you think they

26

do. They own a meager 0.2%.

27
00:01:10,080 --> 00:01:15,600
And if you look closer, the top 5%,

28
00:01:12,720 --> 00:01:20,080
well, they own almost twice as much as

29

the entire squeezed middle 60% have. And

30
00:01:20,080 --> 00:01:25,200
remember, these aren't just economic

31
00:01:22,159 --> 00:01:28,080
statistics. These are people, real

32

lives.

question: What is the best title of the video?
answer: Is Amazon Too Big?
distractor2: How High-Margin Tech Infrastructure Funds Low-Margin Commerce
distractor3: A Legal Framework for Regulating Unchecked Corporate Consolidation

question: How many categories appeared in the chart at 6:06?

1
00:00:00,160 --> 00:00:02,520
This video is sponsored by Brilliant!

2
00:00:02,520 --> 00:00:08,490
The first 200 to use the link in the description
get 20% off the annual subscription.

3
00:00:08,490 --> 00:00:13,420
Elizabeth Warren wants to break up Amazon,
Facebook, Google, and Apple.

4
00:00:13,420 --> 00:00:19,840
The argument goes, roughly, like this: Tech
companies have gotten really big, really fast.

5
00:00:19,840 --> 00:00:24,490
And they’ve abused that power by favoring
their own products over their competitors.

6
00:00:24,490 --> 00:00:29,339
Therefore, once a company reaches a certain
size, it shouldn’t be allowed to own both

7
00:00:29,339 --> 00:00:33,070
the products and the platform on which they’re
sold.

8
00:00:33,070 --> 00:00:37,860
In English, Amazon can’t sell the Kindle
on its own website, and Apple has to pick

9
00:00:37,860 --> 00:00:43,070
between owning Music and iMovie and News or
the App Store itself.

10
00:00:43,070 --> 00:00:49,610
Now, whether Warren is 100% serious or mostly
just generating publicity for her presidential

11
00:00:49,610 --> 00:00:52,300
campaign, she isn’t alone.

12
00:00:52,300 --> 00:00:55,690
This is only the latest part of a much bigger
movement.

13
00:00:55,690 --> 00:01:01,329
We’re at an inflection point in history,
where new, fast, Silicon Valley is crashing

14
00:01:01,329 --> 00:01:04,120
in to slow, old, government.

15
00:01:04,120 --> 00:01:09,950
Everywhere, all at once, the power and influence
of big tech companies are being questioned:

16
00:01:09,950 --> 00:01:15,950
Google was recently fined $1.7 billion in
Europe for being anticompetitive.

17
00:01:15,950 --> 00:01:20,650
Sprint is trying to merge with T-Mobile, despite
significant push back.

18
00:01:20,650 --> 00:01:23,980
Facebook has, well, continued to be Facebook.

19
00:01:23,980 --> 00:01:29,440
And Spotify has launched an all-out attack
against Apple for what it claims is unfair

20
00:01:29,440 --> 00:01:30,440
treatment.

21
00:01:30,440 --> 00:01:33,220
So, who’s right - Apple or Spotify?

22
00:01:33,220 --> 00:01:35,190
Google, or the EU?

23
00:01:35,190 --> 00:01:38,050
Facebook, or, literally everyone else?

24
00:01:38,050 --> 00:01:43,200
First, we need to understand why these companies
have such a huge advantage.

25
00:01:43,200 --> 00:01:48,510
And how, in just a few years, Amazon went
from being synonymous with “cheap, convenient

26
00:01:48,510 --> 00:01:52,720
shopping”, to a scary, political, nebulous
Walmart-like mega-corporation.

27
00:01:52,720 --> 00:01:58,900
Let’s say you wanna start a grocery store.

28
00:01:58,900 --> 00:02:01,460
Maybe you know a little bit about merchandising.

29
00:02:01,460 --> 00:02:06,510
Maybe you come from a long line of grocers
so selling produce is just in your blood.

30
00:02:06,510 --> 00:02:11,500
The other kids were playing with fire trucks
and trains but you, you were daydreaming about

31
00:02:11,500 --> 00:02:14,660
the retail implications of The Engel Curve.

32
00:02:14,660 --> 00:02:18,420
Anyway, the bad news is that the grocery business
sucks.

33
00:02:18,420 --> 00:02:20,590
Like, famously so.

34
00:02:20,590 --> 00:02:24,820
If you’re lucky, you might manage a profit
margin of 3%.

35
00:02:24,820 --> 00:02:29,560
Unless you have some revolutionary way of
arranging bananas on the shelf, you’re just

36
00:02:29,560 --> 00:02:34,740
one of a thousand stores, which customers
have no special loyalty towards.

37
00:02:34,740 --> 00:02:39,610
You don’t see a lot of “Proud mother of
a Safeway shopper” bumper stickers.

38
00:02:39,610 --> 00:02:43,570
But - there is money to be made at the very,
very top.

39
00:02:43,570 --> 00:02:49,220
If you can become a Kroger, or a Whole Foods,
or Trader Joe’s, well, that’s a different

40
00:02:49,220 --> 00:02:50,220
story.

41
00:02:50,220 --> 00:02:54,531
The trick is surviving long enough that you
sell lots of things, so you can, (a), turn

42
00:02:54,531 --> 00:02:59,420
around to the companies making those things
and say “Hey, we’d like to buy 3,000 stores

43
00:02:59,420 --> 00:03:02,270
worth of your bananas, can you make us a deal?”,

44
00:03:02,270 --> 00:03:06,740
and, (b), cut out the middle man by creating
your own generic brand.

45
00:03:06,740 --> 00:03:12,010
With size comes leverage, which lets you buy
cheaper, and, ultimately, make more money.

46
00:03:12,010 --> 00:03:15,430
But, again, the problem is getting there.

47
00:03:15,430 --> 00:03:20,340
Competing with established companies in any
industry usually means losing a lot of money

48
00:03:20,340 --> 00:03:25,069
for a long time with only the hope of making
it back in the future.

49
00:03:25,069 --> 00:03:27,550
But don’t give up on your dream quite yet.

50
00:03:27,550 --> 00:03:33,220
Here’s an idea: Forget groceries for now,
let’s just find some way of making money.

51
00:03:33,220 --> 00:03:36,710
Like, I don’t know, selling cloud storage
to enterprise customers!

52
00:03:36,710 --> 00:03:41,350
It’s a good business, no one else is doing
it very well, and, in a few years, you’ll

53
00:03:41,350 --> 00:03:45,790
have so much money, you can come back to your
dream of starting a grocery store.

54
00:03:45,790 --> 00:03:48,670
What does cloud storage have to do with selling
grapes?

55
00:03:48,670 --> 00:03:52,040
Is that really the most exciting thing you
could be doing?

56
00:03:52,040 --> 00:03:54,810
Pretty much nothing and probably not.

57
00:03:54,810 --> 00:03:56,300
But who cares!

58
00:03:56,300 --> 00:04:00,910
Money is money, and as long as it makes more
than the grocery store loses, you can afford

59
00:04:00,910 --> 00:04:05,500
to slowly grow it into an empire, even while
it isn’t yet profitable.

60
00:04:05,500 --> 00:04:10,900
This, if you haven’t noticed, is my very
crude way of describing Amazon.

61
00:04:10,900 --> 00:04:15,510
It started as a book company, but Bezos had
no special love for books.

62
00:04:15,510 --> 00:04:20,030
That was always just a good way of generating
capital for his real dream.

63
00:04:20,030 --> 00:04:22,100
Today, books are a footnote.

64
00:04:22,100 --> 00:04:26,630
The new distraction is called Amazon Web Services
- AWS.

65
00:04:26,630 --> 00:04:29,230
If you’re already familiar, bear with me
for a sec.

66
00:04:29,230 --> 00:04:35,410
A few videos back I said: > A thousand downloads
don’t cost any more than one.

67
00:04:35,410 --> 00:04:37,780
Scale is (nearly) unlimited.

68
00:04:37,780 --> 00:04:42,070
My point was: it’s a whole lot easier to
sell a thousand note-taking apps than it is

69
00:04:42,070 --> 00:04:47,930
a thousand actual notebooks because software
is made of bits, and bits don’t cost money.

70
00:04:47,930 --> 00:04:53,810
Which, is mostly true in that context, but,
not totally accurate in practice.

71
00:04:53,810 --> 00:04:56,880
Consider the scale at which some companies
operate:

72
00:04:56,880 --> 00:05:03,130
Out of all the bandwidth, from every phone
and every computer, in every country, 15%

73
00:05:03,130 --> 00:05:06,139
is just people watching Netflix.

74
00:05:06,139 --> 00:05:07,630
15%!

75
00:05:07,630 --> 00:05:12,250
Even Uber, which, in theory just connects
the nearest driver to the nearest rider, stores

76
00:05:12,250 --> 00:05:17,610
over 100 petabytes of data - or 100,000,000
GB.

77
00:05:17,610 --> 00:05:20,150
It also fluctuates dramatically.

78
00:05:20,150 --> 00:05:24,430
Every startup dreams of hitting the front
page of Reddit, Unless you’re the engineer,

79
00:05:24,430 --> 00:05:28,660
in which case you have a heart attack trying
to keep up with such a huge spike in views.

80
00:05:28,660 --> 00:05:33,650
Companies, and, especially, startups with
limited budgets, have a tough choice:

81
00:05:33,650 --> 00:05:38,530
Either buy too much capacity, Or save money
and hope they don’t get too popular.

82
00:05:38,530 --> 00:05:41,010
At least, until AWS.

83
00:05:41,010 --> 00:05:46,000
Amazon realized it could solve this problem
with a service: Only pay for what you actually

84
00:05:46,000 --> 00:05:47,050
use.

85
00:05:47,050 --> 00:05:52,310
If your business suddenly explodes in popularity,
no problem, just pay a little more.

86
00:05:52,310 --> 00:05:56,139
Turn the handle for more data, as you would
water or electricity.

87
00:05:56,139 --> 00:06:01,150
Amazon takes care of the rest, the same way
we outsource building windmills to electric

88
00:06:01,150 --> 00:06:02,150
companies.

89
00:06:02,150 --> 00:06:06,000
[Insert subtitle here]

90
00:06:06,000 --> 00:06:11,180
[Insert subtitle here] and you’re probably wondering why

91
00:06:11,180 --> 00:06:12,980
we’re talking so much about AWS.

92
00:06:12,980 --> 00:06:15,190
But what about its income?

93
00:06:15,190 --> 00:06:17,770
Where is it actually making a profit?

94
00:06:17,770 --> 00:06:19,290
This is where it gets interesting.

95
00:06:19,290 --> 00:06:24,979
Now, Amazon looks like a cloud storage company
with an online retail business on the side.

96
00:06:24,979 --> 00:06:31,720
In the 4th quarter of 2018, AWS accounted
for 58% of the company’s operating income.

97
00:06:31,720 --> 00:06:33,970
It alone made more money than McDonalds.

98
00:06:33,970 --> 00:06:39,560
So, yeah, it sells lots of USB cables and
bananas, but that’s not where the money

99
00:06:39,560 --> 00:06:40,560
is.

100
00:06:40,560 --> 00:06:42,210
AWS is camouflage.

101
00:06:42,210 --> 00:06:47,240
It makes the company look good overall and
conceals how much money it loses.

102
00:06:47,240 --> 00:06:49,160
One business subsidizes another.

103
00:06:49,160 --> 00:06:51,280
And this is where it gets tricky.

104
00:06:51,280 --> 00:06:54,950
Because, if you’re one of the other grocery
stores, you’re thinking “This isn’t

105
00:06:54,950 --> 00:06:58,840
really fair - how can we compete with someone
who doesn’t even need to make a profit?”

106
00:06:58,840 --> 00:07:03,990
Safeway and Publix don’t have a $25 billion
a year cloud storage businesses.

107
00:07:03,990 --> 00:07:08,090
When they sell bananas, they have to, like,
ya know, make money.

108
00:07:08,090 --> 00:07:12,930
This is how, one after another, Amazon enters
and dominates a new industry.

109
00:07:12,930 --> 00:07:16,130
It plays by a fundamentally different set
of rules.

110
00:07:16,130 --> 00:07:20,900
Turns out it’s a whole lot easier when you’re
not super worried about the whole profit thing.

111
00:07:20,900 --> 00:07:25,580
Of course, predatory pricing, when a company
lowers its prices to starve out the competition,

112
00:07:25,580 --> 00:07:27,370
isn’t a new idea.

113
00:07:27,370 --> 00:07:31,960
But once they’ve done so, companies usually
raise their prices again - that’s the whole

114
00:07:31,960 --> 00:07:32,960
point.

115
00:07:32,960 --> 00:07:36,170
Amazon, on the other hand, has always kept
its prices low.

116
00:07:36,170 --> 00:07:40,370
It’s not playing the long game, it’s playing
the looooong game.

117
00:07:40,370 --> 00:07:43,400
Here’s it’s revenue, and here’s it’s
profit.

118
00:07:43,400 --> 00:07:47,710
The company touches more money than ever - it
just doesn’t keep it.

119
00:07:47,710 --> 00:07:51,000
Profit has stayed around 0 because it’s
more interested in growth.

120
00:07:51,000 --> 00:07:52,480
That’s the loophole.

121
00:07:52,480 --> 00:07:57,650
In this essay, researcher Lina Khan explains
how, since the ‘70s, antitrust law has used

122
00:07:57,650 --> 00:08:01,840
short-term prices to determine whether a company
is being anticompetitive.

123
00:08:01,840 --> 00:08:07,160
In other words, sure, Amazon is big, it’s
dominant, and it’s killing lots of competitors.

124
00:08:07,160 --> 00:08:10,270
But it’s prices are low, so it flies under
the radar.

125
00:08:10,270 --> 00:08:12,140
You might be thinking - so what?

126
00:08:12,140 --> 00:08:16,810
If a company uses its size to save you and
me money, isn’t that a good thing?

127
00:08:16,810 --> 00:08:21,610
But when products are subsidized, either by
another profitable business like AWS, or,

128
00:08:21,610 --> 00:08:25,410
Venture Capitalists burning money for the
sake of growth, they don’t have to compete

129
00:08:25,410 --> 00:08:26,900
on their own.

130
00:08:26,900 --> 00:08:30,651
Products win not because they’re the best
but because they’re funded by someone, or

131
00:08:30,651 --> 00:08:32,740
something, unrelated.

132
00:08:32,740 --> 00:08:36,399
For example, on iPhone, Apple has the Platform
Advantage.

133
00:08:36,399 --> 00:08:40,529
It controls which apps are allowed on the
App Store, and doesn’t have to give up 30%

134
00:08:40,529 --> 00:08:44,129
of its revenue or follow the same rules, as
everyone else.

135
00:08:44,129 --> 00:08:48,540
If you’re Clash of Clans, this may seem
like a relatively small price to pay for access

136
00:08:48,540 --> 00:08:51,129
to 1.3 billion users.

137
00:08:51,129 --> 00:08:54,300
For someone like Spotify, it’s a very different
story.

138
00:08:54,300 --> 00:08:59,069
Music streaming is the digital equivalent
of a grocery store - Spotify has such tiny

139
00:08:59,069 --> 00:09:03,329
margins that giving Apple 30% breaks the entire
business model.

140
00:09:03,329 --> 00:09:07,800
And even if Apple didn’t make a dime from
its Music or News apps, it might still offer

141
00:09:07,800 --> 00:09:10,509
them just to attract users to the iPhone.

142
00:09:10,509 --> 00:09:14,420
Spotify needs to make money, but Apple Music
just doesn’t.

143
00:09:14,420 --> 00:09:19,290
Apple’s apps, therefore, almost certainly
have more users than they “should”.

144
00:09:19,290 --> 00:09:24,170
Which is not saying they’re good or bad,
but that some number of people, maybe 1, maybe

145
00:09:24,170 --> 00:09:29,019
1 million, use the service only because Apple
had an unfair advantage in putting it in front

146
00:09:29,019 --> 00:09:30,019
of them.

147
00:09:30,019 --> 00:09:33,869
Likewise, Amazon has the Platform Advantage
on its website.

148
00:09:33,869 --> 00:09:38,360
At some point it realized, hey, wait a second,
if we have all the data, and we control what

149
00:09:38,360 --> 00:09:42,720
people see, why on earth are we sending customers
to someone else’s product?

150
00:09:42,720 --> 00:09:47,630
So now it competes with its own sellers, on
everything from batteries to backpacks and

151
00:09:47,630 --> 00:09:48,630
keyboards.

152
00:09:48,630 --> 00:09:51,779
But wait, how is that different than any other
generic brand?

153
00:09:51,779 --> 00:09:56,720
Target has Up&Up, and Walmart, Great Value,
but no one’s complaining they have an unfair

154
00:09:56,720 --> 00:09:57,779
advantage.

155
00:09:57,779 --> 00:09:58,939
The difference is lock-in.

156
00:09:58,939 --> 00:10:03,999
It’s much easier to switch grocery stores
than it is between iPhone and Android.

157
00:10:03,999 --> 00:10:08,620
Companies like Facebook will always say “Look,
you chose to use our service, you chose to

158
00:10:08,620 --> 00:10:13,629
give us your information, didn’t you quit
your job, become a lawyer and read our 3,000-page

159
00:10:13,629 --> 00:10:14,869
terms of service?”

160
00:10:14,869 --> 00:10:16,860
But that’s not really true.

161
00:10:16,860 --> 00:10:21,489
We made one, unrelated choice, like buying
an iPhone or Android, which required that

162
00:10:21,489 --> 00:10:23,910
we make a bunch of other choices later on.

163
00:10:23,910 --> 00:10:25,600
Nobody knows what they’re getting into.

164
00:10:25,600 --> 00:10:29,179
And this will only happen more as companies
get even bigger.

165
00:10:29,179 --> 00:10:35,269
Amazon is an extreme example because AWS is
really profitable and groceries are really

166
00:10:35,269 --> 00:10:40,399
not, but entering new categories with the
resources you already have is kind of what

167
00:10:40,399 --> 00:10:42,079
a company is.

168
00:10:42,079 --> 00:10:46,579
You might start by making smartphones but
then use that money to sell refrigerators.

169
00:10:46,579 --> 00:10:50,720
Fast-forward a few years and now you sell
life insurance and container ships.

170
00:10:50,720 --> 00:10:56,050
Samsung is less a brand and more a Buy-N-Large,
E-Corp conglomerate.

171
00:10:56,050 --> 00:11:00,879
Like Amazon, it barely makes sense to think
of it as a single, unified company.

172
00:11:00,879 --> 00:11:03,449
One division sells parts for the iPhone.

173
00:11:03,449 --> 00:11:07,069
Another fiercely competes against that very
same device.

174
00:11:07,069 --> 00:11:09,239
Even Apple is moving in this direction.

175
00:11:09,239 --> 00:11:13,519
It may not be in the business of refrigerators,
but you now buy your iPhone with an Apple

176
00:11:13,519 --> 00:11:18,980
credit card, download Apple apps, back them
up on Apple’s cloud, and watch Apple-branded

177
00:11:18,980 --> 00:11:20,559
TV-shows.

178
00:11:20,559 --> 00:11:23,649
But there’s also a benefit to this integration.

179
00:11:23,649 --> 00:11:28,009
One of the bests feature of the iPhone is
that it’s all designed by one company, as

180
00:11:28,009 --> 00:11:29,920
one, coherent product.

181
00:11:29,920 --> 00:11:36,019
Because Apple owns both Music and iOS, they’re
easier to use, more convenient, and more powerful

182
00:11:36,019 --> 00:11:37,149
together.

183
00:11:37,149 --> 00:11:41,579
And because you have no choice but to use
Apple’s App Store, your phone is more secure

184
00:11:41,579 --> 00:11:43,379
and your data more private.

185
00:11:43,379 --> 00:11:45,920
Now, of course, you may disagree.

186
00:11:45,920 --> 00:11:50,560
For some, having more freedom might be worth
the trade-off for privacy and security.

187
00:11:50,560 --> 00:11:53,209
But that doesn’t diminish its value for
the rest of us.

188
00:11:53,209 --> 00:11:57,250
In other words, breaking up some of these
companies would actually mean a worse experience

189
00:11:57,250 --> 00:11:58,470
for you and me.

190
00:11:58,470 --> 00:12:03,699
And if your “consumer protection” proposal
makes our lives worse, it’s probably a bad

191
00:12:03,699 --> 00:12:04,699
one.

192
00:12:04,699 --> 00:12:09,329
The EU has shown - time and time and time
again - that governments can make technology

193
00:12:09,329 --> 00:12:13,529
worse simply because they don’t understand
it - even with the best intentions.

194
00:12:13,529 --> 00:12:15,420
So, what’s the solution?

195
00:12:15,420 --> 00:12:17,000
I don’t know.

196
00:12:17,000 --> 00:12:21,230
If anything, we’ve learned you should be
skeptical of any simple solution to a problem

197
00:12:21,230 --> 00:12:22,230
this big.

198
00:12:22,230 --> 00:12:23,839
Instead, here are some ideas:

199
00:12:23,839 --> 00:12:28,660
First, we need to expand the scope of what
qualifies as anticompetitive behavior.

200
00:12:28,660 --> 00:12:31,709
Low prices don’t mean the customer isn’t
being harmed.

201
00:12:31,709 --> 00:12:36,389
On the other hand, closed, locked-down markets
like the App Store aren’t necessarily always

202
00:12:36,389 --> 00:12:37,389
a bad thing.

203
00:12:37,389 --> 00:12:40,949
Second, we need to reexamine some mergers
and acquisitions.

204
00:12:40,949 --> 00:12:45,600
It happens all the time: An exciting young
startup gains some traction only to just be

205
00:12:45,600 --> 00:12:48,029
bought by a Google or an Amazon.

206
00:12:48,029 --> 00:12:50,259
Sometimes we never heard from it again.

207
00:12:50,259 --> 00:12:55,300
Founders are incentivized to sell their companies
- to the tune of billions of dollars.

208
00:12:55,300 --> 00:12:58,860
But society at large would be better off with
more competition.

209
00:12:58,860 --> 00:13:03,421
The key is balancing the benefit we all get
from the scale of companies like Amazon, with

210
00:13:03,421 --> 00:13:07,689
the drawbacks of their immense political and
economic power.

211
00:13:07,689 --> 00:13:12,100
Many of these ideas to break-up tech companies
are designed only to get headlines.

212
00:13:12,100 --> 00:13:17,139
But a real solution requires a deeper, mathematical
understanding of the problem, of the type

213

you can learn on Brilliant.org.

how most of us learn.

We need examples, challenges, and pictures.

8
00:00:18,160 --> 00:00:20,860
This whole election process
over the past year and a half

9
00:00:20,860 --> 00:00:22,540
has been...ugly.

10
00:00:22,540 --> 00:00:24,860
And the rhetoric seemed to be
much more divisive

11
00:00:24,860 --> 00:00:27,260
than any other election

12
00:00:27,260 --> 00:00:31,760
And there's been this idea going around

13
00:00:31,760 --> 00:00:33,080
But is this true?

14
00:00:33,080 --> 00:00:35,280
Are we really that deeply divided?

15

16

♪♪

17
00:00:41,500 --> 00:00:43,400
When people say that

18
00:00:43,400 --> 00:00:45,120
what are they actually
talking about?

19
00:00:45,120 --> 00:00:47,900
Most of you are probably familiar
with this electoral map by now.

20
00:00:47,900 --> 00:00:49,840
The good-old red states and blue states.

21
00:00:49,840 --> 00:00:51,440
And as you are probably aware,

22
00:00:51,440 --> 00:00:53,760
if you zoom in past
the state boundaries,

23
00:00:53,760 --> 00:00:56,180
what you'll find is that
the red and blue divide

24
00:00:56,180 --> 00:00:59,100
is actually much more pronounced
from county to county

25
00:00:59,100 --> 00:01:01,020
rather than between
the states themselves.

26
00:01:01,020 --> 00:01:04,520
This reflects an increasing trend
that has been going on for decades now.

27
00:01:04,520 --> 00:01:09,260
In 1976, roughly 28% of voters lived in
what are called landslide counties.

28
00:01:09,260 --> 00:01:12,740
In 2012, that number
increased to about 50%

29
00:01:12,740 --> 00:01:14,620
and now, in 2016,

30
00:01:14,620 --> 00:01:17,640
60% of voters live
in landslide counties.

31
00:01:17,640 --> 00:01:20,780
That's over double the amount
from just 40 years ago

32
00:01:20,780 --> 00:01:23,620
and this divide is even
more extreme in big cities

33
00:01:23,620 --> 00:01:25,980
and especially rural
and remote areas.

34
00:01:25,980 --> 00:01:28,480
So when it comes to voting for
one of the 2 major parties,

35
00:01:28,480 --> 00:01:31,280
there does seem to be

36
00:01:31,280 --> 00:01:33,220
But what about our beliefs and values?

37
00:01:33,220 --> 00:01:35,400
Is there an ideological divide as well?

38
00:01:35,400 --> 00:01:37,620
In 1994, the Pew Research Center

39
00:01:37,620 --> 00:01:40,980
began a survey where they asked
a large sample group of Americans

40
00:01:40,980 --> 00:01:44,580

41
00:01:44,580 --> 00:01:47,680
and then ranked them on a scale
of consistently liberal

42
00:01:47,680 --> 00:01:49,380
to consistently conservative.

43
00:01:49,380 --> 00:01:51,800
This chart shows
the results from 1994.

44
00:01:51,800 --> 00:01:54,780
The blue represents the democrats
and the red is republicans.

45
00:01:54,780 --> 00:01:57,660
As you can see, there's some red
and blue areas off to the sides,

46
00:01:57,660 --> 00:02:00,360
but there is a large overlapping
region in the middle.

47
00:02:00,360 --> 00:02:04,000
As time goes on, you can see the red

48
00:02:04,000 --> 00:02:06,500
and for some reason,
in the past decade or so,

49
00:02:06,500 --> 00:02:09,460
The two blobs have
very noticeably drifted apart.

50
00:02:09,460 --> 00:02:11,680
The blues have become bluer,
the reds redder,

51
00:02:11,680 --> 00:02:15,000
and the moderate overlapping part

52
00:02:15,000 --> 00:02:18,540
Another study by the Pew Research Center

53
00:02:18,540 --> 00:02:23,480
58% of republicans have a very unfavorable

54
00:02:23,480 --> 00:02:28,420
Up from 46% in 2014,
and just 32% in 2008.

55
00:02:28,420 --> 00:02:31,380
The democrats have followed
a very similar trajectory over the years.

56
00:02:31,380 --> 00:02:34,740
Currently, 55% find Republicans
very unfavorable.

57
00:02:34,740 --> 00:02:37,400
What's even more alarming, though
is that the same study found

58
00:02:37,400 --> 00:02:41,280
45% of Republicans
and 41% of Democrats

59
00:02:41,280 --> 00:02:44,740
actually see the other side as a threat
to the nation's well-being.

60
00:02:44,740 --> 00:02:47,440
This is a sharp increase, even,
from just 2 years ago.

61
00:02:47,440 --> 00:02:49,120
So, what's actually going on here?

62
00:02:49,120 --> 00:02:51,180
What's with all the distrust and animosity?

63
00:02:51,180 --> 00:02:52,500
Well, interestingly enough,

64
00:02:52,500 --> 00:02:56,360
despite the fact that voter's
allegiances to their party seem strong,

65
00:02:56,360 --> 00:03:00,080
there's a lot of evidence to suggest that
people are fed up with the whole system.

66
00:03:00,080 --> 00:03:04,960
A recent poll by GenForward showed
that only 28% of young adults overall

67
00:03:04,960 --> 00:03:08,920
feel that the 2 major parties do a good job of

[Insert subtitle here]

[Insert subtitle here]

But if Americans are so unified

00:03:19,320 --> 00:03:22,080
Well, let's take a look at

73
00:03:22,080 --> 00:03:25,280
Here are the 10 ideological prompts

74
00:03:25,280 --> 00:03:28,320
where a person fell along

75
00:03:28,320 --> 00:03:31,940
Some of these prompts are classic big government 
versus small government situations

76
00:03:31,940 --> 00:03:35,280
like "government is almost always
wasteful and inefficient,"

77
00:03:35,280 --> 00:03:38,840
versus "Government often does a better job

78
00:03:38,840 --> 00:03:40,540
But, as you go further down the list,

79
00:03:40,540 --> 00:03:43,320
you start to see prompts that

80
00:03:43,320 --> 00:03:44,960
like racial discrimination

81
00:03:44,960 --> 00:03:49,140
and whether or not homosexuality

82
00:03:49,140 --> 00:03:51,680
Americans are definitely

83
00:03:51,680 --> 00:03:54,280
but is it really the even split

84
00:03:54,280 --> 00:03:56,300
Public opinion of gay marriage, for example,

85
00:03:56,300 --> 00:04:00,280
has consistently increased over the past decade

86
00:04:00,280 --> 00:04:03,200
even while the political parties

00:04:03,200 --> 00:04:04,660
and according to this chart,

00:04:04,660 --> 00:04:09,140
most Americans now believe that stricter

89
00:04:09,140 --> 00:04:13,340
These are the same questions that the
Pew Research Center has been asking since 1994

90
00:04:13,340 --> 00:04:17,260
and in many ways they do seem to reflect

00:04:17,260 --> 00:04:19,300
but do they reflect us?

00:04:19,300 --> 00:04:21,740
could it be possible that

00:04:21,740 --> 00:04:23,600
is not so much about the issues,

00:04:23,600 --> 00:04:26,900

95
00:04:26,900 --> 00:04:30,100
When I was a kid, politics
were not that big of a deal.

96
00:04:30,100 --> 00:04:32,440
In my neighborhood, you could vote
Republican one year,

97
00:04:32,440 --> 00:04:35,000
and then flip and vote Democrat
for the next election.

98
00:04:35,000 --> 00:04:36,620
We could make jokes about our neighbor's

99
00:04:36,620 --> 00:04:39,500
ultra conservative or liberal
hippie refrigerator magnets,

100
00:04:39,500 --> 00:04:41,580
but we still went to their
Christmas party every year.

101
00:04:41,580 --> 00:04:44,120
It wasn't like we actually thought
that their political beliefs

102
00:04:44,120 --> 00:04:45,860
represented a threat to democracy.

103
00:04:45,860 --> 00:04:46,780
But this year,

104
00:04:46,780 --> 00:04:49,320
the vibe of the election just felt different.

00:05:34,420 --> 00:05:36,000
It's called tribalism.

123
00:05:36,000 --> 00:05:40,440
It's a way of thinking or behaving in which people 
are excessively loyal to their tribe.

124
00:05:40,440 --> 00:05:43,520
But, in terms of human behavior, your tribe
could be a lot of things.

125
00:05:43,520 --> 00:05:45,680
It could be the company you work for,

126
00:05:45,680 --> 00:05:49,040
Your school, family, local sports team,

127
00:05:49,040 --> 00:05:50,520
or your political party.

128
00:05:50,520 --> 00:05:52,480
When people see themselves
as part of a tribe,

129
00:05:52,480 --> 00:05:55,460
they will often go out of their way to
defend the beliefs of their tribe

130
00:05:55,460 --> 00:05:58,040

they're right or wrong.

131
00:05:58,040 --> 00:06:01,860
This could be due to our human desire
for acceptance from within our group

00:06:01,860 --> 00:06:04,460

social psychologists call

133
00:06:04,460 --> 00:06:05,820
naive realism.

134
00:06:05,820 --> 00:06:08,480
Naive realism is the human
tendency to belive

135
00:06:08,480 --> 00:06:11,080
that we see the world around us objectively

136
00:06:11,080 --> 00:06:13,120
and anyone who disagrees with us

137
00:06:13,120 --> 00:06:16,280
is either uninformed, irrational, or biased.

138
00:06:16,280 --> 00:06:21,500
This means that if we think that a person or even a media outlet is part of the other tribe,

139
00:06:21,500 --> 00:06:25,920
that we are far less likely to seriously consider 
anything that they have to say,

140
00:06:25,920 --> 00:06:29,900
which is something that I am,
admittedly, guilty of a lot.

141
00:06:29,900 --> 00:06:34,340
In fact, if you present someone with factual 
evidence that discredits their tribal beliefs,

142
00:06:34,340 --> 00:06:38,120

actually strengthening their beliefs.

143
00:06:38,120 --> 00:06:42,300
And in this modern era of talking points,

144
00:06:42,300 --> 00:06:44,540

00:06:44,540 --> 00:06:47,060

00:06:47,060 --> 00:06:48,380

147
00:06:48,380 --> 00:06:50,300

148
00:06:50,300 --> 00:06:54,000

149
00:06:54,000 --> 00:06:56,580

00:06:56,580 --> 00:06:59,960

153
00:07:10,380 --> 00:07:15,420
Some of this may be a result of Facebook's algorithms, an effect which is known as a 'filter bubble',

154
00:07:15,420 --> 00:07:21,540

155
00:07:21,540 --> 00:07:27,320

156
00:07:27,320 --> 00:07:29,760
Or two tribes retreating deeper into their own camps?

157
00:07:29,760 --> 00:07:35,000
It's hard to say for sure. I know there were definitely times in America's past that we were idealogically

158
00:07:35,000 --> 00:07:41,200
divided, and I think this isn't as bad as some of those times. But it's still- it's still cause for concern.

159
00:07:41,200 --> 00:07:47,700
Democracy functions by people with different beliefs coming together and making compromises and finding

160
00:07:47,700 --> 00:07:52,740

then there's no way we're gonna be able to do that. Government isn't gonna be able to function,

and we're just gonna be angry and resentful. But I don't think it's completely hopeless, there are ways even to

00:08:13,820 --> 00:08:19,440

00:08:19,440 --> 00:08:24,600

it has been shown to discourage negative campaign ads, and it could even give third party candidates a shot.

00:08:31,360 --> 00:08:36,760
I don't know what the solution is to this problem in our country, but in times like these, I am often reminded of

00:08:36,760 --> 00:08:43,640
this quote form the great wizard Albus Dumbledore: "We are only as strong as we are united, as weak as we are

divided." Thank you.

Globalisation.

00:04:16,967 --> 00:04:18,952

136

UN Security Council.

137
00:04:23,132 --> 00:04:25,805

138
00:04:25,805 --> 00:04:28,238

139
00:04:28,238 --> 00:04:30,349

140
00:04:30,349 --> 00:04:32,650
Also, we have an international court for

141
00:04:32,650 --> 00:04:34,297

142
00:04:34,297 --> 00:04:37,323
And that's a very recent innovation.

143
00:04:37,323 --> 00:04:38,313
Four.

144
00:04:38,318 --> 00:04:40,716
Borders are mostly fixed now.

145
00:04:40,716 --> 00:04:42,252
After World War II,

146
00:04:42,252 --> 00:04:44,452
territorial wars generally stopped

147
00:04:44,468 --> 00:04:46,381
when most countries pledged to accept

148
00:04:46,381 --> 00:04:47,441
international borders

149
00:04:47,450 --> 00:04:50,019
and respect other nations autonomy.

150
00:04:50,019 --> 00:04:52,045
But is all of this just an anomaly

151
00:04:52,045 --> 00:04:54,494
or are we on the road to lasting peace?

152
00:04:54,494 --> 00:04:55,294
Truth is

153
00:04:55,294 --> 00:04:56,724
we don't know yet.

154
00:04:56,724 --> 00:04:58,350
We need a big enough sample to rule out

155
00:04:58,350 --> 00:05:00,027
the historical average, which is about

156
00:05:00,027 --> 00:05:01,929
one or two big wars per century.

157
00:05:01,929 --> 00:05:03,659
We just haven't had enough time since

158
00:05:03,659 --> 00:05:05,732

159
00:05:05,732 --> 00:05:07,452

00:05:12,395 --> 00:05:14,222

164
00:05:14,222 --> 00:05:17,166

Yes there are nasty conflicts

166
00:05:18,900 --> 00:05:20,967

167
00:05:20,967 --> 00:05:22,360
things are getting better.

question:
1
00:00:06,549 --> 00:00:07,989
In 1992,

2
00:00:07,989 --> 00:00:12,211
a cargo ship carrying bath toys 
got caught in a storm.

3
00:00:12,211 --> 00:00:14,647
Shipping containers washed overboard,

4
00:00:14,647 --> 00:00:20,837
and the waves swept 28,000 rubber ducks 
and other toys into the North Pacific.

5
00:00:20,837 --> 00:00:22,697
But they didn’t stick together.

6
00:00:22,697 --> 00:00:23,977
Quite the opposite–

7
00:00:23,977 --> 00:00:27,307
the ducks have since washed up 
all over the world,

8
00:00:27,307 --> 00:00:29,557
and researchers have used their paths

9
00:00:29,557 --> 00:00:33,727
to chart a better understanding
of ocean currents.

10
00:00:33,727 --> 00:00:36,493
Ocean currents are driven 
by a range of sources:

11
00:00:36,493 --> 00:00:40,043
the wind, tides, changes in water density,

12
00:00:40,043 --> 00:00:43,073
and the rotation of the Earth.

13
00:00:43,073 --> 00:00:47,733
The topography of the ocean floor 
and the shoreline modifies those motions,

14
00:00:47,733 --> 00:00:49,360
causing currents to speed up,

15
00:00:49,360 --> 00:00:52,200
slow down, or change direction.

16
00:00:52,200 --> 00:00:55,030
Ocean currents fall into 
two main categories:

17
00:00:55,030 --> 00:00:58,290
surface currents and deep ocean currents.

18
00:00:58,290 --> 00:01:00,050
Surface currents control the motion

19
00:01:00,050 --> 00:01:02,660
of the top 10 percent 
of the ocean’s water,

20
00:01:02,660 --> 00:01:06,230
[Insert subtitle here]

21
00:01:06,230 --> 00:01:07,930
Though they have different causes,

22
00:01:07,930 --> 00:01:10,960
surface and deep ocean currents 
influence each other

23
00:01:10,960 --> 00:01:15,160
in an intricate dance that keeps 
the entire ocean moving.

24
00:01:15,160 --> 00:01:16,185
Near the shore,

25
00:01:16,185 --> 00:01:19,635
surface currents are driven 
by both the wind and tides,

26
00:01:19,635 --> 00:01:24,505
which draw water back and forth 
as the water level falls and rises.

27
00:01:24,505 --> 00:01:29,773
Meanwhile, in the open ocean, wind is the 
major force behind surface currents.

28
00:01:29,773 --> 00:01:31,517
As wind blows over the ocean,

29
00:01:31,517 --> 00:01:34,507
it drags the top layers 
of water along with it.

30
00:01:34,507 --> 00:01:37,477
That moving water pulls on 
the layers underneath,

31
00:01:37,477 --> 00:01:39,697
and those pull on the ones beneath them.

32
00:01:39,697 --> 00:01:43,197
In fact, water as deep as 400 meters

33
00:01:43,197 --> 00:01:47,027
is still affected by the wind 
at the ocean’s surface.

34
00:01:47,027 --> 00:01:51,337
If you zoom out to look at the patterns 
of surface currents all over the earth,

35
00:01:51,337 --> 00:01:54,820
you’ll see that they form 
big loops called gyres,

36
00:01:54,820 --> 00:01:57,580
which travel clockwise 
in the northern hemisphere

37
00:01:57,580 --> 00:02:00,430
and counter-clockwise 
in the southern hemisphere.

38
00:02:00,430 --> 00:02:02,620
That’s because of the way 
the Earth’s rotation

39
00:02:02,620 --> 00:02:06,630
affects the wind patterns that
give rise to these currents.

40
00:02:06,630 --> 00:02:08,280
If the earth didn’t rotate,

41
00:02:08,280 --> 00:02:10,740
air and water would simply 
move back and forth

42
00:02:10,740 --> 00:02:12,820
between low pressure at the equator

43
00:02:12,820 --> 00:02:14,610
and high pressure at the poles.

44
00:02:14,610 --> 00:02:16,350
But as the earth spins,

45
00:02:16,350 --> 00:02:20,860
air moving from the equator to the 
North Pole is deflected eastward,

46
00:02:20,860 --> 00:02:24,509
and air moving back down 
is deflected westward.

47
00:02:24,509 --> 00:02:27,299
The mirror image happens 
in the southern hemisphere,

48
00:02:27,299 --> 00:02:29,229
so that the major streams of wind

49
00:02:29,229 --> 00:02:32,789
form loop-like patterns 
around the ocean basins.

50
00:02:32,789 --> 00:02:35,679
This is called the Coriolis Effect.

51
00:02:35,679 --> 00:02:40,129
The winds push the ocean beneath 
them into the same rotating gyres.

52
00:02:40,129 --> 00:02:43,793
And because water holds onto heat 
more effectively than air,

53
00:02:43,793 --> 00:02:48,303
these currents help redistribute 
warmth around the globe.

54
00:02:48,303 --> 00:02:49,864
Unlike surface currents,

55
00:02:49,864 --> 00:02:55,014
deep ocean currents are driven primarily 
by changes in the density of seawater.

56
00:02:55,014 --> 00:02:57,326
As water moves towards the North Pole,

57
00:02:57,326 --> 00:02:58,496
it gets colder.

58
00:02:58,496 --> 00:03:01,036
It also has a higher 
concentration of salt,

59
00:03:01,036 --> 00:03:05,956
because the ice crystals that form 
trap water while leaving salt behind.

60
00:03:05,956 --> 00:03:08,796
This cold, salty water is more dense,

61
00:03:08,796 --> 00:03:09,946
so it sinks,

62
00:03:09,946 --> 00:03:12,616
and warmer surface water takes its place,

63
00:03:12,616 --> 00:03:17,076
setting up a vertical current called 
thermohaline circulation.

64
00:03:17,076 --> 00:03:21,563
Thermohaline circulation of deep water 
and wind-driven surface currents

65
00:03:21,563 --> 00:03:26,319
combine to form a winding loop 
called the Global Conveyor Belt.

66
00:03:26,319 --> 00:03:29,486
As water moves from the depths of 
the ocean to the surface,

67
00:03:29,486 --> 00:03:32,606
it carries nutrients that nourish the 
microorganisms

68
00:03:32,606 --> 00:03:35,726
which form the base of many 
ocean food chains.

69
00:03:35,726 --> 00:03:39,306
The global conveyor belt is the
longest current in the world,

70
00:03:39,306 --> 00:03:41,306
snaking all around the globe.

71
00:03:41,306 --> 00:03:44,906
But it only moves a few 
centimeters per second.

72
00:03:44,906 --> 00:03:49,456
It could take a drop of water 
a thousand years to make the full trip.

73
00:03:49,456 --> 00:03:52,996
However, rising sea temperatures are 
causing the conveyor belt

74
00:03:52,996 --> 00:03:54,956
to seemingly slow down.

75
00:03:54,956 --> 00:03:57,746
Models show this causing havoc with 
weather systems

76
00:03:57,746 --> 00:03:59,616
on both sides of the Atlantic,

77
00:03:59,616 --> 00:04:02,856
and no one knows what would happen if it 
continues to slow

78
00:04:02,856 --> 00:04:05,146
or if it stopped altogether.

79
00:04:05,146 --> 00:04:09,136
The only way we’ll be able to forecast

1
00:00:00,720 --> 00:00:04,280
Over the last decade, milk has become a bit controversial.

2
00:00:04,820 --> 00:00:09,740
Some people say it's a necessary and nutritious food, vital for healthy bones,

3
00:00:10,080 --> 00:00:13,400
but others say it can cause cancer and lead to an early death.

4
00:00:13,680 --> 00:00:15,400
So, who's right?

5
00:00:15,720 --> 00:00:18,020
And why are we drinking it anyway?

6
00:00:19,460 --> 00:00:25,220
[Intro music]

7
00:00:25,980 --> 00:00:29,220
Milk is the basis of every mammal's diet after birth,

8
00:00:29,220 --> 00:00:32,120
when our digestive systems are immature and small.

9
00:00:33,240 --> 00:00:37,240
Basically, it's power food to kick-start our bodies and help us grow.

10
00:00:37,980 --> 00:00:42,740
Milk is rich in fat, vitamins, minerals, and milk-sugar: lactose.

11
00:00:43,620 --> 00:00:48,380
On top of that, for a while after birth, it also contains antibodies and proteins

12
00:00:48,380 --> 00:00:51,900
that protect us from infections and regulate our immune system.

13
00:00:52,600 --> 00:00:54,840
But it's a lot of effort for mothers to produce.

14
00:00:55,320 --> 00:00:58,060
Eventually, humans stop drinking mother's milk

15
00:00:58,060 --> 00:01:00,560
and transition to the diet of their parents.

16
00:01:00,900 --> 00:01:03,280
This is how it's been for thousands of years.

17
00:01:04,000 --> 00:01:06,260
Until about eleven thousand years ago,

18
00:01:06,260 --> 00:01:09,960
when our ancestors settled down in the first agricultural communities.

19
00:01:10,460 --> 00:01:13,480
Soon, they domesticated the first dairy animals:

20
00:01:13,480 --> 00:01:15,340
goats, sheep, and cattle.

21
00:01:16,320 --> 00:01:20,120
They found that dairy animals are able to eat useless and abundant stuff

22
00:01:20,120 --> 00:01:22,580
and turn it into nutritious and tasty food.

23
00:01:23,440 --> 00:01:26,080
This made a huge difference in terms of survival,

24
00:01:26,080 --> 00:01:28,200
especially in hard times.

25
00:01:28,660 --> 00:01:32,500
So groups that had milk available had an evolutionary advantage.

26
00:01:33,120 --> 00:01:34,800
And through natural selection,

27
00:01:34,800 --> 00:01:38,040
it changed the genes of communities who consumed a lot of it.

28
00:01:39,080 --> 00:01:43,400
This adaptation has to do with a specialized enzyme: lactase.

29
00:01:43,720 --> 00:01:45,700
Babies have a lot of it in their system,

30
00:01:45,700 --> 00:01:49,540
so they can break down the milk-sugar lactose and digest milk easily.

31
00:01:50,320 --> 00:01:54,300
But the older we grow, the fewer lactase enzymes our body produces.

32
00:01:55,000 --> 00:02:00,160
Worldwide, about 65% of the population do not have the enzyme after infancy,

33
00:02:00,160 --> 00:02:05,160
which means they are not able to digest more than about 150 milliliters each day.

34
00:02:06,240 --> 00:02:10,480
This lactose intolerance is not spread evenly around the world, though.

35
00:02:11,040 --> 00:02:14,880
In some East Asian communities, for example, it's up to 90%.

36
00:02:15,640 --> 00:02:19,160
In Northern Europe and North America, the rates are the lowest overall.

37
00:02:20,940 --> 00:02:24,040
There are probably a few reasons for this uneven distribution.

38
00:02:24,220 --> 00:02:27,080
The trait was first introduced by random mutation,

39
00:02:27,080 --> 00:02:30,220
which happened independently of each other in a few populations.

40
00:02:31,660 --> 00:02:34,620
The fact that farming replaced hunting and gathering more and more

41
00:02:34,620 --> 00:02:36,480
created natural-selection pressure.

42
00:02:37,840 --> 00:02:41,500
People who were able to digest lactose had more foods at hand,

43
00:02:41,500 --> 00:02:42,780
which was an advantage.

44
00:02:43,140 --> 00:02:50,060
The migration of dairy farmers to the north then spread it further, which probably pushed back populations there that didn't have the trait.

45
00:02:52,180 --> 00:02:57,870
Okay, but if milk has been a valuable part of our diet for thousands of years, why is it so controversial?

46
00:03:01,200 --> 00:03:06,700
There are a number of claims regarding the negative and positive health effects of milk.

47
00:03:06,700 --> 00:03:09,380
The negative ones cover a wide variety,

48
00:03:10,000 --> 00:03:15,520
from brittle bones to cancer, and cardiovascular diseases to intolerance and allergies.

49
00:03:16,209 --> 00:03:18,209
So, how do they hold up?

50
00:03:18,610 --> 00:03:25,049
Some older studies found a connection between milk and a high risk of breast, colon, and prostate cancer

51
00:03:26,410 --> 00:03:30,149
But meta analyses found no impact on your cancer risk.

52
00:03:30,730 --> 00:03:36,119
On the contrary, the calcium in milk might even have a protective effect against colon cancer.

53
00:03:36,130 --> 00:03:41,339
Although this could be calcium in general, it's not clear milk plays a role in this effect.

54
00:03:42,220 --> 00:03:48,449
Only studies on prostate cancer showed an increased risk for people who consumed more than one and a quarter liters of milk a day.

55
00:03:48,850 --> 00:03:54,299
But again, the association is inconsistent and other studies don't find any effects.

56
00:03:55,090 --> 00:04:02,310
We discuss these studies in more detail in our sources document. All in all, the research seems to show that if you drink between

57
00:04:02,440 --> 00:04:07,290
100 to 250 milliliters of milk per day, cancer is not a concern.

58
00:04:09,300 --> 00:04:13,880
Similarly, meta-analyses could not find any impact from milk or dairy products on

59
00:04:13,880 --> 00:04:17,060
your risk of heart disease, stroke, or your total mortality.

60
00:04:18,200 --> 00:04:23,420
Some studies even suggested that high blood pressure might be rarer in people who eat a lot of dairy,

61
00:04:23,420 --> 00:04:26,540
although the evidence is not strong enough to claim this with confidence.

62
00:04:28,160 --> 00:04:31,580
The case gets more complicated though when we look at bones.

63
00:04:31,580 --> 00:04:35,960
A number of studies found neither positive nor negative effects for adults.

64
00:04:36,560 --> 00:04:42,680
What most people worry most about though are harmful amounts of pesticides, antibiotics, or hormones.

65
00:04:43,220 --> 00:04:46,600
There are hormones in milk, but only in very low concentrations.

66
00:04:48,180 --> 00:04:51,800
For example to get the same amount of hormones as from the pill,

67
00:04:51,820 --> 00:04:54,520
you'd need to drink about 5000 litres of milk,

68
00:04:54,520 --> 00:04:58,600
and even if you did, most hormones would be destroyed by your digestive system

69
00:04:58,600 --> 00:05:00,600
before they could affect you,

70
00:05:00,600 --> 00:05:05,629
which is the reason why so much medication is coated to protect it from our digestion.

71
00:05:06,300 --> 00:05:08,300
For pesticides and antibiotics,

72
00:05:08,550 --> 00:05:13,700
there are regulations in most parts of the world that only allow completely harmless amounts.

73
00:05:14,190 --> 00:05:18,260
Milk that surpasses these thresholds is not allowed to go on the shelf.

74
00:05:18,560 --> 00:05:21,740
So there's nothing in particular to worry about.

75
00:05:21,740 --> 00:05:25,060
Besides allergies and those suffering from lactose intolerances,

76
00:05:25,060 --> 00:05:31,960
the best known negative effects of milk are probably acne and general discomfort after drinking milk or eating dairy products,

77
00:05:32,400 --> 00:05:34,340
and here the effects are very real.

78
00:05:34,460 --> 00:05:40,660
For example, skimmed milk has been found to statistically increase the rate of acne by 24%.

79
00:05:40,820 --> 00:05:47,860
Allergies against milk products are especially prevalent among children, with one in 18 kids in Germany suffering from them.

80
00:05:47,860 --> 00:05:52,520
In general, these allergies tend to get better or disappear as they grow older though.

81
00:05:53,300 --> 00:05:55,700
Okay. Is milk healthy then?

82
00:05:55,980 --> 00:06:01,820
Milk, no matter if it comes from mothers, cows, sheep, goats, or camels is a nutrient-dense food.

83
00:06:02,580 --> 00:06:07,580
It contains all necessary macronutrients and many micronutrients.

84
00:06:08,040 --> 00:06:11,020
Especially in regions where people struggle to get enough calories,

85
00:06:11,020 --> 00:06:15,260
milk can contribute to a healthy life and lower child mortality.

86
00:06:15,940 --> 00:06:18,420
For those living in the developed world, in general

87
00:06:18,420 --> 00:06:22,200
milk is not harmful if you are not allergic or intolerant to it.

88
00:06:22,900 --> 00:06:26,800
Especially for children, it's a good way to get large amounts of calcium

89
00:06:26,800 --> 00:06:31,760
and for vegetarians, it's a good source of vitamin b12 and B vitamins in general.

90
00:06:31,930 --> 00:06:38,489
This does not mean there are not other alternatives with the same effect. You do not need to drink milk to be healthy

91
00:06:39,760 --> 00:06:42,989
Milk is also definitely not a substitute for water.

92
00:06:43,510 --> 00:06:49,769
Milk is power food, and the additional calories from drinking a lot of it on a regular basis can contribute to being overweight.

93
00:06:51,130 --> 00:06:58,799
Especially flavored milk or chocolate milk is more comparable to beverages like lemonade than a healthy snack, and there's another thing to consider.

94
00:06:59,530 --> 00:07:02,579
Milk production has a significant impact on the global climate.

95
00:07:03,880 --> 00:07:08,909
About 33 percent of cropland is used to feed grazing animals including dairy cattle

96
00:07:09,639 --> 00:07:13,559
Even though the carbon footprint of dairy products has declined since 1990,

97
00:07:13,680 --> 00:07:18,600
Dairy production is still responsible for 3 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions,

98
00:07:18,600 --> 00:07:21,140
even more than all airplanes combined.

99
00:07:21,640 --> 00:07:27,840
Milk is a huge industry and sadly, most of its production in factory farms causes incredible suffering.

100
00:07:29,229 --> 00:07:33,900
Cows are impregnated over and over, separated from their young shortly after birth,

101
00:07:33,900 --> 00:07:37,260
and slaughtered once their tortured bodies are not productive anymore.

102
00:07:37,680 --> 00:07:41,500
We can't ignore that much of the milk we consume stems from an industry

103
00:07:41,500 --> 00:07:45,040
that is basically torture and contributes to climate change.

104

What about plant-based milk?

107
00:08:00,340 --> 00:08:02,580

108
00:08:04,170 --> 00:08:06,740
And another option might be available soon.

109
00:08:07,380 --> 00:08:09,900
Several startups have created non-animal milk

110
00:08:09,900 --> 00:08:12,660
that is nutritionally identical to dairy milk,

111
00:08:12,660 --> 00:08:16,160
for example, through fermentation by gene modified bacteria.

112
00:08:18,320 --> 00:08:21,460
This lab-grown milk can even be turned into cheese,

113
00:08:21,460 --> 00:08:26,560
something that plant based alternatives struggle with because they lack casein and whey protein,

114
00:08:26,560 --> 00:08:29,920
the key ingredients that give dairy its taste and structure.

00:08:53,040 --> 00:08:56,449
As with almost any topic milk is complicated.

120
00:08:56,790 --> 00:09:01,939
It's not harmful for the majority of the population and it's crucial for many people around the world.
