00:00:00,250 --> 00:00:06,120
79,840 dollars: The average salary of a computer programmer in America.

2
00:00:06,220 --> 00:00:11,300
[Insert subtitle here] or rent a closet in San Francisco.

3
00:00:11,460 --> 00:00:15,400
Even the lowest paid ten percent make more than the average American.

4
00:00:15,400 --> 00:00:22,080
Programming is so well paid because it's so in demand and so in demand because it's growing so quickly in importance.

5
00:00:22,080 --> 00:00:24,120
But it's more than a trend.

6
00:00:24,240 --> 00:00:27,240
Surely it's the inevitable direction of things, right?

7
00:00:27,440 --> 00:00:34,620
Say something big like programming is the future and people conclude that fast forward 20 years if you don't know how to program,

8
00:00:34,760 --> 00:00:37,260
Well, good luck getting a job at McDonald's

9
00:00:37,420 --> 00:00:41,820
But as long as there are jobs, economic laws say people will specialize

10
00:00:41,920 --> 00:00:46,380
and there's no reason to think programming is any different. A valuable skill to learn?

11
00:00:46,380 --> 00:00:51,400
Absolutely, and more so every day. In the way of reading and writing? Not even close.

12
00:00:51,680 --> 00:00:56,480
Not everyone should code, and saying otherwise may only harm those you intend to help.

13
00:00:59,320 --> 00:01:05,580
The biggest fans of "everyone should code" are politicians and technology companies, and that's no coincidence.

14
00:01:05,640 --> 00:01:12,100
To a politician, more of any job that means more taxes, more spending, more everything good.

15
00:01:12,160 --> 00:01:16,340
and programming jobs pay especially well, so they're especially loved

16
00:01:16,340 --> 00:01:20,000
But there's also something unique about these jobs in particular.

17
00:01:20,020 --> 00:01:25,360
Technology companies, often started by programmers, have international influence like no one else.

18
00:01:25,360 --> 00:01:29,360
If someone is going to pull the world's financial and emotional levers,

19
00:01:29,360 --> 00:01:34,200
and unfortunately, we know they are, you as a politician want them in your country.

20
00:01:34,200 --> 00:01:37,740
He who regulates the technology company, regulates the world.

21
00:01:38,040 --> 00:01:43,260
America's power, as home to so many global technology giants, is hard to underestimate.

22
00:01:43,360 --> 00:01:47,520
Few companies have so much financial and cultural influence.

23
00:01:47,700 --> 00:01:52,600
Imagine America's reaction if instead they were based in, I don't know, say Russia.

24
00:01:52,600 --> 00:01:57,960
People like President Obama are so vocal about coding because they understand its potentials.

25
00:01:58,060 --> 00:02:01,580
So does China. they've decided it's too high a price to pay.

26
00:02:01,660 --> 00:02:07,640
And for technology companies, "everyone should code" is "everyone should flood the market with the skills we need".

27
00:02:07,740 --> 00:02:14,000
But it's not all self-interest. There's also a dangerous mix of good intentions and the dunning-kruger effect.

28
00:02:17,400 --> 00:02:19,700
Seeing trends, it's easy to make a prediction.

29
00:02:19,820 --> 00:02:23,960
It won't be long before nearly all jobs require programming,

30
00:02:23,960 --> 00:02:28,540
and the solution is to encourage an already financially troubled generation to pursue

31
00:02:28,540 --> 00:02:31,400
the high-paying safe job of computer programming

32
00:02:31,400 --> 00:02:35,260
But a little bit of foresight can be more dangerous than none at all.

33
00:02:35,360 --> 00:02:39,340
Seeing the potential of programming, without knowing what it's really like.

34
00:02:39,340 --> 00:02:41,240
Programmers do make a lot of money.

35
00:02:41,240 --> 00:02:47,240
But so do surgeons. actually three times as much. and dentists, and psychologists, and lawyers

36
00:02:47,250 --> 00:02:53,119
So why is programming treated in a way surgery isn't? because we're told it's not just another trade,

37
00:02:53,120 --> 00:02:59,750
But an essential skill like reading and writing, and if it is then it totally should be required in every school.

38
00:02:59,750 --> 00:03:06,000
But if not -and I don't think it is- then it's just one admittedly pretty good career path of many.

39
00:03:06,000 --> 00:03:10,700
could anyone perform surgery? given enough time and training, yeah, maybe,

40
00:03:10,700 --> 00:03:14,680
but people have different talents. Surgery may be in high demand

41
00:03:14,680 --> 00:03:18,620
But we know it's not for everyone. in fact specialization is good.

42
00:03:18,620 --> 00:03:23,899
It's the reason we have computers at all. Every single one of us could be completely self-reliant

43
00:03:23,960 --> 00:03:30,320
But you're probably not going to be the best hunter, cobbler, cook, engineer, and scientist in the world

44
00:03:30,420 --> 00:03:36,080
When you have to do everything you can be good at nothing, so how about this? You get really good at farming,

45
00:03:36,200 --> 00:03:43,020
I'll make bricks and we can trade. This way we can both have really nice stuff. That's the basis for civilization!

46
00:03:43,020 --> 00:03:49,480
And you might say, well both farmers and masons still need to read and write, but programming can't be such a skill.

47
00:03:49,480 --> 00:03:54,200
It's difficult enough that it just doesn't make economic sense for everyone to learn it,

48
00:03:54,200 --> 00:04:00,380
unless or until robots take over everything jobs need done. more and more will involve computers,

49
00:04:00,380 --> 00:04:05,900
but it won't be doctors and teachers programming them, because as long as programmers get better at programming,

50
00:04:05,900 --> 00:04:09,960
and teachers get better at teaching, by each sticking to their crafts, they will.

51
00:04:09,960 --> 00:04:16,340
So as far as jobs go, It's so really good one, but it is just a job, not a basic universal skill

52
00:04:19,500 --> 00:04:22,160
A good teacher can take a complicated topic,

53
00:04:22,160 --> 00:04:27,840
Deconstruct it, and explain it in easier terms. To make accessible is necessarily to simplify

54
00:04:27,840 --> 00:04:33,020
But it's really easy to do what looks identical, but actually oversimplifies.

55
00:04:33,020 --> 00:04:37,760
in fact, That's the challenge of YouTube. don't simplify, and you have a boring two-hour video.

56
00:04:37,760 --> 00:04:40,560
Over simplify, and you paint a misleading picture.

57
00:04:40,560 --> 00:04:45,700
In its enthusiasm to make programming accessible, "everyone should code" does exactly that.

58
00:04:45,700 --> 00:04:51,920
Tap-tap-tap, that's programming! definitely not sitting at a desk for long hours solving problems.

59
00:04:51,920 --> 00:04:56,300
Here's the thing; whether you've been to college or have any programming experience,

60
00:04:56,300 --> 00:05:01,500
You can pay a company to teach you how to code in 14 weeks. And for not that much money.

61
00:05:01,540 --> 00:05:06,560
That should be a huge red flag. if you can become a developer in 14 weeks,

62
00:05:06,560 --> 00:05:10,020
either companies overpay for what's really a simple job,

63
00:05:10,020 --> 00:05:13,320
or there's actually much more to it. And of course there is.

64
00:05:13,320 --> 00:05:18,960
It's the difference between programming and computer science. the first you really can learn in 14 weeks.

65
00:05:18,960 --> 00:05:23,760
You can read it in a book. its memorizing what to type to make a computer do a thing.

66
00:05:23,760 --> 00:05:25,740
That's what "everyone should code" teaches.

67
00:05:25,740 --> 00:05:31,650
But it claims the benefits of computer science; solving efficient creative mathematical problems.

68
00:05:31,650 --> 00:05:36,560
That's what companies pay six-figure salaries for. and if that's your thing, awesome!

69
00:05:36,560 --> 00:05:38,520
In fact, I'm one of those people.

70
00:05:38,520 --> 00:05:43,640
but many, maybe most wouldn't actually enjoy it. that doesn't mean you shouldn't teach programming,

71
00:05:43,650 --> 00:05:50,010
but it has to be honest it can be accessible and inclusive, but not misleading. Stem is also cheered for the money,

72
00:05:50,010 --> 00:05:54,480
but that too attracts the wrong people. It would be awesome if teachers were paid more,

73
00:05:54,480 --> 00:06:00,680
but one benefit of what we have, is how it selects for people passionate about the job, not just after a paycheck.

74
00:06:00,680 --> 00:06:05,320
Lots of people go into computer science just for the money, but they may end up hating it,

75
00:06:05,320 --> 00:06:10,980
and the irony is when you sell people on an unrealistic job, supply rises and salaries fall

76
00:06:10,980 --> 00:06:16,980
because you might imagine a huge team of people behind every tech company, but very few are actually engineers

77
00:06:16,980 --> 00:06:21,040
When Instagram had 7 million users, it had four employees

78
00:06:21,040 --> 00:06:26,700
Four. As in, 4.0. There will be more demand for programming, but not unlimited demand.

79
00:06:26,700 --> 00:06:29,640
So we might as well attract who's actually interested.

80
00:06:29,640 --> 00:06:31,780
Programming isn't everyone's cup of tea,

81
00:06:31,780 --> 00:06:36,940
and adding too much sugar will only make it extra bitter when they find out what it's really like.

82
00:06:39,960 --> 00:06:44,840
Maybe programming isn't for everyone, but neither is history, or music, or art

83
00:06:44,849 --> 00:06:49,919
And we all take those classes in school. Surely there are other benefits to learning programming.

84
00:06:50,080 --> 00:06:54,479
There's no doubt programming teaches skills like problem-solving and creative thinking.

85
00:06:54,480 --> 00:06:56,700
But this puts the cart before the horse.

86
00:06:56,700 --> 00:07:01,520
if you're already sold on the importance of programming, it's easy to see everything through that lens.

87
00:07:01,520 --> 00:07:05,420
Coding is a way to understand our world and think differently.

88
00:07:05,428 --> 00:07:09,620
But if those are the skills we care about let's find the best way to teach them.

89
00:07:09,620 --> 00:07:14,400
If we suddenly have 60 minutes of school to spare, I'd suggest a class on personal finance

90
00:07:14,400 --> 00:07:19,680
or critically consuming media or speaking. The class with the biggest impact on my life was debate,

91
00:07:19,680 --> 00:07:24,160
and critical thinking is much needed. Coding classes should be available for those interested,

92
00:07:24,240 --> 00:07:30,600
but not as a requirement. Because everyone learns differently, and at a different pace, and likes different things.

93
00:07:30,600 --> 00:07:33,720
I know my high school didn't teach all the subjects I wanted to learn,

94
00:07:33,760 --> 00:07:37,979
[AD] but that's what's so great about Skillshare. It's an online learning community for you.

95
00:07:37,979 --> 00:07:43,679
Maybe you're interested in animation in which case you can learn from the Masters themselves, the Kurzgesagt (In A Nutshell) team.

96
00:07:43,680 --> 00:07:49,139
They give you graphics to work with, so you can download them follow along and make a fantastic video

00:07:49,209 --> 00:07:52,289
So if you want to make a video like this one or even better,

98
00:07:52,560 --> 00:07:54,860
Skillshare is a great way to get a head start.

99
00:07:54,860 --> 00:07:59,960
If you are interested in programming or want to find out if you are they have classes that can ease you into it

00:08:00,060 --> 00:08:05,159
But it's the real deal that will help you really understand a computer science with classes like this one

And you don't have to pay per class so you're free to learn exactly what you want how much you want

And by who you want

00:08:20,100 --> 00:08:25,620
There are a ton of classes on pretty much any topic so you can pick which one works best for you.

With an annual subscription, Skillshare is less than $10 a month, or you can just try it out.

question:
1
00:00:00,725 --> 00:00:04,015
For most of our history, the human population grew slowly,

2
00:00:04,020 --> 00:00:06,740
until new discoveries brought us more food,

3
00:00:06,740 --> 00:00:08,000
and made us live longer.

4
00:00:08,400 --> 00:00:12,240
[Insert subtitle here]

5
00:00:12,700 --> 00:00:16,300
This led to apocalyptic visions of an overcrowded earth.

6
00:00:16,840 --> 00:00:20,700
But the population growth rate actually peaked in the 1960s.

7
00:00:21,440 --> 00:00:26,060
Since then, fertility rates have crashed as countries industrialize and develop.

8
00:00:26,660 --> 00:00:31,900
The world population is now expected to balance out at around 11 billion by the end of the century.

9
00:00:32,900 --> 00:00:35,940
But the big picture conceals the details.

10
00:00:35,940 --> 00:00:38,320
Let's look at one region in particular.

11
00:00:38,320 --> 00:00:40,220
Sub-Saharan Africa.

12
00:00:40,220 --> 00:00:44,940
In 2019, it was home to a billion people living in 46 countries.

13
00:00:44,940 --> 00:00:48,360
Although its growth rate has slowed down in the last few decades,

14
00:00:48,360 --> 00:00:51,420
it's still much higher than in the rest of the world.

15
00:00:51,420 --> 00:00:55,460
While some projections expect around 2.6 billion people,

16
00:00:55,460 --> 00:00:59,420
others reckon with up to 5 billion by 2100.

17
00:00:59,420 --> 00:01:03,240
Such growth would be a huge challenge for any society.

18
00:01:03,240 --> 00:01:07,360
But Sub-Saharan Africa is also the poorest region on earth.

19
00:01:07,360 --> 00:01:10,320
So, is Sub-Saharan Africa doomed?

20
00:01:10,320 --> 00:01:14,760
And, why did the projections vary by 2.4 billion people?

21
00:01:14,760 --> 00:01:17,300
As always, it's complicated.

22
00:01:17,300 --> 00:01:20,240
Sub-Saharan Africa is a made-up idea,

23
00:01:20,240 --> 00:01:21,900
and in many ways, unhelpful one.

24
00:01:22,380 --> 00:01:25,120
Botswana is as far away from Sierra Leone,

25
00:01:25,120 --> 00:01:27,220
as Ireland is from Kazakhstan.

26
00:01:27,220 --> 00:01:28,920
And they have about as much in common.

27
00:01:29,340 --> 00:01:31,740
But without generalizing a little bit,

28
00:01:31,740 --> 00:01:33,340
this video would be an hour long!

29
00:01:34,020 --> 00:01:37,000
We've also talked to many different scientists for this video,

30
00:01:37,000 --> 00:01:39,100
and they disagreed on a lot of things.

31
00:01:39,580 --> 00:01:43,040
Mainly, on how much fertility matters to poverty.

32
00:01:43,900 --> 00:01:47,140
We've done our best to summarize our research and what they told us,

33
00:01:47,140 --> 00:01:48,520
but take it with a grain of salt,

34
00:01:48,520 --> 00:01:51,780
and check out our sources when we discussed this in more detail.

35
00:01:52,540 --> 00:01:55,660
Okay, let's zoom out to the global perspective again.

36
00:01:56,460 --> 00:02:01,980
A few decades ago, many countries in Asia were at a similar point to Sub-Saharan Africa today.

37
00:02:02,460 --> 00:02:05,440
Large parts of the population were living in extreme poverty,

38
00:02:05,440 --> 00:02:07,300
and birth rates were very high.

39
00:02:07,680 --> 00:02:09,220
Take Bangladesh.

40
00:02:09,220 --> 00:02:13,260
In the 1960s, the average woman had 7 children in her lifetime.

41
00:02:13,700 --> 00:02:16,355
25% of them died before they turned 5,

42
00:02:16,360 --> 00:02:18,320
and of the ones that survived,

43
00:02:18,320 --> 00:02:21,200
only one of five would learn to read and write.

44
00:02:21,200 --> 00:02:23,500
Life expectancy was about 45,

45
00:02:23,500 --> 00:02:26,420
and per capita income was among the lowest in the world.

46
00:02:27,180 --> 00:02:29,220
So, beginning in the 1960s,

47
00:02:29,220 --> 00:02:32,060
Bangladesh started a family planning program,

48
00:02:32,060 --> 00:02:33,640
based on three main pillars.

49
00:02:34,440 --> 00:02:37,600
1. Education helped to change women's outlook.

50
00:02:38,180 --> 00:02:40,980
Women with a higher education tend to want fewer kids,

51
00:02:40,980 --> 00:02:42,620
and become mothers later in life.

52
00:02:43,620 --> 00:02:46,480
2. Better health care lowered child mortality,

53
00:02:46,480 --> 00:02:48,620
leading to parents' wanting fewer children,

54
00:02:48,620 --> 00:02:51,040
because they could expect them to survive.

55
00:02:51,840 --> 00:02:56,380
3. Field workers brought contraceptives even to the remotest areas,

56
00:02:56,380 --> 00:03:00,020
which drove contraceptive use from 8% in 1975,

57
00:03:00,020 --> 00:03:02,360
to 76% in 2019.

58
00:03:02,900 --> 00:03:06,940
Together, these measures greatly slowed down population growth.

59
00:03:07,420 --> 00:03:11,380
In 1960, the average Bangladeshi women had 7 kids.

60
00:03:11,380 --> 00:03:13,280
In 1995, 4,

61
00:03:13,280 --> 00:03:16,080
and, in 2019, it was down to 2.

62
00:03:16,340 --> 00:03:20,360
This also changed the country's demographics and the economy.

63
00:03:20,360 --> 00:03:22,480
Before, many children were born,

64
00:03:22,480 --> 00:03:24,820
but died before they got to contribute to society.

65
00:03:25,160 --> 00:03:29,360
As far fewer kids die and fewer kids are born, things change.

66
00:03:29,360 --> 00:03:30,740
Kids get an education,

67
00:03:30,740 --> 00:03:32,520
and turn into productive adults.

68
00:03:33,120 --> 00:03:35,300
The government was able to shift some of their resources

69
00:03:35,300 --> 00:03:38,520
from lowering child mortality to boosting the economy.

70
00:03:39,320 --> 00:03:45,160
By 2024, Bangladesh is expected to graduate from the category of least developed countries

71
00:03:45,160 --> 00:03:47,160
to the status of a developing economy.

72
00:03:47,960 --> 00:03:52,120
Other Asian countries like South Korea, India, Thailand or the Philippines

73
00:03:52,120 --> 00:03:53,880
have gone through a similar process,

74
00:03:53,885 --> 00:03:55,345
often even faster.

75
00:03:55,680 --> 00:03:59,140
Investment in health and education led to lower birth rates,

76
00:03:59,140 --> 00:04:01,380
which changed the composition of the population,

77
00:04:01,380 --> 00:04:03,940
and enabled governments to boost the economy.

78
00:04:04,440 --> 00:04:08,020
Why didn't the same thing happen everywhere in Sub-Saharan Africa?

79
00:04:08,580 --> 00:04:13,000
Africa, as a whole, has made considerable progress with childhood mortality.

80
00:04:13,000 --> 00:04:15,020
but especially in Sub-Saharan Africa,

81
00:04:15,020 --> 00:04:18,260
education has improved slower than in other parts of the world.

82
00:04:18,680 --> 00:04:22,640
And, while in total, contraceptive use has doubled in the region since 1990,

83
00:04:22,640 --> 00:04:27,840
the unmet need for modern contraception among adolescents is still at about 60%.

84
00:04:28,240 --> 00:04:30,400
The reasons for this are complicated,

85
00:04:30,400 --> 00:04:32,500
and it's impossible to give a single answer here.

86
00:04:33,115 --> 00:04:36,105
Africa is a big place with diverse cultures and people.

87
00:04:36,105 --> 00:04:38,520
But there are a few main factors.

88
00:04:38,520 --> 00:04:43,680
Many Sub-Saharan Nations have suffered under colonization until only a few decades ago,

89
00:04:43,680 --> 00:04:46,880
and had rough transition periods towards independence.

90
00:04:47,460 --> 00:04:51,640
The young nations were often ethnically heterogeneous and lacked unity.

91
00:04:51,920 --> 00:04:54,800
Some areas have been repeatedly racked by civil wars,

92
00:04:54,800 --> 00:04:58,040
military conflicts or suffered under unstable governments,

93
00:04:58,040 --> 00:05:01,280
which made it really hard to expand infrastructure and health care.

94
00:05:01,685 --> 00:05:04,765
So, Africa had a worse starting point than Asia.

95
00:05:05,040 --> 00:05:08,420
Foreign aid and how it was applied, especially during the cold war,

96
00:05:08,420 --> 00:05:10,400
is also a contentious issue.

97
00:05:10,900 --> 00:05:14,040
But this topic is too complex to summarize in a few sentences,

98
00:05:14,040 --> 00:05:16,600
so we'll make a whole new video about it in the future.

99
00:05:17,600 --> 00:05:19,740
And lastly, there are cultural aspects that

100
00:05:19,740 --> 00:05:23,360
make talking about family plan in the context of Africa difficult.

101
00:05:23,900 --> 00:05:28,460
Critics say that trying to bring fertility down is an intrusion into culture and tradition.

102
00:05:29,040 --> 00:05:32,500
But not speaking about an issue will not help solve it.

103
00:05:32,840 --> 00:05:35,740
Not all of these things apply to every country in the region.

104
00:05:35,740 --> 00:05:38,300
We're talking about 46 countries after all,

105
00:05:38,300 --> 00:05:39,700
some of them deeply troubled,

106
00:05:39,700 --> 00:05:41,280
others already flourishing,

107
00:05:41,280 --> 00:05:44,160
all different and facing unique problems.

108
00:05:44,160 --> 00:05:46,980
If population growth continues at its present rate,

109
00:05:46,980 --> 00:05:52,080
then Sub-Saharan Africa could grow to more than 4 billion people by 2100.

110
00:05:52,760 --> 00:05:54,620
Okay. So, what can be done?

111
00:05:55,000 --> 00:05:56,660
Actually, a lot!

112
00:05:56,660 --> 00:06:01,180
Especially, investment and aid that helped to build systems for education,

113
00:06:01,180 --> 00:06:03,040
family planning, and health care.

114
00:06:03,480 --> 00:06:07,460
Surprisingly small changes could have an extreme impact.

115
00:06:07,760 --> 00:06:10,300
For example, if women get a better education,

116
00:06:10,300 --> 00:06:13,240
and have their first child just two years later in life.

117
00:06:13,660 --> 00:06:16,880
This tiny gap between this generation and the next one

118
00:06:16,880 --> 00:06:20,280
would lead to 400 million fewer people in 2100,

119
00:06:20,280 --> 00:06:22,660
with 3.6 billion in total.

120
00:06:23,840 --> 00:06:28,060
If education and family planning are made available to every African women,

121
00:06:28,060 --> 00:06:32,320
universal access to contraception makes having kids a decision.

122
00:06:32,320 --> 00:06:35,220
If families get to choose how many kids they want,

123
00:06:35,220 --> 00:06:39,480
birth projections fall by 30%, to 2.8. billion people.

124
00:06:40,380 --> 00:06:42,240
This isn't just theory.

125
00:06:42,240 --> 00:06:45,520
There are already examples that are reason for optimism.

126
00:06:45,520 --> 00:06:48,620
Ethiopia, the African country with the second-biggest population,

127
00:06:48,620 --> 00:06:51,975
has made a lot of progress in a relatively short amount of time.

128
00:06:51,980 --> 00:06:55,320
Improving health services lead to a drop in child mortality

129
00:06:55,320 --> 00:06:58,800
from 20% to 7% since 1990.

130
00:06:59,280 --> 00:07:03,440
And up to 30% of the annual budget was invested in education,

131
00:07:03,440 --> 00:07:07,620
and the number of schools increased 25-fold over two decades.

132
00:07:07,920 --> 00:07:09,900
So, summarizing,

133
00:07:09,900 --> 00:07:11,700
there are serious challenges ahead,

134
00:07:11,700 --> 00:07:13,580
but they are far from unsolvable.

135
00:07:14,060 --> 00:07:16,855
Sub-Saharan Africa does not need pity or gifts,

136
00:07:16,860 --> 00:07:19,340
but attention and fair investment.

137
00:07:19,340 --> 00:07:23,300
It's a region rich in resources, culture, and potential.

138
00:07:23,300 --> 00:07:24,520
If things go right,

139
00:07:24,520 --> 00:07:28,240
we'll see a turn-around similar to the one we've seen across most of Asia

140
00:07:28,240 --> 00:07:30,040
in the last 30 years.

141
00:07:32,715 --> 00:07:33,945
(quack)
answer: In just a hundred years, the human population quadrupled.

00:00:00,700 --> 00:00:05,580
Never before in history, have there been so many people on Earth as right now.

2
00:00:06,080 --> 00:00:19,660
[Insert subtitle here]

3
00:00:20,580 --> 00:00:26,380
The world population increased fourfold in the last century, so what can we expect for the next century?

4
00:00:27,020 --> 00:00:30,260
And what does population growth mean for our future?

5
00:00:30,780 --> 00:00:32,760
Will there be mass-migration?

6
00:00:32,760 --> 00:00:36,080
Overcrowded slums and megacities covering continents?

7
00:00:36,200 --> 00:00:37,760
Diseases and pollution?

8
00:00:38,020 --> 00:00:41,440
Chaos and violence over energy, water, and food?

9
00:00:41,780 --> 00:00:45,740
And a human species focused only on sustaining itself?

10
00:00:46,520 --> 00:00:49,040
Will population growth destroy our way of life?

11
00:00:49,360 --> 00:00:52,900
Or is this prophecy just ungrounded panic?

12
00:01:02,960 --> 00:01:07,280
In the 1960s population growth reached an unprecedented rate.

13
00:01:07,620 --> 00:01:10,200
Which lead to apocalyptic prophecies.

14
00:01:11,420 --> 00:01:15,680
The poor would pro-create endlessly and overrun the developed world.

15
00:01:15,940 --> 00:01:18,620
The legend of overpopulation was born.

16
00:01:19,880 --> 00:01:26,240
But it turns out high birth rates and the population explosion are not permanent features of some cultures or countries,

17
00:01:26,240 --> 00:01:30,280
But rather a part of a four step process the whole world is going through,

18
00:01:30,480 --> 00:01:32,400
The demographic transition.

19
00:01:32,800 --> 00:01:38,280
Most developed countries have already made the transition, while other countries are doing it right now.

20
00:01:38,960 --> 00:01:45,340
Let's go back to the 18th century, when the entire world, including Europe, was in the first stage of the demographic transition.

21
00:01:45,860 --> 00:01:53,720
By today's standards, Europe was worse off, than a developing region, suffering from poor sanitation, poor diets, and poor medicine.

22
00:01:54,300 --> 00:02:00,080
A lot of people were born, but lots of them died just as fast, so the population hardly grew.

23
00:02:00,300 --> 00:02:05,420
Women had between 4 and 6 children, but only 2 of them would reach adulthood.

24
00:02:06,060 --> 00:02:13,880
Then the industrial revolution happened in the UK and bought the greatest change in human living conditions since the agricultural revolution.

25
00:02:14,260 --> 00:02:17,360
People went from being peasants to workers.

26
00:02:18,580 --> 00:02:22,300
Manufactured goods were mass produced and became widely available.

27
00:02:22,800 --> 00:02:27,900
The sciences flourished and advanced transportation, communication, and medicine.

28
00:02:28,440 --> 00:02:33,640
The role of women in society shifted and created the conditions for their emancipation.

29
00:02:34,440 --> 00:02:42,080
Slowly this economic progress not only formed a middle class, but also raised standards of living and health care for the poor working population.

30
00:02:43,020 --> 00:02:45,180
The second transition stage started.

31
00:02:45,940 --> 00:02:52,720
Better food supplies, hygiene and medicine, meant people stopped dying all the time, especially so, at a very young age.

32
00:02:52,980 --> 00:02:55,620
The result was a population explosion.

33
00:02:55,700 --> 00:02:59,840
Doubling the UK's population between 1750 and 1850.

34
00:03:00,460 --> 00:03:05,720
The main reasons families used to have lots of children was that only a few of them were likely to survive.

35
00:03:05,980 --> 00:03:10,160
Now that had changed, so the third stage of transition was set in motion.

36
00:03:10,400 --> 00:03:14,260
Fewer babies were conceived, and population growth slowed down.

37
00:03:15,060 --> 00:03:22,560
Eventually a balance emerged, fewer people were dying and fewer children were born, so the death rate and birth rate became stable.

38
00:03:23,020 --> 00:03:26,400
Britain had reached the fourth stage of the demographic transition.

39
00:03:27,460 --> 00:03:32,280
This didn't only happen in the UK, more and more countries went through the four stages.

40
00:03:33,020 --> 00:03:36,600
First, many births and many deaths due to bad living conditions.

41
00:03:36,800 --> 00:03:41,420
Second, better living conditions leading to fewer deaths and a population explosion.

42
00:03:41,740 --> 00:03:47,220
Third, fewer deaths resulting in fewer births, and population growth came to an end.

43
00:03:47,800 --> 00:03:53,000
But if birth rates have dropped so much, why is the population still growing so fast?

44
00:03:53,200 --> 00:03:58,640
Well, the children born in the population explosion of the 70s and 80s are having kids themselves now.

45
00:03:58,640 --> 00:04:01,680
Leading to a noticeable spike in overall population.

46
00:04:01,820 --> 00:04:05,160
But they are having far fewer children on average than their parents.

47
00:04:05,540 --> 00:04:09,380
The average today is 2.5, it was 5, 40 years ago.

48
00:04:10,360 --> 00:04:17,460
So as this generation gets older, and fertility declines further, the rate of population growth will keep on slowing.

49
00:04:18,000 --> 00:04:20,100
This is true for every country.

50
00:04:20,480 --> 00:04:23,920
In the west, we tend to overlook progress in other regions of the world.

51
00:04:24,120 --> 00:04:27,580
But actually most of the world's countries have made it to the fourth stage.

52
00:04:28,380 --> 00:04:36,080
Just look at Bangladesh. In 1971, the average woman had 7 kids, but 25% of them would die before the age of 5.

53
00:04:36,520 --> 00:04:42,840
In 2015, the mortality rate was down to 3.8% and women had only 2.2 kids on average.

54
00:04:43,360 --> 00:04:48,360
This is the rule, not an exception, we're not special, we just had a head start.

55
00:04:48,680 --> 00:04:54,880
It took developed countries about 80 years to reduce fertility from more than 6 children, to less than 3.

56
00:04:55,220 --> 00:05:02,260
Others are catching up fast. Malaysia and South Africa did it in only 34 years; Bangladesh took just 20.

57
00:05:02,600 --> 00:05:04,640
Iran managed it in 10 years.

58
00:05:04,980 --> 00:05:11,020
All these countries that are catching up didn't have to start from scratch and the more support they get, the faster they catch up.

59
00:05:11,560 --> 00:05:16,980
This is why programs that help lower child mortality or help poor nations develop, are so important,

60
00:05:17,480 --> 00:05:25,220
No matter what your motivation is, whether you dream of a world where all people live in freedom and wealth, or you just want fewer refugees coming into your country,

61
00:05:25,220 --> 00:05:31,380
The simple truth is, that it's beneficial to you personally if people on the other side of the globe can live a good life.

62
00:05:32,380 --> 00:05:39,120
And we are getting there, the percentage of people living in extreme poverty has never been as low as today.

63
00:05:40,060 --> 00:05:46,060
So the future of global population growth is not an apocalyptic prophecy, it's a promise!

64
00:05:46,180 --> 00:05:48,740
Population growth will come to an end.

65
00:05:48,980 --> 00:05:53,680
The UN forecasts that the 12th billionth human will never be born at all.

66
00:05:54,400 --> 00:06:01,400
And as the development level of the world rises, the number of people a higher education will increase tenfold.

67
00:06:01,860 --> 00:06:06,300
Countries who used to be a need, will help advance development instead.

68
00:06:07,000 --> 00:06:12,900
More people is going to mean more people able to advance our species.

69

This video was a collaboration with Max Roser and ourworldindata, where he explores the progress of humanity through research and data visualisation.

70

Make sure to check it out!

In 2016 we were able to make more and better content than ever before, because of your support on Patreon.com.

Thank you so much and we will be back in the year 12,017.

question: When does electric power demand reach the highest point?

1
00:00:00,280 --> 00:00:04,180
When you flip a light switch, you expect it
to work right?

All of your appliances work, because your

3

For a lot of customers.

4

And utility companies have gotten really good
at anticipating that demand.

5
00:00:26,720 --> 00:00:31,400
But a rise in solar energy production is making
their jobs a bit more complex.

6
00:00:32,360 --> 00:00:34,000
Here's a chart that explains why.

7
00:00:35,080 --> 00:00:38,760
It's showing demand for electricity at any
given time of day.

8
00:00:38,770 --> 00:00:42,230
[Insert subtitle here]

9

Then, it ramps up in the morning.

10
00:00:45,050 --> 00:00:48,150
Everyone's woken up and business gets going.

11
00:00:48,150 --> 00:00:52,150
Then at sunset, energy demand peaks.

12
00:00:52,150 --> 00:00:56,739
Utility companies will update models like
this to operate as efficiently as possible.

13
00:00:56,739 --> 00:01:00,989
But the introduction of renewable energy,
particularly the solar energy, has started

14
00:01:00,989 --> 00:01:05,320
causing problems in these demand curves.

15
00:01:05,320 --> 00:01:10,330
In 2010, solar panel deployment really started
taking off.

16
00:01:10,330 --> 00:01:15,320
Most of those installations took place in
California, so researchers there started looking

17
00:01:15,320 --> 00:01:15,840
into it.

18
00:01:18,530 --> 00:01:21,960
They found that the sun produces the most
energy at mid-day.

19
00:01:21,960 --> 00:01:28,159
And when you factor in that new mid-day production,
your demand curve changes like this.

20
00:01:28,160 --> 00:01:35,760
Every year means new solar capacity, which
makes mid-day demand dip lower and lower.

21
00:01:35,760 --> 00:01:39,600
Researchers call this drop in demand the "duck
curve."

22
00:01:40,000 --> 00:01:46,360
From the grid managers' perspective, the people
whose job it is to constantly balance generation

23
00:01:46,360 --> 00:01:49,920
and demand, it looks like a drop in demand.

24
00:01:49,920 --> 00:01:53,710
That drop in demand creates two problems.

25
00:01:53,710 --> 00:01:57,640
The first has to do with the intense ramps
in the new chart.

26
00:01:57,640 --> 00:02:04,710
As the sun sets, solar energy production ends
just as the demand for energy typically peaks.

27
00:02:04,710 --> 00:02:09,349
Power plants then have to rapidly ramp up
production to compensate for that.

28
00:02:09,360 --> 00:02:13,400
Which is kind of hard to do with the current
fleet of power infrastructure.

29
00:02:14,970 --> 00:02:17,160
The second problem is economic.

30
00:02:17,180 --> 00:02:21,560
Say you have a couple of nuclear and coal
plants.

31
00:02:21,560 --> 00:02:26,680
Those plants are only economic when they are
running all the time, basically.

32
00:02:26,680 --> 00:02:28,879
They run around the clock.

33
00:02:28,879 --> 00:02:34,860
And if you have to turn them off at mid-day,
it completely screws up their economics and

34
00:02:34,860 --> 00:02:39,370
plus lots of utilities just have contracts
with those power plants to keep them running

35
00:02:39,370 --> 00:02:40,370
all the time.

36
00:02:40,370 --> 00:02:43,110
So that creates sort of an artificial floor.

37
00:02:43,600 --> 00:02:51,719
If solar generates too much power and there's
no use for it, there's no one to consume it,

38
00:02:51,719 --> 00:02:55,730
then grid managers just have to turn some
solar panels off.

39
00:02:55,730 --> 00:03:00,840
If they didn't, we could risk overloading
or even damaging the power grid.

40
00:03:00,840 --> 00:03:03,500
So we throw away some of that extra solar
energy.

41
00:03:03,500 --> 00:03:08,889
Effectively, what's happening is that solar
power is being wasted.

42
00:03:08,889 --> 00:03:13,260
That waste, curtailment, is the big challenge
moving forward for solar energy.

43
00:03:13,260 --> 00:03:19,640
If you want solar, eventually to power everything
or close to everything, you've gotta figure

44
00:03:19,640 --> 00:03:22,370
out some way of shifting it to the night time.

45
00:03:22,370 --> 00:03:24,609
Cause the sun's down during the night time.

46
00:03:24,609 --> 00:03:29,890
The more power that can be stored, the more
you can sort of let solar rip.

47
00:03:29,890 --> 00:03:35,430
While the grid managers figure out how to
serve this new supply and demand, this duck

48
00:03:35,440 --> 00:03:38,120
is the greatest challenge facing renewable
energy.

Whether it's securing investment, retirement,

can help you prepare for the unexpected.

00:00:16,120 --> 00:00:19,500

500 companies.

00:00:51,280 --> 00:00:55,000

00:00:55,200 --> 00:00:58,660

00:00:58,679 --> 00:01:00,809

00:01:00,809 --> 00:01:04,680

to many children.

Amazon takes the mouse approach of trying

question:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:03,160
In December 2019 the Chinese authorities

2
00:00:03,160 --> 00:00:06,260
notified the world that a virus was spreading through their communities.

3
00:00:06,260 --> 00:00:11,200
[Insert subtitle here]

4
00:00:11,200 --> 00:00:16,340
This virus is the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome-Related Coronavirus 2

5
00:00:16,340 --> 00:00:21,560
that causes the disease called Covid-19 and that everyone simply calls coronavirus.

6
00:00:21,560 --> 00:00:26,060
What actually happens when it infects a human and what should we all do?

7
00:00:27,100 --> 00:00:33,300
[Intro Music]

8
00:00:34,320 --> 00:00:41,480
A virus is really just a hull around genetic material and a few proteins, arguably not even a living thing.

9
00:00:41,480 --> 00:00:44,880
It can only make more of itself by entering a living cell.

10
00:00:45,280 --> 00:00:47,360
Corona may spread via surfaces,

11
00:00:47,360 --> 00:00:49,720
but it's still uncertain how long it can survive on them.

12
00:00:50,140 --> 00:00:56,700
Its main way of spreading seems to be droplet infection when people cough, or if you touch someone who's ill and then your face,

13
00:00:56,740 --> 00:00:58,740
say rubbing your eyes or nose.

14
00:00:59,080 --> 00:01:04,280
The virus starts its journey here, and then hitches a ride as a stowaway deeper into the body

15
00:01:04,860 --> 00:01:10,860
Its destinations are the intestines, the spleen or the lungs, where it can have the most dramatic effect.

16
00:01:10,900 --> 00:01:15,500
Even just a few corona viruses can cause quite a dramatic situation.

17
00:01:15,640 --> 00:01:19,420
The lungs are lined with billions of epithelial cells.

18
00:01:19,420 --> 00:01:25,300
These are the border cells of your body, lining your organs and mucosa waiting to be infected.

19
00:01:25,560 --> 00:01:31,420
Corona connects to a specific receptor on its victim's membranes to inject its genetic material.

20
00:01:31,680 --> 00:01:36,600
The cell, ignorant of what's happening, executes the new instructions, which are pretty simple:

21
00:01:36,660 --> 00:01:38,760
copy and reassemble.

22
00:01:38,780 --> 00:01:46,240
It fills up with more and more copies of the original virus until it reaches a critical point and receives one final order,

23
00:01:46,240 --> 00:01:47,259
self-destruct.

24
00:01:47,260 --> 00:01:53,520
The cell sort of melts away, releasing new corona particles ready to attack more cells.

25
00:01:53,520 --> 00:01:56,640
The number of infected cells grows exponentially

26
00:01:56,980 --> 00:02:03,480
After about 10 days, millions of body cells are infected, and billions of viruses swarmed the lungs.

27
00:02:03,700 --> 00:02:10,060
The virus has not caused too much damage yet, but corona is now going to release a real beast on you,

28
00:02:10,060 --> 00:02:11,620
your own immune system.

29
00:02:11,800 --> 00:02:18,620
The immune system, while there to protect you, can actually be pretty dangerous to yourself and needs tight regulation.

30
00:02:18,940 --> 00:02:25,780
And as immune cells pour into the lungs to fight the virus, Corona infects some of them and creates confusion.

31
00:02:26,480 --> 00:02:28,280
Cells have neither ears nor eyes.

32
00:02:28,280 --> 00:02:32,840
They communicate mostly via tiny information proteins called cytokines.

33
00:02:32,960 --> 00:02:36,040
Nearly every important immune reaction is controlled by them.

34
00:02:36,680 --> 00:02:41,040
Corona causes infected immune cells to overreact and yell bloody murder.

35
00:02:41,280 --> 00:02:49,740
In a sense, it puts the immune system into a fighting frenzy and sends way more soldiers than it should, wasting its resources and causing damage.

36
00:02:50,360 --> 00:02:53,100
Two kinds of cells in particular wreak havoc.

37
00:02:53,420 --> 00:02:58,580
First, neutrophils, which are great at killing stuff, including our cells.

38
00:02:58,580 --> 00:03:04,560
As they arrive in their thousands, they start pumping out enzymes that destroy as many friends as enemies.

39
00:03:04,940 --> 00:03:12,900
The other important type of cells that go into a frenzy are killer T-cells, which usually order infected cells to commit controlled suicide.

40
00:03:13,300 --> 00:03:17,780
Confused as they are, they start ordering healthy cells to kill themselves too.

41
00:03:18,230 --> 00:03:23,769
The more and more immune cells arrive, the more damage they do, and the more healthy lung tissue they kill.

42
00:03:24,260 --> 00:03:30,639
This might get so bad that it can cause permanent irreversible damage, that leads to lifelong disabilities.

43
00:03:31,100 --> 00:03:34,119
In most cases, the immune system slowly regains control.

44
00:03:34,520 --> 00:03:40,840
It kills the infected cells, intercepts the viruses trying to infect new ones and cleans up the battlefield.

45
00:03:41,080 --> 00:03:42,640
Recovery begins.

46
00:03:42,740 --> 00:03:47,820
The majority of people infected by Corona will get through it with relatively mild symptoms.

47
00:03:48,200 --> 00:03:51,580
But many cases become severe or even critical.

48
00:03:51,680 --> 00:03:55,240
We don't know the percentage because not all cases have been identified,

49
00:03:55,240 --> 00:04:00,120
but it's safe to say that there is a lot more than with the flu. In more severe cases,

50
00:04:00,120 --> 00:04:05,400
Millions of epithelial cells have died and with them, the lungs' protective lining is gone.

51
00:04:05,400 --> 00:04:13,500
That means that the alveoli - tiny air sacs via which breathing occurs - can be infected by bacteria that aren't usually a big problem.

52
00:04:13,900 --> 00:04:15,460
Patients get pneumonia.

53
00:04:15,460 --> 00:04:20,660
Respiration becomes hard or even fails, and patients need ventilators to survive.

54
00:04:20,980 --> 00:04:26,600
The immune system has fought at full capacity for weeks and made millions of antiviral weapons.

55
00:04:26,600 --> 00:04:31,120
And as thousands of bacteria rapidly multiply, it is overwhelmed.

56
00:04:31,120 --> 00:04:36,540
They enter the blood and overrun the body; if this happens, death is very likely.

57
00:04:37,180 --> 00:04:42,240
The Corona virus is often compared to the flu, but actually, it's much more dangerous.

58
00:04:42,240 --> 00:04:46,620
While the exact death rate is hard to pin down during an ongoing pandemic,

59
00:04:46,620 --> 00:04:51,760
we know for sure that it's much more contagious and spreads faster than the flu.

60
00:04:51,980 --> 00:04:56,880
There are two futures for a pandemic like Corona: fast and slow.

61
00:04:56,880 --> 00:05:02,560
Which future we will see depends on how we all react to it in the early days of the outbreak.

62
00:05:02,560 --> 00:05:06,360
A fast pandemic will be horrible and cost many lives;

63
00:05:06,360 --> 00:05:10,120
a slow pandemic will not be remembered by the history books.

64
00:05:10,120 --> 00:05:15,260
The worst case scenario for a fast pandemic begins with a very rapid rate of infection

65
00:05:15,260 --> 00:05:18,180
because there are no counter measures in place to slow it down.

66
00:05:18,520 --> 00:05:20,360
Why is this so bad?

67
00:05:20,360 --> 00:05:24,560
In a fast pandemic, many people get sick at the same time.

68
00:05:24,560 --> 00:05:28,840
If the numbers get too large, health care systems become unable to handle it.

69
00:05:28,840 --> 00:05:34,540
There aren't enough resources, like medical staff or equipment like ventilators, left to help everybody.

70
00:05:34,540 --> 00:05:36,760
People will die untreated.

71
00:05:36,760 --> 00:05:43,260
And as more health care workers get sick themselves, the capacity of health care systems falls even further.

72
00:05:43,660 --> 00:05:49,280
If this becomes the case, then horrible decisions will have to be made about who gets to live and who doesn't.

73
00:05:49,280 --> 00:05:53,700
The number of deaths rises significantly in such a scenario.

74
00:05:53,860 --> 00:06:01,420
To avoid this, the world - that means all of us - needs to do what it can to turn this into a slow pandemic.

75
00:06:01,420 --> 00:06:04,560
A pandemic is slowed down by the right responses.

76
00:06:04,560 --> 00:06:12,320
Especially in the early phase, so that everyone who gets sick can get treatment and there's no crunch point with overwhelmed hospitals.

77
00:06:12,320 --> 00:06:17,780
Since we don't have a vaccine for Corona, we have to socially engineer our behaviour,

78
00:06:17,780 --> 00:06:22,080
to act like a social vaccine. This simply means two things:

79
00:06:22,380 --> 00:06:26,460
1. Not getting infected; and 2. Not infecting others.

80
00:06:26,460 --> 00:06:30,980
Although it sounds trivial, the very best thing you can do is to wash your hands.

81
00:06:30,980 --> 00:06:33,760
The soap is actually a powerful tool.

82
00:06:33,760 --> 00:06:37,840
The corona virus is encased in what is basically a layer of fat;

83
00:06:37,840 --> 00:06:41,620
soap breaks that fat apart and leaves it unable to infect you.

84
00:06:41,620 --> 00:06:47,900
It also makes your hands slippery, and with the mechanical motions of washing, viruses are ripped away.

85
00:06:47,900 --> 00:06:54,960
To do it properly, wash your hands as if you've just cut up some jalapeños and want to put in your contact lenses next.

86
00:06:54,960 --> 00:06:59,520
The next thing is social distancing, which is not a nice experience,

87
00:06:59,520 --> 00:07:03,800
but a nice thing to do. This means: no hugging, no handshakes.

88
00:07:03,800 --> 00:07:09,520
If you can stay at home, stay at home to protect those who need to be out for society to function:

89
00:07:09,520 --> 00:07:17,420
from doctors to cashiers, or police officers;. You depend on all of them; they all depend on you to not get sick.

90
00:07:17,420 --> 00:07:24,600
On a larger level, there are quarantines, which can mean different things, from travel restrictions or actual orders to stay at home.

91
00:07:24,600 --> 00:07:28,400
Quarantines are not great to experience and certainly not popular.

92
00:07:28,400 --> 00:07:34,320
But they buy us - and specially the researchers working on medication and vaccinations - crucial time

93
00:07:34,320 --> 00:07:39,340
So if you are put under quarantine, you should understand why, and respect it.

94
00:07:39,340 --> 00:07:45,700
None of this is fun. But looking at the big picture, it is a really small price to pay.

95
00:07:45,700 --> 00:07:50,020
The question of how pandemics end, depends on how they start;

96
00:07:50,020 --> 00:07:53,560
if they start fast with a steep slope, they end badly.

97
00:07:53,560 --> 00:07:57,980
If they start slow, with a not-so-steep slope, they end okay-ish.

98
00:07:57,980 --> 00:08:02,400
And, in this day and age, it really is in all of our hands.

99
00:08:02,400 --> 00:08:04,060
Literally, and

100
00:08:04,060 --> 00:08:06,060
figuratively.

101
00:08:06,160 --> 00:08:09,880
A huge thanks to the experts who helped us on short notice with this video,

102
00:08:09,880 --> 00:08:11,900
specially Our World In Data,

103
00:08:11,900 --> 00:08:15,620
the online publication for research and data on the world's largest problems

104
00:08:15,620 --> 00:08:17,400
and how to make progress solving them.

105
00:08:17,400 --> 00:08:23,120
Check out their site. It also includes a constantly updated page on the Corona pandemic

106
00:08:23,980 --> 00:08:33,340
[Outro music]

This video is sponsored by Skillshare. Use

2

3
00:00:09,120 --> 00:00:12,889
Visiting Japan feels a bit like taking a trip
to the future.

4
00:00:12,889 --> 00:00:15,309
Robots serve and deliver your food,

5
00:00:15,309 --> 00:00:19,110
Vending machines sell everything from umbrellas
to puppies,

6
00:00:19,110 --> 00:00:24,130
Bullet trains whisk you around the island
at 320 kilometers an hour,

7
00:00:24,130 --> 00:00:30,190
[Insert subtitle here], the second-highest
in the world, warns of the global aging soon

8
00:00:30,190 --> 00:00:31,190
to come.

9
00:00:31,190 --> 00:00:35,430
There’s one way, however, where Japan is
stuck in the past.

10
00:00:35,430 --> 00:00:41,500
Walking around Tokyo, or Osaka, or Kobe, you
might notice something odd: a strangely high

11
00:00:41,500 --> 00:00:43,640
number of music stores.

12
00:00:43,640 --> 00:00:49,239
Compared to the U.S., Japan has 40% as many
people but nearly double the number of music

13
00:00:49,239 --> 00:00:50,350
shops.

14
00:00:50,350 --> 00:00:55,720
As a whole, the Japanese music market is the
second biggest in the world but unlike almost

15
00:00:55,720 --> 00:00:56,910
any other.

16
00:00:56,910 --> 00:01:00,470
In most parts of the world, streaming has
replaced physical sales.

17
00:01:00,470 --> 00:01:05,770
In 2015, for example, 66% of U.S. music sales
were digital.

18
00:01:05,770 --> 00:01:08,259
In Japan, it’s nearly the opposite.

19
00:01:08,259 --> 00:01:13,469
75% of sales were physical, and only 18% were
digital.

20
00:01:13,469 --> 00:01:18,340
This is due, in part, to the country’s stringent
copyright laws, licensing restrictions, and

21
00:01:18,340 --> 00:01:19,340
rental culture.

22
00:01:19,340 --> 00:01:25,289
But there’s another reason CDs are still
loved in countries like Japan and South Korea:

23
00:01:25,289 --> 00:01:26,490
K-Pop.

24
00:01:26,490 --> 00:01:32,600
Korean pop groups have offset losses from
piracy with glossy, premium, collectible CDs,

25
00:01:32,600 --> 00:01:35,350
usually sold to fans who will never play them.

26
00:01:35,350 --> 00:01:41,200
Instead, CDs are sold as merch - often with
different covers to encourage buying several,

27
00:01:41,200 --> 00:01:45,170
and sometimes act as lottery tickets for a
chance to meet your favorite singer.

28
00:01:45,170 --> 00:01:49,969
What’s so interesting about K-Pop, as a
business, is that almost everything, from

29
00:01:49,969 --> 00:01:54,170
the very beginning, is manufactured as a consumer
product.

30
00:01:54,170 --> 00:02:00,130
Artists aren’t found but created - sculpted
for maximum reach, over many years, in a factory

31
00:02:00,130 --> 00:02:01,130
system.

32
00:02:01,130 --> 00:02:03,749
And their international success is no accident.

33
00:02:03,749 --> 00:02:09,479
K-Pop is a deliberate, government-funded project
aimed at growing South Korea’s global power.

34
00:02:09,480 --> 00:02:12,000
Making it, in the process, highly political.

35
00:02:14,340 --> 00:02:18,760
The 1988 Summer Olympics was a turning point
for South Korea.

36
00:02:18,769 --> 00:02:25,270
Like Japan’s 1964 and China’s 2008 games,
it was a rare, historic opportunity to change

37
00:02:25,270 --> 00:02:27,319
the country’s image abroad.

38
00:02:27,319 --> 00:02:32,930
Harsh censorship laws and restrictive TV network
monopolies soon opened up, giving way to a

39
00:02:32,930 --> 00:02:34,650
new generation of artists.

40
00:02:34,650 --> 00:02:40,390
4 years later, in 1992, the Korean government’s
Culture and Tourism Institute began looking

41
00:02:40,390 --> 00:02:42,640
for new, overseas markets.

42
00:02:42,640 --> 00:02:47,370
But rather than waiting for demand, Korean
entertainment hooked foreign viewers and created

43
00:02:47,370 --> 00:02:48,370
it.

44
00:02:48,370 --> 00:02:52,790
The institute translated a popular drama called
“What is love” into Cantonese, which it

45
00:02:52,790 --> 00:02:58,140
sent to the Korean consulate in Hong Kong,
where it was offered free to a local TV station.

46
00:02:58,140 --> 00:03:02,739
Soon, Hong Kong and its neighbor Guangzhou,
were asking for more.

47
00:03:02,739 --> 00:03:08,230
Not long after that, demand spread to Taiwan,
Vietnam, Japan, and further into mainland

48
00:03:08,230 --> 00:03:12,920
China, which established diplomatic relations
with South Korea that same year.

49
00:03:12,920 --> 00:03:18,230
The media called this mass cultural dispersion
“Hallyu”, or “the Korean Wave”.

50
00:03:18,230 --> 00:03:23,460
The next turning point came after the 1997
Asian Financial Crisis, when manufacturing

51
00:03:23,460 --> 00:03:27,670
industries across South and Southeast Asia
saw huge losses.

52
00:03:27,670 --> 00:03:32,840
In response, President Kim Dae-Jung turned
to the entertainment sector, hiring a PR firm

53
00:03:32,840 --> 00:03:35,370
to launch a new national image.

54
00:03:35,370 --> 00:03:40,840
The cultural budget increased 600%, and a
new Ministry of Culture was formed, including

55
00:03:40,840 --> 00:03:41,840
an entire K-Pop department.

56
00:03:41,840 --> 00:03:48,560
The second Korean Wave came in 2012 with the
explosive viral hit “Gangnam Style”.

57
00:03:48,560 --> 00:03:54,200
Overnight, the whole world became curious
about Korean music, dramas, fashion, and language.

58
00:03:54,200 --> 00:03:58,780
And while it wasn’t truly representative
of K-Pop as a genre, it was useful for one

59
00:03:58,780 --> 00:04:03,760
big thing: proving a song didn’t need to
be written in English to succeed in the West,

60
00:04:03,760 --> 00:04:06,540
later confirmed by hits like “Despacito”.

61
00:04:06,540 --> 00:04:11,280
No one could’ve predicted the success of
Gangnam Style, but the rise of Korean entertainment,

62
00:04:11,280 --> 00:04:16,640
in some form, was inevitable. Engineered-for,
in fact, by the K-Pop Formula.

63
00:04:16,640 --> 00:04:21,310
The difference between it and other genres
is that K-Pop is reverse-engineered based

64
00:04:21,310 --> 00:04:23,170
on consumer preferences.

65
00:04:23,170 --> 00:04:27,000
Where most musicians start off practicing
in their parents’ garages, driven only by

66
00:04:27,000 --> 00:04:32,670
a passion for the art and eventually get discovered
by a record label, K-Pop groups usually begin,

67
00:04:32,670 --> 00:04:36,130
rise, and change directions from a conference
room.

68
00:04:36,130 --> 00:04:41,620
There are four big labels: YG, SM, JYP, and
Big Hit Entertainment.

69
00:04:41,620 --> 00:04:46,770
Although, again, the word “label” is slightly
deceiving - these companies aren’t so much

70
00:04:46,770 --> 00:04:51,770
agents as product designers - they create
and shape every aspect of their groups.

71
00:04:51,770 --> 00:04:54,560
First, they begin with recruitment.

72
00:04:54,560 --> 00:04:59,980
Because K-Pop singers are as much public idols
as musicians, the composition of personalities

73
00:04:59,980 --> 00:05:01,550
is very important.

74
00:05:01,550 --> 00:05:05,900
Companies look for a set of distinct yet cohesive
personalities so as to appeal to as large

75
00:05:05,900 --> 00:05:11,320
a fan base as possible, while not generating
unnecessary internal conflict.

76
00:05:11,320 --> 00:05:16,780
Some labels turn recruitment into a reality-TV
competition - ideal for creating fan loyalty

77
00:05:16,780 --> 00:05:18,290
and dramatizing personalities.

78
00:05:18,290 --> 00:05:25,750
In 2012, 4% of the entire South Korean population
tried-out for Superstar K, its most popular

79
00:05:25,750 --> 00:05:27,530
singing competition.

80
00:05:27,530 --> 00:05:32,280
Other companies recruit based only on qualities
like appearance: because the next component

81
00:05:32,280 --> 00:05:33,770
is Training.

82
00:05:33,770 --> 00:05:38,660
Potential stars, sometimes as young as 11
years old, go through roughly 5-10 years of

83
00:05:38,660 --> 00:05:40,480
arduous preparation.

84
00:05:40,480 --> 00:05:46,740
A training schedule might be as follows: 5
am, Wake up; Practice Choreography, Go to

85
00:05:46,740 --> 00:05:53,260
school, Get out at 3 pm, Practice vocals until
6, Language lessons until 9, and then exercise

86
00:05:53,260 --> 00:05:58,060
until 11, leaving an hour to get home before
the trains shut down for the night in Seoul

87
00:05:58,060 --> 00:05:59,830
and 5 hours for sleep.

88
00:05:59,830 --> 00:06:05,030
Still, after all that, after sacrificing all
other hobbies and dreams, after learning English

89
00:06:05,030 --> 00:06:09,610
or Japanese, only about 10% of trainees will
ever début.

00:06:09,610 --> 00:06:15,750
K-Pop stars complain of long, miserable hours,
low pay, and unfair 7-year contracts which

00:06:15,750 --> 00:06:20,470

92
00:06:20,470 --> 00:06:22,170

93
00:06:22,170 --> 00:06:27,160
Labels, in turn, argue these stipulations

94
00:06:27,160 --> 00:06:32,370
hundreds of thousands, or even millions of
dollars and years they invest in each trainee.

95
00:06:32,370 --> 00:06:36,690
The third ingredient, and perhaps most important,
is localization.

96
00:06:36,690 --> 00:06:41,610
Because K-Pop is so diverse - incorporating
everything from pop to techno, rock, and hip-hop,

97
00:06:41,610 --> 00:06:45,340
it’s hard to define what, exactly, it is.

98
00:06:45,340 --> 00:06:50,570
One of the few, unifying characteristics which
sets it apart from, say, Japanese Pop, is

99
00:06:50,570 --> 00:06:53,510
the way it caters to an international audience.

100
00:06:53,510 --> 00:06:57,920
Group names generally consist of a short,
easily-recognized English word or acronym

101
00:06:57,920 --> 00:07:02,050
- TWICE, BTS, EXO, AOA.

102
00:07:02,050 --> 00:07:07,030
Another common strategy is to have at least
one Chinese, Japanese, Thai, or Taiwanese

103
00:07:07,030 --> 00:07:08,350
group member.

104
00:07:08,350 --> 00:07:14,980
Songs and their extravagant music videos are
often produced two or three times: in Korea,

105
00:07:14,980 --> 00:07:18,330
Japanese, and Mandarin, with English words
sprinkled throughout.

106
00:07:18,330 --> 00:07:22,770
In addition to being hugely profitable, this
international focus provides Seoul with something

107
00:07:22,770 --> 00:07:25,940
even more valuable, although, intangible.

108
00:07:25,940 --> 00:07:30,550
While soft power can’t be precisely measured,
it tells a nation’s story in a way no amount

109
00:07:30,550 --> 00:07:33,180
of tanks or factories ever can.

110
00:07:33,180 --> 00:07:37,190
K-Pop is so political because it paints such
a vivid national image.

111
00:07:37,190 --> 00:07:42,520
Thus, why South Korea brought the girl group
Red Velvet to sing for Kim Jong-Un in Pyongyang

112
00:07:42,520 --> 00:07:43,680
last year.

113
00:07:43,680 --> 00:07:49,140
Separately, in 2016, the U.S. began deploying
a defense system in South Korea against potential

114
00:07:49,140 --> 00:07:53,390
North Korean missiles called the Terminal
High Altitude Area Defense.

115
00:07:53,390 --> 00:07:57,650
Soon after, South Korean products began disappearing
from Chinese shelves.

116
00:07:57,650 --> 00:08:02,930
Although never explicitly announced, China’s
government effectively banned K-Pop.

117
00:08:02,930 --> 00:08:06,960
Tour groups were forbidden from traveling
to the South and previously welcome K-Pop

118
00:08:06,960 --> 00:08:11,530
groups suddenly found their performances canceled or
visas denied.

119
00:08:11,530 --> 00:08:16,140
Music videos were even blocked from the internet,
as groups turned to Hong Kong and Macau concerts

120
00:08:16,140 --> 00:08:18,530
until the ban was relaxed in 2017.

121
00:08:18,530 --> 00:08:24,180
It’s another example of China using its
large consumer market as leverage - not unlike

122
00:08:24,180 --> 00:08:29,930

the unwavering fortitude of Chinese patriotism

123
00:08:29,930 --> 00:08:34,719
- stronger even, than the support of a Kobe
Bryant or BTS super-fan.

124
00:08:34,719 --> 00:08:40,280
Finally, the last step is to sell every millimeter
of unused space.

125
00:08:40,280 --> 00:08:45,790
Extreme fan loyalty translates into extremely
effective paid endorsements, product placements,

126
00:08:45,790 --> 00:08:46,790
and sponsorships.

127
00:08:46,790 --> 00:08:52,180
The quintessential example of the formula’s
success is the 7-member boy band, BTS.

128
00:08:52,180 --> 00:08:56,540
Their Twitter account generates 4 times the
engagement of President Donald Trump’s,

129
00:08:56,540 --> 00:08:57,800
They appeared on the Ellen show,

130
00:08:57,800 --> 00:09:03,940
Gave a speech at the United Nations, and contribute
an estimated $3.6 billion US Dollars a year

00:09:05,740 --> 00:09:10,520

00:09:10,520 --> 00:09:16,060
It’s now building an entire themed-district

00:09:23,350 --> 00:09:28,070
Some say K-Pop is too commercialized, too

00:09:28,070 --> 00:09:33,830
But while some artists invent touching origin

00:09:33,830 --> 00:09:34,830

139
00:09:34,830 --> 00:09:40,660
Like professional wrestling, yes it’s exaggerated

140
00:09:40,660 --> 00:09:45,600
But there’s something respectably authentic
about how transparently manufactured it all

141
00:09:45,600 --> 00:09:46,600

142
00:09:46,600 --> 00:09:52,440
It may be fake but very real is the joy it

Behind every great K-Pop idol is an intense

19
00:01:05,290 --> 00:01:09,460
Start with the regular base fare, add the

20
00:01:09,460 --> 00:01:13,659

21

00:01:17,820 --> 00:01:22,450
Then add the booking fee, and possibly airport,

fees.

00:01:23,450 --> 00:01:27,940
UNLESS there are too many riders and not enough

00:01:27,940 --> 00:01:28,940
price,

26

2, 3, or, on New Years Eve Two-Thousand-Eleven,

27
00:01:33,640 --> 00:01:36,890
And as YoutUBERs have shown, algorithms can

28

If drivers log out at the same time, they

29
00:01:41,420 --> 00:01:45,900
Oh, it also uses machine learning to predict

30

route,

31

so maybe don’t call an Uber from the Burj

33
00:01:52,270 --> 00:01:57,030
Even despite this, Uber is almost always cheaper,

34
00:01:57,030 --> 00:01:59,820
It took the most outdated, inefficient industry,

35
00:01:59,820 --> 00:02:02,210
sprinkled in something called “Technology”

36
00:02:02,210 --> 00:02:04,420
and completely reinvented the wheel.

37
00:02:04,420 --> 00:02:11,450
Oh, come on, you should know by now, there’s

38
00:02:11,450 --> 00:02:14,540
In the 1930’s, The Great Depression… happened.

39
00:02:14,540 --> 00:02:17,180
It wasn’t great, but it was depressing.

40
00:02:17,180 --> 00:02:20,800
[Insert subtitle here]

41
00:02:20,800 --> 00:02:24,470
Especially low-skill, low barrier-to-entry
jobs,

42
00:02:24,470 --> 00:02:30,070
But, YouTube hadn’t been invented, so, they
drove taxis - lots and lots of taxis.

43
00:02:30,070 --> 00:02:32,670
Meanwhile, fewer people could afford a ride.

44
00:02:32,670 --> 00:02:37,569
And, as I was taught by a monopoly educating
me about the danger of monopolies, When this

45
00:02:37,569 --> 00:02:42,170
line goes up, and this ones goes down, prices
fall and drivers get angry.

46
00:02:42,170 --> 00:02:45,040
Like, violent protests in the street angry.

47
00:02:45,040 --> 00:02:47,190
So New York City wrote the Haas Act.

48
00:02:47,190 --> 00:02:53,380
Now, to legally operate a taxi, you’d need
one of 17,000 licenses called medallions.

49
00:02:53,380 --> 00:02:58,090
But 81 years later, with a million more people,
it’s only 13,000.

50
00:02:58,090 --> 00:02:59,440
You can see the problem.

51
00:02:59,440 --> 00:03:03,629
The number of medallions issued is more political
than it is practical.

52
00:03:03,629 --> 00:03:07,550
Before, extreme competition made prices unsustainably
low.

53
00:03:07,550 --> 00:03:09,849
Good for riders, bad for drivers.

54
00:03:09,849 --> 00:03:14,920
And then, the pendulum reversed - too little
competition made taxis expensive and inefficient

55
00:03:14,920 --> 00:03:17,590
- bad for riders, good for drivers.

56
00:03:17,590 --> 00:03:22,980
One medallion, the right to operate a single
taxi, was once worth over a million dollars.

57
00:03:22,980 --> 00:03:25,680
But advice like this hasn’t aged so well.

58
00:03:25,680 --> 00:03:27,220
Because: Uber happened.

59
00:03:27,220 --> 00:03:32,040
Its drivers flood the market by not requiring
medallions, draining their value.

60
00:03:32,040 --> 00:03:37,170
High competition, low prices, and angry calls
for regulation - Sound familiar?

61
00:03:37,170 --> 00:03:41,920
This time, we aren’t in an economic depression,
but many households are, which means lots

62
00:03:41,920 --> 00:03:42,959
of drivers.

63
00:03:42,959 --> 00:03:48,239
For you and I, Uber is revolutionary - the
low prices of last century plus the magic

64
00:03:48,239 --> 00:03:49,510
of these things.

65
00:03:49,510 --> 00:03:55,950
And for drivers, well, yes and no…

66
00:03:55,950 --> 00:04:03,150
If you ask Uber what the average driver makes
an hour, they point you to this study: $19.19.

67
00:04:03,150 --> 00:04:04,530
Another says 21.

68
00:04:04,530 --> 00:04:07,090
Not too bad - unless, you look under the hood.

69
00:04:07,090 --> 00:04:11,560
What they don’t include are the car, its
depreciation, maintenance, gas, and some of

70
00:04:11,560 --> 00:04:12,560
the insurance.

71
00:04:12,560 --> 00:04:14,940
Adjust for these and things aren’t so rosy
-

72
00:04:14,940 --> 00:04:19,680
This study estimates the median hourly profit
is eight fifty five before taxes,

73
00:04:19,680 --> 00:04:23,300
less than minimum wage for 54% of drivers.

74
00:04:23,300 --> 00:04:25,059
8% actually lose money.

75
00:04:25,059 --> 00:04:30,199
You might say: But Uber is supplementary - a
quick way to make extra cash between jobs.

76
00:04:30,199 --> 00:04:34,369
And, that’s mostly true, about 60% have
another primary income.

77
00:04:34,369 --> 00:04:39,720
Plus, unlike taxis, who are even legally required
to wear black socks in LA, with Uber, you

78
00:04:39,720 --> 00:04:40,720
have some freedom.

79
00:04:40,720 --> 00:04:44,669
But the reason people don’t drive more might
only be they can’t.

80
00:04:44,669 --> 00:04:49,460
Because Uber considers its drivers not employees,
but independent contractors.

81
00:04:49,460 --> 00:04:54,650
Employees are entitled to minimum wage, gas
reimbursement, overtime, breaks, collective

82
00:04:54,650 --> 00:04:56,960
bargaining, paid leave, and health insurance,

83
00:04:56,960 --> 00:05:00,400
Which would cost the company about 4 billion
dollars a year.

84
00:05:00,400 --> 00:05:05,650
So they’re extremely careful to call drivers
“partners”, and itself, not a transportation

85
00:05:05,650 --> 00:05:06,960
company, but a “platform” -

86
00:05:06,960 --> 00:05:12,009
Simply connecting riders to drivers, who decide
when to work, what to wear, and so on.

87
00:05:12,009 --> 00:05:14,169
But, Uber controls the prices.

88
00:05:14,169 --> 00:05:18,759
And that’s the catch - if drivers are just
independent businesses, Uber setting their

89
00:05:18,759 --> 00:05:21,210
fares could be considered price fixing.

90
00:05:21,210 --> 00:05:22,550
So, which are they?

91
00:05:22,550 --> 00:05:27,740
That depends on who you ask and when, and
the answer will shape the future of the industry.

92
00:05:27,740 --> 00:05:32,589
But something doesn’t add up, The golden
age for drivers came from regulating competition,

93
00:05:32,589 --> 00:05:36,279
the same regulation Uber spends millions of
dollars fighting.

94
00:05:36,279 --> 00:05:39,779
Going back to the days of high competition
and low prices.

95
00:05:39,779 --> 00:05:40,869
But …why?

96
00:05:40,869 --> 00:05:44,580
If Uber takes a cut from drivers, their interests
should be the same.

97
00:05:44,580 --> 00:05:49,330
Regulation, of course, slows its growth, but
there’s also another reason:

98
00:05:49,330 --> 00:05:53,810
Drivers compete - but Uber makes the same
commission regardless of who picks you up.

99
00:05:53,810 --> 00:05:56,379
Uber makes more money with more drivers.

100
00:05:56,379 --> 00:05:59,310
But drivers want the opposite - less competition.

101
00:05:59,310 --> 00:06:05,120
They look like other platform-vendor relationships
- Amazon and its sellers, Apple and app developers,

102
00:06:05,120 --> 00:06:09,849
Both of which need their vendors - if YouTube
leaves the app store, Apple can’t replace

103
00:06:09,849 --> 00:06:10,849
it.

104
00:06:10,849 --> 00:06:15,909
But drivers are drivers - Uber needs them
- but no one in particular; they’re disposable.

105
00:06:15,909 --> 00:06:20,259
Something like 96% stop driving for the company
in their first year.

106
00:06:20,259 --> 00:06:25,430
The two seem economically intertwined, but
as long as Uber can find more drivers, they

107
00:06:25,430 --> 00:06:28,740
can keep fares unsustainably competitive with
rivals.

108
00:06:28,740 --> 00:06:32,919
The real winners of the Haas Act weren’t
cabdrivers, who couldn’t afford million

109
00:06:32,919 --> 00:06:34,960
dollar medallions, but their owners.

110
00:06:34,960 --> 00:06:40,139
Instead of drivers giving away their first
$100 a day to rent a medallion, now it’s

111
00:06:40,139 --> 00:06:41,580
25% all day.

112
00:06:41,580 --> 00:06:46,159
For many drivers, it’s still a very welcome
and useful opportunity, but it isn’t quite

113
00:06:46,159 --> 00:06:49,009

114
00:06:49,009 --> 00:06:53,979
And it may not last…

115
00:06:53,979 --> 00:06:57,090
On paper, Uber has the perfect business model:

116
00:06:57,090 --> 00:07:00,039
Its huge network of drivers dominate the globe,

117
00:07:00,039 --> 00:07:03,399
but it need not buy a single car or gallon
of fuel.

118
00:07:03,399 --> 00:07:05,499
All perk, and no work.

119
00:07:05,499 --> 00:07:08,589
Something thousands of startups desperately
try to emulate.

120
00:07:08,589 --> 00:07:12,569
Most of which belong on Flopstarter, with
products like the TIMELESS watch, which…

00:07:12,569 --> 00:07:13,869
doesn’t tell the time.

122
00:07:13,869 --> 00:07:17,529
So how did Uber lose four and a half billion
dollars last year?

123
00:07:17,529 --> 00:07:19,710
That’s 12 million dollars a day!

124
00:07:19,710 --> 00:07:24,379
Many startups sacrifice profit for growth,
But Uber is nine years old.

125
00:07:24,379 --> 00:07:26,340
Facebook made money after two.

126
00:07:26,340 --> 00:07:31,319
The company’s biggest problem may not be
its legality, or controversy although there’s

127
00:07:31,319 --> 00:07:34,559

model.

128
00:07:34,559 --> 00:07:37,749
The magic of so many companies is the network
effect.

129
00:07:37,749 --> 00:07:41,249
Every new customer makes it that much easier

130
00:07:41,249 --> 00:07:45,830
You join Facebook because Steve is on it,

131
00:07:45,830 --> 00:07:46,830
on.

00:07:46,830 --> 00:07:48,749
For Uber though, this is only regional.

133
00:07:48,749 --> 00:07:51,419
More drivers in New York does nothing for

134
00:07:51,419 --> 00:07:54,000
In fact, it failed in all of China.

00:07:54,000 --> 00:07:56,740
Every city is a new chicken-and-egg problem:

00:07:56,740 --> 00:08:00,710
Drivers need riders before they’ll drive,

137
00:08:00,710 --> 00:08:02,429
I do not like them, Sam-I-Am.

138
00:08:02,429 --> 00:08:04,610
I do not like green eggs and - oh.

139
00:08:04,610 --> 00:08:07,599
This helps keep prices low, and profits, nonexistent.

140
00:08:07,599 --> 00:08:12,789
It’s inescapable and leaves only one path
for Uber: self-driving cars.

141
00:08:12,789 --> 00:08:15,779
Remove the driver, remove the money-eating
machine.

142
00:08:15,779 --> 00:08:20,300
But it means competing with the technology
of Google and the auto-expertise of GM.

143
00:08:20,300 --> 00:08:25,059
Either it’ll transform into one of the biggest
transportation companies in the world, or,

144
00:08:25,059 --> 00:08:27,110
it’ll be the end of the road.

which’ll be fascinating to watch, doubly
