21
00:01:42,840 --> 00:01:44,119
environment.

22
00:01:44,119 --> 00:01:49,689
Some simply got unlucky - their WiFi stopped
working or their phones froze, and had to

23
00:01:49,689 --> 00:01:50,930
retake it.

24
00:01:50,930 --> 00:01:54,369
The SAT was in even worse shape.

25
00:01:54,369 --> 00:01:59,700
In March, as new Coronavirus cases exploded
in the U.S., many testing centers were forced

26
00:01:59,700 --> 00:02:03,399
to close, sometimes on short or no notice.

27
00:02:03,399 --> 00:02:10,140
The May and then June SATs were canceled,
and preparations are now being made for Fall.

28
00:02:10,140 --> 00:02:15,420
After first announcing it would also go online,
the College Board has now reversed that decision,

29
00:02:15,420 --> 00:02:20,500
saying it plans on holding one test a month
from August through the end of the year, all

30
00:02:20,500 --> 00:02:21,840
in-person.

31
00:02:21,840 --> 00:02:27,980
Knowing these circumstances, a number of schools
began dropping their SAT and ACT requirements.

32
00:02:27,980 --> 00:02:34,140
Dartmouth, Harvard, Princeton, Yale, Stanford,
Cornell, all UC-schools, and hundreds of others

33
00:02:34,140 --> 00:02:38,190
have announced they’re becoming ‘test-optional’
for at least the next year.

34
00:02:38,190 --> 00:02:43,250
But, rather than delaying the course of history,
the Coronavirus seems to be propelling it

35
00:02:43,250 --> 00:02:47,250
forward, five, ten, or even fifteen years.

36
00:02:47,250 --> 00:02:51,220
What was before unthinkable:
Not going to the movies,

37
00:02:51,220 --> 00:02:54,060
Working from home,
and learning from your laptop,

38
00:02:54,060 --> 00:02:59,940
is now being forced upon us, setting a precedent
that may extend far beyond the virus.

39
00:02:59,940 --> 00:03:04,650
If employees can work just as effectively
from home, without the cost of running an

40
00:03:04,650 --> 00:03:07,090
office, why not keep doing so?

41
00:03:07,090 --> 00:03:12,310
And if this batch of students can skip the
SAT, why can’t all?

42
00:03:12,310 --> 00:03:17,290
The first thing to note is that ‘test-optional’
may not mean what you think it does.

43
00:03:17,290 --> 00:03:22,480
Many schools require scores from all applicants,
but, on the other end of the spectrum, only

44
00:03:22,480 --> 00:03:27,540
a very small number are ‘test-blind’,
meaning, even if students submit them, they’ll

45
00:03:27,540 --> 00:03:32,130
only be used for things like financial aid,
not admissions.

46
00:03:32,130 --> 00:03:34,260
Most are somewhere in-between.

47
00:03:34,260 --> 00:03:39,070
Some schools forgo test scores for students
who meet a certain threshold GPA or class

48
00:03:39,070 --> 00:03:47,570
rank, others vary based on major, and, finally,
about 700 allow students to decide themselves.

49
00:03:47,570 --> 00:03:52,520
Test-optional doesn’t necessarily mean scores
aren’t important, make admissions easier,

50
00:03:52,520 --> 00:03:54,610
or that you shouldn’t submit them.

51
00:03:54,610 --> 00:03:58,720
It does mean that if you don’t submit them,
you’ll need other strong qualifications

52
00:03:58,720 --> 00:04:00,770
to stay competitive.

53
00:04:00,770 --> 00:04:05,970
And here lies the puzzle: If a school believes
standardized tests to be a strong predictor

54
00:04:05,970 --> 00:04:10,120
of college success, one would expect them
to be mandatory.

55
00:04:10,120 --> 00:04:15,090
On the other hand, if they don’t, you’d
expect schools to not even consider them.

56
00:04:15,090 --> 00:04:21,150
Why would so many schools allow students to
decide how much information to give them?

57
00:04:21,150 --> 00:04:26,550
Information which could affect their graduation
rate, academic performance, and, eventually,

58
00:04:26,550 --> 00:04:27,550
endowment.

59
00:04:27,550 --> 00:04:30,979
A few clues may help answer this question.

60
00:04:30,979 --> 00:04:35,550
Research shows a few things usually happen
when schools go test-optional:

61
00:04:35,550 --> 00:04:37,750
First, more students apply.

62
00:04:37,750 --> 00:04:43,169
Naturally, when universities make it easier
to do so, whether by using the Common Application,

63
00:04:43,169 --> 00:04:47,080
or removing requirements like test scores,
more will.

64
00:04:47,080 --> 00:04:51,490
Of course, schools aren’t accepting more
applicants, which means their acceptance rates

65
00:04:51,490 --> 00:04:54,600
go down, and they appear more selective.

66
00:04:54,600 --> 00:04:57,960
Second, their average test scores are higher.

67
00:04:57,960 --> 00:05:02,460
Each student knows all of his or her scores,
and individually decides whether to submit

68
00:05:02,460 --> 00:05:06,990
them based on whether or not they’ll increase
their odds of getting admitted.

69
00:05:06,990 --> 00:05:11,120
Students with higher scores will choose to
submit them, while those with lower ones will

70
00:05:11,120 --> 00:05:16,189
more likely not, inflating their accepted
school’s average statistics.

71
00:05:16,189 --> 00:05:18,180
In theory, this shouldn’t matter.

72
00:05:18,180 --> 00:05:23,380
The College Board explicitly states that SAT
scores should not be used to compare schools.

73
00:05:23,380 --> 00:05:25,389
And, yet, they are.

74
00:05:25,389 --> 00:05:31,030
By going test-optional, schools may improve
on college rankings, even if their true average

75
00:05:31,030 --> 00:05:33,720
scores actually decreased.

76
00:05:33,720 --> 00:05:42,029
[Insert subtitle here]

77
00:05:42,029 --> 00:05:46,999
Although this number is discounted by 15%
if fewer than three-quarters of new students

78
00:05:46,999 --> 00:05:51,580
in a particular year don’t submit scores,
it still leaves plenty of room for schools

79
00:05:51,580 --> 00:05:58,120
to game the system, either by ensuring 75.1%
of students submit, or by making up for the

80
00:05:58,120 --> 00:06:01,479
discount with extremely high average scores.

81
00:06:01,479 --> 00:06:06,639
Bond-rating agencies also use average scores
to assess a school’s student demand, and

82
00:06:06,639 --> 00:06:08,560
from it, determine creditworthiness.

83
00:06:08,560 --> 00:06:16,100
Finally, a third effect of going test-optional
is disputed: it may increase diversity.

84
00:06:16,100 --> 00:06:22,469
The question is: Do standardized tests help
alleviate or amplify inequality?

85
00:06:22,469 --> 00:06:27,150
Some studies suggest the former, while others
come to the later conclusion.

86
00:06:27,150 --> 00:06:32,569
In general, admissions officers agree that
the #1 best predictors of college success

87
00:06:32,569 --> 00:06:36,940
are similar high school classes - like AP,
IB, and honors.

88
00:06:36,940 --> 00:06:42,729
It’s no surprise that arduous semester or
year long courses would better prepare students

89
00:06:42,729 --> 00:06:49,469
for, arduous semester or year long courses,
than, say, a three hour exam by itself.

90
00:06:49,469 --> 00:06:54,360
The difficulty is that every teacher in every
high school in every city, county, and state

91
00:06:54,360 --> 00:06:56,070
teaches and grades differently.

92
00:06:56,070 --> 00:06:59,629
It’s also been observed that grades are
inflating over time.

93
00:06:59,629 --> 00:07:06,139
There are far fewer Cs and Ds and far more
As and Bs today than there were ten years

94
00:07:06,139 --> 00:07:07,139
ago.

95
00:07:07,139 --> 00:07:12,840
Thus, admissions offices can and should treat
high school GPA as the most important metric,

96
00:07:12,840 --> 00:07:18,520
the College Board argues, but combined with
national, standardized SAT scores to compare

97
00:07:18,520 --> 00:07:21,830
and confirm these numbers between schools.

98
00:07:21,830 --> 00:07:27,370
How much the SAT adds in predictive power,
researchers disagree, but admissions officers

99
00:07:27,370 --> 00:07:31,910
tend to agree that high grades and low test
scores are better than the reverse.

100
00:07:31,910 --> 00:07:36,509
And it’s these students who stand to benefit
from test-optional policies.

101
00:07:36,509 --> 00:07:42,039
They’re disproportionately first-generation
to college, women, low-income, and speak a

102
00:07:42,039 --> 00:07:44,160
second language at home.

103
00:07:44,160 --> 00:07:48,969
While the SAT may ‘confirm’ high GPAs
for most students, it may make someone in

104
00:07:48,969 --> 00:07:51,939
this group look worse for no good reason.

105
00:07:51,939 --> 00:07:56,439
For example, they may not have access to test
prep or have the free time to take the exam

106
00:07:56,439 --> 00:07:57,680
several times.

107
00:07:57,680 --> 00:08:02,810
It’s widely known that household income
is strongly correlated with test performance,

108
00:08:02,810 --> 00:08:05,339
and, for obvious reasons:

109
00:08:05,339 --> 00:08:11,089
Test fees, while insignificant for high-income
households, can be prohibitive for the poor.

110
00:08:11,089 --> 00:08:16,779
Many low-income students are given two free
SAT exams, but wealthy students are still

111
00:08:16,779 --> 00:08:20,900
more likely to have taken the SAT multiple
times.

112
00:08:20,900 --> 00:08:26,379
Schools in wealthier areas also provide greater
assistance with the SAT and college admissions,

113
00:08:26,379 --> 00:08:28,520
not to mention private help.

114
00:08:28,520 --> 00:08:34,910
Many studies suggest test prep leads to an
overall 20-30 point increase on the SAT - sometimes

115
00:08:34,910 --> 00:08:39,750
only by teaching test-taking strategies, rather
than actual material.

116
00:08:39,750 --> 00:08:44,810
Test coaches, another branch of the SAT economy,
sometimes help their clients apply for learning

117
00:08:44,810 --> 00:08:48,640
disabilities in order to obtain more time
on the exam.

118
00:08:48,640 --> 00:08:52,910
On the other hand, test-optional policies
place greater emphasis on things like high

119
00:08:52,910 --> 00:08:58,230
school curriculum and extracurricular activities,
both of which are less accessible in some

120
00:08:58,230 --> 00:09:01,490
areas and for some socioeconomic groups.

121
00:09:01,490 --> 00:09:06,820
Avoiding the SAT, in other words, may simply
introduce a new form of inequality.

122
00:09:06,820 --> 00:09:13,770
But, while not requiring the SAT and ACT may
or may not help increase diversity, it definitely

123
00:09:13,770 --> 00:09:18,870
helps strengthen other metrics like acceptance
rate, which make schools look more selective.

124
00:09:18,870 --> 00:09:24,240
It’s impossible to know which of these reasons
truly motivate schools to try test-optional

125
00:09:24,240 --> 00:09:30,000
policies, but it does strongly suggest why
they stay that way.

126
00:09:30,000 --> 00:09:33,690
Schools now say they’re adjusting this and
next year’s requirements to help ease the

127
00:09:33,690 --> 00:09:38,700
hardships faced by students, which should
come as no surprise at a time when they expect

128
00:09:38,700 --> 00:09:42,160
fewer applicants and greater financial difficulties.

129
00:09:42,160 --> 00:09:46,910
This year the University of California schools
president made headlines for announcing that

130
00:09:46,910 --> 00:09:53,000
all UC schools will be test-optional for the
next two years, then test-blind for 2 more

131
00:09:53,000 --> 00:09:57,970
after that, and then phase out the SAT and
ACT completely.

132
00:09:57,970 --> 00:10:03,090
Critics have praised the decision for making
higher education more fair and diverse.

133
00:10:03,090 --> 00:10:08,870
Except the UC system isn’t abandoning standardized
testing, but creating its own test to use

134
00:10:08,870 --> 00:10:09,970
instead.

135
00:10:09,970 --> 00:10:15,140
In many ways, it’s reminiscent of 2001,
when the then-UC president delivered a speech

136
00:10:15,140 --> 00:10:20,250
recommending its schools abandon the SAT,
which prompted the College Board to redesign

137
00:10:20,250 --> 00:10:21,790
the test.

138
00:10:21,790 --> 00:10:25,900
Whether intentional or not, these are negotiations.

139
00:10:25,900 --> 00:10:30,570
Not-so-subtle reminders to the College Board
that it’s true customers aren’t students,

140
00:10:30,570 --> 00:10:37,820
but schools, and that if it can’t create
the test schools want, they can make it themselves.

But there’s something else that might.

14
00:00:51,100 --> 00:00:55,530
To understand how background checks work,
it helps to imagine two very different people,

15
00:00:55,530 --> 00:00:56,790
who both want to buy a gun.

16
00:00:56,790 --> 00:01:02,350
This first person is dangerous. Maybe he has
a history of domestic violence or mental illness.

17
00:01:02,350 --> 00:01:05,120
And most importantly — he has a record.

18
00:01:05,120 --> 00:01:09,890
And the second one is not dangerous. He just
wants a gun for protection or to go hunting

19
00:01:09,890 --> 00:01:12,650
or cause shooting guns is kinda fun.

20
00:01:12,650 --> 00:01:18,160
Before either one can buy a gun, they first have to go through an FBI instant background check.

21
00:01:18,160 --> 00:01:22,860
And I mean instant — it only takes an average
of 108 seconds to get a response from the

22
00:01:22,870 --> 00:01:24,310
FBI’s database.

23
00:01:24,310 --> 00:01:28,700
That database is made up of records sent in
by state police and other agencies. And it’s

24
00:01:28,700 --> 00:01:32,310
checked to see if the buyer has things like
a criminal record, addiction, a restraining

25
00:01:32,310 --> 00:01:35,510
order or has been hospitalized for a mental
illness.

26
00:01:35,510 --> 00:01:39,960
Under a universal background check system,
anyone buying a gun — whether in a gun store,

27
00:01:39,960 --> 00:01:43,900
or through a private sale — would have to
be checked through that database. That means

28
00:01:43,900 --> 00:01:48,380
our second person walks out with a gun.
And our first person, with a criminal record,

29
00:01:48,380 --> 00:01:49,440
doesn’t.

30
00:01:49,440 --> 00:01:50,860
Or, at least he shouldn’t.

31
00:01:50,860 --> 00:01:55,400
I’ve done a lot of reporting on this, we
have just seen time and time again background

32
00:01:55,400 --> 00:01:59,439
checks just do not stop people we don’t
want having guns from actually getting the

33
00:01:59,439 --> 00:02:00,549
weapons.

34
00:02:00,549 --> 00:02:05,049
There are a couple problems with the background
check system. One is that the FBI database

35
00:02:05,049 --> 00:02:07,180
is about as outdated as its logo.

36
00:02:07,180 --> 00:02:09,090
It’s missing millions of records.

37
00:02:09,090 --> 00:02:14,250
That’s why the Charleston church shooter
was able to buy a gun, despite having a record.

38
00:02:14,250 --> 00:02:19,069
Or why the man who killed 26 Texan churchgoers
was also able to pass a background check,

39
00:02:19,069 --> 00:02:23,500
after the Air Force failed to send his domestic
abuse convictions to the FBI.

40
00:02:23,500 --> 00:02:27,860
So even with a background check for every
type of sale, there’s still a chance this

41
00:02:27,870 --> 00:02:29,360
guy gets a gun.

42
00:02:29,360 --> 00:02:33,480
That’s partly why study after study has
found that while background checks “prevent,

43
00:02:33,480 --> 00:02:37,800
or make substantially more difficult, the
criminal acquisition of firearms.”

44
00:02:37,800 --> 00:02:42,260
Making them universal doesn’t actually have
any effect on the actual gun crisis in America:

45
00:02:42,260 --> 00:02:43,260
gun deaths.

46
00:02:43,260 --> 00:02:48,230
A Johns Hopkins study of California, where
comprehensive background checks were implemented

47
00:02:48,230 --> 00:02:54,200
in 1991, found the law was “not associated
with changes in firearm suicide or homicide.”

48
00:02:54,200 --> 00:02:57,760
Thanks in part to those incomplete and missing
records.

49
00:02:57,760 --> 00:03:02,590
The other problem is that background checks
only look at “good” people and “already

50
00:03:02,590 --> 00:03:05,230
bad” people. But there is an in between.

51
00:03:05,230 --> 00:03:10,390
The background checks are supposed to catch
people who have a record already. It just

52
00:03:10,390 --> 00:03:16,480
misses all the people who haven’t done anything
bad yet but might do something bad in the

53
00:03:16,480 --> 00:03:17,480
future.

54
00:03:17,480 --> 00:03:20,030
German is not advocating for a Minority Report
situation.

55
00:03:20,030 --> 00:03:24,731
He’s talking about someone like this guy,
who is also dangerous, but

56
00:03:24,731 --> 00:03:26,629
who doesn’t have a record.

57
00:03:26,629 --> 00:03:32,420
Under a universal background check system
— he could get a gun. In 108 seconds.

58
00:03:32,420 --> 00:03:34,960
But there’s another system that could prevent
this.

59
00:03:34,960 --> 00:03:39,520
Twelve states and Washington, DC have gone
one step further and established a licensing

60
00:03:39,520 --> 00:03:40,120
system.

61
00:03:40,120 --> 00:03:43,420
How’s it different? Well, Here’s how it
works in Massachusetts:

62
00:03:43,420 --> 00:03:48,660
Before you ever go to a gun store, you first
have to take a firearm safety course.

63
00:03:48,660 --> 00:03:53,400
Then you go to the police department and submit
an application, give references and give your

64
00:03:53,400 --> 00:03:55,590
fingerprints for a background check.

65
00:03:55,590 --> 00:04:00,780
Then not only is the FBI database checked,
but all local law enforcement agencies wherever

66
00:04:00,780 --> 00:04:05,379
you’ve lived are directly contacted, along
with the Department of Mental Health.

67
00:04:05,379 --> 00:04:10,930
That entire process in Massachusetts usually
takes about 3 weeks. And most people‚ about

68
00:04:10,930 --> 00:04:13,120
97% — pass.

69
00:04:13,500 --> 00:04:18,920
Nothing about a gun licensing system will
prevent a law-abiding citizen from going through

70
00:04:18,920 --> 00:04:21,040
the process and obtaining a firearm.

71
00:04:21,040 --> 00:04:26,340
That’s Dr. Cassandra Crifasi, she researches
health policy at Johns Hopkins, and she’s

72
00:04:26,340 --> 00:04:27,830
one of the authors of the studies earlier.

73
00:04:27,830 --> 00:04:31,970
And she says the reason licensing works is
that it’s designed to do both of the big

74
00:04:31,970 --> 00:04:33,900
things background checks fail at.

75
00:04:33,900 --> 00:04:39,660
A, to properly identify and screen out people
who shouldn’t have guns.

76
00:04:39,660 --> 00:04:45,010
And B, create a system to reduce impulsive
gun purchases.

77
00:04:45,010 --> 00:04:49,919
The licensing system is more comprehensive
than the one-database background check system,

78
00:04:49,919 --> 00:04:53,050
so our criminal will be reliably denied a
gun.

79
00:04:53,050 --> 00:04:57,080
But because it’s so meticulous it also stands
a chance of keeping our third guy, without

80
00:04:57,080 --> 00:04:59,190
a record, from getting a gun.

81
00:04:59,190 --> 00:05:04,389
There are people who, may want to impulsively
acquire a firearm, for example to harm themselves

82
00:05:04,389 --> 00:05:05,389
or others.

83
00:05:05,389 --> 00:05:11,750
And the process of obtaining a license can
at least delay that person during that time

84
00:05:11,750 --> 00:05:17,430
of crisis or maybe deter them from getting
that firearm at all.

85
00:05:17,430 --> 00:05:20,840
In 1995, Connecticut implemented a licensing
system.

86
00:05:20,840 --> 00:05:26,040
[Insert subtitle here]

87
00:05:26,040 --> 00:05:31,630
Compare that to Missouri, which once had a
licensing system, but got rid of it in 2007.

88
00:05:31,630 --> 00:05:36,700
Over the next decade, they had a huge spike
in homicides and gun suicides.

89
00:05:36,700 --> 00:05:41,139
In both states there were lots of factors
involved. But researchers say this shows that

90
00:05:41,140 --> 00:05:42,640
licensing works.

91
00:05:42,640 --> 00:05:47,540
It’s also… pretty popular. Among voters
who live in a house with a gun, more than

92
00:05:47,540 --> 00:05:52,360
two-thirds think that it’s a good idea.
Ask all Americans and more than three-quarters

93
00:05:52,360 --> 00:05:53,590
support it.

94
00:05:53,590 --> 00:05:58,580
Background checks are supposed to stop bad
people from getting guns. But they often don’t.

95
00:05:58,580 --> 00:06:01,000
Licensing picks up that slack.

96
00:06:01,000 --> 00:06:09,480
By making sure that people are crossing these hurdles,
we just make sure, in a much better, stronger

97
00:06:09,480 --> 00:06:12,900
way, that people are not getting firearms
when they shouldn’t have them.
answer: Over the next 10 years, they saw a drop in gun homicides and gun suicides.

question:
1
00:00:01,170 --> 00:00:07,830
These 50 cards represent every person who
took the SAT college entrance exam in 2017.

2
00:00:07,830 --> 00:00:13,100
In America, this score -- this ranking of
students -- is hugely important.

3
00:00:13,100 --> 00:00:16,400
Elite schools like Yale or Harvard select
the large majority of their students from

4
00:00:16,400 --> 00:00:19,500
this pile --
the top 1 percent of test takers.

5
00:00:19,500 --> 00:00:21,180
And it's not just super elite schools.

6
00:00:21,180 --> 00:00:25,410
A public flagship state school, like the University
of Georgia, admits most of its students from

7
00:00:25,410 --> 00:00:26,789
this pile.

8
00:00:26,789 --> 00:00:31,029
And even a less selective school, like Wichita
State University, admits most of its students

9
00:00:31,029 --> 00:00:32,660
from this pile.

10
00:00:32,660 --> 00:00:36,199
All three of these ranges are higher than
the average score.

11
00:00:36,199 --> 00:00:39,730
This why people pay lots of money to train
for the test with companies like Princeton

12
00:00:39,730 --> 00:00:41,510
Review, Kaplan, and PrepScholar.

13
00:00:41,510 --> 00:00:44,600
A slightly higher score can make a big difference.

14
00:00:44,600 --> 00:00:48,879
That’s also why some really rich people
got caught paying lots of money to help their

15
00:00:48,880 --> 00:00:50,350
kids cheat on the test.

16
00:00:50,420 --> 00:00:53,100
"Dozens of coaches, actors, and CEOs..."

17
00:00:53,100 --> 00:00:56,720
"Felicity Huffman accused of paying $15,000

18
00:00:56,720 --> 00:01:03,080
to have someone either take the exam for their child, or to correct their child's answers afterward.."

19
00:01:03,720 --> 00:01:09,100
Your place in this ranking can have a huge
impact on what opportunities come your way.

20
00:01:09,109 --> 00:01:10,450
So it’s worth asking...

21
00:01:10,450 --> 00:01:13,080
what exactly does the SAT measure?

22
00:01:13,460 --> 00:01:15,460
What does this score actually say about you?

23
00:01:18,420 --> 00:01:22,000
To answer this question, we have to start
with this man: Carl Brigham.

24
00:01:22,000 --> 00:01:25,439
He was a young psychologist during World War
I

25
00:01:25,439 --> 00:01:28,509
who was obsessed with measuring human
intelligence.

26
00:01:28,509 --> 00:01:32,100
He would devise puzzles for soldiers that
supposedly measured their intelligence by

27
00:01:32,100 --> 00:01:33,100
testing whether they could

28
00:01:33,100 --> 00:01:34,439
decode symbols,

29
00:01:34,439 --> 00:01:35,770
draw missing parts of a picture,

30
00:01:35,770 --> 00:01:38,359
or even complete maze.

31
00:01:38,359 --> 00:01:42,430
He concluded that white people of English,
Scottish, and Dutch descent were smartest.

32
00:01:42,430 --> 00:01:48,060
At the very bottom were black people and recent
immigrants from Poland and Italy.

33
00:01:48,060 --> 00:01:50,909
He ignored the fact that some test takers
didn't speak English.

34
00:01:50,909 --> 00:01:56,049
So answering a question like "How many are
60 guns and 5 guns" could be difficult.

35
00:01:56,049 --> 00:02:00,390
He ignored how some people were barred from
receiving an adequate education.

36
00:02:00,390 --> 00:02:03,880
Which meant some puzzles, like this one, could
be quite challenging.

37
00:02:03,880 --> 00:02:07,460
He just assumed the scores reflected the innate
intelligence of different races.

38
00:02:07,460 --> 00:02:12,610
And because of this, he wrote that black people
were so much less intelligent that America

39
00:02:12,610 --> 00:02:17,770
should worry about "racial admixture" which
would "incorporate the negro into our racial

40
00:02:17,770 --> 00:02:21,120
stock" -- and "taint" the population.

41
00:02:21,120 --> 00:02:24,750
After World War I, Brigham wrote a new test
to measure the intelligence of prospective

42
00:02:24,750 --> 00:02:26,010
college students.

43
00:02:26,010 --> 00:02:27,930
He included word and number puzzles, like:

44
00:02:27,930 --> 00:02:30,819
Pick the three words below that are most related:

45
00:02:30,820 --> 00:02:35,250
Chops, liver, round, fore-quarter, rump, sirloin.

46
00:02:36,880 --> 00:02:38,940
Yeah, I don't know, either.

47
00:02:38,950 --> 00:02:43,440
Anyway, Brigham's exam was called the Scholastic
Aptitude Test.

48
00:02:43,440 --> 00:02:45,980
The SAT.

49
00:02:47,580 --> 00:02:50,340
The SAT wasn't very popular at first.

50
00:02:50,340 --> 00:02:53,480
In 1941, just 10,000 people took the exam.

51
00:02:53,480 --> 00:02:56,189
That was just 1 percent of high school seniors.

52
00:02:56,189 --> 00:02:58,480
Most colleges just didn't need it.

53
00:02:58,480 --> 00:03:01,880
They didn't have that many applicants, partially
because less than 10 percent of people Americans

54
00:03:01,880 --> 00:03:03,239
went to college.

55
00:03:03,239 --> 00:03:05,560
So they could spend more time with each application.

56
00:03:05,560 --> 00:03:08,840
And many elite schools administered their
own entrance exams.

57
00:03:08,840 --> 00:03:11,280
Then, World War II ended.

58
00:03:16,340 --> 00:03:18,640
Millions of troops returned to the US.

59
00:03:18,650 --> 00:03:23,690
And there was a new benefit white veterans
could take advantage of: the GI Bill

60
00:03:23,690 --> 00:03:25,640
— which helped them pay for college.

61
00:03:25,640 --> 00:03:28,800
And college enrollment skyrocketed.

62
00:03:28,800 --> 00:03:32,760
All of a sudden, colleges had way more applications
to sort through.

63
00:03:32,760 --> 00:03:35,819
And they needed a tool to help them figure
out who to accept.

64
00:03:35,819 --> 00:03:39,890
So they started requiring the SAT, which gave
them some numerical way to rank applicants.

65
00:03:39,890 --> 00:03:41,349
Meanwhile, the College Board recognized that
Americans didn't love the idea of an "intelligence

66
00:03:41,349 --> 00:03:42,349
test" determining their future.

67
00:03:42,349 --> 00:03:44,530
So they started saying their exam measured
college preparedness.

68
00:03:44,530 --> 00:03:48,140
And every few years, they proved it -- by
saying their exam, along with high school

69
00:03:48,140 --> 00:03:51,710
grades, were a good predictor of how well
students do in college.

70
00:03:51,710 --> 00:03:52,909
They still do this.

71
00:03:52,909 --> 00:03:55,260
For example, here's that analysis from this
year.

72
00:03:55,260 --> 00:03:59,609
It shows that high school GPA alone gets us
about halfway to predicting college GPA.

73
00:03:59,609 --> 00:04:04,810
But the College Board sold schools on this
next part: If we consider SAT scores along

74
00:04:04,810 --> 00:04:07,819
with high school GPA, this prediction can
get a bit better.

75
00:04:07,819 --> 00:04:12,650
And colleges bought into this rebranding,
and started asking for SAT scores.

76
00:04:12,650 --> 00:04:16,010
In 1941, just 10,000 students took the SAT.

77
00:04:16,010 --> 00:04:18,090
By 1950, 80,000 students took the exam.

78
00:04:18,090 --> 00:04:22,700
By 1960, 800,000 students took the SAT.

79
00:04:22,700 --> 00:04:24,880
By the next decade, it rose to a million..

80
00:04:25,800 --> 00:04:30,000
Now, more than 2 million students take the
exam each year.

81
00:04:30,000 --> 00:04:34,180
And as the competition for college ramped
up, the applications got stronger.

82
00:04:34,180 --> 00:04:39,070
In 1982, the average high school graduate
completed Algebra or maybe Algebra 2.

83
00:04:39,070 --> 00:04:42,650
By 2004, the average student was closer to
Trigonometry.

84
00:04:42,650 --> 00:04:46,710
Also, more students had extracurriculars on
their applications.

85
00:04:46,710 --> 00:04:51,690
In 1992, just 19 percent of high school students
were leaders in an extracurricular activity.

86
00:04:51,690 --> 00:04:55,560
Just 12 years later, in 2004, that number
doubled.

87
00:04:55,560 --> 00:04:59,450
As the competition got stiffer, students started
applying to way more schools.

88
00:04:59,450 --> 00:05:04,540
In 1967, about 40 percent of students applied
to more than two schools.

89
00:05:04,540 --> 00:05:07,260
Now, it's more than 80 percent of students.

90
00:05:07,260 --> 00:05:10,470
And a decent chunk of them apply to more than
6 schools.

91
00:05:10,470 --> 00:05:13,370
All of this overwhelmed admissions offices.

92
00:05:13,370 --> 00:05:16,540
So they started to rely even more on the SATs.

93
00:05:16,540 --> 00:05:21,880
In 1993, [Insert subtitle here]

94
00:05:21,880 --> 00:05:26,139
By 2005, it was 59 percent.

95
00:05:26,139 --> 00:05:30,240
But looming over the increasing weight of
this number, was this other thing the SAT

96
00:05:30,240 --> 00:05:32,040
seemed to measure.

97
00:05:32,040 --> 00:05:33,580
Wealth.

98
00:05:33,580 --> 00:05:34,850
It's apparent in the data.

99
00:05:34,850 --> 00:05:38,080
Here's a chart of the average SAT scores by
family income.

100
00:05:38,080 --> 00:05:43,400
Students whose families earn less than $20,000
score around 890 -- way below average.

101
00:05:43,400 --> 00:05:47,180
And as we move up the income brackets, students
score higher and higher.

102
00:05:47,180 --> 00:05:51,400
The wealthiest students -- whose parents earn
more than $200,000 -- score an average of

103
00:05:51,400 --> 00:05:52,440
1150.

104
00:05:52,440 --> 00:05:57,050
Now, defenders of the SAT have often said
there's nothing wrong with the test itself.

105
00:05:57,050 --> 00:06:00,480
They say this score is just reflecting the
inequality in America.

106
00:06:00,480 --> 00:06:01,510
And that's not wrong.

107
00:06:01,510 --> 00:06:03,780
We can follow that logic up the chain.

108
00:06:03,780 --> 00:06:08,280
We can start with America's highly unequal
neighborhoods.

109
00:06:08,280 --> 00:06:12,000
Schools in poor neighborhoods are more likely
to be under-resourced.

110
00:06:12,000 --> 00:06:16,280
And students from more affluent neighborhoods
and schools tend to score higher on the SAT.

111
00:06:16,280 --> 00:06:21,700
In turn, students with better SAT scores go
to more selective colleges.

112
00:06:21,700 --> 00:06:23,840
And this system is a cycle.

113
00:06:23,840 --> 00:06:27,180
When Stanford researcher Raj Chetty and his
colleagues tracked people born in the early-1980s,

114
00:06:27,180 --> 00:06:30,949
he found that these people -- who went to
the most selective colleges --

115
00:06:30,949 --> 00:06:35,320
-- had parents who earned, on average, $171,000
a year.

116
00:06:35,320 --> 00:06:41,230
The parents of these people, who went to selective
public colleges, earned $87,000.

117
00:06:41,230 --> 00:06:46,430
And those who attended community colleges
had parents who earned $67,000 a year.

118
00:06:46,430 --> 00:06:50,150
And through this system, that wealth was passed
on.

119
00:06:50,150 --> 00:06:54,380
Chetty and his colleagues found that students
who graduated from these elite colleges earned,

120
00:06:54,380 --> 00:06:59,630
on average, $82,500 a year by their early-30s.

00:06:59,630 --> 00:07:04,080
Those who went to a selective public college
earned half that -- $41,600.

122
00:07:04,080 --> 00:07:07,210
And those who went to a community college
were at about $30,000.

123
00:07:08,200 --> 00:07:11,960
But Chetty and his colleagues found that,
if low-income student gets the opportunity

124
00:07:11,960 --> 00:07:15,500
to attend a more selective school, they're able to graduate -- and earn just

125
00:07:15,500 --> 00:07:17,420
as much money as their classmates.

126
00:07:19,920 --> 00:07:23,360
In 2016, the College Board redesigned the
SAT.

127
00:07:23,360 --> 00:07:27,610
The old test tried to trip up test-takers
-- for example, asking about the meaning of

128
00:07:27,610 --> 00:07:30,160
obscure words like "acrimonious."

129
00:07:30,160 --> 00:07:33,460
The new one tries to test what you've learned
in school -- to try to make it less of an

130
00:07:33,460 --> 00:07:34,800
intelligence test.

131
00:07:34,800 --> 00:07:39,800
For example, it'll show you a sentence like:
The jungle has an intense clustering of bugs.

132
00:07:39,800 --> 00:07:40,800
And then ask:

133
00:07:40,800 --> 00:07:42,220
What does "intense" most nearly mean?

134
00:07:42,220 --> 00:07:43,940
Emotional
Concentrated

135
00:07:43,940 --> 00:07:45,090
Brilliant
Determined

136
00:07:47,960 --> 00:07:51,660
Still, your SAT score measures how well you'll
do in college, to a degree.

137
00:07:51,660 --> 00:07:55,830
It also measures where you grew up -- and
what opportunities you had.

138
00:07:55,830 --> 00:08:00,830
But it’s also a tool that keeps this inequality
machine going.

139
00:08:00,830 --> 00:08:03,310
College Board president David Coleman sees
this happening.

140
00:08:03,310 --> 00:08:07,320
He recently wrote:
"We need a far humbler view of the SAT.

141
00:08:07,320 --> 00:08:11,490
They should never be more than one factor
in an admissions decision.

142
00:08:11,490 --> 00:08:15,190
Low scores should never be a veto on a student’s
life."

143
00:08:15,190 --> 00:08:18,680
The SAT was created in the pursuit of precision.

144
00:08:18,680 --> 00:08:20,410
An effort to measure what we're capable of

145
00:08:20,410 --> 00:08:23,230
-- to predict what we can do.

146
00:08:23,230 --> 00:08:25,310
What we might do.

147
00:08:25,310 --> 00:08:30,590
What we've forgotten is that, often, that
can't be untangled from where we've been,

148
00:08:30,590 --> 00:08:32,000
what we've been through,

149
00:08:32,000 --> 00:08:34,160
and what we’ve been given.

question:
1
00:00:02,520 --> 00:00:07,000
If, for the same work, women make only 77
cents for every dollar a man makes,

2
00:00:07,000 --> 00:00:09,500
why don’t businesses hire only women?

3
00:00:09,500 --> 00:00:12,080
Wages are the biggest expense for most businesses.

4
00:00:12,100 --> 00:00:15,620
So, hiring only women would reduce costs by
nearly a quarter

5
00:00:15,620 --> 00:00:17,760
– and that would go right to the bottom line.

6
00:00:17,780 --> 00:00:19,860
Don’t businesses want to be profitable?

7
00:00:19,880 --> 00:00:22,800
Or, are they just really bad at math?

8
00:00:22,800 --> 00:00:28,420
Well, actually, it’s the feminists, celebrities
and politicians spreading this wage gap myth

9
00:00:28,420 --> 00:00:30,140
who have the math problem.

10
00:00:30,140 --> 00:00:31,840
Here’s why:

11
00:00:31,840 --> 00:00:38,140
The 77-cents-on-the-dollar statistic is calculated
by dividing the median earnings of all women

12
00:00:38,220 --> 00:00:42,440
working full-time by the median earnings of
all men working full-time.

13
00:00:42,440 --> 00:00:47,960
In other words, if the average income of all
men is, say, 40,000 dollars a year,

14
00:00:47,960 --> 00:00:53,060
and the average annual income of all women is, say,
30,800 dollars, that would mean that women

15
00:00:53,060 --> 00:00:56,500
earn 77 cents for every dollar a man earns.

16
00:00:56,500 --> 00:01:00,960
30,800 divided by 40,000 equals .77.

17
00:01:00,970 --> 00:01:06,440
But these calculations don’t reveal a gender
wage injustice because it doesn’t take into

18
00:01:06,440 --> 00:01:11,900
account occupation, position, education or
hours worked per week.

19
00:01:11,900 --> 00:01:17,540
Even a study by the American Association of
University Women, a feminist organization,

20
00:01:17,540 --> 00:01:21,960
[Insert subtitle here]

21
00:01:21,980 --> 00:01:24,860
[Insert subtitle here]

22
00:01:24,900 --> 00:01:27,520
And the key word here is “choice.”

23
00:01:27,530 --> 00:01:32,390
The small wage gap that does exist has nothing
to do with paying women less, let alone with

24
00:01:32,390 --> 00:01:39,520
sexism; it has to do with differences in individual
career choices that men and women make.

25
00:01:39,520 --> 00:01:45,840
In 2009, the U.S. Department of Labor released
a paper that examined more than 50 peer-reviewed

26
00:01:45,850 --> 00:01:51,700
studies and concluded that the oft-cited 23
percent wage gap “may be almost entirely

27
00:01:51,700 --> 00:01:57,080
the result of individual choices being made
by both male and female workers.”

28
00:01:57,080 --> 00:01:59,240
Well, let’s look at some of those choices.

29
00:01:59,240 --> 00:02:04,020
Georgetown University compiled a list of the
five best-paying college majors,

30
00:02:04,060 --> 00:02:07,700
and the percentage of men or women majoring in those fields:

31
00:02:07,700 --> 00:02:12,520
Number 1 best-paying major: Petroleum Engineering:
87% male

32
00:02:12,520 --> 00:02:21,000
Number 2: Pharmaceutical Sciences: 48% male
3: Mathematics and Computer Science: 67% male

33
00:02:21,000 --> 00:02:28,690
4: Aerospace Engineering: 88% male
5: Chemical Engineering: 72% male

34
00:02:28,690 --> 00:02:34,600
Notice that women out-represent men in only
one of the five top-paying majors

35
00:02:34,600 --> 00:02:36,840
– by only a few percentage points.

36
00:02:36,840 --> 00:02:41,900
Now consider the same study’s list of the
five worst paying college majors:

37
00:02:41,920 --> 00:02:50,880
Number 1: Counseling and Psychology: 74% female
Number 2: Early Childhood Education: 97% female

38
00:02:50,880 --> 00:02:59,140
3: Theology and Religious Vocations: 66% male
4: Human Services and Community Organization:

39
00:02:59,140 --> 00:03:05,040
81% female
5: Social Work: 88% female

40
00:03:05,160 --> 00:03:09,320
Here, it’s the women who lead in all but
one category.

41
00:03:09,320 --> 00:03:13,599
Even within the same profession, men and women
make different career choices that impact

42
00:03:13,600 --> 00:03:15,300
how much money they make.

43
00:03:15,300 --> 00:03:20,480
Take nursing, where male nurses on the whole
earn 18% more than female nurses.

44
00:03:20,489 --> 00:03:21,489
The reason?

45
00:03:21,489 --> 00:03:25,800
Male nurses gravitate to the best-paying nursing
specialties, they work longer hours,

46
00:03:25,900 --> 00:03:30,600
and disproportionately find jobs in cities with the highest compensation.

47
00:03:30,600 --> 00:03:35,020
Now, here’s how one expert on nursing compensation,
Professor Linda Aiken of the University of

48
00:03:35,020 --> 00:03:40,780
Pennsylvania, sums up the data: “Career
choices and educational differences explain most,

49
00:03:40,780 --> 00:03:43,900
if not all, the gender gap in nursing.”

50
00:03:43,920 --> 00:03:49,239
The Department of Labor paper concluded that
once these differences are accounted for across

51
00:03:49,240 --> 00:03:55,340
all professions, the unexplained wage gap
is somewhere between 4.8 and 7 percent

52
00:03:55,340 --> 00:04:01,560
– almost identical to the 6.6 percentage gap found
by the AAUW.

53
00:04:01,569 --> 00:04:03,640
But why is there any gap at all?

54
00:04:03,640 --> 00:04:09,099
No one knows for sure, as both the AAUW and
the Labor Department concede.

55
00:04:09,100 --> 00:04:14,120
There are so many variables that drive wages
that no single study can cover them all.

56
00:04:14,120 --> 00:04:18,820
Few wage gap studies control for variables
such as dangerous work environment;

57
00:04:18,820 --> 00:04:22,800
men are vastly overrepresented, for example, on oil
rigs.

58
00:04:22,840 --> 00:04:27,260
And here’s another variable: men are more
willing and able to work long hours

59
00:04:27,260 --> 00:04:28,920
without advance notice.

60
00:04:28,920 --> 00:04:34,400
According to Harvard economist Claudia Goldin,
even if two lawyers have the same education,

61
00:04:34,400 --> 00:04:39,820
same specialty, and work the same number
of hours — firms pay more to someone who is

62
00:04:39,820 --> 00:04:44,700
willing to always be “on call” and ready
to be in the office when the firm needs them,

63
00:04:44,700 --> 00:04:47,540
as opposed to wanting a more regular schedule.

64
00:04:47,600 --> 00:04:50,980
This isn’t sexism, it’s just common sense.

65
00:04:50,990 --> 00:04:55,979
With more realistic categories and definitions,
whatever wage gap remains would certainly

66
00:04:55,979 --> 00:04:58,479
narrow to point of vanishing.

67
00:04:58,480 --> 00:05:01,780
So it seems that business leaders aren’t
bad at math simply because they don’t

68
00:05:01,780 --> 00:05:03,620
only hire women.

69
00:05:03,620 --> 00:05:08,500
Those who claim that for the same work women
earn 77 cents on the dollar compared to men,

70
00:05:08,500 --> 00:05:13,520
on the other hand, are not merely bad at math
--but at telling the truth.

71
00:05:13,520 --> 00:05:19,280
I’m Christina Hoff Sommers of the American
Enterprise Institute for Prager University.
answer: shows that the actual wage gap shrinks to only 6.6 cents when you factor in different choices men and women make.

00:00:23,339 --> 00:00:29,519
fun to explore it further in this episode
of The Infographics Show; Vegans vs Meat-eaters.

11
00:00:29,519 --> 00:00:33,780
A vegan is someone who follows a diet that
contains no animal meat, fish, eggs, dairy

12
00:00:33,780 --> 00:00:36,440
products, or any other food that comes from
animals.

13
00:00:36,440 --> 00:00:39,809
They differ from vegetarians, who generally
still eat dairy and eggs as part of their

14
00:00:39,809 --> 00:00:41,120
diets.

15
00:00:41,120 --> 00:00:44,820
Vegans also typically abstain from using any
other products that come from animals, such

16
00:00:44,820 --> 00:00:46,519
as honey and leather jackets.

17
00:00:46,519 --> 00:00:51,910
Back in 2008, vegans only accounted for around
0.5% of the US population, or about 1 million

18
00:00:51,910 --> 00:00:52,930
people.

19
00:00:52,930 --> 00:00:57,339
As of polls taken in 2014, vegans now make
up roughly 2.5% of the population.

20
00:00:57,339 --> 00:01:01,809
At least in the United States, women seem
to be far bigger fans of veganism, making

21
00:01:01,809 --> 00:01:02,809
up around 79% of vegans.

22
00:01:02,809 --> 00:01:08,189
The number of meat eaters obviously far outweighs
the number of vegans throughout the world,

23
00:01:08,189 --> 00:01:13,420
[Insert subtitle here]

24
00:01:13,420 --> 00:01:17,402
By not consuming any animal products, vegans
follow a dietary path similar to an herbivore.

25
00:01:17,402 --> 00:01:23,030
Herbivores are animals that feed exclusively
on plants, such as cows, giraffes, and adorable

26
00:01:23,030 --> 00:01:24,090
deer.

27
00:01:24,090 --> 00:01:28,329
Meat-eaters are typically omnivores, which
means that they eat both plants and animals.

28
00:01:28,329 --> 00:01:32,290
The term comes from the latin words Omni,
meaning “all or everything,” and the word

29
00:01:32,290 --> 00:01:34,200
Vorare, which means “to devour.”

30
00:01:34,200 --> 00:01:37,390
So basically omnivores are down to eat whatever.

31
00:01:37,390 --> 00:01:40,930
Most meat-eaters don’t solely eat just meat,
like a carnivore would do.

32
00:01:40,930 --> 00:01:43,579
That is, unless you’re Ron Swanson from
Parks and Rec.

33
00:01:43,579 --> 00:01:46,729
Then it’s beautiful bacon and sizzling steaks
all day!

34
00:01:46,729 --> 00:01:50,360
So humans are widely thought of as natural
omnivores, but some believe that humans are

35
00:01:50,360 --> 00:01:54,000
at their optimal health when following the
dietary habits of an herbivore.

36
00:01:54,000 --> 00:01:57,310
People often cite potential health benefits
and ethical dilemmas as the main reasons to

37
00:01:57,310 --> 00:01:58,460
go on a vegan diet.

38
00:01:58,460 --> 00:02:01,890
We won’t get into the ethics today, but
we are curious about the health differences

39
00:02:01,890 --> 00:02:04,380
between vegans and their meat-eating friends.

40
00:02:04,380 --> 00:02:06,500
People on a vegan diet tend to be leaner.

41
00:02:06,500 --> 00:02:10,519
In a cross-sectional study of nearly 40,000
(37,875) adults, meat-eaters had the highest

42
00:02:10,519 --> 00:02:13,599
mean body-mass-index, or BMI.

43
00:02:13,599 --> 00:02:16,090
Vegetarians were in the middle and vegans
had the lowest.

44
00:02:16,090 --> 00:02:19,760
Based on several studies from Finland, some
scientists have suggested that vegan diets

45
00:02:19,760 --> 00:02:22,670
may be helpful in the treatment of rheumatoid
arthritis.

46
00:02:22,670 --> 00:02:27,390
Vegans also appear to have lower rates of
hypertension than both meat-eaters and vegetarians.

47
00:02:27,390 --> 00:02:31,720
Vegans also typically have lower cardiometabolic
risks for conditions like heart disease or

48
00:02:31,720 --> 00:02:32,720
strokes.

49
00:02:32,720 --> 00:02:36,220
The problem, however, doesn't seem to be with
meat itself, but rather with the quality of

50
00:02:36,220 --> 00:02:37,220
meat.

51
00:02:37,220 --> 00:02:40,550
Recent findings have found that coronary heart
disease problems do not seem to be linked

52
00:02:40,550 --> 00:02:45,080
with red meat and saturated fats like previously
thought, but rather with processed meats.

53
00:02:45,080 --> 00:02:49,480
Based on a study of nearly 1.25 million people
(1,218,380), consumption of processed meats,

54
00:02:49,480 --> 00:02:53,640
not simply red meat, was associated with higher
rates of coronary heart disease.

55
00:02:53,640 --> 00:02:57,670
>From an evolutionary standpoint, meat-eating
omnivores also seem to be the reason behind

56
00:02:57,670 --> 00:03:00,230
the growth of our larger, more intelligent
brains.

57
00:03:00,230 --> 00:03:03,790
This is the result of the higher protein content
associated with meat consumption.

58
00:03:03,790 --> 00:03:08,700
The American Dietetic Association, or ADA,
states that the protein from plants can easily

59
00:03:08,700 --> 00:03:13,290
meet and exceed protein requirements, and
that being an omnivore merely increases the

60
00:03:13,290 --> 00:03:17,599
amount of protein sources a person can have
by including animal meat.

61
00:03:17,599 --> 00:03:20,970
Obviously, protein is important to both bone
health and muscle mass.

62
00:03:20,970 --> 00:03:24,810
One study even found that women who ate meat
had higher amounts of muscle mass than their

63
00:03:24,810 --> 00:03:28,939
vegetarian counterparts, even if the protein
intake was the same.

64
00:03:28,939 --> 00:03:32,819
While there certainly may be some health advantages
in going vegan, there seems to be some common

65
00:03:32,819 --> 00:03:34,720
deficiencies in the diet.

66
00:03:34,720 --> 00:03:36,920
One of these deficiencies is with the vitamin
B-12.

67
00:03:36,920 --> 00:03:41,240
The ADA states that there are no natural plant
foods that contain any significant amount

68
00:03:41,240 --> 00:03:42,240
of the vitamin.

69
00:03:42,240 --> 00:03:46,660
Vegans can still get it, but they need to
take a vitamin or consume fortified foods

70
00:03:46,660 --> 00:03:49,069
like soy milk and certain breakfast cereals.

71
00:03:49,069 --> 00:03:53,450
Omega-3 fatty acids are also very difficult
to come by on a vegan diet, but this can be

72
00:03:53,450 --> 00:03:56,329
overcome through the consumption of algae
supplements.

73
00:03:56,329 --> 00:04:00,750
With vegans requiring supplementation to meet
their nutritional needs, it supports the claim

74
00:04:00,750 --> 00:04:05,360
that veganism is unnatural, but that doesn’t
necessarily mean it's unhealthy.

75
00:04:05,360 --> 00:04:09,430
At this point, some of you may be wondering
which diet leads to longer life spans.

76
00:04:09,430 --> 00:04:11,750
For that information, we turn to Okinawa.

77
00:04:11,750 --> 00:04:15,989
The traditional Okinawan diet is typically
regarded as the best for health and longevity,

78
00:04:15,989 --> 00:04:20,890
with the Okinawan islands having the greatest
concentration of centenarians in the world.

79
00:04:20,890 --> 00:04:26,150
An archipelago hundreds of miles off the coast
of Japan, Okinawa has about 740 centenarians

80
00:04:26,150 --> 00:04:29,210
out of its population of 1.3 million people.

81
00:04:29,210 --> 00:04:33,020
While their diets have been changing recently
due to globalization and factors like fast

82
00:04:33,020 --> 00:04:37,210
food chains, the traditional Okinawan diet
is made up of large amounts of plant-based

83
00:04:37,210 --> 00:04:38,530
carbohydrates (about 85% of their diet).

84
00:04:38,530 --> 00:04:43,800
Although they are primarily vegans, traditional
Okinawans still eat meat on special occasions,

85
00:04:43,800 --> 00:04:47,140
usually pork, as well as small amounts of
fish on a weekly basis.

86
00:04:47,140 --> 00:04:50,640
This doesn’t prove that small amounts of
animal products are vital to good health,

87
00:04:50,640 --> 00:04:55,420
but it does hint that the optimal human diet
can be achieved without going completely vegan.

88
00:04:55,420 --> 00:05:00,090
That said, many health organizations, including
the ADA, state that well-planned vegan diets

89
00:05:00,090 --> 00:05:03,730
are healthy and nutritionally adequate, and
may provide health benefits in the prevention

90
00:05:03,730 --> 00:05:05,340
and treatment of certain diseases.

91
00:05:05,340 --> 00:05:09,130
It seems like no matter what your dietary
preferences are, a healthy lifestyle can be

92
00:05:09,130 --> 00:05:11,590
achieved on or off a vegan diet.

93
00:05:11,590 --> 00:05:14,860
Are you or would you ever consider becoming
a vegan?

Why or why not?

00:03:02,200 --> 00:03:07,819
beer and alcohol industries are two of the
biggest anti-marijuana advocates. Obviously,

40
00:03:07,819 --> 00:03:13,140
marijuana is a serious threat to alcohol sales.
Due to its safer nature, marijuana is often

41
00:03:13,140 --> 00:03:16,140
suggested as an alternative to alcohol.

42
00:03:16,140 --> 00:03:21,680
However, heavy use can be harmful. Since pot
smoke is chemically very similar to tobacco

43
00:03:21,680 --> 00:03:26,739
smoke, heavy pot smokers are at risk for some
of the same health effects as cigarette smokers,

44
00:03:26,739 --> 00:03:31,680
like bronchitis and other respiratory illnesses.
Though, the risks are from smoking, which

45
00:03:31,680 --> 00:03:37,159
isn't the only way to use marijuana. Another
hazard: car accidents caused by driving while

46
00:03:37,159 --> 00:03:40,109
high, though the risk is lower than from drunk
driving.

47
00:03:40,109 --> 00:03:42,209
A smoker would theoretically have to consume

48
00:03:42,209 --> 00:03:55,980
nearly 1,500 pounds of marijuana within about
fifteen minutes to induce a lethal response.

question: What is the best title of the video?
answer: What people miss about the gender wage gap
distractor1: Why women earn 79 cents for every dollar a man makes
distractor2: How to ask for a raise: A guide for female MBAs
distractor3: The history of women in the workforce: 1970 to present

question:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:09,000
When we talk about gender equality in the US there’s this one statistic you see all the time: "Women earn 79 cents for every dollar men make."

2
00:00:09,000 --> 00:00:12,600
And while that statistic is factually correct, there’s a lot it doesn’t tell you.

3
00:00:12,600 --> 00:00:17,320
It simply compares the median wages of men and women who work full time.

4
00:00:17,320 --> 00:00:24,320
It doesn’t tell you how the wage gap plays out for women with different educational levels or different ages, or who work in different fields.

5
00:00:24,320 --> 00:00:28,180
And you need that information if you want to start closing the gap.

6
00:00:30,160 --> 00:00:35,520
Part of the wage gap reflects the fact that women are more concentrated in lower-paying occupations.

7
00:00:35,520 --> 00:00:40,180
But to fully understand the issue, you  have to look within occupations too.

8
00:00:40,180 --> 00:00:43,620
Back in 2009, three economists set out to understand the wage gap

9
00:00:43,620 --> 00:00:48,660
by following a group of MBA graduates from the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business.

10
00:00:48,660 --> 00:00:53,860
They looked at thousands of men and women who graduated between 1990 and 2006.

11
00:00:53,860 --> 00:00:58,180
And their data showed that men had slightly higher salaries right out of the gate.

12
00:00:58,180 --> 00:01:05,180
One year out of business school, women were making an average salary of $115,000 while men earned $130,000.

13
00:01:05,520 --> 00:01:14,240
But nine years out of business school, things looked really different. Men were earning an average salary of $400,000, while women were earning 60 percent less

14
00:01:14,240 --> 00:01:18,320
—$250,000 on average. The gap had widened considerably.

15
00:01:18,320 --> 00:01:24,420
But research suggests the gap doesn’t stay that wide — that it shrinks as women enter middle age.

16
00:01:24,420 --> 00:01:31,420
This chart shows how the wage gap for college graduates changes as women age. The lower the line, the bigger the wage gap between men and women.

17
00:01:31,820 --> 00:01:38,820
If you look at women born in 1973, you can see the wage gap growing as they go from their mid-twenties to their mid thirties.

18
00:01:39,020 --> 00:01:43,000
Better than previous generations but heading in the same direction.

19
00:01:43,000 --> 00:01:45,440
Same thing for women born in 1968.

20
00:01:45,440 --> 00:01:51,220
The pay difference for men and women continues to grow as they move from their mid-thirties to their mid-forties.

21
00:01:51,220 --> 00:01:58,220
And for women born in 1948, things started off the same. The gap widens as they get older. But then, all of a sudden, it starts shrinking.

22
00:01:58,220 --> 00:02:05,220
As working women approach their 50s and 60s, the difference between men’s and women’s salaries gets smaller

23
00:02:05,220 --> 00:02:10,820
Which makes sense if you think about what often happens during a woman’s 20s and 30s.

24
00:02:10,880 --> 00:02:16,640
In the Chicago MBA study, women with kids had a wage gap twice as large as women without.

25
00:02:16,640 --> 00:02:21,680
The truth is that women take on a disproportionate share of child-rearing tasks.

26
00:02:21,740 --> 00:02:28,740
A survey from Pew found that in 2-parent households, women did more than men when it came to managing kids’ schedules,

27
00:02:28,740 --> 00:02:33,480
taking care of them when they’re sick, and handling the majority of household chores.

28
00:02:33,480 --> 00:02:37,140
And that was a survey of families where both parents worked full-time.

29
00:02:37,140 --> 00:02:41,420
But these additional responsibilities seem to hurt some women more than others.

30
00:02:41,420 --> 00:02:48,420
This is a key research finding from Claudia Goldin, an economist at Harvard who is a leading researcher on the gender wage gap.

31
00:02:48,420 --> 00:02:52,600
She shows this by exploring how gender pay gaps vary in different fields.

32
00:02:52,600 --> 00:02:57,320
This is one of her charts. Each of these dots is a different higher-paying job.

33
00:02:57,320 --> 00:03:04,320
The lower the dot, the larger the gender pay gap. The further to the right, the more the job pays, based on the average income of men in that job.

34
00:03:04,560 --> 00:03:07,500
These green dots represent jobs in the tech sector.

35
00:03:07,500 --> 00:03:14,660
For the most part, the jobs are pretty close to the 0 line, meaning the difference in pay between men and women is fairly small.

36
00:03:14,760 --> 00:03:17,160
The same is true for jobs in science.

37
00:03:17,160 --> 00:03:18,120
The yellow dots.

38
00:03:18,120 --> 00:03:18,960
But look as these red dots.

39
00:03:18,960 --> 00:03:21,200
They represent jobs in business.

40
00:03:21,200 --> 00:03:26,780
And they’re mostly clustered toward the middle and the bottom of the chart, meaning they have some of the largest wage gaps.

41
00:03:26,780 --> 00:03:34,800
There’s a fairly simple way to explain some of these differences—some jobs require specific hours. Others are more flexible.

42
00:03:34,800 --> 00:03:45,280
Take your prototypical businesswoman. Maybe she’s a venture capitalist, maybe she’s an accountant. Either way, she has a standard 9-5 schedule so she can meet with other businesspeople or with clients.

43
00:03:45,280 --> 00:03:50,180
If she’s not available to her clients when they need her, her bosses won’t think she’s doing a good job.

44
00:03:50,180 --> 00:03:55,360
Compare that to a scientist who works in a lab. Most of her work is self-directed.

45
00:03:55,360 --> 00:04:01,580
It doesn't’ really matter when she runs her experiments, as long as she gets them done. If she gets her work done, her bosses think she’s doing a good job.

46
00:04:01,580 --> 00:04:10,320
For the millions of women in with jobs that demand very specific hours, the wage gap is larger than it is for women in jobs with more flexible hours

47
00:04:10,320 --> 00:04:17,880
There’s one job where we can see this really clearly. In 1970s, [Insert subtitle here]

48
00:04:17,880 --> 00:04:25,700
Pharmacies used to be mostly independent businesses where a single pharmacist might be responsible for keeping his shop open whenever people needed it.

49
00:04:25,700 --> 00:04:32,060
Today, most pharmacies are owned by large chains. They stay open longer, which means they need more pharmacists.

50
00:04:32,060 --> 00:04:41,260
Women pharmacists now have a lot more options and a 6am to 2pm shift is just as good as a 9 - 5 shift. Nobody gets rewarded for working exceptionally long hours.

51
00:04:41,260 --> 00:04:49,180
And the wage gap for pharmacists has shrunk dramatically. Today, female pharmacists make 92 percent of what their male counterparts do.

52
00:04:49,180 --> 00:04:55,380
Of course, we can’t all be pharmacists. There will always be jobs where it’s important to  work particular hours.

53
00:04:55,380 --> 00:05:00,180
But there are lots of jobs where hours could potentially become more flexible than they are right now.

54
00:05:00,180 --> 00:05:05,760
And research tells us the more we can make that work, the more the wage gap is going to shrink.
answer: women pharmacists earned about 66 percent of what men did.

question: What is the best title of the video?

question:
1
00:00:00,099 --> 00:00:04,990
Americans love their meat, with the average
person consuming roughly 198 lbs (90 kg) of

2
00:00:04,990 --> 00:00:06,850
pork, beef and chicken every year.

3
00:00:06,850 --> 00:00:11,190
The global average is considerably less, at
around 75 lbs (34 kg) per year, but not everyone

4
00:00:11,190 --> 00:00:15,270
is a meat lover, as around 5% of the world’s
population choose to be vegetarian.

5
00:00:15,270 --> 00:00:20,740
In the USA, [Insert subtitle here]

6
00:00:20,740 --> 00:00:21,740
[Insert subtitle here]

7
00:00:21,740 --> 00:00:25,300
With the majority of the population currently
consuming meat and enjoying burgers, ribs,

8
00:00:25,300 --> 00:00:29,630
bacon, wings, and steak on a daily basis,
what would happen if everyone just stopped?

9
00:00:29,630 --> 00:00:33,170
How would it affect the economy, our livelihoods,
the environment, and our health?

10
00:00:33,170 --> 00:00:36,760
That’s what we’re going to look into,
in this episode of the Infographics Show,

11
00:00:36,760 --> 00:00:39,059
What Would Happen If the World Suddenly Turned
Vegetarian?

12
00:00:39,059 --> 00:00:42,149
Do not forget to subscribe and click the bell
button so that you can be part of our Notification

13
00:00:42,149 --> 00:00:43,149
Squad.

14
00:00:43,149 --> 00:00:44,390
Economy
It is estimated by the North American Meat

15
00:00:44,390 --> 00:00:50,370
Institute (NAMI) that the meat industry brings
$894 billion to the US economy with $95 billion

16
00:00:50,370 --> 00:00:52,179
of that being for beef alone.

17
00:00:52,179 --> 00:00:57,320
800,000 people are employed in the meat and
poultry business in the US, and millions worldwide,

18
00:00:57,320 --> 00:01:00,710
so a sudden turn to vegetarianism would mean
a huge loss of jobs.

19
00:01:00,710 --> 00:01:04,110
It would, at the same time, create jobs in
different fields.

20
00:01:04,110 --> 00:01:08,250
Moving into a meat-free lifestyle would have
a significant impact on the world’s economy,

21
00:01:08,250 --> 00:01:13,380
with the meat industry being perceived in
value of up to $1.6 trillion by 2050.

22
00:01:13,380 --> 00:01:16,250
Social Impacts
The social impacts of global vegetarianism

23
00:01:16,250 --> 00:01:18,180
could be devastating for many communities.

24
00:01:18,180 --> 00:01:22,820
Currently, around 1 billion people dedicate
their lives to tending to livestock and lands

25
00:01:22,820 --> 00:01:27,180
or working in meat factories, so if we stopped
eating meat, their livelihoods would be stripped

26
00:01:27,180 --> 00:01:29,640
from them, losing their income and lands.

27
00:01:29,640 --> 00:01:31,259
What work could they do instead?

28
00:01:31,259 --> 00:01:34,929
Many may take to growing and selling fruit,
vegetables or wheat crops, or finding another

29
00:01:34,929 --> 00:01:35,929
source of income.

30
00:01:35,929 --> 00:01:39,340
The poor could be hit hard with their diet
no longer including the nutrition that they

31
00:01:39,340 --> 00:01:43,759
get from meat with animal products containing
many more nutrients than grains and rice.

32
00:01:43,759 --> 00:01:47,340
There are many cultural and religious traditions
that include meat as a focal point, which

33
00:01:47,340 --> 00:01:51,330
would no longer exist or would have to be
altered due to a vegetarian lifestyle.

34
00:01:51,330 --> 00:01:55,969
Many of the 1.8 billion Muslims around the
world celebrate Eid al-Adha every year as

35
00:01:55,969 --> 00:02:00,409
part of the Islamic calendar and as part of
this tradition, a goat or sheep is slaughtered

36
00:02:00,409 --> 00:02:03,320
and some of the meat is offered to poor and
needy families.

37
00:02:03,320 --> 00:02:07,579
In the USA, a longstanding tradition is having
a turkey on the table for Thanksgiving dinner,

38
00:02:07,579 --> 00:02:10,500
but in a meat-free environment, what would
be the feature food on our plates?

39
00:02:10,500 --> 00:02:11,500
Tofurkey?

40
00:02:11,500 --> 00:02:15,310
Now let’s look at some of the positive impacts
a sudden change to vegetarianism would have.

41
00:02:15,310 --> 00:02:17,470
Environment
In a vegetarian world, our environment would

42
00:02:17,470 --> 00:02:22,140
be much better off, leaving way to a healthier
and cleaner planet for future generations.

43
00:02:22,140 --> 00:02:25,510
Livestock production and the meat industry
is thought to be one of the biggest contributors

44
00:02:25,510 --> 00:02:30,400
to climate change, with a larger impact on
the planet than anything else, as 14.5% of

45
00:02:30,400 --> 00:02:34,620
the world’s greenhouse gas emissions are
caused by the human activity of meat production.

46
00:02:34,620 --> 00:02:38,390
Most people do not even think about the effect
food has on climate change, but if we stopped

47
00:02:38,390 --> 00:02:42,780
eating meat, we would be doing our planet
a favour with gas emissions being reduced

48
00:02:42,780 --> 00:02:43,850
significantly.

49
00:02:43,850 --> 00:02:48,100
Meat production emits much higher gas emissions
than fruit and vegetable production, and research

50
00:02:48,100 --> 00:02:52,060
has shown that the production of beef is so
environmentally destructive that it causes

51
00:02:52,060 --> 00:02:55,560
5 times more climate warming emissions than
other animals.

52
00:02:55,560 --> 00:02:59,940
In the US, an average family of four emit
more greenhouse gases due to the meat they

53
00:02:59,940 --> 00:03:02,770
consume than from having two cars on the road.

54
00:03:02,770 --> 00:03:06,540
With the sudden change to vegetarianism and
the elimination of meat, our food related

55
00:03:06,540 --> 00:03:08,870
emissions could drop by up to 60-70%.

56
00:03:08,870 --> 00:03:11,870
Water
Another major environmental cost of meat production

57
00:03:11,870 --> 00:03:16,400
is water usage, with livestock consuming more
of our water than anything else, and also

58
00:03:16,400 --> 00:03:18,850
being one of the largest causes of polluted
water.

59
00:03:18,850 --> 00:03:24,360
The total water footprint for one pound of
beef is 200 times that of one pound of plant

60
00:03:24,360 --> 00:03:25,360
foods.

61
00:03:25,360 --> 00:03:29,710
One kilo of beef requires 15,000 litres of
water before it arrives on your dinner plate,

62
00:03:29,710 --> 00:03:33,760
while a roast chicken would take up 4,325
litres.

63
00:03:33,760 --> 00:03:37,390
Globally there are millions of people that
do not have access to clean drinking water,

64
00:03:37,390 --> 00:03:41,080
so if there were less livestock to feed, there
would be a lot more water to go around.

65
00:03:41,080 --> 00:03:43,570
Land
According to Dutch scientists, there are currently

66
00:03:43,570 --> 00:03:48,510
2.7 billion hectares of land being used for
cattle grazing with between 20-30% of the

67
00:03:48,510 --> 00:03:52,870
globe’s ice-free land solely for farming
pigs, chicken and cattle.

68
00:03:52,870 --> 00:03:57,510
Another 100 million hectares on top of that
are dedicated to growing the crops that feed

69
00:03:57,510 --> 00:03:58,530
the livestock.

70
00:03:58,530 --> 00:04:04,320
In the US, around 700 million tons of food
are consumed by livestock alone each year,

71
00:04:04,320 --> 00:04:08,860
which could actually be given to humans instead
to help combat world hunger, which could be

72
00:04:08,860 --> 00:04:12,160
eliminated with an estimated 40 million tons
of food.

73
00:04:12,160 --> 00:04:16,049
Global vegetarianism could free up this land
currently used by livestock, and even though

74
00:04:16,049 --> 00:04:20,400
a lot of it would not be suitable for habitation
for humans, some of it could be used to cater

75
00:04:20,400 --> 00:04:24,560
to the growing global population, to grow
more plants, and to lead way for other innovative

76
00:04:24,560 --> 00:04:25,720
ways to use the land.

77
00:04:25,720 --> 00:04:28,400
Health
56 billion animals are farmed and killed each

78
00:04:28,400 --> 00:04:32,930
year for human consumption with many being
kept alive by a steady diet of drugs so they

79
00:04:32,930 --> 00:04:36,240
withstand the stressful and unsanitary farming
conditions.

80
00:04:36,240 --> 00:04:42,320
At any time of year, there are approximately
20 billion chickens, 1.5 billion cows, 1 billion

81
00:04:42,320 --> 00:04:47,360
pigs, and 1 billion sheep in farms and factories
around the world – that is three times the

82
00:04:47,360 --> 00:04:49,960
amount of humans and they are all there to
feed us.

83
00:04:49,960 --> 00:04:54,770
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization,
the number of animals that require land for

84
00:04:54,770 --> 00:04:58,340
grazing is growing by 25 million each year.

85
00:04:58,340 --> 00:05:02,010
Factory farmed animals are full of diseases
and can be a breeding ground for new strains

86
00:05:02,010 --> 00:05:03,570
of viruses and superbugs.

87
00:05:03,570 --> 00:05:08,400
By eliminating these factory farms, we could
lower the risk of antibiotic resistant bacteria

88
00:05:08,400 --> 00:05:11,620
and diseases such as Mad Cow Disease being
released into our environment.

89
00:05:11,620 --> 00:05:12,620
Protein?

90
00:05:12,620 --> 00:05:15,480
Another point to consider would be that without
meat to provide all-important protein in our

91
00:05:15,480 --> 00:05:17,750
diets, what would be our primary source?

92
00:05:17,750 --> 00:05:20,010
Fortunately, there are many alternatives.

93
00:05:20,010 --> 00:05:24,570
Soybeans are historically known as ‘meat
without bones’ and contain 35% protein,

94
00:05:24,570 --> 00:05:26,770
meaning it is a quality protein source.

95
00:05:26,770 --> 00:05:30,660
There is a current perception that vegetarians
drain the world’s plant sources but in fact

96
00:05:30,660 --> 00:05:34,110
most of the soybean crops and grains grown
go to livestock.

97
00:05:34,110 --> 00:05:38,160
Other ways we could get a healthy dose of
daily protein would be to eat more peas, nuts,

98
00:05:38,160 --> 00:05:40,380
beans, quinoa, greens and buckwheat.

99
00:05:40,380 --> 00:05:44,730
Dairy milk and chicken eggs are also an excellent
source, provided that milk and egg farms would

100
00:05:44,730 --> 00:05:45,800
still be in operation.

101
00:05:45,800 --> 00:05:47,350
So, what do you think?

102
00:05:47,350 --> 00:05:49,750
Would the world benefit from a global vegetarian
diet?

103
00:05:49,750 --> 00:05:51,580
Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

104
00:05:51,580 --> 00:05:55,390
Also, be sure to check out our other video
called Vegans vs Meat Eaters!

105
00:05:55,390 --> 00:05:58,270
Thanks for watching, and, as always, don’t
forget to like, share, and subscribe.

106
00:05:58,270 --> 00:05:58,850
See you next time!

question:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:02,003
Matter, as we know it;

2
00:00:02,003 --> 00:00:07,700
Atoms, stars and galaxies, planets and 
trees, rocks and us.

3
00:00:08,135 --> 00:00:12,176
This matter accounts for less than
5% of the known universe.

4
00:00:12,483 --> 00:00:18,062
About 25% is dark matter; 
and 70% is dark energy.

5
00:00:18,196 --> 00:00:20,699
Both of which are invisible.

6
00:00:20,864 --> 00:00:25,497
This is kind of strange because it
suggests that everything we experience is

7
00:00:25,497 --> 00:00:28,218
really only a tiny fraction of reality.

8
00:00:28,653 --> 00:00:29,818
But it gets worse.

9
00:00:29,972 --> 00:00:34,526
We really have no clue what dark matter
and energy are, or how they work.

10
00:00:34,940 --> 00:00:36,776
We are pretty sure they exist though.

11
00:00:37,060 --> 00:00:39,214
So, what do we know?

12
00:00:45,771 --> 00:00:50,568
Dark matter is the stuff that makes 
it possible for galaxies to exist.

13
00:00:50,956 --> 00:00:54,154
When we calculated why the universe
is structured the way it is,

14
00:00:54,347 --> 00:00:57,927
it quickly became clear that there's just
not enough normal matter.

15
00:00:58,167 --> 00:01:01,335
The gravity of the visible matter
is not strong enough to form

16
00:01:01,368 --> 00:01:03,734
galaxies and complex structures.

17
00:01:03,930 --> 00:01:08,629
The stars would more likely be scattered
all over the place and not form galaxies.

18
00:01:09,052 --> 00:01:12,715
So, we know there is something else inside
and around them.

19
00:01:13,196 --> 00:01:16,185
Something that doesn't
emit or reflect light.

20
00:01:16,276 --> 00:01:17,975
Something dark...

21
00:01:18,207 --> 00:01:22,284
but besides being able to calculate
the existence of dark matter,

22
00:01:22,586 --> 00:01:24,587
we can see it... kind of.

23
00:01:24,711 --> 00:01:29,394
Places with a high concentration of dark
matter bend light passing near by.

24
00:01:29,483 --> 00:01:32,966
So we know there's something there that
interacts with gravity.

25
00:01:33,142 --> 00:01:39,034
Right now, we have more ideas about
what dark energy is not, than what it is!

26
00:01:39,393 --> 00:01:43,601
We know dark matter is not just clouds of
normal matter without stars,

27
00:01:43,800 --> 00:01:46,408
because it would emit particles
we could detect.

28
00:01:46,586 --> 00:01:48,924
Dark matter is not anti-matter,

29
00:01:48,933 --> 00:01:53,320
because anti-matter produces unique gamma
rays when it reacts with normal matter.

30
00:01:53,515 --> 00:01:57,190
Dark matter is also not
made up of black holes,

31
00:01:57,217 --> 00:02:00,902
very compact objects that violently affect
their surroundings,

32
00:02:00,902 --> 00:02:04,702
while dark matter seems to be
scattered all over the place.

33
00:02:04,941 --> 00:02:07,703
Basically, we only know 3 things for sure;

34
00:02:08,017 --> 00:02:10,274
1. Something is out there.

35
00:02:10,444 --> 00:02:13,107
2. It interacts with gravity.

36
00:02:13,228 --> 00:02:15,688
3. There is a lot of it.

37
00:02:15,898 --> 00:02:19,842
Dark matter is probably made up of a 
complicated exotic particle

38
00:02:19,848 --> 00:02:23,731
that doesn't interact with 
light and matter in a way we expect,

39
00:02:23,741 --> 00:02:25,755
but right now, we just don't know.

40
00:02:25,994 --> 00:02:29,428
Dark energy is even more
strange and mysterious.

41
00:02:29,518 --> 00:02:33,470
We can't detect it, we can't measure it
and we can't taste it.

42
00:02:33,715 --> 00:02:36,724
But we do see its effects very clearly.

43
00:02:36,944 --> 00:02:41,358
In 1929, Edward Hubble examined how 
the wavelength of light

44
00:02:41,358 --> 00:02:44,858
emitted by distant galaxies, shifts
towards the red end

45
00:02:44,865 --> 00:02:48,208
of the electromagnetic spectrum
as it travels through the space.

46
00:02:48,399 --> 00:02:54,043
He found that fainter, more distant galaxies
showed a large degree of red shift;

47
00:02:54,337 --> 00:02:56,617
closer galaxies, not so much.

48
00:02:56,982 --> 00:03:01,094
Hubble determined that this was because
the universe itself is expanding.

49
00:03:01,267 --> 00:03:04,835
The red shift occurs,
because the wavelengths of light

50
00:03:04,835 --> 00:03:07,418
are stretched as the universe expands.

51
00:03:07,635 --> 00:03:12,552
More recent discoveries have shown that, 
[Insert subtitle here].

52
00:03:12,745 --> 00:03:16,922
Before that, it was thougth that the pull
of gravity would cause the expansion to

53
00:03:16,922 --> 00:03:21,169
either slow down or even retract and 
collapse in on itself at some point.

54
00:03:21,435 --> 00:03:26,835
Space doesn't change its properties
as it expands; there's just more of it.

55
00:03:26,921 --> 00:03:29,932
New space is constantly
created everywhere,

56
00:03:30,081 --> 00:03:34,922
galaxies are tight bound clusters of stuff
held together by gravity

57
00:03:34,944 --> 00:03:38,210
so we don't experience this expansion
in our daily lives.

58
00:03:38,293 --> 00:03:40,248
But we see it everywhere around us.

59
00:03:40,302 --> 00:03:44,852
Wherever there is empty space in the 
universe, more is forming every second.

60
00:03:45,052 --> 00:03:50,057
So, dark energy seems to be some
kind of energy intrinsic to empty space.

61
00:03:50,142 --> 00:03:52,851
Energy that is stronger than
anything else we know

62
00:03:52,851 --> 00:03:55,871
and it keeps getting stronger
as time passes by.

63
00:03:56,161 --> 00:04:01,601
Empty space has more energy than
everything else in the universe combined.

64
00:04:02,072 --> 00:04:06,012
We have multiple ideas about 
what dark energy might be.

65
00:04:06,124 --> 00:04:11,469
One idea is, the dark energy is not
a thing, but just a property of space.

66
00:04:11,890 --> 00:04:15,356
Empty space is not nothing, it has its own
energy.

67
00:04:15,382 --> 00:04:18,451
It can generate more space and
is quite active.

68
00:04:18,531 --> 00:04:22,829
So, as the universe expands,
it could be that just more and more space

69
00:04:22,829 --> 00:04:27,975
appears to fill the gaps and this leads
to a faster expanding universe.

70
00:04:28,494 --> 00:04:32,772
This idea is close to an idea that 
Einstein had back in 1917,

71
00:04:32,772 --> 00:04:35,199
of the concept of a cosmological constant,

72
00:04:35,199 --> 00:04:38,422
a force that counteracted
the force of gravity.

73
00:04:38,494 --> 00:04:42,367
The only problem is, that when we tried
to calculate the amount of this energy

74
00:04:42,536 --> 00:04:47,239
the result was so wrong and weird,
that it only added to the confusion.

75
00:04:47,371 --> 00:04:50,418
Another idea is, that empty space is
actually full of

76
00:04:50,418 --> 00:04:54,428
temporary, virtual particles that 
spontaneously and continually

77
00:04:54,428 --> 00:04:58,035
form from nothing and then dissapear into
nothing again.

78
00:04:58,405 --> 00:05:01,753
The energy form those particles
could be dark energy.

79
00:05:01,907 --> 00:05:06,572
Or maybe dark energy is an unknown kind of
dynamic energy fluid or field

80
00:05:06,572 --> 00:05:11,122
which permeates the entire universe,
but somehow has the opposite effect

81
00:05:11,122 --> 00:05:13,771
on the universe than normal
energy and matter.

82
00:05:14,015 --> 00:05:18,591
But if it exists, we don't know
how and where or how we could detect it.

83
00:05:18,742 --> 00:05:22,214
So there are still a lot of questions to
answer.

84
00:05:22,321 --> 00:05:26,036
Our theories about dark matter and
dark energy are still just that;

85
00:05:26,056 --> 00:05:27,056
theories.

86
00:05:27,186 --> 00:05:32,217
On one hand, this is kind of frustrating,
on the other hand this is frontier science

87
00:05:32,296 --> 00:05:34,025
making it very exciting.

88
00:05:34,121 --> 00:05:37,185
It shows us that no matter how much
we feel we're on top of things,

89
00:05:37,185 --> 00:05:40,378
we are still very much
apes with smartphones, on a tiny

90
00:05:40,378 --> 00:05:45,466
fragile island in space looking into
the sky wondering how our universe works

91
00:05:45,787 --> 00:05:50,751
There is so much left to learn,
and that is awesome.

92

which promotes and supports

Learn more about this topic

95
00:06:03,207 --> 00:06:06,599
It was a blast of work with them

96

Our videos are also made possible

00:00:33,250 --> 00:00:36,020

00:00:36,020 --> 00:00:39,940
This concept, of taxing the poor at a lower

00:00:39,941 --> 00:00:41,589

13
00:00:41,589 --> 00:00:43,960
It’s how taxes work in most countries.

14
00:00:43,960 --> 00:00:46,719

15
00:00:46,719 --> 00:00:48,539

00:00:48,539 --> 00:00:53,289
"The middle class and the poor that pay, if

00:00:53,289 --> 00:00:59,540
"Why is it that 45 percent of the population

00:00:59,540 --> 00:01:02,360

23
00:01:14,360 --> 00:01:18,370
Now, you might be thinking, don’t billionaires

24
00:01:18,370 --> 00:01:19,760

00:01:19,760 --> 00:01:24,210

And this analysis, where this data came from?

00:01:54,280 --> 00:01:55,760

00:02:00,150 --> 00:02:04,070

00:02:04,070 --> 00:02:06,860

00:02:10,280 --> 00:02:12,230

00:02:12,230 --> 00:02:15,280
Put these taxes together, and it’s clear

00:02:15,280 --> 00:02:18,340
rich -- including billionaires.

44
00:02:18,340 --> 00:02:20,800
Add these back onto the income taxes,

45
00:02:20,800 --> 00:02:25,180

46
00:02:25,180 --> 00:02:27,640
But now let's talk about another tax.

47
00:02:27,640 --> 00:02:29,440
This one's buried in your paystub.

48
00:02:29,440 --> 00:02:33,510
Look closely, and you'll see something called
a Medicare tax and a Social Security tax.

49
00:02:33,510 --> 00:02:35,440
Sometimes paystubs call them FICA.

50
00:02:35,440 --> 00:02:38,220
Anyway, combined, these are called payroll
taxes.

51
00:02:38,220 --> 00:02:42,280
Medicare and Social Security are two really
important programs: they provide health care

52
00:02:42,280 --> 00:02:45,140

53
00:02:45,140 --> 00:02:46,580

54
00:02:46,580 --> 00:02:49,440
Which is why we have these payroll taxes -- separate from the income tax --

00:02:49,440 --> 00:02:50,780

56
00:02:50,780 --> 00:02:55,100
So on your paycheck, you'll notice that you're

00:02:55,100 --> 00:02:59,520

58
00:02:59,520 --> 00:03:03,960

00:03:03,960 --> 00:03:06,500

60
00:03:06,500 --> 00:03:11,620
So in reality, many workers pay nearly the full 15.3

00:03:11,620 --> 00:03:15,500

00:03:15,500 --> 00:03:17,640
But the wealthy?

00:03:24,819 --> 00:03:26,569

00:03:26,569 --> 00:03:31,010
