00:03:45,140 --> 00:03:47,600

00:03:47,600 --> 00:03:51,640

00:03:51,640 --> 00:03:53,940

Meanwhile, everyone, even people with almost no money,

00:04:30,140 --> 00:04:32,140
needs to buy certain basic things to survive.

84
00:04:32,140 --> 00:04:36,260
And for poor people, those basic things and the taxes that come with them

85
00:04:36,260 --> 00:04:39,360
cost them almost everything they earn.

86
00:04:39,360 --> 00:04:43,780
So if we chart how much of their income each
of these people pays in consumption taxes...

87
00:04:43,780 --> 00:04:48,600
… we can see that poor people pay a much larger
portion.

88
00:04:49,900 --> 00:04:52,340
When we put these taxes together…

89
00:04:52,340 --> 00:04:56,620
Suddenly we see a big change.

90
00:04:56,620 --> 00:05:01,150
The chart shows us that this line, from before,
is a lie.

91
00:05:01,150 --> 00:05:05,160
That America’s tax system as a whole, isn’t
very progressive.

92
00:05:05,160 --> 00:05:07,060
Instead, it’s mostly flat.

93
00:05:07,060 --> 00:05:11,800
Poor people pay about the same portion of
their income in taxes as rich people.

94
00:05:11,800 --> 00:05:16,020
And this guy — this billionaire — is paying
a smaller portion than everyone else.

95
00:05:16,020 --> 00:05:17,720
Even the poorest.

96
00:05:18,300 --> 00:05:21,100
If you look at just certain types of taxes,

97
00:05:21,100 --> 00:05:25,080
it’s natural to assume that rich people pay a bigger tax burden in the US,

98
00:05:25,080 --> 00:05:28,940
and that poor people aren’t exactly paying their fair share.

99
00:05:28,940 --> 00:05:32,520
But a more complete look at the bigger picture,
challenges that.

100
00:05:32,520 --> 00:05:36,960
And it suggests that, if we’re looking for
a group that isn’t paying their fair share,

101
00:05:36,960 --> 00:05:40,880
we might be looking on the wrong end.
answer: he is the very richest 10 percent.

question: What is the difference in voter turnout percentage between Sweden and the U.S.?

1
00:00:03,639 --> 00:00:08,930
In Sweden, more than 82.6% of people over
18 turn out to vote in elections.

2
00:00:08,930 --> 00:00:11,830
82.6%!

3
00:00:11,830 --> 00:00:16,139
In the U.S., [Insert subtitle here]

4
00:00:16,139 --> 00:00:20,930
We’re getting our asses kicked by Denmark,
South Korea, the Netherlands and a whole host

5
00:00:20,930 --> 00:00:22,830
of other developed democracies.

6
00:00:22,830 --> 00:00:28,660
If we re-sort this chart to show what percent
of registered voters actually voted - we’re

7
00:00:28,660 --> 00:00:30,400
near the top of the list!

8
00:00:30,400 --> 00:00:35,269
The U.S. has a huge gap between the share
of people who can vote, and the share of people

9
00:00:35,269 --> 00:00:36,809
who actually do.

10
00:00:36,809 --> 00:00:40,780
But it turns out, a lot of these countries
are doing something really simple, that could

11
00:00:40,780 --> 00:00:42,700
make that gap disappear.

12
00:00:46,889 --> 00:00:51,219
If you take all 50 states, and rank them by
the share of eligible voters — that’s

13
00:00:51,219 --> 00:00:56,699
citizens over 18 who aren’t felons — that
actually voted in 2016, you can see a huge

14
00:00:56,699 --> 00:00:57,729
variation.

15
00:00:57,729 --> 00:01:01,869
Now let’s look at the states that let you
register when you show up to vote on election

16
00:01:01,869 --> 00:01:02,949
day.

17
00:01:02,949 --> 00:01:04,129
Notice something?

18
00:01:04,129 --> 00:01:07,280
The states with the highest turnout rates
all have it.

19
00:01:07,280 --> 00:01:10,890
All the states below the national
average— well, they don’t.

20
00:01:10,890 --> 00:01:13,800
Most of them make you register nearly a month
in advance.

21
00:01:13,800 --> 00:01:18,140
And there’s a whole host of reasons people
might not be registered - nearly a third

22
00:01:18,140 --> 00:01:22,620
of unregistered Americans say they intend
to and just haven’t gotten around to it,

23
00:01:22,620 --> 00:01:26,390
others say it’s inconvenient or they just
don’t know how.

24
00:01:26,390 --> 00:01:32,280
In Minnesota, 12% of the people who voted
in 2016 registered on election day.

25
00:01:32,280 --> 00:01:35,180
That’s 350,000 people.

26
00:01:35,180 --> 00:01:39,560
Maine, New Hampshire, Wisconsin and Idaho
all had lots of people registering last-minute,

27
00:01:39,560 --> 00:01:40,930
too.

28
00:01:46,460 --> 00:01:48,760
Oregon has figured that out.

29
00:01:48,760 --> 00:01:55,580
Turnout increased nearly 4% from 2012 to 2016
— that's more than double than what we saw nationally.

30
00:01:55,590 --> 00:02:01,130
It’s no coincidence that in 2015 Oregon
became the first state to enact automatic

31
00:02:01,130 --> 00:02:03,490
voter registration - or AVR.

32
00:02:03,490 --> 00:02:05,690
Here’s how it works.

33
00:02:05,690 --> 00:02:10,209
Anyone who has an interaction with Oregon’s
Department of Motor Vehicles is automatically

34
00:02:10,209 --> 00:02:13,719
added to the list of registered voters, called
a voter roll.

35
00:02:13,719 --> 00:02:18,110
The state sends them postcards giving them
a chance to register with a party or decline

36
00:02:18,110 --> 00:02:19,510
to be registered.

37
00:02:19,510 --> 00:02:22,900
It changes the system from opt-in to opt-out.

38
00:02:22,900 --> 00:02:26,549
So a sixteen year old getting their
driver license will be automatically registered

39
00:02:26,549 --> 00:02:27,810
to vote when they turn 18.

40
00:02:27,810 --> 00:02:33,400
A new resident who changes their ID or
car registration will also be automatically registered

41
00:02:33,400 --> 00:02:38,000
In total, 272,000 people were registered this
way.

42
00:02:38,000 --> 00:02:41,400
And more than a third of them actually voted
in 2016.

43
00:02:41,400 --> 00:02:45,019
Of those voters, 37% of them were under 30.

44
00:02:45,019 --> 00:02:49,129
Compare that to the voters who were registered
through the traditional fill-out-the-vote--for

45
00:02:49,129 --> 00:02:52,150
method, and only 13% were under 30.

46
00:02:52,150 --> 00:02:55,779
AVR got more young people to come out on election
day.

47
00:02:55,779 --> 00:03:01,079
13 states and Washington, DC have already
passed AVR legislation and will have it running

48
00:03:01,079 --> 00:03:02,609
by the 2020 election.

49
00:03:02,609 --> 00:03:07,760
It’ll have massive effects in California
alone, where there are nearly 7 million eligible

50
00:03:07,760 --> 00:03:09,810
people not registered to vote yet.

51
00:03:09,810 --> 00:03:13,540
Let’s go back to that chart with all the other
countries.

52
00:03:13,540 --> 00:03:16,959
These are the ones who have some form of automatic
voter registration.

53
00:03:16,959 --> 00:03:21,739
If the US implemented it nationally, we could
literally move up in the world.

54
00:03:21,740 --> 00:03:25,669
Plus, it’ll make our voting system more
secure and more accurate.

55
00:03:26,860 --> 00:03:30,219
Now when you move, you have to
re-register to vote.

56
00:03:30,219 --> 00:03:35,379
That creates duplicate registrations and makes
it harder for voter rolls to be kept updated.

57
00:03:35,379 --> 00:03:39,370
With AVR, your registration moves with you
- no duplicates.

58
00:03:39,370 --> 00:03:41,340
It’ll also be cheaper.

59
00:03:41,340 --> 00:03:46,300
Everything will be electronic and there will be millions
less registrations to process.

60
00:03:47,100 --> 00:03:52,159
But most importantly, it could automatically
register nearly 50 million Americans, who

61
00:03:52,159 --> 00:03:55,670
would then gets a chance to help decide how
the country should be run.
answer: just over half the voting age population shows up to the polls.

question:
1
00:00:02,250 --> 00:00:06,770
This is Portugal playing Morocco at the 2018
World Cup.

2
00:00:06,770 --> 00:00:09,800
Portugal was the heavy favorite and won the
game 1-0.

3
00:00:09,800 --> 00:00:14,040
The result wasn’t all that interesting,
but this photo is.

4
00:00:14,040 --> 00:00:19,650
This Portugal player wasn’t born in Portugal
and these two Morocco players weren’t born

5
00:00:19,650 --> 00:00:20,650
in Morocco.

6
00:00:20,650 --> 00:00:25,770
See, soccer’s regulating body, FIFA, allows
athletes to play for any nation they have

7
00:00:25,770 --> 00:00:27,310
a clear connection to,

8
00:00:27,310 --> 00:00:30,820
including the country a player’s parents
or grandparents are from.

9
00:00:30,820 --> 00:00:35,790
In this year’s World Cup, 82 players are
playing for countries that they weren’t

10
00:00:35,790 --> 00:00:36,940
born in.

11
00:00:36,940 --> 00:00:39,300
So… where are they coming from?

12
00:00:39,300 --> 00:00:42,020
If we plot it on a map,
one country stands out.

13
00:00:42,020 --> 00:00:47,970
France is where the largest number
of all World Cup players were born.

14
00:00:47,970 --> 00:00:51,930
Brazil has the next highest total but it’s
not even close.

15
00:00:51,930 --> 00:00:56,739
France has had the most native players and
coaches in the last 4 World Cups and their

16
00:00:56,739 --> 00:00:59,399
dominance has been on the rise.

17
00:00:59,400 --> 00:01:03,020
So, what’s so special about France?

18
00:01:10,780 --> 00:01:13,500
At the end of World War II, much of France

19
00:01:13,510 --> 00:01:14,810
was destroyed.

20
00:01:14,810 --> 00:01:19,570
The government began recruiting laborers,
from southern and eastern Europe as well as colonies in

21
00:01:19,570 --> 00:01:24,740
northern Africa, to rebuild the country during
the late 1940s and 1950s.

22
00:01:24,740 --> 00:01:29,260
During that time France brought in more immigrants than any other European country.

23
00:01:29,270 --> 00:01:35,659
And in the 1960s and early 70s France’s economy
grew rapidly and a labor shortage led to another

24
00:01:35,660 --> 00:01:40,780
wave of immigrants - with even more arrivals
from French colonies throughout Africa

25
00:01:40,780 --> 00:01:41,720
and the Caribbean.

26
00:01:41,720 --> 00:01:47,000
Many of them settled in major housing developments
just outside of the major cities.

27
00:01:49,080 --> 00:01:52,450
At the same time, France was also in a sports
crisis.

28
00:01:52,450 --> 00:01:54,479
Especially the national football team.

29
00:01:54,479 --> 00:02:02,060
Between 1960 and 1974, France failed to qualify
for three world cups and three European championships.

30
00:02:02,060 --> 00:02:06,131
The French Football Federation decided the
way to get better was to create a national

31
00:02:06,140 --> 00:02:11,420
structure for developing talent, so it established
one of Europe's first football academy systems.

32
00:02:11,420 --> 00:02:16,800
In 1972, a national training center was opened
in Vichy, and four years later, the Federation

33
00:02:16,810 --> 00:02:21,370
worked with top French football clubs to set
up a wider network of academies to recruit

34
00:02:21,370 --> 00:02:23,400
and train local youth.

35
00:02:23,400 --> 00:02:28,170
In 1988, the national training center moved
to a forested suburb south of Paris called

36
00:02:28,170 --> 00:02:29,310
Clairefontaine

37
00:02:29,310 --> 00:02:34,450
and by the early 1990s, this French soccer
system was one of the best in the world - developing

38
00:02:34,450 --> 00:02:36,940
talented players from all over France.

39
00:02:36,940 --> 00:02:39,500
And the system delivered results.

40
00:02:55,100 --> 00:02:58,960
In 1998, the 
French national team, called Les Bleues, won

41
00:02:58,970 --> 00:02:59,980
the World Cup.

42
00:02:59,980 --> 00:03:03,060
A moment that was celebrated throughout the
country.

43
00:03:03,060 --> 00:03:07,319
And it seemed to be a breakthrough for French
multiculturalism as well,

44
00:03:07,319 --> 00:03:09,980
since several players were either immigrants
themselves

45
00:03:09,980 --> 00:03:13,830
or children of immigrants who came to France
in the 20th century.

46
00:03:13,830 --> 00:03:18,080
The team was called the “Black, Blanc, Beur”,
meaning “black, white, arab” - a spin

47
00:03:18,080 --> 00:03:20,409
on the three colors of the French flag

48
00:03:20,409 --> 00:03:26,280
But not everyone supported diversity, particularly
nationalist politicians like Jean-Marie Le Pen.

49
00:03:48,790 --> 00:03:54,080
Despite racist criticism, players from immigrant
families have continued to make up more and

50
00:03:54,080 --> 00:03:56,220
more of France’s best talent.

51
00:03:56,220 --> 00:03:58,849
Many come from one place in particular.

52
00:03:58,849 --> 00:04:04,019
38% of immigrants to France settle in Greater Paris.

53
00:04:04,019 --> 00:04:07,180
Most end up in these areas called banlieues.

54
00:04:07,180 --> 00:04:11,940
The French word literally means “suburb”;
but it can also imply immigrant-dominated

55
00:04:11,940 --> 00:04:12,940
ghettos.

56
00:04:12,940 --> 00:04:15,651
Over the years, these areas have frequently
seen riots.

57
00:04:16,651 --> 00:04:22,389
They have high levels of unemployment, crime,
and poverty and are in a crisis.

58
00:04:22,389 --> 00:04:26,840
Yet the banlieues continue to produce some
of the most talented soccer players.

59
00:04:26,840 --> 00:04:31,190
That’s because this is where France’s
immigration history meets its soccer system,

60
00:04:31,190 --> 00:04:36,260
and it’s the reason why the city is the
world’s number one talent pool for soccer.

61
00:04:37,720 --> 00:04:43,020
Since 2002, [Insert subtitle here]

62
00:04:43,020 --> 00:04:49,660
Out of all French players at the 2018 World
Cup (50), 16 were born or raised in Greater Paris.

63
00:04:50,360 --> 00:04:55,100
The French national team has eight from banlieues, all children of immigrants.

64
00:04:56,480 --> 00:05:00,400
That includes Kylian Mbappe, France’s 19 year-old
super star

65
00:05:00,400 --> 00:05:05,710
who was born to an Algerian mother and Cameroonian
father in the Parisian suburb of Bondy and

66
00:05:05,710 --> 00:05:08,740
was trained through the French system at Clairefontaine.

67
00:05:11,490 --> 00:05:14,660
But Parisian players don’t just play for
France.

68
00:05:14,660 --> 00:05:18,080
Over the years, FIFA’s eligibility rules
have allowed them to play for countries like

69
00:05:18,080 --> 00:05:23,040
the Ivory Coast, Morocco, Algeria, Portugal,
Cameroon, and Togo.

70
00:05:24,180 --> 00:05:29,810
4 players on this year’s Senegal team are
from the Greater Paris area as well as this

71
00:05:29,810 --> 00:05:31,930
player on Tunisia.

72
00:05:31,930 --> 00:05:33,730
And remember this photo?

73
00:05:33,730 --> 00:05:36,390
Both of these players were born in Paris.

74
00:05:36,390 --> 00:05:41,050
That’s what’s special about French soccer
- the combination of an established academy

75
00:05:41,050 --> 00:05:47,250
system and its unique immigration history
is producing incredible talent - for France

76
00:05:47,250 --> 00:05:48,820
and the rest of the world.
answer: the number of Parisian-born players at the World Cup has continued to rise.

question: What is the best title of the video?

question:
1
00:00:00,299 --> 00:00:02,669
This video is sponsored by Brilliant.

2
00:00:02,669 --> 00:00:08,420
The first 200 to use the link in the description

3
00:00:08,420 --> 00:00:13,780
Anyone whose ever been to In-N-Out knows to
expect, no matter where you are, the same,

4
00:00:13,780 --> 00:00:17,449
consistent burger, smiling cashier, and long
lines.

5
00:00:17,449 --> 00:00:22,849
Residents of Portland, Oregon were known to
drive four hours each way to the nearest restaurant

6
00:00:22,849 --> 00:00:24,300
in Grants Pass,

7
00:00:24,300 --> 00:00:29,380
and before there were any in Phoenix, locals
supposedly flew to Ontario, California, had

8
00:00:29,380 --> 00:00:31,499
lunch, and promptly flew back.

9
00:00:31,499 --> 00:00:37,530
And yet, despite seemingly unlimited demand,
In-N-Out is one of the smallest major fast-food

10
00:00:37,530 --> 00:00:42,109
chains in the world, with only 347 locations.

11
00:00:42,109 --> 00:00:46,970
There are over twice as many Whataburgers,
almost four times as many Five Guys, and forty

12
00:00:46,970 --> 00:00:50,579
times as many McDonalds, just in the U.S.

13
00:00:50,579 --> 00:00:56,210
Since it began in 1948, it’s only opened
an average of five restaurants a year - two

14
00:00:56,210 --> 00:01:00,039
less than Subway opened in a single day, at
its peak.

15
00:01:00,039 --> 00:01:05,330
In other words, In-N-Out deliberately leaves
money on the table, refusing to expand even

16
00:01:05,330 --> 00:01:08,240
where huge profits are guaranteed.

17
00:01:08,240 --> 00:01:09,880
Why?

18
00:01:09,880 --> 00:01:14,290
Profitable, high-margin industries are often,
kind-of… boring.

19
00:01:14,290 --> 00:01:17,000
How do you make money selling toothbrushes?

20
00:01:17,000 --> 00:01:19,160
Uh, well, you…

21
00:01:19,160 --> 00:01:20,160
sell them!

22
00:01:20,160 --> 00:01:24,420
Plastic handles with bristles on the end,
as it turns out, don’t cost very much to

23
00:01:24,420 --> 00:01:27,100
make, and therefore, have healthy margins.

24
00:01:27,100 --> 00:01:31,500
Someone, of course, will try to turn them
into a subscription, make them out of aluminum,

25
00:01:31,500 --> 00:01:35,820
oooh, and call it the Youthbrush, but most
of us don’t have a passion for consumer

26
00:01:35,820 --> 00:01:41,340
dental products, so the business model is
simple: You hand me a couple of dollars, I’ll

27
00:01:41,340 --> 00:01:43,600
give you a rod with some bristles.

28
00:01:43,600 --> 00:01:47,220
Things get interesting when companies have
to get creative.

29
00:01:47,220 --> 00:01:52,360
When competition is high, or consumer willingness
to spend money low, they have to find some

30
00:01:52,360 --> 00:01:54,360
other way to make a profit.

31
00:01:54,360 --> 00:01:56,960
For restaurants, it’s all about selling
drinks.

32
00:01:56,960 --> 00:01:59,450
With printers, the money’s really in the
ink.

33
00:01:59,450 --> 00:02:01,230
And Costco’s low prices?

34
00:02:01,230 --> 00:02:04,090
Those are offset by annual membership fees.

35
00:02:04,090 --> 00:02:09,270
Selling millions of french fries for a few
cents each isn’t a bad business for McDonald’s,

36
00:02:09,270 --> 00:02:12,220
but it’s found something even better: real
estate.

37
00:02:12,220 --> 00:02:17,440
While the company only owns and operates 15%
of its restaurants and the rest are franchised,

38
00:02:17,440 --> 00:02:21,530
it owns almost all of their buildings and
the land beneath them.

39
00:02:21,530 --> 00:02:27,060
Franchisees pay about 8-15% of their revenue
as rent to McDonald’s, who makes money whether

40
00:02:27,060 --> 00:02:32,370
they’re profitable or not, and that’s
on top of the normal franchise royalty.

41
00:02:32,370 --> 00:02:36,950
After going on a huge shopping spree during
the 2008 recession, McDonald’s now owns

42
00:02:36,950 --> 00:02:40,640
more than $30 billion worth of real estate.

43
00:02:40,640 --> 00:02:45,470
Not only is its business diversified but much
of that income is tax-deductible.

44
00:02:45,470 --> 00:02:51,380
In other words, McDonald’s is actually more
real estate investor than fast-food franchise.

45
00:02:51,380 --> 00:02:56,450
Likewise, if you think of In-N-Out only as
a burger chain, it doesn’t make much sense.

46
00:02:56,450 --> 00:02:58,510
Why not open more locations?

47
00:02:58,510 --> 00:03:02,610
Why not change and perfect the recipes, or
add new menu items?

48
00:03:02,610 --> 00:03:08,160
But, if In-N-Out is really about serving a
predictable, familiar experience more than

49
00:03:08,160 --> 00:03:13,709
the food itself, opening new locations and
trying new things are huge risks.

50
00:03:13,709 --> 00:03:19,330
In-N-Out’s secret ingredient, the thing
it’s really selling is: consistency.

51
00:03:19,330 --> 00:03:24,410
Nearly every location has the same, familiar
layout, drive-thru lane, and iconic crossed

52
00:03:24,410 --> 00:03:27,720
palm-trees, a reference to the founder’s
favorite movie.

53
00:03:27,720 --> 00:03:33,830
Unlike other fast-food restaurants, the interior
is clean, well-lit, and easy on the eyes.

54
00:03:33,830 --> 00:03:39,280
Most importantly, the menu is dead simple:
hamburger, cheeseburger, french fries, three

55
00:03:39,280 --> 00:03:43,680
flavors of shakes, and the two hamburger patty,
two slices of cheese, double-double.

56
00:03:43,680 --> 00:03:45,310
That’s it.

57
00:03:45,310 --> 00:03:50,880
To drink, there’s milk, hot cocoa, coffee,
classic and diet Coke, root beer, Dr. Pepper,

58
00:03:50,880 --> 00:03:53,489
7Up, lemonade, and iced tea.

59
00:03:53,489 --> 00:03:59,030
Even with a few, secret variations, like grilled
cheese, animal fries, and the Neapolitan milkshake,

60
00:03:59,030 --> 00:04:03,819
there’s nowhere near the selection of, say,
a Dairy Queen or McDonald’s, which have

61
00:04:03,819 --> 00:04:08,060
about twice as many drinks alone as everything
at In-N-Out.

62
00:04:08,060 --> 00:04:14,069
Its menu changes not seasonally, or annually,
but, maybe once a generation.

63
00:04:14,069 --> 00:04:20,979
In 1958, bottled sodas became fountain drinks,
Milkshakes were added in ’75, Dr. Pepper,

64
00:04:20,979 --> 00:04:27,110
21-years later, Lemonade, in 2003, and hot
chocolate fifteen years after that.

65
00:04:27,110 --> 00:04:32,090
When a fourth beverage size was proposed,
a fight reportedly broke out inside the company.

66
00:04:32,090 --> 00:04:39,310
And, in 2018, it closed all 37 locations in
Texas for a full 48-hours when it found buns

67
00:04:39,310 --> 00:04:41,520
that didn’t meet its quality standards.

68
00:04:41,520 --> 00:04:46,169
The downside of this consistency is that it
can’t respond to changes in the industry.

69
00:04:46,169 --> 00:04:51,740
In 2015, McDonald’s was able to turn around
declining sales with its all-day breakfast.

70
00:04:51,740 --> 00:04:56,470
And, caught off guard by Chipotle’s success,
many chains have tried capturing that market

71
00:04:56,470 --> 00:04:59,379
by introducing more healthy alternatives.

72
00:04:59,379 --> 00:05:04,300
On the other hand, by keeping things simple,
In-N-Out can carefully optimize every ingredient

73
00:05:04,300 --> 00:05:05,990
in its business formula.

74
00:05:05,990 --> 00:05:11,740
Inevitably, new items mean longer lines, confused
employees, and added complexity.

75
00:05:11,740 --> 00:05:17,610
The McCafé Coffee, for example, required
each store buy a $15-20,000 espresso machine

76
00:05:17,610 --> 00:05:21,659
and train employees on how to use it.

77
00:05:21,659 --> 00:05:27,449
At In-N-Out, there are five levels of employees:
Level 1, the janitor and counter handout,

78
00:05:27,449 --> 00:05:33,629
2, for the drive-thru, 3 and 4 who make french
fries, 5, who is allowed to assemble burgers,

79
00:05:33,629 --> 00:05:39,129
and 6, the only person authorized to man the
grill, which requires at least 3-6 months

80
00:05:39,129 --> 00:05:40,360
of training.

81
00:05:40,360 --> 00:05:45,610
Not only does this ensure well-trained cooks,
but it also turns fast-food into a proper,

82
00:05:45,610 --> 00:05:47,409
well-paid profession.

83
00:05:47,409 --> 00:05:52,070
Level one employees are generally paid more
than minimum wage, and managers make an average

84
00:05:52,070 --> 00:05:58,960
of $160,000 a year, with some making well
over a quarter of a million dollars overseeing

85
00:05:58,960 --> 00:06:00,240
a single location.

86
00:06:00,240 --> 00:06:05,960
It’s not hard to see why they stay with
the company for an average of 14 years.

87
00:06:05,960 --> 00:06:11,689
Almost all current and ex-In-N-Out employees
say the same thing: it’s a stressful, chaotic,

88
00:06:11,689 --> 00:06:14,089
and, yet, highly desirable job.

89
00:06:14,089 --> 00:06:20,120
Everyone, full and part-time, receives 401k
plans, dental and vision coverage, and paid

90
00:06:20,120 --> 00:06:21,810
vacation days.

91
00:06:21,810 --> 00:06:27,060
Even more impressive, it does all that despite
having some of the lowest prices in the industry.

92
00:06:27,060 --> 00:06:34,259
A hamburger, fries, and milkshake costs just
$6.85, about half the price of the same order

93
00:06:34,259 --> 00:06:35,689
at Shake Shack.

94
00:06:35,689 --> 00:06:40,849
Any other company would, without hesitation,
export this formula of highly-skilled employees,

95
00:06:40,849 --> 00:06:46,539
a simple menu, and consistent quality, across
the country, and then, when that worked, across

96
00:06:46,539 --> 00:06:47,559
the globe.

97
00:06:47,559 --> 00:06:53,241
The fact that it hasn’t is, more than anything
else, a reflection of its values, set 70 years

98
00:06:53,241 --> 00:06:59,150
ago in Baldwin Park, California by husband
and wife founders Esther and Harry Snyder.

99
00:06:59,150 --> 00:07:03,800
It was the first place ever to use a two-way
speaker system, allowing drivers to place

100
00:07:03,800 --> 00:07:05,439
orders while in line.

101
00:07:05,439 --> 00:07:10,319
They would eventually open 18 more locations,
but, strictly, only when they could afford

102
00:07:10,319 --> 00:07:14,000
to buy the property outright, never on a loan.

103
00:07:14,000 --> 00:07:18,699
Principled, thoughtful founders like the Snyders
aren’t all that hard to find, but rarely

104
00:07:18,699 --> 00:07:22,399
does the second generation inherit those same
values.

105
00:07:22,399 --> 00:07:27,900
[Insert subtitle here] and another 50% don’t

106
00:07:27,900 --> 00:07:29,529
last until the third.

107
00:07:29,529 --> 00:07:33,539
In-N-Out is one of the few chains that has
stayed true to its beginnings, despite going

108
00:07:33,539 --> 00:07:35,809
through several traumatic changes.

109
00:07:35,809 --> 00:07:42,449
When Harry died in 1967, his son Rich took
over, who then died in a plane crash in ’93,

110
00:07:42,449 --> 00:07:46,689
after which his brother Guy replaced him,
only to die six years later.

111
00:07:46,689 --> 00:07:48,909
Esther then returned to manage the company.

112
00:07:48,909 --> 00:07:54,340
Finally, in the riskiest move of all, after
she died in 2006, presidency was given to

113
00:07:54,340 --> 00:07:59,679
someone outside the family, Mark Taylor, until
Guy’s daughter, Lynsi, reached the age of

114
00:07:59,679 --> 00:08:05,940
30, when she inherited 50% of the business,
and then almost full control in 2017 at age

115
00:08:05,940 --> 00:08:07,139
35.

116
00:08:07,139 --> 00:08:11,680
In-N-Out has seen six different leaders, been
heavily pressured by outsiders to franchise

117
00:08:11,680 --> 00:08:16,499
the business, and watched the industry it
helped create change dramatically, and yet,

118
00:08:16,499 --> 00:08:21,400
today, 70-years later, any of its very first
customers would feel right at home in any

119
00:08:21,400 --> 00:08:23,379
of its 300 locations.

120
00:08:23,379 --> 00:08:28,919
It’s current president is the highest-rated
female CEO in the U.S. by employees.

121
00:08:28,919 --> 00:08:35,589
And while the company continues growing - entering
Texas in 2011, Oregon in 2015, and soon Colorado

122
00:08:35,589 --> 00:08:37,979
- it does so very carefully.

123
00:08:37,979 --> 00:08:43,210
Lynsi, still in her 30’s, doesn’t expect
to expand east of Texas in her lifetime, and

124
00:08:43,210 --> 00:08:45,519
never in every U.S. state.

125
00:08:45,519 --> 00:08:50,519
With so few locations, every grand opening
is a major event - with free, organic marketing

126
00:08:50,519 --> 00:08:52,150
and much fanfare.

127
00:08:52,150 --> 00:08:57,950
Lines are so long that the company hires off-duty
police officers to manage traffic and flies-in

128
00:08:57,950 --> 00:09:03,959
“All-Star” employees - experienced workers
who manage the chaos in long 10-hour shifts.

129
00:09:03,959 --> 00:09:06,620
The biggest bottleneck is distribution.

130
00:09:06,620 --> 00:09:12,360
Buns are baked daily, milkshakes 100% dairy,
and there are no freezers or microwaves.

131
00:09:12,360 --> 00:09:17,020
That means ingredients have to be prepared
at distribution centers - currently in Baldwin

132
00:09:17,020 --> 00:09:22,940
Park; Lathrop, California; Dallas; Phoenix,
Draper, Utah; and Colorado Springs.

133
00:09:22,940 --> 00:09:27,029
From there, they need to be delivered within
a single days drive to each of their stores

134
00:09:27,029 --> 00:09:32,980
- which limits new locations to a roughly
500-mile radius from each distribution center.

135
00:09:32,980 --> 00:09:38,130
Whether you’re a fan of Shake Shack, Whataburger,
Five Guys, or McDonald’s, you have to admit

136
00:09:38,130 --> 00:09:40,690
there’s something special about In-N-Out.

137
00:09:40,690 --> 00:09:46,269
While McDonald’s will always make more money,
serve more customers, and be more widely known,

138
00:09:46,269 --> 00:09:51,079
In-N-Out has arguably done something even
harder: keep a legacy alive while staying

139
00:09:51,079 --> 00:09:56,740
true to its original ideals over 70-years
and through six generations of leadership.

140
00:09:56,740 --> 00:10:01,860
The lesson is: whether in business, life,
or learning, the hardest part is often just

141
00:10:01,860 --> 00:10:03,720
keeping a good thing going.

142
00:10:03,720 --> 00:10:08,649
Enrolling in a class is easy, but remembering
to actually go and retaining the knowledge,

00:00:19,490 --> 00:00:26,360

00:00:26,360 --> 00:00:28,939

00:00:28,939 --> 00:00:30,039

00:00:30,039 --> 00:00:35,150
Your first guess might be San Jose, maybe

10
00:00:35,150 --> 00:00:40,341
That is, unless you noticed the lack of Teslas,

11
00:00:40,341 --> 00:00:41,341
video.

12
00:00:41,341 --> 00:00:46,560
This is Silicon Wadi, a cluster of cities
in Israel with one of the highest concentrations

13
00:00:46,560 --> 00:00:49,050
of tech companies and startups on Earth.

14
00:00:49,050 --> 00:00:55,420
It’s home to Waze, Wix, SodaStream, and
Fiverr, files more patents per capita than

15
00:00:55,420 --> 00:01:01,770
all but 4 countries, and is ranked the 4th
most startup friendly nation overall, behind

16
00:01:01,770 --> 00:01:04,830
only Canada, the UK, and the U.S.

17
00:01:04,830 --> 00:01:08,850
The difference is, those countries aren’t
next door to the Syrian Civil War.

18
00:01:08,850 --> 00:01:14,200
30 members of the UN still don’t recognize
the existence of Israel, including most of

19
00:01:14,200 --> 00:01:15,260
its neighbors.

20
00:01:15,260 --> 00:01:19,860
In fact, any evidence of traveling there,
on any passport, prevents you from visiting

21
00:01:19,860 --> 00:01:21,780
eight of those countries.

22
00:01:21,780 --> 00:01:27,280
Because of this, Israeli customs stamps not
your passport but a separate piece of paper.

23
00:01:27,280 --> 00:01:32,620
But despite all of this, Despite the constant
threat of terrorism, Despite being only slightly

24
00:01:32,620 --> 00:01:37,810
bigger than Fiji and having just two and a
half percent the population of the U.S., Israel

25
00:01:37,810 --> 00:01:42,660
creates some of the most successful tech companies
and entrepreneurs in the world.

26
00:01:42,840 --> 00:01:45,600
Why?

27
00:01:45,600 --> 00:01:50,159
As one of the very important world leaders
who consult my channel for advice, you want

28
00:01:50,159 --> 00:01:52,710
to know how to start your very own Silicon
Valley.

29
00:01:52,710 --> 00:01:54,470
Well, you’re in luck.

30
00:01:54,470 --> 00:01:56,810
The recipe is actually quite simple:

31
00:01:56,810 --> 00:02:02,060
First, buy some ping-pong tables, throw down
a couple of bean bags, and, within minutes,

32
00:02:02,060 --> 00:02:08,110
a cavalcade of Soylent-drinking, smartwatch-wearing
CS-grads will assemble at your door.

33
00:02:08,110 --> 00:02:12,810
Even better, why not build some apartments,
a grocery store, and, while you’re at it,

34
00:02:12,810 --> 00:02:13,810
a pharmacy.

35
00:02:13,810 --> 00:02:15,940
Then they’ll never leave!

36
00:02:15,940 --> 00:02:17,360
Work-life what?

37
00:02:17,360 --> 00:02:18,300
Just kidding!

38
00:02:18,300 --> 00:02:18,800
Mostly.

39
00:02:19,040 --> 00:02:24,000
More than a few countries and cities have
tried charming tech companies with tax breaks,

40
00:02:24,120 --> 00:02:31,060
grants, free 21-foot cacti, and other totally
normal things, but almost as many have failed.

41
00:02:31,060 --> 00:02:35,650
On the other side of the Arabian Peninsula,
Dubai built what it calls “Free Zones”,

42
00:02:35,650 --> 00:02:41,420
areas with special incentives to attract certain
types of companies, like Biotech firms, movie

43
00:02:41,420 --> 00:02:43,400
studios, and tech companies.

44
00:02:43,400 --> 00:02:47,050
At first glance, Dubai Internet City looks
like a great success.

45
00:02:47,050 --> 00:02:49,620
And, to some degree, that’s true.

46
00:02:49,620 --> 00:02:55,590
It convinced Microsoft, Cisco, IBM, HP, and
Canon to invest millions of dollars in the

47
00:02:55,590 --> 00:03:00,680
middle of the desert, at a time when the future
of Dubai was much more uncertain.

48
00:03:00,680 --> 00:03:05,020
But having beautiful buildings with famous
logos on them is not the same as creating

49
00:03:05,020 --> 00:03:06,760
an environment of innovation.

50
00:03:06,760 --> 00:03:11,080
You’ll find plenty of the former in the
Cayman Islands, but it’s not exactly the

51
00:03:11,080 --> 00:03:14,480
first place that comes to mind when you think
“cutting-edge research”.

52
00:03:14,480 --> 00:03:19,870
Meanwhile, Silicon Valley is, despite its
very high cost of doing business.

53
00:03:19,870 --> 00:03:25,090
In other words, tax breaks may bring companies,
but not necessarily innovation.

54
00:03:25,090 --> 00:03:29,930
Corporations come to Dubai largely for its
promise of no income or corporate tax for

55
00:03:29,930 --> 00:03:36,430
50-years, but often only for marketing, support,
and sales, while hiring most of their engineers

56
00:03:36,430 --> 00:03:38,750
in the U.S., India, and Israel.

57
00:03:38,750 --> 00:03:42,550
So, what do those countries have that others
don’t?

58
00:03:42,550 --> 00:03:46,190
There are three basic ingredients to a successful
tech scene.

59
00:03:46,190 --> 00:03:48,040
The first is Talent.

60
00:03:48,040 --> 00:03:50,730
One of the best predictors of which is, unsurprisingly,
education.

61
00:03:50,730 --> 00:03:56,540
In the words of Scott Galloway, “Find the
universities that are gaining the most traction

62
00:03:56,540 --> 00:04:02,010
in engineering or STEM and you’re going
to find an ecosystem that can produce a unicorn.”

63
00:04:02,010 --> 00:04:07,110
Basically, put a bunch of smart, ambitious
people in a small, contained space, sprinkle-in

64
00:04:07,110 --> 00:04:11,410
some idealism, ideas will collide and good
things will happen.

65
00:04:11,410 --> 00:04:16,650
At the level of a nation, universities are
about proximity, and hey, if you also learn

66
00:04:16,650 --> 00:04:19,370
something along the way, that’s a bonus!

67
00:04:19,370 --> 00:04:24,139
Which is great news for Israel, one of the
most educated countries in the world.

68
00:04:24,139 --> 00:04:28,380
[Insert subtitle here]

69
00:04:28,380 --> 00:04:33,690
The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Tel-Aviv
University, and the Israel Institute of Technology

70
00:04:33,690 --> 00:04:35,990
are all globally competitive schools.

71
00:04:35,990 --> 00:04:41,470
And because the country is just so small,
and its population so highly-concentrated

72
00:04:41,470 --> 00:04:47,190
in just a few regions, it has the same fertile
ground for entrepreneurship as a college campus,

73
00:04:47,190 --> 00:04:49,290
at a much larger scale.

74
00:04:49,290 --> 00:04:54,800
About 92% of Israelis live in urban areas,
almost entirely in the Northern half of the

75
00:04:54,800 --> 00:04:55,800
country.

76
00:04:55,800 --> 00:05:01,240
Startups, therefore, are surrounded by their
customers, business partners, and competitors.

77
00:05:01,240 --> 00:05:06,880
The other aspect of Talent that’s often
overlooked, but just as important, is demographics.

78
00:05:06,880 --> 00:05:10,710
Not just how big a population is, but also
what it’s like.

79
00:05:10,710 --> 00:05:17,360
For example, it’s misleading to say only
that Japan has 126 million people and Ethiopia,

80
00:05:17,360 --> 00:05:18,360
98.

81
00:05:18,360 --> 00:05:22,240
What those raw numbers hide are their age
and background, which can either act as a

82
00:05:22,240 --> 00:05:26,220
free economic multiplier or a bleak and costly
undoing.

83
00:05:26,220 --> 00:05:31,919
Japan’s population may be large, but it
takes an unfortunate shape - far too many

84
00:05:31,919 --> 00:05:34,889
old people for not enough young.

85
00:05:34,889 --> 00:05:39,870
Unless millions of Japanese suddenly change
their mind and start having children tomorrow,

86
00:05:39,870 --> 00:05:45,979
the land of the rising sun will slowly set,
as Africa grows into the next major consumer

87
00:05:45,979 --> 00:05:46,979
market.

88
00:05:46,979 --> 00:05:52,080
Now, Israel’s growth is not quite so dramatic,
but it is growing, which is more than you

89
00:05:52,080 --> 00:05:57,020
can say about the future of most developed
countries, including all of Europe, the U.S.,

90
00:05:57,020 --> 00:05:58,479
Canada, Australia, and China.

91
00:05:58,479 --> 00:06:03,520
The problem is not that Japan doesn’t have
working-aged people.

92
00:06:03,520 --> 00:06:08,910
Even as its population shrinks, there will
long be millions and millions of workers.

93
00:06:08,910 --> 00:06:13,540
But they’ll be busy caring for their parents,
not inventing the next big thing.

94
00:06:13,540 --> 00:06:19,150
Israel, meanwhile, has enough people to care
for the old and young, with plenty left over.

95
00:06:19,150 --> 00:06:22,110
It also has some extra help: immigration.

96
00:06:22,110 --> 00:06:28,090
The Law of Return allows any Jew, their spouse,
children, grandchildren, and even their non-Jewish

97
00:06:28,090 --> 00:06:31,350
spouse to come to Israel and receive citizenship.

98
00:06:31,350 --> 00:06:35,340
There are even scholarships to cover your
expenses while you learn Hebrew.

99
00:06:35,340 --> 00:06:40,410
The result of all this is that there are 140
scientists, technicians, and engineers for

100
00:06:40,410 --> 00:06:45,550
every 10,000 Israeli employees, compared to
just 85 in the U.S.

101
00:06:45,550 --> 00:06:49,400
The second, much-simpler ingredient is Capital.

102
00:06:49,400 --> 00:06:53,350
Starting a business is expensive, and someone
needs to write the checks.

103
00:06:53,350 --> 00:06:57,539
The good news is that the only thing Silicon
Valley hates more than affordable housing

104
00:06:57,539 --> 00:06:59,160
is missing out.

105
00:06:59,160 --> 00:07:02,750
Investors pour money into companies whose
only skill is improving the rate at which

106
00:07:02,750 --> 00:07:06,880
they can flush hundred dollar bills down the

00:07:06,880 --> 00:07:09,139
feeling of having lost an opportunity.

109
00:07:10,630 --> 00:07:15,680
Once word gets out that somewhere, like Israel,
is good at producing high-value startups,

110
00:07:15,680 --> 00:07:18,710
finding investors became exponentially easier.

111
00:07:18,710 --> 00:07:22,330
The more checks are written, the more venture
capital firms pay attention.

112
00:07:22,330 --> 00:07:26,930
Israel’s government got the ball rolling
in the ’90s with big incentives for anyone

113
00:07:26,930 --> 00:07:29,160
willing to come invest in the country.

114
00:07:29,160 --> 00:07:35,500
Today, 4.5% of its total GDP is spent on Research
& Development, which is just barely less than

115
00:07:35,500 --> 00:07:37,300
first place South Korea.

116
00:07:37,300 --> 00:07:42,139
Now, producing lots of smart, young graduates
and giving them bundles of cash is cool and

117
00:07:42,139 --> 00:07:46,990
all unless they take those skills and that
capital to California, giving Americans the

118
00:07:46,990 --> 00:07:48,889
jobs and tax dollars.

119
00:07:48,889 --> 00:07:53,100
The third ingredient is, therefore, a High
Standard of Living.

120
00:07:53,100 --> 00:07:55,139
Israelis have to want to stay in the country.

121
00:07:55,139 --> 00:08:00,500
It’s a fun fact for South Africa that Elon
Musk grew up there, but not much use because

122
00:08:00,500 --> 00:08:03,830
Tesla and SpaceX are American companies.

123
00:08:03,830 --> 00:08:06,229
And this is harder than it sounds.

124
00:08:06,229 --> 00:08:11,630
On one hand, entrepreneurs and employees care
about healthcare, crime, public transit, and

125
00:08:11,630 --> 00:08:12,630
so on.

126
00:08:12,630 --> 00:08:13,919
But, it’s a balance.

127
00:08:13,919 --> 00:08:18,630
Because, as salaries rise, companies are less
drawn to the lower cost of hiring an Israeli

128
00:08:18,630 --> 00:08:25,380
engineer - currently $73 thousand over, say,
a Californian - 114 thousand.

129
00:08:25,380 --> 00:08:29,510
Salaries are so high in the San Francisco
Bay Area, for example, that, if you’re feeling

130
00:08:29,510 --> 00:08:34,779
particularly cheap, you might just buy a $20
million private jet to save money, so you

131
00:08:34,779 --> 00:08:39,529
can hire employees in less-expensive Houston
and fly them over for the workday.

132
00:08:39,529 --> 00:08:44,510
Israel has to be attractive enough for people
but not so expensive that businesses look

133
00:08:44,510 --> 00:08:45,510
elsewhere.

134
00:08:45,510 --> 00:08:49,429
Together, these three ingredients go a long
way towards making Israel one of the tech

135
00:08:49,429 --> 00:08:51,179
capitals of the world.

136
00:08:51,179 --> 00:08:57,230
But there’s also another, harder to measure,
but, no less real, factor to consider: culture.

137
00:08:57,230 --> 00:09:01,310
If you graduate from Stanford with a degree
in Computer Science on Friday, there’s a

138
00:09:01,310 --> 00:09:06,450
very real chance you could walk into a Facebook
or a Microsoft on Monday and start making

139
00:09:06,450 --> 00:09:09,199
$100+ thousand dollars a year.

140
00:09:09,199 --> 00:09:14,050
Or you could spend your days begging for money
with the possibility of losing a lot only

141
00:09:14,050 --> 00:09:16,459
to end up back at square one.

142
00:09:16,459 --> 00:09:21,870
When the vast majority of new companies fail,
starting one is a huge risk, especially considering

143
00:09:21,870 --> 00:09:23,160
how lucrative the alternative.

144
00:09:23,160 --> 00:09:29,179
It takes a certain kind of personality that’s
willing to fail - and do so very publicly.

145
00:09:29,179 --> 00:09:34,639
In many Asian countries, the culture of saving
face makes entrepreneurship unthinkable for

146
00:09:34,639 --> 00:09:35,639
many.

147
00:09:35,639 --> 00:09:38,679
The reputational damage of failure is simply
too great.

148
00:09:38,679 --> 00:09:44,410
In Israel, however, a spirit of Chutzpah - roughly,
audacity or bravery - has just the opposite

149
00:09:44,410 --> 00:09:45,500
effect.

150
00:09:45,500 --> 00:09:49,860
The author of the book Start-up Nation writes
“Somewhere along the way - either at home,

151
00:09:49,860 --> 00:09:54,759
in school, or in the army - Israelis learn
that assertiveness is the norm, reticence

152
00:09:54,759 --> 00:09:57,689
something that risks your being left behind.”

153
00:09:57,689 --> 00:10:02,459
Israel is one of a handful of countries that
requires long military service for everyone

154
00:10:02,459 --> 00:10:05,689
- 3 years for men and 2 for women.

155
00:10:05,689 --> 00:10:10,110
During their service, Israelis learn skills
that apply to the workplace, make lifelong

156
00:10:10,110 --> 00:10:15,149
friends and business partners, and are reminded
that their country can’t be complacent.

157
00:10:15,149 --> 00:10:20,660
Ultimately, Israel proves that there is no
single factor to economic success.

158
00:10:20,660 --> 00:10:25,970
It has high rates of education, lots of government
investment, and, especially considering its

159
00:10:25,970 --> 00:10:28,869
geography, an impressive standard of living.

160
00:10:28,869 --> 00:10:31,529
But it isn’t ranked number one in any of
those categories.

161
00:10:31,529 --> 00:10:37,610
Instead, a combination of all these things,
along with factors like American foreign aid,

162
00:10:37,610 --> 00:10:39,549
allow the country to prosper.

163
00:10:39,549 --> 00:10:46,100
It also shows that top-down, government policies
are only so effective at encouraging entrepreneurship.

164
00:10:46,100 --> 00:10:50,489
Countries can hand out money left and right,
but innovation occurs at the level of the

165
00:10:50,489 --> 00:10:56,660
individual - his or her ability to take risks,
start new projects, and learn new things.

166
00:10:56,660 --> 00:11:00,600
If that sounds like you, let me recommend

If you already have a business idea in mind,

question: What percent of the world's population are left-handed?
answer: one tenth

question:
1
00:00:06,674 --> 00:00:09,301
If you know an older left-handed person,

2
00:00:09,301 --> 00:00:14,103
chances are they had to learn to write
or eat with their right hand.

3
00:00:14,103 --> 00:00:15,635
And in many parts of the world,

4
00:00:15,635 --> 00:00:20,036
it's still common practice to force
children to use their "proper" hand.

5
00:00:20,615 --> 00:00:24,378
Even the word for right
also means correct or good,

6
00:00:24,378 --> 00:00:27,557
not just in English,
but many other languages, too.

7
00:00:28,366 --> 00:00:30,838
But if being left-handed is so wrong,

8
00:00:30,838 --> 00:00:32,962
then why does it happen
in the first place?

9
00:00:33,499 --> 00:00:37,618
Today, [Insert subtitle here].

10
00:00:37,618 --> 00:00:40,127
Archeological evidence shows
that it's been that way

11
00:00:40,127 --> 00:00:43,400
for as long as 500,000 years,

12
00:00:43,400 --> 00:00:45,216
with about 10% of human remains

13
00:00:45,216 --> 00:00:49,925
showing the associated differences
in arm length and bone density,

14
00:00:49,925 --> 00:00:54,542
and some ancient tools and artifacts
showing evidence of left-hand use.

15
00:00:55,099 --> 00:00:59,496
And despite what many may think,
handedness is not a choice.

16
00:00:59,496 --> 00:01:04,175
It can be predicted even before birth
based on the fetus' position in the womb.

17
00:01:04,861 --> 00:01:08,349
So, if handedness is inborn,
does that mean it's genetic?

18
00:01:08,823 --> 00:01:10,127
Well, yes and no.

19
00:01:10,500 --> 00:01:15,294
Identical twins, who have the same genes,
can have different dominant hands.

20
00:01:15,294 --> 00:01:19,357
In fact, this happens as often as it does
with any other sibling pair.

21
00:01:20,185 --> 00:01:22,689
But the chances of being
right or left-handed

22
00:01:22,689 --> 00:01:25,810
are determined by the handedness
of your parents

23
00:01:25,810 --> 00:01:28,639
in surprisingly consistent ratios.

24
00:01:28,639 --> 00:01:31,947
If your father was left-handed
but your mother was right-handed,

25
00:01:31,947 --> 00:01:36,063
you have a 17% chance
of being born left-handed,

26
00:01:36,063 --> 00:01:39,769
while two righties will have
a left-handed child only 10% of the time.

27
00:01:40,522 --> 00:01:43,678
Handedness seems to be determined
by a roll of the dice,

28
00:01:43,702 --> 00:01:45,811
but the odds are set by your genes.

29
00:01:46,354 --> 00:01:48,077
All of this implies there's a reason

30
00:01:48,077 --> 00:01:51,582
that evolution has produced
this small proportion of lefties,

31
00:01:51,582 --> 00:01:53,821
and maintained it
over the course of millennia.

32
00:01:54,236 --> 00:01:56,304
And while there have been several theories

33
00:01:56,304 --> 00:01:59,830
attempting to explain why handedness
exists in the first place,

34
00:01:59,830 --> 00:02:01,928
or why most people are right-handed,

35
00:02:01,928 --> 00:02:03,434
a recent mathematical model

36
00:02:03,434 --> 00:02:06,899
suggests that the actual ratio
reflects a balance

37
00:02:06,899 --> 00:02:11,181
between competitive and cooperative
pressures on human evolution.

38
00:02:11,697 --> 00:02:13,489
The benefits of being left-handed

39
00:02:13,489 --> 00:02:17,409
are clearest in activities
involving an opponent,

40
00:02:17,409 --> 00:02:20,205
like combat or competitive sports.

41
00:02:20,205 --> 00:02:25,285
For example, about 50% of top hitters
in baseball have been left-handed.

42
00:02:25,285 --> 00:02:26,286
Why?

43
00:02:26,310 --> 00:02:28,278
Think of it as a surprise advantage.

44
00:02:28,836 --> 00:02:31,584
Because lefties are a minority
to begin with,

45
00:02:31,584 --> 00:02:34,220
both right-handed
and left-handed competitors

46
00:02:34,220 --> 00:02:36,846
will spend most of their time
encountering

47
00:02:36,846 --> 00:02:39,679
and practicing against righties.

48
00:02:39,679 --> 00:02:41,223
So when the two face each other,

49
00:02:41,223 --> 00:02:45,430
the left-hander will be better prepared
against this right-handed opponent,

50
00:02:45,430 --> 00:02:47,577
while the righty will be thrown off.

51
00:02:48,260 --> 00:02:49,897
This fighting hypothesis,

52
00:02:49,897 --> 00:02:51,699
where an imbalance in the population

53
00:02:51,699 --> 00:02:55,228
results in an advantage for left-handed
fighters or athletes,

54
00:02:55,228 --> 00:02:58,787
is an example of negative
frequency-dependent selection.

55
00:02:59,279 --> 00:03:01,599
But according to the principles
of evolution,

56
00:03:01,599 --> 00:03:03,361
groups that have a relative advantage

57
00:03:03,385 --> 00:03:06,556
tend to grow until
that advantage disappears.

58
00:03:07,219 --> 00:03:10,553
If people were only fighting and competing
throughout human evolution,

59
00:03:10,553 --> 00:03:14,434
natural selection would lead to more
lefties being the ones that made it

60
00:03:14,434 --> 00:03:16,014
until there were so many of them,

61
00:03:16,014 --> 00:03:18,438
that it was no longer a rare asset.

62
00:03:18,962 --> 00:03:21,094
So in a purely competitive world,

63
00:03:21,094 --> 00:03:23,731
50% of the population
would be left-handed.

64
00:03:24,345 --> 00:03:29,068
But human evolution has been shaped
by cooperation, as well as competition.

65
00:03:29,068 --> 00:03:30,223
And cooperative pressure

66
00:03:30,223 --> 00:03:33,627
pushes handedness distribution
in the opposite direction.

67
00:03:34,786 --> 00:03:38,449
In golf, where performance
doesn't depend on the opponent,

68
00:03:38,449 --> 00:03:41,562
only 4% of top players are left-handed,

69
00:03:41,562 --> 00:03:44,620
an example of the wider phenomenon
of tool sharing.

70
00:03:45,620 --> 00:03:47,338
Just as young potential golfers

71
00:03:47,338 --> 00:03:50,489
can more easily find
a set of right-handed clubs,

72
00:03:50,489 --> 00:03:53,796
many of the important instruments
that have shaped society

73
00:03:53,796 --> 00:03:56,945
were designed for
the right-handed majority.

74
00:03:56,945 --> 00:03:59,227
Because lefties are worse
at using these tools,

75
00:03:59,227 --> 00:04:01,737
and suffer from higher accident rates,

76
00:04:01,737 --> 00:04:04,913
they would be less successful
in a purely cooperative world,

77
00:04:04,913 --> 00:04:08,251
eventually disappearing
from the population.

78
00:04:08,251 --> 00:04:10,251
So by correctly predicting
the distribution

79
00:04:10,275 --> 00:04:12,846
of left-handed people
in the general population,

80
00:04:12,846 --> 00:04:15,653
as well as matching data
from various sports,

81
00:04:15,653 --> 00:04:16,699
the model indicates

82
00:04:16,699 --> 00:04:20,499
that the persistence of lefties
as a small but stable minority

83
00:04:20,499 --> 00:04:22,458
reflects an equilibrium

84
00:04:22,458 --> 00:04:24,990
that comes from competitive
and cooperative effects

85
00:04:24,990 --> 00:04:28,071
playing out simultaneously over time.

86
00:04:28,071 --> 00:04:29,738
And the most intriguing thing

87
00:04:29,738 --> 00:04:33,477
is what the numbers can tell us
about various populations.

88
00:04:33,477 --> 00:04:37,457
From the skewed distribution of pawedness
in cooperative animals,

89
00:04:37,457 --> 00:04:39,666
to the slightly larger
percentage of lefties

90
00:04:39,666 --> 00:04:42,592
in competitive hunter-gatherer societies,

91
00:04:42,592 --> 00:04:47,636
we may even find that the answers
to some puzzles of early human evolution

92
00:04:47,636 --> 00:04:49,639
are already in our hands.
answer: about 1/10 of the world's population are left-handed

question:
1
00:00:00,459 --> 00:00:01,459
This is an EpiPen.

2
00:00:01,460 --> 00:00:06,400
It’s a device that injects you with adrenaline
if you’re having a possibly deadly allergic reaction.

3
00:00:06,400 --> 00:00:09,580
If you have severe allergies, you basically
need it.

4
00:00:09,580 --> 00:00:14,640
And if you live in the UK, an EpiPen will
cost you the equivalent of 38 US dollars.

5
00:00:14,640 --> 00:00:18,300
But if you live in the US, it’ll cost you
$300.

6
00:00:18,300 --> 00:00:19,720
And it’s not just the EpiPen.

7
00:00:19,720 --> 00:00:22,640
Let’s look at five of the top selling prescription
drugs in the world.

8
00:00:22,640 --> 00:00:26,130
Advair, a brand-name asthma inhaler: more
expensive in the US.

9
00:00:26,130 --> 00:00:29,809
Lantus, a type of Insulin: more expensive
in the US.

10
00:00:29,809 --> 00:00:31,160
Sovaldi for hepatitis C?

11
00:00:31,260 --> 00:00:31,760
Yup.

12
00:00:31,820 --> 00:00:33,180
Costs more in the US.

13
00:00:33,280 --> 00:00:35,100
Humira for arthritis.

14
00:00:35,100 --> 00:00:37,930
Crestor for cholesterol: more expensive in
the US.

15
00:00:38,720 --> 00:00:40,840
So here’s an unsurprising chart:

16
00:00:40,840 --> 00:00:44,880
Americans spend more on prescription drugs
than anyone else in the world.

17
00:00:44,880 --> 00:00:45,920
Why?

18
00:00:47,080 --> 00:00:51,059
The first thing you have to understand is
that in the US, drugs get to patients differently

19
00:00:51,059 --> 00:00:52,710
than almost everywhere else.

20
00:00:52,710 --> 00:00:55,780
Let’s look at that popular hepatitis C drug,
Sovaldi.

21
00:00:55,780 --> 00:01:00,510
In 2014 Sovaldi became the first drug to completely
cure hepatitis C.

22
00:01:01,480 --> 00:01:04,540
Here’s how it got to market in, for example,
the UK.

23
00:01:04,540 --> 00:01:09,240
First a government agency had to decide that
Sovaldi was safe and that it actually worked.

24
00:01:09,240 --> 00:01:13,280
Then it was evaluated by a regulatory agency
to see if was worthwhile:

25
00:01:13,280 --> 00:01:14,440
Are there too many side effects?

26
00:01:14,440 --> 00:01:16,450
Is there already a similar drug?

27
00:01:16,450 --> 00:01:17,979
Is there a cheaper option?

28
00:01:17,980 --> 00:01:19,860
Sovaldi was deemed worthwhile.

29
00:01:19,860 --> 00:01:22,079
Next, they negotiated the price.

30
00:01:22,079 --> 00:01:25,250
In the UK, the government buys the stock of
medicine for the country.

31
00:01:25,250 --> 00:01:29,650
That means they’re usually able to get a
lower rate, kind of like a bulk discount.

32
00:01:29,650 --> 00:01:32,920
Which keeps prescription drugs cheaper for
UK citizens.

33
00:01:32,920 --> 00:01:37,540
In almost every developed country besides
the US, this is what the system looks like:

34
00:01:37,540 --> 00:01:42,040
Safety evaluation, assessment of whether the
country needs it, price negotiations, sold

35
00:01:42,040 --> 00:01:43,360
to patients.

36
00:01:43,600 --> 00:01:46,140
Now let’s look at the system in the US.

37
00:01:46,140 --> 00:01:49,140
First, the drug is evaluated for safety,
but that’s it.

38
00:01:49,149 --> 00:01:51,760
If it’s safe, they can sell it, end of story.

39
00:01:51,760 --> 00:01:55,740
Drugs are sold by the drug companies to patients,
usually through insurance.

40
00:01:55,740 --> 00:01:59,980
And since the US system lets them sell it
for any price, Gilead, the company that makes

41
00:01:59,980 --> 00:02:01,760
Sovaldi, charged Americans more for it.

42
00:02:02,220 --> 00:02:07,340
When it first came to market, the entire treatment
cost $84,000 in the US.

43
00:02:07,340 --> 00:02:08,260
In the UK?

44
00:02:08,260 --> 00:02:10,480
Just about $58,000 US dollars.

45
00:02:10,480 --> 00:02:14,260
That’s still a lot of money, but it’s
a full 30% less.

46
00:02:14,720 --> 00:02:17,680
So it seems like the UK has the better system
right?

47
00:02:17,680 --> 00:02:19,120
Well, it’s complicated.

48
00:02:19,600 --> 00:02:23,960
These photos are from protests in the US against
the high price of EpiPens.

49
00:02:23,960 --> 00:02:27,640
And these are photos from protests in the
UK, over the lack of access

50
00:02:27,640 --> 00:02:30,500
to a cystic fibrosis drug called Orkambi.

51
00:02:31,040 --> 00:02:34,480
That’s because when there’s a committee
that determines whether a new drug is worthwhile

52
00:02:34,480 --> 00:02:36,320
— sometimes they say no.

53
00:02:36,320 --> 00:02:40,320
And when they negotiate the prices, sometimes
they don’t come to an agreement and hit

54
00:02:40,320 --> 00:02:41,260
a standoff.

55
00:02:41,260 --> 00:02:43,020
That’s what’s happening with Orkambi.

56
00:02:43,780 --> 00:02:45,780
Both systems require trade offs.

57
00:02:45,780 --> 00:02:50,900
Regulated drug markets tend to make drugs
more affordable, but some drugs are completely unavailable.

58
00:02:51,320 --> 00:02:55,340
And while the US has more drugs technically
available, they’re often too expensive to

59
00:02:55,340 --> 00:02:56,740
actually afford.

60
00:02:57,060 --> 00:03:01,950
Americans without insurance are the most likely
to skip medication because of the cost.

61
00:03:01,950 --> 00:03:04,860
[Insert subtitle here].

62
00:03:05,580 --> 00:03:09,260
But the commonality between these two systems
— is the drug companies.

63
00:03:09,260 --> 00:03:14,000
Developing new drug products isn’t cheap
and they’re for-profit businesses.

64
00:03:14,010 --> 00:03:17,970
If Gilead didn’t think that researching
and developing a hepatitis C cure, would make

65
00:03:17,970 --> 00:03:21,100
them money in the end, they might not have.

66
00:03:21,100 --> 00:03:24,980
And with these regulated markets keeping costs
down, the only place the drug companies can

67
00:03:24,980 --> 00:03:28,440
really make their money is, you guessed it, the US.

68
00:03:28,440 --> 00:03:32,830
Americans are essentially subsidizing the
cost of drugs for the rest of the world.

69

In other words, a big part of why prescription
drugs are more expensive in the US

70
00:03:37,080 --> 00:03:39,340
is because they’re cheaper everywhere else.

00:00:23,340 --> 00:00:27,890
Every day in the US, nearly half a million
people sitting in local jails haven’t been

8
00:00:27,890 --> 00:00:30,650
convicted of anything.

9
00:00:30,650 --> 00:00:32,060
Why are most of them there?

10
00:00:32,060 --> 00:00:34,200
Because they can’t afford cash bail.

11
00:00:34,200 --> 00:00:39,880
In 2009, the last year relevant federal data
was released, the median bail was $10,000

12
00:00:39,880 --> 00:00:44,010
for felony defendants, much higher than many
Americans can afford.

13
00:00:44,010 --> 00:00:49,250
And in a 2014 analysis of New York City jails,
researchers found that only 14 percent of

14
00:00:49,250 --> 00:00:52,580
people given bail were able to pay at their
initial hearing.

15
00:00:52,580 --> 00:00:56,970
Now, lawmakers and activists are trying to
get rid of cash bail.

16
00:00:56,970 --> 00:01:02,600
When bail is set unreasonably high, people
are behind bars only because they are poor.

17
00:01:02,600 --> 00:01:08,310
And I congratulate California to help lead
the effort to do away with cash bail.

18
00:01:08,310 --> 00:01:12,380
A bill to reform New Hampshire’s bail system
now headed to the Governor’s desk.

19
00:01:12,380 --> 00:01:18,320
Courts are starting to eliminate cash bail,
but that’s creating another problem: What

20
00:01:18,320 --> 00:01:19,720
comes next?

21
00:01:21,500 --> 00:01:25,680
Let’s look at someone committing a minor
offense, like breaking an open container law.

22
00:01:25,690 --> 00:01:31,400
They are arrested and brought before a judge,
who typically has three options.

23
00:01:31,400 --> 00:01:35,160
Deny bail and keep the defendant in jail until
trial,

24
00:01:35,160 --> 00:01:38,940
release them without bail, which might include
monitored supervision,

25
00:01:38,940 --> 00:01:40,600
or set bail.

26
00:01:40,600 --> 00:01:42,400
Cash bail is intended as collateral.

27
00:01:42,400 --> 00:01:47,049
It’s supposed to be used to make sure people
show up for their trials — not as a punishment

28
00:01:47,049 --> 00:01:48,409
or a way to imprison.

29
00:01:48,409 --> 00:01:51,490
If the defendant pays bail, they can go free
until trial.

30
00:01:51,490 --> 00:01:55,150
And when they return to court and their trial
ends, they get their money back.

31
00:01:55,150 --> 00:01:59,930
But if they don’t have enough money for
bail, they go to jail.

32
00:01:59,930 --> 00:02:04,530
In 2013, the average number of days detained
pretrial was 28 for Philadelphia defendants

33
00:02:04,530 --> 00:02:06,780
with bail of 2000 dollars or less.

34
00:02:08,090 --> 00:02:11,300
During that time a person’s life can fall
apart.

35
00:02:11,319 --> 00:02:14,530
If they don’t show up for work, they can
lose their job.

36
00:02:14,530 --> 00:02:17,300
If they are a parent, a child loses their
caregiver.

37
00:02:17,680 --> 00:02:21,620
And if they live in a shelter, their housing
is gone.

38
00:02:21,629 --> 00:02:25,150
While in jail, it’s likely they will be
given the option of pleading guilty.

39
00:02:25,150 --> 00:02:30,450
With so much on the line, many people choose
to plead guilty instead of waiting for a trial.

40
00:02:30,450 --> 00:02:35,029
That deal gives them their freedom, but a
criminal conviction has long-term consequences.

41
00:02:35,029 --> 00:02:38,460
Particularly for someone’s ability to find
work or housing.

42
00:02:39,800 --> 00:02:41,269
Cash bail isn’t fair.

43
00:02:41,269 --> 00:02:45,549
For those who can’t afford it, the system
presents a series of problems that wealthier

44
00:02:45,549 --> 00:02:48,200
defendants are often able to avoid.

45
00:02:48,200 --> 00:02:52,310
The only difference between the two paths
is how much money you have, not how guilty

46
00:02:52,310 --> 00:02:53,140
you are.

47
00:02:53,140 --> 00:02:56,319
So what’s a better alternative?

48
00:02:56,319 --> 00:03:01,359
D.C. courts effectively eliminated cash bail
in 1992.

49
00:03:01,359 --> 00:03:06,269
Instead, judges use risk assessments to inform
pretrial release decisions.

50
00:03:06,269 --> 00:03:10,590
If the person breaking an open container law
had been arrested in DC, a court official

51
00:03:10,590 --> 00:03:13,639
would enter data about them into a risk assessment.

52
00:03:13,639 --> 00:03:17,840
Algorithms analyze the data, and the defendant
is scored for their likelihood to commit new

53
00:03:17,840 --> 00:03:20,019
crimes and return for trial.

54
00:03:20,019 --> 00:03:24,700
In most assessments, those results are delivered
to the judge with a pretrial release recommendation

55
00:03:24,700 --> 00:03:28,419
that they can choose to follow at their own
discretion.

56
00:03:28,419 --> 00:03:32,140
Risk assessments are supposed to help ensure
that a judge’s decisions are accountable

57
00:03:32,140 --> 00:03:35,879
to an objective standard, instead of just
a hunch.

58
00:03:35,879 --> 00:03:37,799
The data is encouraging.

59
00:03:37,799 --> 00:03:44,799
In 2017, [Insert subtitle here],
88% of those returned for every single court

60
00:03:44,799 --> 00:03:48,449
date, 86% weren’t arrested during that time.

61
00:03:48,449 --> 00:03:53,819
And overall the decision to remove cash bail
saves D.C. courts close to $400 million a

62
00:03:53,820 --> 00:03:54,380
year.

63
00:03:54,380 --> 00:03:59,440
As more courts consider eliminating cash bail,
it’s likely that risk assessments will be

64
00:03:59,440 --> 00:04:00,780
used instead.

65
00:04:01,660 --> 00:04:07,379
But that’s raising a concern that one biased
system is being traded for another.

66
00:04:07,379 --> 00:04:11,469
Risk assessments use data about defendants’
criminal histories without always considering

67
00:04:11,469 --> 00:04:12,810
other factors.

68
00:04:12,810 --> 00:04:17,109
And social prejudices and over-policing make
it more likely that low-income and minority

69
00:04:17,109 --> 00:04:20,120
Americans will have prior convictions.

70
00:04:20,120 --> 00:04:24,560
Reformers worry that relying on a score that
doesn’t acknowledge that bias risks perpetuating

71
00:04:24,560 --> 00:04:25,560
it.

72
00:04:25,900 --> 00:04:31,270
The ACLU even decided to oppose California’s
decision to eliminate cash bail, in part because

73
00:04:31,270 --> 00:04:33,360
of the debate over risk assessments.

74
00:04:33,360 --> 00:04:38,060
Let’s say our defendant accepted the plea
deal after being arrested for an open container.

75
00:04:38,060 --> 00:04:43,449
Then they get arrested again, for another
low-level offense, like shoplifting.

76
00:04:43,449 --> 00:04:47,300
The conviction from their earlier guilty plea
would increase their risk assessment score

77
00:04:47,300 --> 00:04:51,440
— making it more likely that a judge sends
them to jail this time.

78
00:04:51,440 --> 00:04:54,440
But the assessment wouldn’t show that they
pleaded guilty because they couldn't afford

79
00:04:54,440 --> 00:04:59,389
to stay in jail awaiting trial after being
unable to afford bail.

80
00:04:59,389 --> 00:05:03,590
On the plus side, judges also have other tools
to inform their decisions.

81
00:05:03,590 --> 00:05:08,479
Conditional release programs give judges more
pretrial release options, including drug testing,

82
00:05:08,480 --> 00:05:11,569
in-person check ins, and electronic monitoring.

83
00:05:12,320 --> 00:05:17,080
Still, those programs cost courts money and
can be invasive for defendants.

84
00:05:17,080 --> 00:05:22,199
Less intensive support services like sending
court reminders and providing transportation

85
00:05:22,199 --> 00:05:26,370
can also increase the chance that people return
for trial.

86
00:05:26,370 --> 00:05:30,099
Providing additional pre-trial options and
services can help reduce the likelihood that

87
00:05:30,099 --> 00:05:35,639
judges become over-reliant on risk assessments
— or resort to their first option: keeping

88
00:05:35,640 --> 00:05:37,120
defendants in jail.

89
00:05:37,120 --> 00:05:42,199
Because US judges are elected by voters, they’re
incentivized to keep people locked up.

90
00:05:42,199 --> 00:05:46,020
When you’re running to keep your job, you
don’t want to be the judge who let the violent

91
00:05:46,020 --> 00:05:47,820
criminal go free before trial.

92
00:05:50,040 --> 00:05:55,840
Using money to decide who goes to jail creates
two very different paths: one for those who

93
00:05:55,840 --> 00:05:59,370
have money and one for those who don’t.

94
00:06:00,540 --> 00:06:03,340
And while alternatives present their own problems,

95
00:06:04,700 --> 00:06:06,699
having more steps in the process can mean

96
00:06:06,699 --> 00:06:10,770
that fewer defendants overall are funneled to jail
while waiting for their trial.

question: In which year did deaths caused by measles in USA reach the highest point?
How many states have MMR vaccination rates below 93%?
What is the highest value shown on the vertical axis for the 2004-2019 measles chart?

1
00:00:00,620 --> 00:00:03,960
This is a chart of reported measles cases
in the US.

2
00:00:03,960 --> 00:00:09,460
In the 1950s, measles was one of those diseases
that nearly every child got.

3
00:00:09,460 --> 00:00:13,040
It caused a high fever and a spotty rash all
over the body.

4
00:00:13,040 --> 00:00:17,950
And while most recovered easily, [Insert subtitle here]

5
00:00:17,950 --> 00:00:21,130
Then in 1963, a vaccine became available.

6
00:00:21,130 --> 00:00:25,030
And measles became an easily preventable and
unnecessary disease.

7
00:00:25,030 --> 00:00:28,700
By 2000, measles was officially eliminated
in the US.

8
00:00:28,700 --> 00:00:32,369
And for a time, less than a hundred Americans
a year got it.

9
00:00:32,369 --> 00:00:35,480
But In the last decade, that number has started
to grow.

10
00:00:35,480 --> 00:00:41,760
Now, there have been more cases through the
first three months of 2019 than all of 2018.

11
00:00:41,760 --> 00:00:43,120
Measles is back.

12
00:00:43,120 --> 00:00:47,100
And to understand why, you have to understand
where it’s back.

13
00:00:47,100 --> 00:00:51,500
Measles can be quite serious, but now no one
needs to get them.

14
00:00:51,510 --> 00:00:53,449
Here are those recent measles cases again.

15
00:00:53,449 --> 00:00:57,159
If we look at the 2013 spike, we notice
something.

16
00:00:57,160 --> 00:01:02,200
A good chunk of those cases can be attributed
to an outbreak among Orthodox Jews in New York.

17
00:01:02,300 --> 00:01:04,440
That huge spike in 2014?

18
00:01:04,440 --> 00:01:08,900
Most of those cases are all from one outbreak
among the Amish in Ohio.

19
00:01:08,900 --> 00:01:09,970
2017?

20
00:01:09,970 --> 00:01:13,190
One outbreak in the Somali-American community
in Minnesota,.

21
00:01:13,190 --> 00:01:14,220
2018?

22
00:01:14,220 --> 00:01:17,190
Different communities of New York Orthodox
Jews.

23
00:01:17,190 --> 00:01:19,290
And again in 2019.

24
00:01:19,290 --> 00:01:23,360
What all of this shows is that the return
of measles isn’t as widespread as you might think.

25
00:01:23,600 --> 00:01:28,680
75% of recent cases have happened in these
close-knit communities.

26
00:01:28,680 --> 00:01:32,970
People in these communities tend to read the
same news, watch the same TV programs, speak

27
00:01:32,970 --> 00:01:34,220
the same language.

28
00:01:34,220 --> 00:01:36,200
Julia Belluz, Vox health reporter.

29
00:01:36,200 --> 00:01:38,700
They go to school together, they worship together.

30
00:01:38,700 --> 00:01:42,990
When not enough of them are vaccinated - you
know, it tends to spread like wildfire.

31
00:01:42,990 --> 00:01:49,360
Like in early 2019 outside Vancouver, Washington
where a measles outbreak sickened 73 people.

32
00:01:49,360 --> 00:01:53,490
It originated at a local Slavic church, likely
from someone who picked up the disease in

33
00:01:53,490 --> 00:01:54,700
Eastern Europe.

34
00:01:54,700 --> 00:02:00,160
It quickly spread through the community, infecting
mostly small children who weren’t immunized.

35
00:02:00,160 --> 00:02:04,230
One reason this happened is that the Slavic
community in Washington has one of the lowest

36
00:02:04,230 --> 00:02:06,300
rates of vaccination in the state.

37
00:02:06,300 --> 00:02:09,380
Some of the people in this community don’t
trust doctors.

38
00:02:09,380 --> 00:02:11,180
Yuriy is a member of that community.

39
00:02:11,180 --> 00:02:12,859
He’s also a health data analyst.

40
00:02:12,859 --> 00:02:16,829
They have a view that big pharma is too ingrained
with the medical establishment.

41
00:02:16,829 --> 00:02:20,849
They are much more willing to listen to members
of the community.

42
00:02:20,849 --> 00:02:26,230
Anti-vaccination misinformation can reach
anyone - but it’s in these small communities

43
00:02:26,230 --> 00:02:27,709
where it does the most damage.

44
00:02:27,709 --> 00:02:30,900
Most people in these communities are vaccinated.

45
00:02:30,900 --> 00:02:35,209
The problem starts when not enough people
are vaccinated - it prevents them from reaching

46
00:02:35,209 --> 00:02:36,640
what’s called herd immunity.

47
00:02:36,640 --> 00:02:38,240
Here’s how it works.

48
00:02:38,250 --> 00:02:41,959
With every vaccine you need a certain perc
entage of the community to be immunized in

49
00:02:41,959 --> 00:02:43,670
order for the vaccine to work.

50
00:02:43,670 --> 00:02:48,480
If a group of people comes into contact with
one person contagious with measles - and none

51
00:02:48,480 --> 00:02:52,620
of them are vaccinated - virtually everyone
will get sick.

52
00:02:52,620 --> 00:02:57,680
If 50% of the group is vaccinated, that’s
not enough - the rest are likely to get sick

53
00:02:57,689 --> 00:02:59,819
and spread the disease.

54
00:02:59,819 --> 00:03:04,280
But at a certain point, if enough people are
vaccinated, - they can actually protect the

55
00:03:04,280 --> 00:03:08,440
few that aren’t vaccinated from getting
sick, stopping the spread of the disease —

56
00:03:08,440 --> 00:03:09,680
herd immunity.

57
00:03:10,340 --> 00:03:13,980
This is important because there are people
who can’t get vaccinated because of their

58
00:03:13,989 --> 00:03:18,010
immune system: people like cancer patients
and newborn babies.

59
00:03:18,010 --> 00:03:23,280
And with measles because it’s so contagious,
that number is just really really high - it's 95%

60
00:03:23,780 --> 00:03:27,620
So basically everyone who can get vaccinated
needs to be vaccinated.

61
00:03:27,620 --> 00:03:30,700
We’re protecting all those people who can’t
get vaccines.

62
00:03:30,700 --> 00:03:35,859
That 95% number doesn't leave much wiggle
room, and a lot of US states are now struggling

63
00:03:35,860 --> 00:03:36,880
to meet it.

64
00:03:36,880 --> 00:03:39,260
These are the states where the number of kindergarteners

65
00:03:39,260 --> 00:03:42,700
vaccinated for measles is below the herd immunity threshold.

66
00:03:42,800 --> 00:03:44,840
It's half of states.

67
00:03:44,859 --> 00:03:49,500
So how do we make sure everyone who can get
vaccinated does?

68
00:03:49,500 --> 00:03:51,250
It might help it look at it this way.

69
00:03:51,250 --> 00:03:54,409
These are the states that allow parents to
opt-out for religious reasons.

70
00:03:54,409 --> 00:03:59,599
And these are the states that allow parents
to opt out for any philosophical reason.

71
00:03:59,599 --> 00:04:01,920
And then, there are a few states that allow
neither.

72
00:04:01,920 --> 00:04:06,720
The two states that have had no exemptions
for a very long time - Mississippi and West Virginia -

73
00:04:06,720 --> 00:04:09,780
they haven’t seen outbreaks in

For the franchisee, this model is attractive

4,500.
