question: By how many percentage points was the corporation tax rate lower in early 2021 compared to the rate before Reagan's cuts?

1
00:00:07,754 --> 00:00:11,674
When President Ronald Reagan began
his first term in 1981,

2
00:00:11,674 --> 00:00:13,551
the US economy was struggling.

3
00:00:13,718 --> 00:00:16,345
Unemployment rates were high
and getting higher,

4
00:00:16,345 --> 00:00:21,559
and in 1979, inflation had peaked 
at an all-time high for peacetime.

5
00:00:22,310 --> 00:00:24,437
In an effort to combat these issues,

6
00:00:24,437 --> 00:00:28,399
Reagan's administration introduced
a number of economic policies,

7
00:00:28,775 --> 00:00:33,654
including tax cuts for large corporations
and high-income earners.

8
00:00:33,905 --> 00:00:37,033
The idea was that tax savings for the rich

9
00:00:37,033 --> 00:00:40,495
would cause extra money 
to trickle down to everyone else,

10
00:00:40,495 --> 00:00:41,704
and for that reason,

11
00:00:41,704 --> 00:00:46,292
these policies are often referred 
to as trickle-down economics.

12
00:00:46,709 --> 00:00:48,669
From the 80s to the late 90s,

13
00:00:48,669 --> 00:00:51,839
the US saw one of its longest 
and strongest periods

14
00:00:51,839 --> 00:00:53,966
of economic growth in history.

15
00:00:54,550 --> 00:00:58,221
Median income rose, 
as did rates of job creation.

16
00:00:58,304 --> 00:01:01,974
Since then, many politicians have invoked
trickle-down theory

17
00:01:01,974 --> 00:01:04,393
as a justification for tax cuts—

18
00:01:04,519 --> 00:01:07,021
but did these policies actually work,

19
00:01:07,021 --> 00:01:09,732
either in the sense of stimulating 
economic growth,

20
00:01:09,732 --> 00:01:13,319
or in terms of improving circumstances
for Americans?

21
00:01:13,486 --> 00:01:15,655
Would they work in other circumstances?

22
00:01:16,155 --> 00:01:17,615
To answer these questions,

23
00:01:17,615 --> 00:01:20,952
the main things to consider are whether
the impact of the tax cut

24
00:01:20,952 --> 00:01:23,621
on the government’s tax revenue 
is harmful,

25
00:01:24,330 --> 00:01:28,292
whether the money saved in taxes actually
stimulates the economy,

26
00:01:28,417 --> 00:01:32,713
and whether stimulating the economy
actually improves people’s lives.

27
00:01:33,339 --> 00:01:36,759
The idea behind tax cuts is 
that if taxes are too high,

28
00:01:36,759 --> 00:01:38,761
people will be less willing to work,

29
00:01:38,761 --> 00:01:41,264
which would ultimately
decrease tax revenue.

30
00:01:41,764 --> 00:01:46,352
So at a lower tax rate, the government
might actually gain more tax money

31
00:01:46,352 --> 00:01:50,314
that it can theoretically put 
towards improving life for its citizens,

32
00:01:50,940 --> 00:01:54,694
because people will work more when they
get to keep more of their earnings.

33
00:01:55,111 --> 00:01:58,906
Of course, there’s a limit to how much
the government can cut taxes:

34
00:01:58,906 --> 00:02:03,953
at a zero tax rate there is no tax revenue
regardless of how much people are working.

35
00:02:04,203 --> 00:02:07,748
So while cuts from a very high
tax rate might be fine,

36
00:02:07,748 --> 00:02:11,043
cuts from a lower tax rate might
be counterproductive,

37
00:02:11,419 --> 00:02:14,589
hampering the government's ability
to accomplish crucial things.

38
00:02:14,881 --> 00:02:17,925
Tax rates were extremely high
when Reagan took office.

39
00:02:17,925 --> 00:02:23,723
[Insert subtitle here]

40
00:02:23,723 --> 00:02:27,435
and corporation tax from 48% to 34%.

41
00:02:28,144 --> 00:02:31,522
By comparison, as of early 2021,

42
00:02:31,522 --> 00:02:35,318
those rates were 37% and 21% respectively.

43
00:02:35,693 --> 00:02:39,822
When tax rates are lower, tax cuts
for the wealthy can be harmful.

44
00:02:39,822 --> 00:02:42,742
For example, in 2012 to 2013,

45
00:02:42,742 --> 00:02:47,872
lawmakers cut the top tax-rate in the
state of Kansas by almost 30%

46
00:02:47,872 --> 00:02:50,917
and reduced some business
tax rates to zero.

47
00:02:51,292 --> 00:02:54,503
As a result, the government’s balance
sheet immediately fell

48
00:02:54,503 --> 00:02:57,381
into negative territory 
and did not recover,

49
00:02:57,381 --> 00:03:00,968
implying that wealthy individuals 
and companies did not invest

50
00:03:00,968 --> 00:03:02,511
back into the economy.

51
00:03:02,887 --> 00:03:05,848
In short, the money did not trickle down.

52
00:03:06,432 --> 00:03:08,351
This appears to be a trend:

53
00:03:08,351 --> 00:03:12,813
in a study over multiple periods 
of history and across 18 countries,

54
00:03:12,813 --> 00:03:16,567
The London School of Economics 
found that cutting taxes

55
00:03:16,567 --> 00:03:19,570
increased the wealth
of the top 1% of people,

56
00:03:19,570 --> 00:03:22,156
but had little effect 
on the economy as a whole.

57
00:03:22,907 --> 00:03:26,911
In order for tax cuts for the rich
to truly stimulate the economy,

58
00:03:26,911 --> 00:03:29,372
they would have to spend the saved money

59
00:03:29,372 --> 00:03:32,708
putting it back into, for example, 
local businesses—

60
00:03:32,708 --> 00:03:35,044
but this isn’t what happens in practice.

61
00:03:35,336 --> 00:03:38,673
No economic policy operates in isolation:

62
00:03:38,673 --> 00:03:43,469
each time and place is unique with
multiple policies in place simultaneously,

63
00:03:43,636 --> 00:03:47,431
so there is only ever one test case
for each set of scenarios.

64
00:03:47,682 --> 00:03:51,143
This makes it difficult to deliver
definitive rulings on whether

65
00:03:51,143 --> 00:03:52,728
an economic policy worked,

66
00:03:52,728 --> 00:03:54,981
whether something else might
have worked better,

67
00:03:54,981 --> 00:03:57,566
or whether it would work 
in a different situation.

68
00:03:57,900 --> 00:04:01,195
And yet, rhetoric 
around trickle-down economics,

69
00:04:01,195 --> 00:04:03,739
both during the Reagan era and since,

70
00:04:03,823 --> 00:04:06,242
often promises something definitive:

71
00:04:06,242 --> 00:04:11,038
that spending by society’s richest members
on things other than taxes

72
00:04:11,038 --> 00:04:15,209
directly improves the financial 
circumstances of the less wealthy.

73
00:04:15,418 --> 00:04:18,045
And there’s not
much evidence to support that.
answer: His administration cut the highest income tax bracket from 70% to 28%

More importantly

00:06:38,698 --> 00:06:40,833

payout requirements...

152
00:06:41,067 --> 00:06:42,068

153
00:06:42,068 --> 00:06:43,870

00:06:43,870 --> 00:06:46,773

Donor advice funds have been

00:06:52,078 --> 00:06:53,579

00:06:53,579 --> 00:06:56,048

1
00:00:00,549 --> 00:00:03,679
I have to admit that when it comes to food,

2

3
00:00:07,979 --> 00:00:14,730
And I spend a lot of time in Montana, so for

4
00:00:14,730 --> 00:00:16,059
Pretty much as good as it gets.

5
00:00:16,059 --> 00:00:17,059
I know.

6
00:00:17,059 --> 00:00:21,090
I don’t do it often and when I do, I gotta
admit I feel a little conflicted.

7
00:00:21,090 --> 00:00:24,230
And that’s for a lot of reasons, including
the planet.

8
00:00:24,230 --> 00:00:26,519
But how big of a problem is what I eat?

9
00:00:26,520 --> 00:00:31,740
I mean, does it really make much of a dent
in something as huge as global warming?

10
00:00:37,680 --> 00:00:41,579
It turns out, what we put on our plates matters
a lot.

11
00:00:41,579 --> 00:00:45,730
About 25 percent of all the global climate
change problems we’re seeing can be attributed

12
00:00:45,730 --> 00:00:49,899
back to the food and the choices that we’re
actually making about what we eat on a daily

13
00:00:49,899 --> 00:00:50,899
basis.

14
00:00:50,899 --> 00:00:52,969
This is greater than all of the cars on the
planet.

15
00:00:52,969 --> 00:00:57,199
In fact, it’s about twice as much global
warming pollution as the cars.

16
00:00:57,199 --> 00:01:02,790
Ben Houlton and Maya Almaraz study the connection
between climate and diet at the University

17
00:01:02,790 --> 00:01:04,070
of California, Davis.

18
00:01:04,070 --> 00:01:09,360
They track how the way we produce food creates
greenhouse gases that contribute to global

19
00:01:09,360 --> 00:01:10,360
warming.

20
00:01:10,360 --> 00:01:14,340
With their data, the team has crunched the
numbers to figure out how much carbon pollution

21
00:01:14,340 --> 00:01:17,210
is produced by different foods and different
diets.

22
00:01:17,210 --> 00:01:20,500
A lot of people feel really helpless when
it comes to climate change, like they can’t

23
00:01:20,500 --> 00:01:21,520
make a difference.

24
00:01:21,520 --> 00:01:26,220
And what our research is showing is that your
personal decisions really can have a big impact.

25
00:01:26,220 --> 00:01:29,160
So, take that grass fed ribeye steak I love.

26
00:01:29,160 --> 00:01:32,631
If you really look at everything that went
into making a single serving of beef, you

27
00:01:32,631 --> 00:01:36,090
end up emitting about 330 grams of carbon.

28
00:01:36,090 --> 00:01:38,130
That’s like driving a car three miles.

29
00:01:38,130 --> 00:01:43,140
Now, if I choose to have chicken instead,
there’s more than a five-fold drop in emissions.

30
00:01:43,140 --> 00:01:45,790
Switch to fish and you see the number go down
even more.

31
00:01:45,790 --> 00:01:47,430
Now, look at veggies.

32
00:01:47,430 --> 00:01:52,030
If I swapped beef out entirely for lentils,
well, I’m down to practically nothing!

33
00:01:52,030 --> 00:01:56,780
So, why does beef and lamb, too, for that
matter - pack such a powerful punch to the

34
00:01:56,780 --> 00:01:58,280
planet?

35
00:01:58,280 --> 00:02:02,880
Livestock accounts for a little over 14 percent
of global greenhouse gas emissions.

36
00:02:02,880 --> 00:02:07,240
If that sort of seems low to you, consider
it’s about equal to transportation.

37
00:02:07,240 --> 00:02:13,470
We’re talking all the cars, trucks, planes,
trains and ships on the planet combined!

38
00:02:13,470 --> 00:02:20,010
This is partly because ruminant animals like
cows and sheep - they’re just gassy!

39
00:02:20,010 --> 00:02:25,530
And the methane they produce is at least 25
times more potent than carbon dioxide.

40
00:02:25,530 --> 00:02:31,170
Plus it takes lot of land, fertilizer and
about a billion tons of grain to feed all

41
00:02:31,170 --> 00:02:32,170
that livestock.

42
00:02:32,170 --> 00:02:37,500
And you could feed 3.5 billion people with
that grain; if we were just directly eating

43
00:02:37,500 --> 00:02:42,030
these grains ourselves, it would eliminate
a lot of the CO2 that is emitted from cattle

44
00:02:42,030 --> 00:02:43,030
production.

45
00:02:43,030 --> 00:02:46,710
So it’s clear that meat has a pretty big
carbon load, but it’s also worth remembering

46
00:02:46,710 --> 00:02:49,790
that not all livestock is raised equally.

47
00:02:49,790 --> 00:02:53,990
In parts of the American West, for instance,
ranchers are working to raise livestock in

48
00:02:53,990 --> 00:02:56,060
ways that actually help restore the land.

49
00:02:56,060 --> 00:03:01,880
And they’re experimenting with ways that
soil and grasslands can be used to keep carbon

50
00:03:01,880 --> 00:03:03,590
pollution out of the air.

51
00:03:03,590 --> 00:03:07,870
But even these sustainable ranchers will really
tell you, we’re probably eating too much

52
00:03:07,870 --> 00:03:08,870
meat.

53
00:03:08,870 --> 00:03:12,300
I know a lot of people who if you don’t
serve them meat for lunch or dinner, they’re

54
00:03:12,300 --> 00:03:14,400
kind of like "well, when is the meat coming out?"

55
00:03:14,400 --> 00:03:18,700
It's to the point now where the U.S. actually
has one of the highest meat footprints per

56
00:03:18,700 --> 00:03:19,700
capita.

57
00:03:19,700 --> 00:03:21,910
So, what about not eating meat at all?

58
00:03:21,910 --> 00:03:25,880
Vegan is the way to go for the least impact
on the planet, but it’s not that much different,

59
00:03:25,880 --> 00:03:28,640
in terms of emissions, than say, a vegetarian
diet.

60
00:03:28,640 --> 00:03:33,349
And the team found that the environmental
impact of the Mediterranean diet is pretty

61
00:03:33,349 --> 00:03:35,890
similar to vegan and vegetarian diets.

62
00:03:35,890 --> 00:03:41,420
It’s a lot less meat-heavy than what Americans
are used to - so, fish and poultry a few times

63
00:03:41,420 --> 00:03:46,970
a week; beef maybe once a month, plenty of
plant-based foods, and of course, loads of

64
00:03:46,970 --> 00:03:48,180
olive oil.

65
00:03:48,180 --> 00:03:52,630
Eliminating like 90 percent of your meat intake
is more important than eliminating all of

66
00:03:52,630 --> 00:03:53,630
your meat.

67
00:03:53,630 --> 00:03:54,630
We don’t all have to be vegan.

68
00:03:54,630 --> 00:03:56,300
We don’t all even have to be vegetarian.

69
00:03:56,300 --> 00:03:58,910
If we can just reduce our meat intake, every
little bit helps.

70
00:03:58,910 --> 00:04:01,910
And if you can bring it down a lot, you can
help the climate a lot.

71
00:04:01,910 --> 00:04:06,800
If we all just switched to a Mediterranean
diet, it could actually solve 15 percent of

72
00:04:06,800 --> 00:04:09,520
global warming pollution by 2050.

73
00:04:09,520 --> 00:04:13,709
If everyone were to move towards it, that
is equivalent to taking somewhere around a

74
00:04:13,709 --> 00:04:17,479
billion cars off of the streets, in terms
of vehicle emissions each year.

75
00:04:17,479 --> 00:04:19,969
So, that kind of a footprint is big-time.

76
00:04:19,969 --> 00:04:23,939
But say you still want more meat than the
Mediterranean diet recommends?

77
00:04:23,939 --> 00:04:29,240
Just cutting down your portion size to the
doctor-recommended 4 ounces can reduce your

78
00:04:29,240 --> 00:04:30,449
emissions by half.

79
00:04:30,449 --> 00:04:31,449
That’s huge!

80
00:04:31,449 --> 00:04:35,710
In fact, the doctors are telling us we’re
eating about twice as much meat as we really

81
00:04:35,710 --> 00:04:37,370
need for a healthy diet.

82
00:04:37,370 --> 00:04:39,889
The good news is, we are listening to our
doctors.

83
00:04:39,889 --> 00:04:44,650
In the last decade, [Insert subtitle here]

84
00:04:44,650 --> 00:04:48,449
All these things that you're already being
told are good for you also happen to be good

85
00:04:48,449 --> 00:04:49,449
for the planet.

86
00:04:49,449 --> 00:04:52,740
So what we eat really is a big part of the
climate puzzle.

87
00:04:52,740 --> 00:04:57,830
I mean, we may not all be able to afford an
electric car or putting solar panels on our

88
00:04:57,830 --> 00:05:00,240
house, but we all have to eat every day.

89
00:05:00,240 --> 00:05:03,400
And these choices we make can add up to really
big numbers.

90
00:05:03,400 --> 00:05:08,009
And since meat has a pretty big carbon load,
we need to be thoughtful about how much we

91
00:05:08,009 --> 00:05:09,009
eat.

92
00:05:09,009 --> 00:05:13,819
As for that ribeye steak that I really love,
I am honestly trying to cut back!

93
00:05:13,819 --> 00:05:19,060
Maybe it’s just a smaller piece of steak;
or simply swapping out a meat dish for a veggie

94
00:05:19,060 --> 00:05:20,060
burger.

95
00:05:20,060 --> 00:05:23,340
It may seem like a small thing, but it really
does add up to big impacts.

96
00:05:23,340 --> 00:05:26,199
Hey, so what did you have for dinner last
night?

97
00:05:26,199 --> 00:05:33,059
Find out how your choices are affecting global
warming by taking a quiz at climate.universityofcalifornia.edu

00:05:33,059 --> 00:05:38,599
or watch one of our other episodes to discover
what happened when I brought a box of donuts

99

to MIT.

40
00:03:02,530 --> 00:03:09,431
The result of clearcutting and burning strategies

That’s the third-highest increase in the

45
00:03:32,220 --> 00:03:40,950
at a 30% jump from the prior year, second

millions of pounds of carbon dioxide each

00:04:18,489 --> 00:04:19,489

00:04:24,970 --> 00:04:33,440

Central Africa is engulfed in flames.

00:04:41,889 --> 00:04:45,990
A region decidedly larger than the Amazon.

60
00:04:45,990 --> 00:04:50,930
But there’s a difference between Amazonian

61
00:04:50,930 --> 00:04:55,410
The fires in Central African countries like

00:04:55,410 --> 00:04:57,740

00:04:57,740 --> 00:05:02,720

In part, this is due to the way grasslands

00:05:33,460 --> 00:05:37,419

00:06:07,830 --> 00:06:10,300
problem its ecosystem.

00:06:51,800 --> 00:06:56,050

00:07:04,259 --> 00:07:09,479
Or tied to long-held agricultural traditions

92
00:07:09,479 --> 00:07:14,810
But the increased intensities of the infernos

93
00:07:14,810 --> 00:07:21,290

00:07:21,290 --> 00:07:25,720

00:01:59,856 --> 00:02:04,850
The coaster itself is trying to push you up
into a new direction.

35
00:02:04,850 --> 00:02:09,229
Your head, your spine, everything else wants
to keep going in a straight line.

36
00:02:09,229 --> 00:02:12,285
But the coaster is saying, no, you gotta curve

00:02:28,342 --> 00:02:29,424

47

with the circular loop problem

00:02:49,790 --> 00:02:53,586

00:02:53,586 --> 00:02:57,090
This line represents a circular loop like
the Flip Flap's.

50
00:02:57,090 --> 00:03:01,930
After jumping from 1 to 14 Gs, it would decrease
as you reached the top of the loop

51
00:03:01,930 --> 00:03:05,530
then ramp all the way up again to 14 at the
bottom,

52
00:03:05,530 --> 00:03:08,695
and then back to 1 as the coaster 
leaves the curve.

53
00:03:08,695 --> 00:03:11,125
Passengers were completely rattled.

54
00:03:11,125 --> 00:03:14,922
The Flip Flap, being made mostly of wood,
didn’t help either.

55
00:03:14,922 --> 00:03:17,100
Wood is stretchy and compress-y.

56
00:03:17,100 --> 00:03:21,360
You can see the circle moving as the cart
goes around.

57
00:03:21,735 --> 00:03:23,890
It's stressing it this way and then it's stressing
it that way.

58
00:03:23,890 --> 00:03:29,238
It just looks like an engineering catastrophe
about to happen.

59
00:03:29,238 --> 00:03:32,484
The next looping coaster built on Coney Island,
the Loop the Loop,

60
00:03:32,484 --> 00:03:34,900
Was crafted to avoid all those issues.

61
00:03:35,159 --> 00:03:38,770
It was made entirely out of steel, which offered
more stability.

62
00:03:38,770 --> 00:03:42,050
And the circle was switched to more of an
upside down teardrop shape.

63
00:03:42,050 --> 00:03:46,570
Squeezing the sides in helped ease the transition
into and out of the curvature

64
00:03:46,570 --> 00:03:50,960
reducing the G forces and creating a
smoother, less body-damaging ride.

65
00:03:51,291 --> 00:03:54,568
But still, they had the capacity problem.

66
00:03:54,568 --> 00:03:57,190
Neither the Flip Flap or the Loop the Loop
could support

67
00:03:57,190 --> 00:03:59,005
more than a few riders at a time

because the loops were small, and so

69
00:04:03,043 --> 00:04:05,680
Most of the cars, they seated 4 people

70
00:04:05,680 --> 00:04:09,728

71
00:04:09,728 --> 00:04:11,560
They just couldn't make enough money.

00:04:11,978 --> 00:04:15,010

than ride.

00:04:15,500 --> 00:04:19,404
The Flip Flap lasted 7 years,

And all other looping coasters 
around the world

It seemed like the end of the track for loops.

77
00:04:26,929 --> 00:04:30,442
That is... until something new came along.

78
00:04:30,442 --> 00:04:33,582
In 1959, Disney unveiled the Matterhorn.

79
00:04:33,582 --> 00:04:37,649
It didn’t have a loop but it was the very
first tubular steel coaster.

80
00:04:37,649 --> 00:04:40,440
Unlike regular steel which was solid throughout,

81
00:04:40,440 --> 00:04:43,400
tubular steel was hollow in the middle, 
making it lighter-weight,

82
00:04:43,400 --> 00:04:46,190
and easier to bend into smooth arcs and curves.

83
00:04:46,190 --> 00:04:50,477
Unlike wood, tubular steel could support heavy
weight, and more dynamic movement.

84
00:04:50,477 --> 00:04:54,610
And in 1976, Six Flags Magic Mountain 
debuted the first

85
00:04:54,610 --> 00:04:58,640
modern vertical looping coaster, 
made with tubular steel.

86
00:04:58,640 --> 00:05:01,680
The Great American Revolution squeezed the
loop even more

87
00:05:01,680 --> 00:05:02,780
than the Loop the Loop

88
00:05:02,780 --> 00:05:05,127
creating what’s known as a “clothoid loop".

89
00:05:05,127 --> 00:05:08,840
It gets smaller and smaller as you get to
the top

90
00:05:08,840 --> 00:05:11,440
to try and even out the G forces.

91
00:05:11,440 --> 00:05:15,214
And then it does exact opposite as it comes
back down.

92
00:05:15,214 --> 00:05:19,600
With clothoid loop-shaped coasters, designers
could distribute the G’s more evenly

93
00:05:19,600 --> 00:05:22,900

94
00:05:22,900 --> 00:05:25,460

Revolution.

A much smoother experience compared to the

This clothoid loop — crafted using strong

meant that the Great American Revolution

"The entire basis of the Republican strategy

[Insert subtitle here]

The national debt is at an all-time high.

37
00:02:01,597 --> 00:02:04,587
But how should we feel about this debt?

38
00:02:04,587 --> 00:02:08,270
And what happens if we don’t pay it back?

39
00:02:12,230 --> 00:02:17,490
The US national debt is nearing 
29 trillion dollars, with a capital T.

40
00:02:17,490 --> 00:02:20,887
Depending on when you watch this, 
it might already be there.

41
00:02:20,887 --> 00:02:23,298

43
00:02:27,225 --> 00:02:31,860

the country spends a lot: because of wars,

44
00:02:31,860 --> 00:02:36,767

and… now, pandemics.

45
00:02:36,767 --> 00:02:40,661
And the department in charge of all this 
is the US Treasury.

46
00:02:40,661 --> 00:02:44,176
They collect taxes and spend them 
to fund the government.

47
00:02:44,176 --> 00:02:48,750
And, for the record, it's Congress and the
President who decide how much taxes should

48
00:02:48,750 --> 00:02:51,280

49
00:02:51,280 --> 00:02:54,348
The Treasury just handles the flow of money.

50
00:02:54,348 --> 00:02:59,828
But for—essentially, ever—they approve
more spending than they bring in with taxes.

51
00:02:59,828 --> 00:03:04,080
So the Treasury has to make up that difference
by taking on debt.

52
00:03:04,080 --> 00:03:07,144
And it does that by selling bonds.

53
00:03:07,144 --> 00:03:09,950
They can vary, but generally 
it works like this:

54
00:03:09,950 --> 00:03:15,000
You buy a $1,000 30-year bond 
at a locked-in 2% interest rate.

55
00:03:15,000 --> 00:03:20,344
Every year the Treasury sends you $20, 
the 2% interest you’ve earned.

56
00:03:20,344 --> 00:03:25,773
And after 30 years, you can cash out the bond
and get your $1,000 back.

57
00:03:25,773 --> 00:03:27,689
It’s a win-win situation.

58
00:03:27,689 --> 00:03:33,389
The US gets money to fund the government 
and you make some profit on a safe investment.

59
00:03:33,389 --> 00:03:38,650
More than a third of these bonds — and therefore
the total US debt — are owned by Americans

60
00:03:38,650 --> 00:03:40,544

61
00:03:40,544 --> 00:03:43,243

62

in bonds.

63
00:03:47,572 --> 00:03:51,233

the federal government.

64
00:03:51,233 --> 00:03:55,307
Yes, the federal government owns part of 
the federal government’s debt.

65
00:03:55,307 --> 00:03:58,989

66
00:03:58,989 --> 00:04:00,950

67

68

69

70

71

75

76
00:04:27,339 --> 00:04:29,341

78

00:06:28,240 --> 00:06:29,475
are going up.

112
00:06:30,790 --> 00:06:35,410
If you borrow for anything, whether it's for
a dishwasher, or a car, college, or your credit

113
00:06:35,410 --> 00:06:37,390
card, that's going to become more costly.

114
00:06:37,390 --> 00:06:38,800
We're going to lose jobs.

115
00:06:38,800 --> 00:06:41,172
Wages won't go up as high.

116
00:06:41,172 --> 00:06:45,303
We could be like these countries and just
not have a debt limit.

117
00:06:45,303 --> 00:06:49,473
Or have one so high it’s never a threat
to the economy.

118
00:06:49,473 --> 00:06:53,179
Because if Congress and the President really
want to take on less debt

119
00:06:53,179 --> 00:06:54,833
they can change the tax system.

120
00:06:54,833 --> 00:06:57,059
Or reduce spending.

121
00:06:57,059 --> 00:07:01,930
The debt limit does make sense if you are
a functioning Congress, you're saying we need

122
00:07:01,930 --> 00:07:06,169
to put in place some policy to make sure that
we don't borrow more than we mean to

123
00:07:06,169 --> 00:07:09,287
or we stop and we pause and we check 
on the borrowing.

124
00:07:09,287 --> 00:07:11,152
That certainly isn't how it is working.

125
00:07:11,152 --> 00:07:13,283
The simplest thing would just be 
to repeal it

126
00:07:13,283 --> 00:07:16,263
and be like almost every other country in the world.

127
00:07:16,263 --> 00:07:21,860
Even if the US never actually defaults on
its debt, just the mere political fights and

128
00:07:21,860 --> 00:07:26,990
“will they or won’t they” unease 
could make the United States

129
00:07:26,990 --> 00:07:28,453
a less desirable place to invest.

130
00:07:28,453 --> 00:07:33,515
It's long been seen as this kind of the safest
asset that you can invest in, and so

131
00:07:33,515 --> 00:07:35,743
that's given the U.S. a lot of advantages.

132
00:07:35,743 --> 00:07:42,039
But the more our political system is so polarized
and dysfunctional, the more that it becomes

133
00:07:42,039 --> 00:07:46,090
a little bit questioned of whether the US
should have the incredible advantage

134
00:07:46,090 --> 00:07:47,421
that it has thus far.

What happens when you strip away

Where is the best spot

14
00:00:51,259 --> 00:00:55,972
In football, the beautiful game,
the penalty kick places a player here

00:00:55,972 --> 00:00:58,449

16
00:00:59,976 --> 00:01:03,605
A penalty kick shootout helps
decide a game in the event of a tie.

17
00:01:03,855 --> 00:01:06,816
It's the same thing,
but with kickers from each team

18
00:01:06,816 --> 00:01:11,531
in succession, to see which team

19
00:01:11,531 --> 00:01:14,754
A PK shootout from Spain 1982

00:01:14,754 --> 00:01:18,286

00:01:18,286 --> 00:01:21,081
or Qatar in 2022.

22
00:01:21,081 --> 00:01:27,000
So you could record every PK shootout shot

23
00:01:27,003 --> 00:01:30,965
“The most frustrating part was,
you know, finding the video.

24
00:01:30,965 --> 00:01:33,718
I remember, I think

25
00:01:33,760 --> 00:01:37,555
Once I found it, I actually struggled

26
00:01:37,555 --> 00:01:38,431
“Which is kind of crazy,

27
00:01:38,431 --> 00:01:41,518
if you think about it, because that's
how people watching the games,

28
00:01:41,518 --> 00:01:43,761
like they had no idea
what was happening.”

29
00:01:43,761 --> 00:01:45,000
“Exactly.”

30
00:01:45,000 --> 00:01:49,772
Pablo López Landeros is a data scientist
and sports-obsessive hobbyist

31
00:01:49,772 --> 00:01:52,570
who recorded every World Cup shootout kick

32
00:01:52,570 --> 00:01:55,198
from 1982 to 2018.

33
00:01:55,698 --> 00:01:59,744
“I had to watch the same shootout
from five different videos

34
00:01:59,744 --> 00:02:00,913
if I could find it.”

35
00:02:00,913 --> 00:02:03,331
Those shootouts provided a lot of data.

36
00:02:03,331 --> 00:02:06,376
He recorded the team,
the foot the kicker shot with,

37
00:02:06,584 --> 00:02:09,963
where the keeper went,
whether the ball was on target or not,

38
00:02:10,171 --> 00:02:13,550
if it did go in,
and if it was an elimination goal.

39
00:02:15,218 --> 00:02:19,013
“Fans get kind of angry

40
00:02:19,013 --> 00:02:22,392

it's a coin flip.

41
00:02:22,392 --> 00:02:26,479
But if you look at the data,
then it's a very unfair coin flip,

42
00:02:26,563 --> 00:02:30,624
just because 70% of the goals
go in.”

43
00:02:30,624 --> 00:02:32,543
Keepers affected that.

44
00:02:32,543 --> 00:02:34,859
They dove to the left,
from the player's perspective,

45
00:02:34,859 --> 00:02:37,258
more than they dove right.

46
00:02:37,258 --> 00:02:40,076
They often dive
before seeing a shot's trajectory,

47
00:02:40,076 --> 00:02:42,912
so it can really be worth
knowing the probabilities.

48
00:02:43,204 --> 00:02:44,330
They stayed in the middle

49
00:02:44,330 --> 00:02:48,793
only about 13% of the time, where the
save percentage was also the lowest.

50
00:02:48,793 --> 00:02:53,464
These stats work in concert
with where the kicks ended up.

51
00:02:53,464 --> 00:02:56,344
If you divide the goal into
nine common zones,

52
00:02:56,344 --> 00:03:00,210
it's possible to see where players
kick the most.

53
00:03:00,210 --> 00:03:02,294
For all shots, including misses,

54
00:03:02,294 --> 00:03:05,114
[Insert subtitle here]

55
00:03:05,114 --> 00:03:06,811
But that doesn't mean they were best.

56
00:03:06,936 --> 00:03:10,690
These are the success rates by zone,
and there are clear trends.

57
00:03:11,024 --> 00:03:14,485
The top middle has a high miss rate,
likely a combination of it

58
00:03:14,485 --> 00:03:18,156
getting stopped by the keeper
or missing the goal completely,

59
00:03:18,364 --> 00:03:23,244
like in this classic shot
from a 1994 penalty kick shootout.

60
00:03:23,494 --> 00:03:27,123
Meanwhile, the most popular area,
that lower left corner,

61
00:03:27,540 --> 00:03:31,211
actually has a lower success rate
than the opposite corner.

62
00:03:31,502 --> 00:03:34,172
The top spot is that top right corner,

63
00:03:34,464 --> 00:03:37,800
where 88% of shots in World Cup shootouts

64
00:03:38,009 --> 00:03:41,221
resulted in a goal.

65
00:03:42,931 --> 00:03:46,351
When you combine the keeper dives
with the shooting data,

66
00:03:46,601 --> 00:03:50,230
that right side
looks like it's undervalued by kickers.

67
00:03:50,563 --> 00:03:52,190
So is that the final answer?

68
00:03:52,190 --> 00:03:53,821
Always shoot it there if you can?

69
00:03:53,821 --> 00:03:57,654
“There's two approaches in statistics,
two main, like, schools of

70
00:03:57,654 --> 00:03:58,446
thought , I guess.

71
00:03:58,446 --> 00:04:02,283
The frequentist approach,
which is like the clear cut example

72
00:04:02,283 --> 00:04:06,037
of what we're doing,
just getting ratios, looking at the data.

73
00:04:06,371 --> 00:04:11,292
And then there's this other approach
called the Bayesian approach.”

74
00:04:11,918 --> 00:04:15,004
A Bayesian might
look at increasingly complex predictors

75
00:04:15,004 --> 00:04:18,311
rather than a count.
It could go on forever:

76
00:04:18,311 --> 00:04:21,652
from the footedness of the kicker...
to the the country the kicker is playing for...

77
00:04:21,652 --> 00:04:24,000
(voices
overlap with many reasons).

78
00:04:25,436 --> 00:04:27,475
Let's go back to the 1976 European

79
00:04:27,475 --> 00:04:31,521
football championship:

80
00:04:32,563 --> 00:04:36,067
This is Antonin Panenka,

81

82
00:04:40,655 --> 00:04:42,657

00:04:54,085 --> 00:04:58,631
Today, that's known as a Panenka kick.

00:04:58,923 --> 00:05:01,759
It's a bluff in poker, a bunt in baseball,

00:05:17,692 --> 00:05:20,903
In 2006,

00:05:20,903 --> 00:05:23,740

00:05:24,032 --> 00:05:29,538

All the way back in the 2nd century BC, the Han

3
00:00:18,000 --> 00:00:23,600
recurrent issue of conflict with the Xiongnu

4
00:00:23,600 --> 00:00:32,000
Han emperor, Emperor Wu, decided in 138 BC to send 
an envoy off to try and form some type of alliance

5
00:00:32,000 --> 00:00:38,240
or garner support from the Yuezhi in the west. As 
he traveled through Central Asia, the emissary,

6
00:00:38,240 --> 00:00:44,400
Zhang Qian witnessed for the first time a variety 
of new people and cultures and was particularly

7
00:00:44,400 --> 00:00:51,040
fascinated by the Da-yuan people. To be specific, 
Qian was drawn to the horses of the Da-yuan.

8
00:00:51,040 --> 00:00:56,080
Although the Han Dynasty had long been using 
horses in warfare, and even as far back as

9
00:00:56,080 --> 00:01:03,280
during the 11th century BC Shang Dynasty cavalry 
and chariots were popular, the horses of Da-yuan

10
00:01:03,280 --> 00:01:09,920
appeared to Qian to be far superior to those 
that were bred in China. Admiring their size,

11
00:01:09,920 --> 00:01:17,040
strength, and speed, Qian returned to Emperor 
Wu and informed him of these magnificent beasts.

12
00:01:17,040 --> 00:01:23,120
As a result, Wu decided to purchase some of these 
western horses and in a short matter of time,

13
00:01:23,120 --> 00:01:29,200
with the help of their new horsepower, the Han 
Dynasty was able to address the Xiongnu threat.

14
00:01:29,200 --> 00:01:34,240
Impressed by the success of Qian’s journey 
west and the collaboration it inspired,

15
00:01:34,240 --> 00:01:40,560
Emperor Wu decided to take things a step further, 
triggering the official opening of the Silk

16
00:01:40,560 --> 00:01:48,160
Road in 130 BC, connecting the East to the West 
through a network of trade routes spanning roughly

17
00:01:48,720 --> 00:01:54,960
4,000 miles from end to end, reaching from

18
00:01:57,040 --> 00:02:01,040
This was not the first such

19
00:02:01,040 --> 00:02:05,040
roads, to create an international 
trade route though. In fact,

20
00:02:05,040 --> 00:02:11,120
it was the Persians under Darius I and the

21
00:02:11,120 --> 00:02:17,360
This was known as the Royal Road and it stretched 
from Susa, which lies in modern-day Iran,

22
00:02:17,360 --> 00:02:22,880
all the way nearly 2,000 miles to 
the west in Sardis, which is today

23
00:02:22,880 --> 00:02:28,320
a part of Turkey. The Persians would also add 
smaller routes to the main one which reached

24
00:02:28,320 --> 00:02:34,160
parts of the Indian subcontinent and northern 
Africa as well, and this network came to be

25
00:02:34,160 --> 00:02:40,960
roughly 300 years prior to the opening of the Silk 
Road. Although later outdone by the Silk Road,

26
00:02:40,960 --> 00:02:46,640
the Persian Royal Road was quite impressive in 
itself, and the writings about its messengers,

27
00:02:46,640 --> 00:02:52,720
provided to us by Herodotus, would later form the 
basis of the United States Postal Service creed.

28
00:02:53,280 --> 00:02:59,040
Nonetheless, the Silk Road would soon be 
the ultimate route or routes for messengers,

29
00:02:59,040 --> 00:03:03,360
merchants, and explorers alike. The 
roads were used in a few manners,

30
00:03:03,360 --> 00:03:06,160
with the main being for commercial trade.

31
00:03:06,160 --> 00:03:11,280
Despite the fact that the term we know it by 
now was not actually coined until the late

32
00:03:11,280 --> 00:03:17,360
19th century, the Silk Road did, in fact, 
serve as a major contributor to the trade of

33
00:03:17,360 --> 00:03:23,520
silks throughout the regions it spanned over. 
For a long while, silk only came out of China

34
00:03:23,520 --> 00:03:26,800
due to the fact that it was the 
Chinese who had discovered how

35
00:03:26,800 --> 00:03:32,000
to harvest the material from the cocoons of 
silkworms and had strategically hidden this

36
00:03:32,000 --> 00:03:37,520
discovery from the rest of the world. Thanks to 
the creation of the Silk Road network though,

37
00:03:37,520 --> 00:03:43,440
the material and products produced from it could 
now be sold all throughout the path to Europe,

38
00:03:43,440 --> 00:03:50,240
and it was the far west Romans, in particular, who 
really fell in love with this Chinese commodity…

39
00:03:50,240 --> 00:03:55,200
This near-obsession with silk that the Romans 
developed would actually also prove to be

40
00:03:55,200 --> 00:04:01,680
a prime example of how the Silk Road not only 
spread goods from west to east and east to west,

41
00:04:01,680 --> 00:04:07,200
but also brought culture and new ideas to each 
state that it touched. In the case of Rome and

42
00:04:07,200 --> 00:04:13,040
silk, the remarkable demand for the product within 
the empire eventually put Rome in a position of an

43
00:04:13,040 --> 00:04:18,880
“unfavorable balance of trade”, which deeply 
bothered the emperors. While nothing would ever

44
00:04:18,880 --> 00:04:25,920
be done to rectify this before the 476 fall of the 
Western Roman Empire, the Eastern Roman Empire,

45
00:04:25,920 --> 00:04:32,720
or the Byzantines, would take on the burden and it 
would be their emperor who now put an end to it.

46
00:04:32,720 --> 00:04:38,000
After discovering the source of this 
infatuating material, Emperor Justinian

47
00:04:38,000 --> 00:04:44,400
sent two men undercover as monks into China to 
steal enough silkworms to start a new production

48
00:04:44,400 --> 00:04:50,720
stream of silk back in Byzantium. The expedition 
worked, and now the Eastern Roman Empire could

49
00:04:50,720 --> 00:04:56,800
save itself from the same high-priced silk-induced 
trade imbalance of their Western counterpart…

50
00:04:56,800 --> 00:05:01,920
Silk was still not the only popular 
export along the Silk Road though.

51
00:05:01,920 --> 00:05:10,400
Additionally from East to West, products such as 
teas, dyes, spices, porcelain, paper, gunpowder,

52
00:05:10,400 --> 00:05:16,960
and medicine were all frequently traded. Paper and 
gunpowder would go on to make significant impacts

53
00:05:16,960 --> 00:05:23,520
in the contemporary European world, with gunpowder 
changing warfare as they knew it, and paper soon

54
00:05:23,520 --> 00:05:29,280
becoming the primary canvas for writing. As 
the Eastern trade changed the Western culture

55
00:05:29,280 --> 00:05:35,760
and world, the West did the same for the East. 
Western merchants would sell goods like glassware,

56
00:05:35,760 --> 00:05:43,600
textiles, animal furs, certain foods such as 
fruits or honey, live animals, rugs and blankets,

57
00:05:43,600 --> 00:05:50,880
armor, and horse-riding necessities. Here alone we 
see the inspiration for new thinking and new ways

58
00:05:50,880 --> 00:05:56,640
of life being passed along the network of trade 
routes, and this does not even include the spread

59
00:05:56,640 --> 00:06:02,560
of religions and ideologies that would occur 
thanks to the merchants and travels themselves.

60
00:06:02,560 --> 00:06:07,840
And yet, all of this was done whilst 
most merchants, messengers, and the like,

61
00:06:07,840 --> 00:06:13,920
never went across the whole Silk Road network. 
In reality, the vast majority of the traders

62
00:06:13,920 --> 00:06:20,000
especially would only go part way, sell or trade 
their goods to another merchant, and then that man

63
00:06:20,000 --> 00:06:26,240
would go and do the same. This created a large 
system of middlemen and also allowed for the

64
00:06:26,240 --> 00:06:32,320
opening of new businesses. Inns and resting places 
for the common caravans would soon begin popping

65
00:06:32,320 --> 00:06:38,160
up along the routes, and on the less legal 
side, robbers became frequently employed.

66
00:06:38,720 --> 00:06:43,360
There was one man who would travel from one end 
to the other though, and he would later make the

67
00:06:43,360 --> 00:06:50,160
road famous through his writing about the journey. 
It was Marco Polo who spent three years alongside

68
00:06:50,160 --> 00:06:57,440
his father, aged only 17, traversing the Silk Road 
until they finally reached the Chinese palace of

69
00:06:57,440 --> 00:07:04,880
Kublai Khan in 1275 AD. The Polos would stay 
in Asia for years more, where the young man

70
00:07:04,880 --> 00:07:10,320
traveled to places, he’d never seen and met 
people and cultures he’d never imagined.

71
00:07:10,320 --> 00:07:17,440
When Marco Polo yet again traveled along the Silk 
Road, this time to return home to Venice in 1295,

72
00:07:17,440 --> 00:07:22,400
he brought back with him all of the knowledge 
and experience that he had gained from his

73
00:07:22,400 --> 00:07:28,720
time in Asia and shared it all with the European 
world in his book, “The Travels of Marco Polo”.

74
00:07:29,520 --> 00:07:36,400
Language, culture, religion, discovery, and so on 
and so forth were all shared along the Silk Road,

75
00:07:36,400 --> 00:07:40,080
making the ancient trade network

entirely cut off any trade with the west and shut 
down the Silk Road. Looking for ways around this,

81
00:08:10,560 --> 00:08:17,040
many Europeans began to explore the seas instead, 
hoping for a means around the blockage on land.

82
00:08:17,040 --> 00:08:23,840
This birthed the Age of Discovery, lending soon to 
the eventual European expeditions to the New World

83
00:08:23,840 --> 00:08:30,240
that would shape so many countries as we know them 
today. In many ways, it was the Silk Road itself

84
00:08:30,240 --> 00:08:35,920
that can be credited for these monumental moments 
in history, as it was the possibilities provided

85
00:08:35,920 --> 00:08:41,840
by the incredible trade network that would give 
Europeans a craving for further exploration and

86
00:08:41,840 --> 00:08:47,680
global trade, which would send them to the 
seas in response to the Ottoman intervention.

87
00:08:47,680 --> 00:08:54,960
Thus, the Silk Road worked in a plethora of ways. 
It served, obviously, as a hub for international

88
00:08:54,960 --> 00:09:00,560
trade and commerce. Additionally, these routes 
would open up new journeys for explorers,

89
00:09:00,560 --> 00:09:06,800
allow for easier passage of messengers from East 
to West, and through all of this helped to share

90
00:09:06,800 --> 00:09:21,840
and exchange cultures, languages, religions, 
ideas, development, and sadly even disease.
answer: Even disease spread along the routes, and many historians point to the Silk Road in particular as being the possible culprit for the spread of the devastating Black Death in the 14th century

This is the Indo-European language family. It

2
00:00:12,480 --> 00:00:19,600
to western Europe. Almost half of the global 
population speaks an Indo-European language

3
00:00:19,600 --> 00:00:26,160
and that includes you and me. English is an 
Indo-European language, specifically part

4
00:00:26,160 --> 00:00:32,480
of the Germanic branch of the family along 
with languages like German, Dutch and Swedish.

5
00:00:34,400 --> 00:00:41,600
in the early 5th century the Romans, who 
had ruled over England for over 400 years

6
00:00:41,600 --> 00:00:47,840
withdrew their hold over the island. Filling this 
vacuum, a number of Germanic tribes from Denmark

7
00:00:47,840 --> 00:00:54,160
and the north of Germany ventured onto the island, 
and slowly replaced the Celtic and Romano-British

8
00:00:54,160 --> 00:01:00,000
cultures that had been dominant in the area. 
Celtic speakers became concentrated in Wales,

9
00:01:00,000 --> 00:01:06,880
Scotland and Cornwall while the area we now 
know as England became culturally Germanic.

10
00:01:07,920 --> 00:01:13,840
The Germanic peoples in Britain, while from a 
number of separate tribes, eventually developed a

11
00:01:13,840 --> 00:01:26,840
common cultural identity as Anglo-Saxons. And with 
these Anglo-Saxons our story truly begins [Music]

12
00:01:31,360 --> 00:01:38,240
the Anglo-Saxons, in their many kingdoms, spoke 
a language we now call Old English. Old English

13
00:01:38,240 --> 00:01:44,640
really sounds nothing like our modern language and 
is largely incomprehensible to us modern speakers.

14
00:01:44,640 --> 00:01:51,920
Here's an example of the language from 
the epic poem Beowulf: Hwæt. We Gardena

15
00:01:51,920 --> 00:02:01,760
in geardagum, þeodcyninga, þrym 
gefrunon, hu ða æþelingas ellen fremedon.

16
00:02:01,760 --> 00:02:07,600
So I assume you understood none of that. 
not to worry, no modern English speaker

17
00:02:07,600 --> 00:02:12,880
would be able to understand. It's so 
old, and English has evolved so much

18
00:02:12,880 --> 00:02:17,520
that it may as well be a foreign 
language. While not understandable today,

19
00:02:17,520 --> 00:02:24,320
half of our most commonly used words come from 
this Anglo-Saxon tongue. Words like 'water,'

20
00:02:24,320 --> 00:02:32,320
'child,' 'ear,' 'talk' and 'the.' Basically 
most short simple words come from this Old

21
00:02:32,320 --> 00:02:39,520
English language. Now Old English was not a static 
language; no languages ever are, but most of the

22
00:02:39,520 --> 00:02:46,800
major changes to the English language through its 
history came not from within, but from without.

23
00:02:48,000 --> 00:02:54,880
The first major influx of change to English came 
with the Viking invasions in the 8th century

24
00:02:54,880 --> 00:03:01,200
onward. Norsemen from Norway and Denmark invaded 
the north of England and even set up a kingdom

25
00:03:01,200 --> 00:03:07,680
of their own called the Danelaw. These Vikings 
spoke a language called Old Norse which is the

26
00:03:07,680 --> 00:03:14,800
ancestor of the modern Scandinavian languages. 
Its influence on English was mostly vocabulary,

27
00:03:14,800 --> 00:03:24,520
with words like 'sky,' 'bag,' 'law,' 'hit' 
and even 'they' coming from Old Norse. [Music]

28
00:03:27,280 --> 00:03:33,840
In 1066 William the Bastard, later called William 
the Conqueror invaded England with his Norman

29
00:03:33,840 --> 00:03:41,360
army, and at the Battle of Hastings successfully 
conquered it. These Normans, now the ruling class

30
00:03:41,360 --> 00:03:48,640
of England spoke a dialect of Old French. This 
Norman French came to be the language of the

31
00:03:48,640 --> 00:03:55,280
royal court, while Old English continued to 
be the language of the peasantry. After around

32
00:03:55,280 --> 00:04:01,600
100 years of this the two languages began to 
merge, creating what we call Middle English.

33
00:04:02,640 --> 00:04:09,040
If you've ever wondered why English, a Germanic 
language, has so many cognates with romance

34
00:04:09,040 --> 00:04:18,720
languages like Spanish or French, this is why. [Insert subtitle here]

35
00:04:18,720 --> 00:04:27,920
[Insert subtitle here] These words are most commonly 
seen in the spheres of law, religion, and science.

36
00:04:27,920 --> 00:04:33,280
This French connection is also why English 
has so many words that mean the same thing,

37
00:04:33,920 --> 00:04:39,360
called synonyms. If you look at an English 
dictionary it is almost always much larger

38
00:04:39,360 --> 00:04:46,160
than a dictionary of another language. The most 
famous example of these synonyms comes from the

39
00:04:46,160 --> 00:04:52,000
realm of food. In English we use two different 
words when referring to an animal and the meat

40
00:04:52,000 --> 00:05:00,160
that comes from said animal. Words like pig, cow 
and chicken are all Anglo-Saxon, as the farmers

41
00:05:00,160 --> 00:05:08,480
who raised these animals were English speakers, 
while pork, beef and poultry are all Norman French

42
00:05:08,480 --> 00:05:16,960
because the elites who ate the fine food were 
French speakers. With this influx of French words,

43
00:05:16,960 --> 00:05:23,440
as well as a simplification of the grammar rules 
of Old English, Middle English is one step closer

44
00:05:23,440 --> 00:05:30,800
to the language we know today. Still, it is by and 
large incomprehensible to most English speakers.

45
00:05:31,600 --> 00:05:38,400
Here is an example from the Canterbury Tales by 
Chaucer, the most famous Middle English writer:

46
00:05:40,000 --> 00:05:47,120
Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote, The 
droghte of March hath perced to the roote,

47
00:05:47,120 --> 00:05:53,280
And bathed every veyne in swich licóur 
Of which vertú engendred is the flour.

48
00:05:59,120 --> 00:06:05,120
In the 15th century a phenomenon known as the 
great vowel shift started occurring, which

49
00:06:05,120 --> 00:06:11,760
propelled English into its Early Modern version. 
This vowel shift affected almost all English

50
00:06:11,760 --> 00:06:17,600
pronunciation in quite dramatic ways. We won't 
get too into the specifics because I don't want

51
00:06:17,600 --> 00:06:25,040
to get into complicated linguistics, but basically 
English long vowels like 'ooh' started becoming

52
00:06:25,040 --> 00:06:32,880
shorter diphthongs like 'oh.' A diphthong by 
the way is basically a sound made of two vowels.

53
00:06:33,600 --> 00:06:39,600
Also there were many consonants that became 
unpronounced which we now call silent letters.

54
00:06:40,800 --> 00:06:47,280
A good example of this change is in the word 
knife. In Middle English it was pronounced

55
00:06:47,280 --> 00:06:52,720
'kneef' but after the vowel shift 
the 'k' became silent and the 'e'

56
00:06:53,520 --> 00:07:00,800
turned to the diphthong 'ai.' As you can see while 
the pronunciation of the word has changed, the

57
00:07:00,800 --> 00:07:06,720
spelling has not. This is one of the major reasons 
why English spelling is so notoriously difficult.

58
00:07:07,680 --> 00:07:14,080
So with this change over around 200 years the 
English language landed in a place most of us will

59
00:07:14,080 --> 00:07:21,440
recognize. A good example of what we call Early 
Modern English is the work of Shakespeare. Two

60
00:07:21,440 --> 00:07:29,120
households, both alike in dignity (In fair Verona 
where we lay our scene), From ancient grudge break

61
00:07:29,120 --> 00:07:37,440
to new mutiny, where civil blood makes civil hands 
unclean. That was a small part of the prologue

62
00:07:37,440 --> 00:07:44,240
from Romeo and Juliet. It is understandable, 
but the word choice is quite different from

63
00:07:44,240 --> 00:07:51,040
how Modern English speakers speak, making it 
sometimes difficult to comprehend entirely.

64
00:07:54,160 --> 00:08:00,640
Beginning in the 16th century the British 
started exploring and subsequently created

65
00:08:00,640 --> 00:08:06,240
an empire. At its height in the 19th century the 
British Empire covered a quarter of the Earth,

66
00:08:06,240 --> 00:08:12,800
and had control over almost a quarter of the 
Earth's inhabitants. This spread of English,

67
00:08:12,800 --> 00:08:18,160
as well as the later industrial revolution 
transformed English even further,

68
00:08:18,880 --> 00:08:24,080
mostly in the realm of vocabulary. New 
words from English colonies as well as

69
00:08:24,080 --> 00:08:30,320
new words for new technology ballooned the 
English vocabulary into what it is today.

70
00:08:30,960 --> 00:08:37,600
Also the spread of English created many English 
varieties, most prominently in North America where

71
00:08:37,600 --> 00:08:45,200
English pronunciation froze in place. The standard 
American accent like my accent is actually closer

72
00:08:45,200 --> 00:08:52,160
to the accent of Shakespeare than most modern 
British accents. American English is particularly

73
00:08:52,160 --> 00:08:56,400
influential because of the success of 
American pop culture around the world.

74
00:08:57,520 --> 00:09:03,040
English today is still evolving as much as 
it ever was, with new words being added to

75
00:09:03,040 --> 00:09:09,280
dictionaries every year, as well as many old 
words falling out of use. English grammar is

76
00:09:09,280 --> 00:09:15,120
also changing and it will continue to change 
so much so that in a few hundred years our

77
00:09:15,120 --> 00:09:22,221
language will sound just as foreign to future 
English speakers as Chaucer does to us [Music]
